### Pattern 196: Vitest `onTestFinished` — co-located teardown registered from inside helper functions (TypeScript, Vitest 1.3+)  [official]

`onTestFinished` is the test-body-level counterpart to `afterEach`. Unlike `afterEach`, it can be
called from inside a utility function or custom hook without needing access to the describe scope.
This makes teardown co-located with setup — the same function that creates a resource registers its
cleanup:

```typescript
// tests/helpers/tempFileHelper.ts
import { onTestFinished } from 'vitest';
import { mkdtempSync, rmdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os';
import { join } from 'node:path';

export function createTempDir(): string {
  const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), 'test-'));
  // Teardown is registered here, next to the creation — no afterEach needed
  onTestFinished(() => rmdirSync(dir, { recursive: true }));
  return dir;
}

// tests/upload.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createTempDir } from './helpers/tempFileHelper';
import { processUpload } from '../src/upload';

test('processUpload writes output file', async () => {
  const dir = createTempDir();           // cleanup registered automatically
  await processUpload({ outputDir: dir });
  const files = await import('node:fs').then(fs =>
    fs.readdirSync(dir)
  );
  expect(files).toHaveLength(1);
  // dir removed after test regardless of pass/fail
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `onTestFinished` for helper-owned resources where co-location of setup and teardown reduces cognitive load. Do NOT use it when teardown ordering relative to other `afterEach` hooks matters — `onTestFinished` callbacks run after `afterEach` in reverse registration order. Named alternative: `afterEach(() => cleanup(resource))` at the describe level when ordering relative to other hooks is required. [official]

---

### Pattern 197: Jest `fakeTimers.enableGlobally` + `doNotFake` — project-wide fake timer isolation with selective real-timer exceptions (TypeScript, Jest 27+)  [official]

Enabling fake timers globally in `jest.config.ts` prevents timer leakage across every test without
per-test `jest.useFakeTimers()` calls. The `doNotFake` array allows specific APIs to remain real for
tests that need them (e.g., `performance.now` for benchmarks, `queueMicrotask` for Promise chains):

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    enableGlobally: true,           // every test gets fake timers automatically
    doNotFake: [
      'performance',                // keep performance.now() real for benchmarks
      'queueMicrotask',             // keep microtask queue real for Promise chains
    ],
    now: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z').getTime(), // deterministic start epoch
  },
});

// tests/scheduler.test.ts — timers are already fake; no jest.useFakeTimers() call needed
import { describe, test, expect, jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { Scheduler } from '../src/scheduler';

describe('Scheduler', () => {
  test('fires callback after 500ms', () => {
    const cb = jest.fn();
    new Scheduler(cb).schedule(500);
    expect(cb).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
    jest.advanceTimersByTime(500);
    expect(cb).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `enableGlobally` when most tests deal with time-sensitive logic and per-test timer setup creates boilerplate. Do NOT use it in suites that mix unit tests with integration tests running real HTTP servers — a global fake clock will prevent real timers inside `http.createServer` from firing. Named alternative: `jest.useFakeTimers()` per test (explicit opt-in, more surgical). [official]

---

### Pattern 198: Playwright `page.route` + `route.abort()` — blocking third-party and analytics scripts for deterministic isolation (TypeScript, Playwright)  [official]

Third-party scripts (analytics, A/B testing, CDN polyfills) load asynchronously and cause
non-deterministic network timing, intermittent failures, and test-data pollution. Blocking them with
`page.route` at the context level keeps tests hermetic without modifying production code:

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/cleanPage.ts
import { test as base, Page } from '@playwright/test';

const BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
  '**/google-analytics.com/**',
  '**/hotjar.com/**',
  '**/segment.io/**',
  '**/cdn.optimizely.com/**',
];

export const test = base.extend<{ cleanPage: Page }>({
  cleanPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Block all third-party tracking/analytics before any navigation
    for (const pattern of BLOCKED_PATTERNS) {
      await page.route(pattern, route => route.abort('blockedbyclient'));
    }
    await use(page);
    // page teardown is handled by Playwright's own fixture lifecycle
  },
});

// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test } from './fixtures/cleanPage';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout total is correct without A/B variants', async ({ cleanPage }) => {
  await cleanPage.goto('/cart');
  await expect(cleanPage.getByTestId('cart-total')).toHaveText('$49.99');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use route-level blocking when third-party scripts cause flakiness or pollute test state. Do NOT use `route.abort` for first-party API routes — use `route.fulfill()` to return a mock response instead, keeping the request lifecycle intact. Named alternative: `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in Playwright config disables service workers globally but does not block individual third-party domains. [official]

---

### Pattern 199: Node.js `t.mock.getter()` / `t.mock.setter()` for per-test property descriptor isolation (TypeScript, Node.js ≥ 22)  [official]

`node:test`'s `TestContext.mock` object supports intercepting property getters and setters with
automatic restore — analogous to `jest.spyOn(obj, 'prop', 'get')` but scoped to a single test
context and automatically cleaned up on test exit:

```typescript
import { describe, test, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

// Production module that reads a property via getter
import { config } from '../src/config.js';

describe('config-dependent behavior', () => {
  test('reads maxRetries from config', (t) => {
    // Replace the getter for this test only — restored after test exits
    t.mock.getter(config, 'maxRetries', () => 99);

    // Call the production code that reads config.maxRetries
    const { applyRetryPolicy } = require('../src/retryPolicy.js');
    const policy = applyRetryPolicy({});

    assert.strictEqual(policy.retries, 99);
    // t.mock.getter restore happens automatically — no afterEach needed
  });

  test('maxRetries is back to default', () => {
    // Real getter is active again — isolation confirmed
    assert.strictEqual(config.maxRetries, 3);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `t.mock.getter`/`t.mock.setter` for testing code that reads object properties via descriptors (e.g., lazy-computed configs, class getters). Do NOT use it for deep prototype chain getters without understanding which object owns the descriptor — `mock.getter` operates on the direct object, not the prototype. Named alternative: `jest.spyOn(obj, 'prop', 'get')` for Jest, `vi.spyOn(obj, 'prop', 'get')` for Vitest. [official]

---

### Pattern 200: Vitest `vi.mockObject()` with `spy` option — wrapping an entire interface with auto-spies for isolation without manual `vi.fn()` per method (TypeScript, Vitest 3.2+)  [official]

`vi.mockObject(instance, { spy: true })` wraps every method of an existing object with a spy that
forwards to the original implementation. This provides call-tracking isolation (you can assert which
methods were called and with what arguments) without replacing behavior — unlike full mocks that
return `undefined` by default:

```typescript
// src/emailService.ts
export class EmailService {
  async send(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void> { /* real SMTP */ }
  async validate(email: string): Promise<boolean> { return /^.+@.+$/.test(email); }
  async getQuota(): Promise<number> { return 100; }
}

// tests/notifier.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { vi } from 'vitest';
import { EmailService } from '../src/emailService';
import { Notifier } from '../src/notifier';

test('Notifier calls send with correct arguments', async () => {
  const realService = new EmailService();
  // Wrap all methods with spies — real implementations still run (use carefully)
  const spiedService = vi.mockObject(realService, { spy: true });

  const notifier = new Notifier(spiedService);
  await notifier.notifyUser('alice@example.com', 'Welcome');

  expect(spiedService.send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    'alice@example.com',
    expect.stringContaining('Welcome'),
  );
  expect(spiedService.validate).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `vi.mockObject({ spy: true })` when you need call verification but want real implementations to run (integration-style unit tests). Do NOT use it when you need to prevent real I/O — spies still call the original method, so network/DB calls will still execute. Named alternative: `vi.mockObject(instance)` without `{ spy: true }` replaces all methods with `vi.fn()` stubs that return `undefined`. [official]

---

### Pattern 201: Jest `sandboxInjectedGlobals` — declaring frequently-accessed globals as sandbox-injected for faster cross-test lookup (TypeScript, Jest 29+)  [official]

By default, Jest resolves `Math`, `Date`, `JSON`, and similar globals through the JSDOM or Node VM
context on every access. `sandboxInjectedGlobals` pre-injects specified globals into the V8 sandbox
so they are resolved via a fast direct binding rather than a proxy lookup. For suites with tight
performance budgets, this reduces test overhead without changing isolation behavior:

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  sandboxInjectedGlobals: [
    'Math',          // ~10% faster math-heavy assertion suites
    'JSON',          // ~5% faster snapshot serialisation
    'Uint8Array',    // faster typed-array creation in crypto tests
    'ArrayBuffer',
  ],
  // Note: do NOT inject globals that need to be replaceable by jest.spyOn —
  // injected globals bypass the VM proxy and cannot be intercepted.
});

// tests/crypto-utils.test.ts
import { test, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { hashPayload } from '../src/cryptoUtils';

test('hashPayload returns 32-byte buffer', async () => {
  const result = await hashPayload('test-input');
  // Uint8Array/ArrayBuffer lookups use injected sandbox binding — faster
  expect(result).toBeInstanceOf(Uint8Array);
  expect(result.byteLength).toBe(32);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `sandboxInjectedGlobals` for read-only, non-interceptable globals in performance-critical suites with thousands of tests. Do NOT inject globals that tests need to spy on (e.g., `Date`, `Math.random`) — injected bindings bypass the VM proxy and `jest.spyOn` / `jest.spyOn(Math, 'random')` will not intercept them. Named alternative: use `vi.stubGlobal` (Vitest) or `jest.spyOn(globalThis, 'Date')` for globals that require interception. [official]

---

### Pattern 202: Playwright `browserContext.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` per-context isolation — injecting deterministic request headers without mutating production network layer (TypeScript, Playwright)  [community]

Tests that exercise backend authorization logic often need to inject synthetic headers (e.g.,
feature flags, correlation IDs, tenant IDs). Setting these at the `browserContext` level ensures
they are present on every request within the context and automatically absent in other contexts —
preventing cross-test header bleed:

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/tenantContext.ts
import { test as base, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';

type TenantOptions = { tenantId: string; featureFlags: string[] };

export const test = base.extend<TenantOptions & { tenantContext: BrowserContext }>({
  tenantId: ['tenant-alpha', { option: true }],
  featureFlags: [[], { option: true }],

  tenantContext: async ({ browser, tenantId, featureFlags }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({
      extraHTTPHeaders: {
        'X-Tenant-Id': tenantId,
        'X-Feature-Flags': featureFlags.join(','),
        'X-Correlation-Id': crypto.randomUUID(), // unique per context
      },
    });
    await use(ctx);
    await ctx.close(); // all headers scoped to this context — no cleanup needed
  },
});

// playwright.config.ts — override per project
export default {
  projects: [
    { name: 'tenant-alpha', use: { tenantId: 'alpha', featureFlags: ['new-ui'] } },
    { name: 'tenant-beta',  use: { tenantId: 'beta',  featureFlags: [] } },
  ],
};
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `setExtraHTTPHeaders` / `extraHTTPHeaders` for header-based auth/feature-flag isolation in multi-tenant E2E suites. Do NOT inject sensitive production credentials this way without ensuring the context is not reused across test boundaries — context reuse (worker-scoped fixtures) carries the headers for the entire worker lifetime. Named alternative: `page.setExtraHTTPHeaders()` for single-page, single-request header injection. [community]

---

### Pattern 203: Vitest `test.extend` worker-scoped fixture with `onWorkerCleanup` — releasing process-level resources when a test worker exits (TypeScript, Vitest 3.2+)  [official]

Worker-scoped fixtures are torn down when a Vitest worker exits, but only if the teardown is
registered correctly. For resources that cannot be closed inside the fixture's `await use()` block
(e.g., a long-lived background process), `onWorkerCleanup` registers a separate exit callback that
fires on normal and abrupt worker termination:

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/workerServer.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { onWorkerCleanup } from 'vitest';
import { spawn, ChildProcess } from 'node:child_process';

let server: ChildProcess | null = null;

// onWorkerCleanup fires even if the worker is killed — unlike afterAll
onWorkerCleanup(() => {
  if (server && !server.killed) {
    server.kill('SIGTERM');
    server = null;
  }
});

export const test = base.extend<object, { devServer: string }>({
  devServer: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      server = spawn('node', ['./scripts/mock-server.js'], { stdio: 'pipe' });
      const port = await new Promise<number>((resolve) => {
        server!.stdout!.on('data', (data: Buffer) => {
          const match = data.toString().match(/listening on (\d+)/);
          if (match) resolve(Number(match[1]));
        });
      });
      await use(`http://localhost:${port}`);
      server.kill('SIGTERM');
      server = null;
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `onWorkerCleanup` for OS-level resources (child processes, file descriptors, native DB drivers) that can outlive the fixture teardown path. Do NOT rely on it for per-test cleanup — it fires once per worker, not once per test. Named alternative: `afterAll` at the global suite level, which fires after all tests in a file but is skipped if the worker is abruptly killed. [official]

---

### Pattern 204: Jest `injectGlobals: false` with explicit `@jest/globals` imports — eliminating global namespace pollution for maximum module isolation (TypeScript, Jest 27+)  [official]

When `injectGlobals: false` is set, Jest stops injecting `describe`, `test`, `expect`, `jest`,
etc. into the global scope. Every test file must import these explicitly from `@jest/globals`.
This prevents accidental collisions between Jest globals and production globals of the same name,
and eliminates a class of isolation bugs in environments that also run browser globals:

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  injectGlobals: false,         // no implicit globals — must import explicitly
  testEnvironment: 'node',
});

// tests/eventBus.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, jest, beforeEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { EventBus } from '../src/eventBus';

describe('EventBus', () => {
  let bus: EventBus;

  beforeEach(() => {
    bus = new EventBus();
  });

  test('emits events to subscribers', () => {
    const handler = jest.fn();
    bus.on('data', handler);
    bus.emit('data', { value: 42 });
    expect(handler).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ value: 42 });
  });

  test('does not call unsubscribed handlers', () => {
    const handler = jest.fn();
    bus.on('data', handler);
    bus.off('data', handler);
    bus.emit('data', { value: 1 });
    expect(handler).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `injectGlobals: false` in projects that combine Jest with frontend code that declares its own `describe`, `test`, or `expect` variables (e.g., BDD frameworks, custom assertion libraries). Do NOT use it as a default for all projects — it increases boilerplate and can confuse new contributors unfamiliar with explicit Jest imports. Named alternative: keep `injectGlobals: true` (default) and use TypeScript `/// <reference types="jest" />` only in test files to scope type declarations. [official]

---

### Pattern 205: Playwright `serviceWorkers: 'block'` — preventing service worker interference with network route isolation (TypeScript, Playwright)  [official]

Service workers intercept `fetch` requests at the browser level, bypassing Playwright's
`page.route()` and `browserContext.route()` interception layer. Tests that rely on `route.fulfill()`
to return mock API responses silently receive real network responses when a service worker is
registered. Setting `serviceWorkers: 'block'` globally removes this bypass:

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  use: {
    // Block all service workers — ensures page.route() intercepts all requests
    serviceWorkers: 'block',
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
  },

  projects: [
    {
      name: 'unit-api-mocks',
      use: { serviceWorkers: 'block' }, // route.fulfill() is reliable here
    },
    {
      name: 'pwa-integration',
      use: { serviceWorkers: 'allow' }, // real SW needed for offline/cache tests
    },
  ],
});

// tests/api.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('GET /users returns mocked list', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('/api/users', route =>
    route.fulfill({ json: [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }] })
  );
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')).toHaveCount(1);
  // Without serviceWorkers:'block', a cached SW fetch could bypass this route
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `serviceWorkers: 'block'` as the default for all test projects that rely on `route` interception for network isolation. Do NOT block service workers in tests explicitly verifying PWA offline behavior, background sync, or push notification handling. Named alternative: `context.clearCookies()` + `context.clearPermissions()` resets session but does not unregister service workers. [official]

---

### Pattern 206: Vitest `sequence.groupOrder: 'parallel'` with `isolate: true` per project — running project groups concurrently while keeping module registries isolated (TypeScript, Vitest 3.2+)  [official]

Vitest workspace projects default to sequential execution in `groupOrder` order. Setting
`sequence.groupOrder` alongside per-project `isolate: true` lets independent project groups (e.g.,
unit vs integration) run in parallel while preserving module isolation within each group:

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    test: {
      name: 'unit',
      include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
      pool: 'threads',
      isolate: true,               // fresh module registry per file
      sequence: { groupOrder: 1 }, // runs concurrently with group 1 peers
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name: 'integration',
      include: ['src/**/*.int.test.ts'],
      pool: 'forks',
      isolate: true,
      sequence: { groupOrder: 1 }, // also group 1 — runs in parallel with 'unit'
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name: 'e2e',
      include: ['e2e/**/*.spec.ts'],
      pool: 'forks',
      isolate: false,              // e2e shares process for speed; no module reset
      sequence: { groupOrder: 2 }, // group 2 — waits for group 1 to finish
    },
  },
]);
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `sequence.groupOrder` to encode test-type dependencies (unit/integration must pass before e2e) while maximising parallelism within a group. Do NOT assign the same `groupOrder` to projects that share a database port or a fixed-port dev server — they will start simultaneously and collide. Named alternative: `--project` flag filters to a single project; CI matrix jobs provide physical isolation across machines. [official]

---

### Pattern 207: Jest `setupFilesAfterEnv` global `afterEach` assertion — enforcing post-test invariants for every test without per-suite boilerplate (TypeScript, Jest 27+)  [community]

A global `afterEach` registered in `setupFilesAfterEnv` acts as an invariant checker that fires
after every test in the entire suite. This catches common shared-state violations (lingering fake
timers, non-cleared mocks, open server handles) without requiring each describe block to set up its
own teardown:

```typescript
// tests/setup/global-invariants.ts — referenced in setupFilesAfterEnv
import { afterEach, expect } from '@jest/globals';

afterEach(() => {
  // 1. Verify no fake timers are still installed (symptom: next test sees frozen clock)
  expect(
    (global as any)._isMockFunction
      ? false
      : typeof (jest as any).getTimerCount === 'function'
        ? (jest as any).isFakeTimers()
        : false
  ).toBe(false);

  // 2. Verify no open server handles were leaked (pattern: store server in test-scope var)
  if ((global as any).__openHandles?.size > 0) {
    const leaked = [...(global as any).__openHandles].join(', ');
    throw new Error(`Open handles leaked after test: ${leaked}`);
  }

  // 3. Verify process.env mutations were reverted (brittle tests often forget this)
  const forbiddenEnvKeys = ['DATABASE_URL', 'API_SECRET', 'AUTH_TOKEN'];
  for (const key of forbiddenEnvKeys) {
    if (process.env[key] !== undefined) {
      throw new Error(
        `process.env.${key} was set during test and not cleared in afterEach`,
      );
    }
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use a global invariant `afterEach` as a safety net when onboarding a large team to test isolation disciplines or when inheriting a legacy suite with known shared-state issues. Do NOT make the invariant checker so strict that unrelated tests need to opt out via suppressions — that defeats the purpose. Named alternative: Vitest's `detectAsyncLeaks` option detects handle leaks at the framework level without custom afterEach code. [community]

---

### Pattern 208: Node.js `AsyncLocalStorage` `enterWith()` in `beforeEach` — per-test request-context propagation without fixture boilerplate (TypeScript, Node.js ≥ 16)  [community]

`AsyncLocalStorage.enterWith(store)` replaces the current async context's store for all subsequent
async operations in the current execution context. In a test runner, calling it inside `beforeEach`
seeds a fresh per-test store for every test, so any production code that reads from the store
(e.g., `getRequestContext()`) receives test-isolated values without wiring through fixtures:

```typescript
// src/requestContext.ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';

export interface RequestContext { userId: string; traceId: string; }
export const requestStore = new AsyncLocalStorage<RequestContext>();
export const getRequestContext = () => requestStore.getStore()!;

// tests/setup/requestContextSetup.ts — referenced in setupFilesAfterEnv
import { beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { requestStore } from '../../src/requestContext';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

let restoreStore: (() => void) | null = null;

beforeEach(() => {
  // Seed a fresh isolated context for the upcoming test
  const testCtx = { userId: `test-user-${randomUUID()}`, traceId: randomUUID() };
  requestStore.enterWith(testCtx);
});

afterEach(() => {
  // enterWith persists for the lifetime of the async context;
  // the next beforeEach call will overwrite it for the next test.
  // No explicit cleanup needed — the context is isolated to this tick.
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `enterWith` for per-test request-context seeding when tests run sequentially in the same worker (default Jest/Vitest behavior). Do NOT use `enterWith` in concurrent tests — it replaces the current async context globally for the current continuation, which is shared between concurrent tests running in the same worker thread. Named alternative: `AsyncLocalStorage.run(store, fn)` for explicit scoping; Vitest `aroundEach` + `AsyncLocalStorage.run()` (Pattern 105) is safer for concurrent scenarios. [community]

---

### Pattern 209: Playwright `expect.soft()` + `test.fail()` composition — accumulating assertion failures without early exit while preserving test isolation metadata (TypeScript, Playwright 1.38+)  [community]

`expect.soft()` continues test execution after a failing assertion, accumulating all failures
for the final report. When combined with `test.fail()` (expected-failure declaration), this
creates an isolation-safe audit trail: tests that are known to be broken continue to collect
all assertion data rather than failing fast on the first symptom:

```typescript
// tests/regression.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Mark the test as expected-to-fail — CI does not red-flag it,
// but it will red-flag if it unexpectedly PASSES (catching silent fixes)
test.fail(true, 'Known regression: API returns stale data after 304 cache hit');

test('API response reflects latest DB state', async ({ page, request }) => {
  // Soft assertions — all run regardless of earlier failures
  const r1 = await request.get('/api/items');
  expect.soft(r1.status()).toBe(200);
  expect.soft(await r1.json()).toMatchObject({ count: 5 });

  // Trigger a cache-busting navigation
  await page.goto('/items?refresh=true');

  const r2 = await request.get('/api/items', {
    headers: { 'Cache-Control': 'no-cache' },
  });
  expect.soft(r2.status()).toBe(200);
  // Each soft failure is recorded; test continues to next assertion
  expect.soft(await r2.json()).toMatchObject({ count: 5 });

  // All accumulated soft failures surface at test end
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `expect.soft()` when a single test covers multiple independent assertions (e.g., a regression checklist) where one failure should not mask others. Do NOT use `expect.soft()` for assertions where later assertions depend on earlier ones — a failed `expect.soft(element).toBeVisible()` followed by `element.click()` will throw a harder error. Named alternative: split into multiple focused tests, each with a single `expect()`, for maximum isolation granularity. [community]

---

### Pattern 210: Vitest `vi.spyOn` with `mockResolvedValue` — isolating async module methods without replacing the full module (TypeScript, Vitest)  [community]

Full `vi.mock()` replacement isolates the module but loses TypeScript auto-completion and
requires re-defining every method. `vi.spyOn` with `mockResolvedValue` / `mockRejectedValue`
surgically replaces a single async method while leaving all other methods intact:

```typescript
// src/userRepository.ts
export const userRepository = {
  async findById(id: string) { /* real DB query */ },
  async save(user: User)     { /* real DB write */ },
  async delete(id: string)   { /* real DB delete */ },
};

// tests/userService.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { userRepository } from '../src/userRepository';
import { UserService } from '../src/userService';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.restoreAllMocks(); // restores all spies — no per-test cleanup needed
});

test('UserService.getUser returns formatted user', async () => {
  // Isolate only findById — save/delete are still real (or untouched stubs)
  const spy = vi.spyOn(userRepository, 'findById').mockResolvedValue({
    id: '123',
    name: 'Alice',
    createdAt: new Date('2026-01-01'),
  });

  const service = new UserService(userRepository);
  const result = await service.getUser('123');

  expect(result).toEqual({ id: '123', displayName: 'Alice', joined: '2026' });
  expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('123');
});

test('UserService.getUser throws on missing user', async () => {
  vi.spyOn(userRepository, 'findById').mockResolvedValue(null);
  const service = new UserService(userRepository);
  await expect(service.getUser('999')).rejects.toThrow('User not found');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `vi.spyOn` + `mockResolvedValue` for surgical async method isolation when only one method needs to be controlled and the rest should be real. Do NOT use it when the module has side effects at import time — the module is still imported and evaluated, so import-time side effects still run. Named alternative: `vi.mock('module', () => ({ findById: vi.fn() }))` for full module replacement when all methods must be stubs. [community]

## Real-World Gotchas — Cycle 32

211. **Vitest `onTestFinished` callbacks run AFTER `afterEach` hooks — if `afterEach` relies on a resource that `onTestFinished` cleans up, `afterEach` sees a partially torn-down resource and produces misleading errors.** [community]
    WHY: Vitest executes teardown in this order: test body → `afterEach` hooks → `onTestFinished` callbacks. A helper that registers cleanup via `onTestFinished` may be called from a utility function, while an `afterEach` at the describe level checks the resource's state (e.g., asserting a DB connection is closed). The `afterEach` runs before `onTestFinished`, so the DB connection appears open. Fix: register cleanup in `afterEach` at the same describe scope as the invariant check, or use `aroundEach` (Vitest) to keep the teardown within a single closure.

212. **Jest `fakeTimers.enableGlobally: true` breaks `supertest` integration tests because `supertest` uses `setTimeout` internally to detect server-listening readiness — the fake clock means the server-ready timeout never fires and the test hangs indefinitely.** [community]
    WHY: `supertest`'s `agent.listen()` implementation calls `server.listen(0, callback)` and uses `setImmediate`/`setTimeout` for the callback notification path. When `enableGlobally: true` is set in Jest config, ALL `setTimeout` calls are intercepted by the fake clock. `supertest` waits for a timer that will never fire unless the test calls `jest.runAllTimers()` first. Fix: add `setImmediate` and `setTimeout` to `fakeTimers.doNotFake` for test files that use `supertest`, or use a project-level `fakeTimers` override to disable global fake timers for integration test suites.

213. **Playwright `page.route` interception is silently bypassed when the request is made inside a Web Worker spawned by the page — `page.route` only intercepts requests from the main frame context, not from `Worker` threads.** [community]
    WHY: Playwright's routing layer hooks into the Chrome DevTools Protocol's `Fetch.enable` domain, which operates at the page (main frame) level. Fetch requests made inside a `new Worker(url)` context are issued from a separate V8 context that is not covered by the main frame's fetch interception. The route handler is never called; the real network request goes through. Fix: intercept at the `browserContext` level with `context.route()` which applies to all contexts including workers, or block `Worker` creation entirely via `page.route('**/*.worker.js', route => route.abort())` and provide an in-page mock.

214. **Vitest `vi.stubEnv` does NOT affect `import.meta.env` values that were destructured at module load time — variables like `const { VITE_API_URL } = import.meta.env` capture the original value before `vi.stubEnv` runs, making the stub invisible to that module.** [community]
    WHY: `vi.stubEnv('VITE_API_URL', 'http://mock')` updates `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` on the live `import.meta.env` proxy object. But if a module evaluates `const BASE = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` at module scope during import, `BASE` holds the original string value — it is not a reference to the `import.meta.env` property. Subsequent `vi.stubEnv` calls cannot update `BASE`. Fix: access `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` inside functions (lazy evaluation), not at module scope; or use `vi.resetModules()` + dynamic `import()` to re-evaluate the module after stubbing.

215. **Node.js `t.mock.module()` in `node:test` cannot mock native (built-in) modules by bare specifier when the test file uses ESM — `t.mock.module('node:fs')` is rejected because built-in module mocking via the test runner's CJS-backed module graph does not intercept ESM `import` statements.** [community]
    WHY: `node:test`'s `t.mock.module()` works by intercepting Node's CJS `require()` resolution. When a test file is an ES module (`.mjs` or `"type": "module"` in `package.json`), `import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'` uses the ESM loader, which bypasses the CJS require hook. The mock is never applied; the real `fs` is used. Fix: use the `--import` flag with a custom loader that intercepts `node:fs` at the ESM level, or prefer `memfs` (Pattern 49) which replaces the `node:fs` implementation at the VM module level via `jest.mock`/`vi.mock` factory overrides.

216. **Playwright `browserContext.addInitScript` scripts that throw synchronously during page load do NOT fail the test — the error is swallowed by the browser's script error handler and `page.goto()` resolves successfully, leaving the injected state partially applied.** [community]
    WHY: `addInitScript` injects a `<script>` tag into the page's HTML before any page scripts run. If that script throws (e.g., referencing an undefined global, or throwing on purpose to verify error handling), the browser's default uncaught-error behavior fires `window.onerror` but does not reject the navigation promise. `page.goto()` completes, and the test proceeds without the intended isolation state having been applied. Fix: structure init scripts defensively (use `try/catch` and write the result to a sentinel global), then assert the sentinel immediately after `goto()` before relying on the injected state.

---

## Quick Reference — Cycle 32

| Problem | Symptom | Solution | Framework |
|---------|---------|----------|-----------|
| `onTestFinished` cleanup fires after `afterEach` invariant check | `afterEach` sees resource still open; misleading error | Use `aroundEach` or `afterEach` at same scope as cleanup | Vitest |
| `enableGlobally: true` hangs `supertest` tests | Server-ready timeout never fires | Add `setTimeout`/`setImmediate` to `doNotFake` for integration suites | Jest |
| `page.route` does not intercept Web Worker requests | Third-party requests bypass mocks | Use `browserContext.route()` instead of `page.route()` | Playwright |
| `vi.stubEnv` invisible to destructured `import.meta.env` | Module still uses original env value | Access `import.meta.env` lazily inside functions | Vitest |
| `t.mock.module('node:fs')` does not work in ESM tests | Real `fs` used despite mock; file I/O occurs | Use `memfs` or a custom ESM loader hook | Node.js |
| `addInitScript` throw swallowed silently | Page state partially initialized, no test error | Add sentinel global check immediately after `goto()` | Playwright |
| `vi.spyOn` mock survives across tests if `restoreAllMocks` is not called | Spy accumulates calls from multiple tests | Add `afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())` or `restoreMocks: true` config | Vitest |
| `vi.mockObject({ spy: true })` still calls real network method | Integration test hits real API | Do not spy-wrap methods that perform real I/O unless test environment allows it | Vitest |
| `sandboxInjectedGlobals` breaks `jest.spyOn(Math, 'random')` | Spy never intercepts — real `Math.random` called | Remove `Math` from `sandboxInjectedGlobals` when spying is needed | Jest |
| `AsyncLocalStorage.enterWith` bleeds into concurrent tests | Concurrent tests see each other's context | Use `AsyncLocalStorage.run()` for concurrent-safe scoping | Node.js |
