### Pattern 230: Vitest `sequence.hooks: 'stack'` — Jest-compatible vs. Vitest-default hook execution order decision table  [official]

Vitest 4.0 changed the default hook execution order: `afterEach` hooks now execute in reverse (LIFO) order within nested `describe` blocks, matching how a call stack unwinds. Jest runs `afterEach` in the order they were registered (FIFO). This asymmetry causes subtle isolation failures when migrating from Jest to Vitest: a teardown that expected to run first (as it did in Jest) now runs last, potentially cleaning up a resource that a later teardown still references.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — choose the model explicitly; do not rely on defaults
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    sequence: {
      // 'stack' (default in Vitest 4): afterEach runs in reverse registration order (LIFO)
      // 'list': afterEach runs in forward registration order (FIFO) — Jest-compatible
      hooks: 'list', // set during Jest migration to avoid hook-order surprises
    },
  },
});

// tests/hook-order.test.ts
import { describe, beforeEach, afterEach, test, expect } from 'vitest';

const log: string[] = [];

describe('outer', () => {
  beforeEach(() => log.push('outer-before'));
  afterEach(() => {
    log.push('outer-after');
    log.length = 0; // clean up log for next test
  });

  describe('inner', () => {
    beforeEach(() => log.push('inner-before'));
    afterEach(() => log.push('inner-after'));

    test('hooks execute in expected order', () => {
      expect(log).toEqual(['outer-before', 'inner-before']);
      // With hooks:'list':  afterEach fires inner-after then outer-after
      // With hooks:'stack': afterEach fires in reverse — outer-after then inner-after
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `sequence.hooks: 'list'` when migrating a Jest project to Vitest to preserve hook-order semantics and avoid teardown regressions. Do NOT leave `sequence.hooks` unset in a mixed team — explicit is safer than relying on the default. Named alternative: restructure teardown to be order-independent (each `afterEach` is self-contained and does not depend on another `afterEach` having run first); this is the strongest approach but requires more refactoring. [official]

---

### Pattern 231: Jest `jest.unstable_mockModule()` + dynamic `import()` — canonical ESM module isolation per test  [official]

Jest's `jest.mock()` relies on Babel static hoisting, which does not work for native ESM. `jest.unstable_mockModule()` is the ESM-native replacement: it registers the mock in the registry before the module is loaded, and must be paired with a dynamic `await import()` AFTER the `unstable_mockModule` call. Calling `jest.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` ensures each test gets a fresh registry, preventing mock state from accumulating across tests.

```typescript
// src/emailService.ts  (ESM module)
export async function sendWelcomeEmail(to: string): Promise<void> {
  const { transporter } = await import('./transporter.js');
  await transporter.sendMail({ to, subject: 'Welcome!' });
}

// tests/emailService.test.ts
import { beforeEach, test, expect, jest } from '@jest/globals';

let sendWelcomeEmail: typeof import('../src/emailService')['sendWelcomeEmail'];
let mockSendMail: jest.Mock;

beforeEach(async () => {
  jest.resetModules(); // clear registry before each test

  mockSendMail = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'test-id' });

  jest.unstable_mockModule('../src/transporter.js', () => ({
    transporter: { sendMail: mockSendMail },
  }));

  // Dynamic import AFTER unstable_mockModule — picks up the mock registry
  ({ sendWelcomeEmail } = await import('../src/emailService.js'));
});

test('sendWelcomeEmail calls transporter with correct args', async () => {
  await sendWelcomeEmail('alice@example.com');
  expect(mockSendMail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({ to: 'alice@example.com' }),
  );
});

test('mock is fresh — no accumulated call history from previous test', async () => {
  expect(mockSendMail).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  await sendWelcomeEmail('bob@example.com');
  expect(mockSendMail).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `jest.unstable_mockModule()` for any ESM module that is imported at the top of the module under test — static hoisting via `jest.mock()` will not intercept native ESM. Do NOT mix `jest.mock()` (CJS-style) and `jest.unstable_mockModule()` (ESM-style) in the same test file — the hoisting semantics conflict. Named alternative: Vitest `vi.mock()` with ESM (Vitest performs compile-time hoisting of `vi.mock()` for ESM natively); no runtime workarounds needed. [official]

---

### Pattern 232: Playwright `page.clock.install()` before `page.goto()` — deterministic time-travel for date-sensitive UI tests  [official]

Playwright v1.45+ ships a `page.clock` API that installs a fake clock into the browser page context before navigation. Calling `page.clock.install({ time: '2025-01-15T09:00:00Z' })` before `page.goto()` ensures all `Date.now()`, `new Date()`, `setTimeout`, and `setInterval` calls within the page operate on the frozen time. Without this, any UI component that renders "Today is..." or schedules timers relative to the current time will produce different screenshots on different days.

```typescript
// tests/dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard shows correct date in header', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install fake clock BEFORE navigation — page scripts see frozen time
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2025-06-15T12:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Headline renders "Today: Sunday, June 15 2025"
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /June 15 2025/ })).toBeVisible();

  // Advance clock by 1 hour to test expiry banner
  await page.clock.tick(60 * 60 * 1000);

  // Session timeout banner should appear after 1-hour idle
  await expect(page.getByText('Your session will expire soon')).toBeVisible();
});

test('date picker defaults to today', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2025-03-22T00:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/booking');

  const datePicker = page.getByLabel('Check-in date');
  await expect(datePicker).toHaveValue('2025-03-22');
  // Without page.clock, this assertion fails on any day that is not March 22
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `page.clock.install()` for any UI test that renders dates, times, relative durations ("3 days ago"), countdowns, or scheduled notifications — these are the most common sources of flaky screenshot regression tests. Do NOT call `page.goto()` before `page.clock.install()` — if the page loads real scripts before the fake clock is installed, some timers may already be scheduled against real time. Named alternative: inject a fixed `Date` implementation via a mock service worker intercepting a `/time` endpoint that the app calls to get the current time — more complex but framework-agnostic. [official]

---

### Pattern 233: Vitest `test.override()` — per-test configuration override without a new `describe` scope  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced `test.override()` (replacing the deprecated `test.scoped()`) to override Vitest configuration options on a per-test basis without wrapping the test in a dedicated `describe` block. This is useful for adjusting `timeout`, `retry`, or environment variables for a single test in the middle of a file that otherwise shares a configuration.

```typescript
// tests/mixed-timeouts.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { cacheClient } from '../src/cache';
import { db } from '../src/db';

// Most tests in this file use the default 5000ms timeout
test('fast cache lookup returns in 50ms', async () => {
  const result = await cacheClient.get('warm-key');
  expect(result).toBeDefined();
});

// This single test needs a longer timeout for a cold-start query
test.extend({ timeout: 30_000 })(
  'cold-start DB query completes within 30 seconds',
  async () => {
    const result = await db.query('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM large_archive');
    expect(result.rows[0].count).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  },
);

// test.override also works for environment variable isolation
test('uses override DB URL for this test only', {
  env: { DATABASE_URL: 'postgresql://localhost/test_override' },
}, async () => {
  expect(process.env.DATABASE_URL).toBe('postgresql://localhost/test_override');
});

test('original DATABASE_URL is restored here', () => {
  expect(process.env.DATABASE_URL).not.toBe('postgresql://localhost/test_override');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `test.override()` for one-off adjustments (timeout, environment variables, retry count) that apply to a single test in a file where the other tests use default config. Do NOT use `test.override()` to switch `pool` type per-test — pool and worker configuration is resolved at project/file level, not individual test level. Named alternative: wrap the test in a separate `describe` block with `vi.setConfig()` in `beforeEach` and `vi.resetConfig()` in `afterEach`; more verbose but compatible with Vitest 3.x. [official]

---

### Pattern 234: Node.js `node:test` `t.mock.timers` + `t.mock.fn()` — built-in timer and function isolation without external frameworks  [official]

Node.js v20+ ships a full test runner in `node:test` with `TestContext.mock.timers` (fake timer control) and `TestContext.mock.fn()` (function mocking). Both are automatically restored at the end of the test's scope — no `afterEach` cleanup, no global `vi.useRealTimers()` calls. For projects that want to avoid Jest/Vitest entirely (e.g., runtime libraries published as pure Node.js packages), this is a zero-dependency isolation path.

```typescript
// src/scheduler.ts
export function scheduleReminder(
  callback: () => void,
  delayMs: number,
): ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> {
  return setTimeout(callback, delayMs);
}

// tests/scheduler.test.ts (Node.js native test runner)
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { scheduleReminder } from '../src/scheduler.js';

describe('scheduleReminder', () => {
  test('invokes callback after delay', (t) => {
    // t.mock.timers is scoped to this test context; restored automatically
    t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout'] });

    const callback = t.mock.fn(); // scoped mock; call count fresh per test
    scheduleReminder(callback, 1000);

    assert.strictEqual(callback.mock.callCount(), 0); // not yet called

    t.mock.timers.tick(1000);
    assert.strictEqual(callback.mock.callCount(), 1); // called after tick
  });

  test('timer state from previous test is gone', (t) => {
    // t.mock.timers is fresh — no carry-over from the previous test
    const cb = t.mock.fn();
    scheduleReminder(cb, 500);
    // Not calling tick — timer has NOT fired
    assert.strictEqual(cb.mock.callCount(), 0);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `node:test` timer + function mocks for libraries that must run in Node.js without a test framework dependency (published packages, CLIs, server-side utilities). Do NOT use `node:test` for projects that need snapshot testing, coverage reporting via Istanbul/V8, or component testing — Jest and Vitest have more mature ecosystems for those. Named alternative: Vitest's `vi.useFakeTimers()` and `vi.fn()` — more ergonomic, better TypeScript types, richer mock API including `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()`. [official]

---

### Pattern 235: MSW v2 `server.boundary()` — per-render/per-component network isolation in React test suites  [community]

MSW v2 introduced `server.boundary()` to create scoped handler registries that are automatically disposed when their scope exits. Wrapping a React Testing Library `render()` in `server.boundary()` means any `server.use()` calls inside that boundary only affect that render's network requests, preventing handler bleed into parallel renders in the same test file.

```typescript
// tests/UserProfile.test.tsx
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import { server } from '../mocks/server';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { UserProfile } from '../src/UserProfile';

test('shows loading skeleton then user name', async () => {
  await server.boundary(async () => {
    // This handler only applies within this boundary scope
    server.use(
      http.get('/api/users/:id', ({ params }) =>
        HttpResponse.json({ id: params.id, name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' }),
      ),
    );

    render(<UserProfile userId="42" />);

    expect(screen.getByRole('progressbar')).toBeInTheDocument();
    await waitFor(() =>
      expect(screen.getByText('Alice')).toBeInTheDocument(),
    );
  });
  // Handler is automatically removed when boundary exits
});

test('shows error state on 500', async () => {
  await server.boundary(async () => {
    server.use(
      http.get('/api/users/:id', () =>
        new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 }),
      ),
    );

    render(<UserProfile userId="99" />);
    await waitFor(() =>
      expect(screen.getByText('Failed to load profile')).toBeInTheDocument(),
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `server.boundary()` in React component tests where different tests in the same file need conflicting handler implementations for the same endpoint. Do NOT call `server.use()` outside a `boundary()` in test files with concurrent tests — the handler stack is global and concurrent tests will interfere. Named alternative: `beforeEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` + `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` pair; simpler but resets ALL handlers, not just the ones the current test added. [community]

---

### Pattern 236: Vitest `onWorkerCleanup` — process-level resource release robust to worker bail and OOM crash  [official]

`onWorkerCleanup()` (Vitest 3.0+) registers a callback that runs when a worker process is about to exit, whether cleanly or due to an uncaught exception. Unlike `afterAll`, it fires even when `bail: 1` stops the suite early or when an OOM crash triggers a worker restart. Use it to close database connection pools, stop embedded servers, and flush metrics sinks that live at the worker-process level.

```typescript
// tests/setup/worker-lifecycle.ts  (referenced via vitest.config.ts setupFiles)
import { onWorkerCleanup } from 'vitest';
import { connectionPool } from '../src/db/pool';
import { metricsFlushAll } from '../src/monitoring/metrics';

onWorkerCleanup(async () => {
  // Called on clean exit AND on uncaught-exception worker death
  await metricsFlushAll();       // ensure no metrics are dropped in CI
  await connectionPool.end();    // release all DB connections
  // If this callback throws, Vitest logs the error but continues teardown
});

// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    setupFiles: ['./tests/setup/worker-lifecycle.ts'],
    pool: 'forks',
    bail: 1, // even with bail, onWorkerCleanup still fires
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `onWorkerCleanup` for any resource that must be released regardless of whether the suite completed — metrics clients, DB pools, open sockets that would otherwise produce "process did not exit" warnings. Do NOT use `onWorkerCleanup` for per-test resource cleanup (use `aroundEach` or `afterEach` instead) — it runs only once per worker process, not per test. Named alternative: Jest's `globalTeardown` runs once per Jest process; similar concept but does not cover mid-run worker crashes in parallel mode. [official]

---

### Pattern 237: Vitest per-project `isolate: false` for speed-critical unit test projects with shared immutable modules  [official]

Vitest 4.0's pool overhaul allows `isolate: false` to be set on individual workspace projects rather than globally. This lets you run unit tests against a shared module registry (no per-file module reload) at maximum speed, while keeping integration tests in a separate project with `isolate: true` for full isolation. The key requirement is that shared modules must be truly immutable — no module-level mutable state.

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    // Unit tests: pure functions, no singletons, speed is critical
    test: {
      name: 'unit',
      include: ['src/**/*.unit.test.ts'],
      pool: 'threads',
      isolate: false,          // shared module registry — 3-5x faster startup
      fileParallelism: true,
    },
  },
  {
    // Integration tests: DB, HTTP, stateful services — must be isolated
    test: {
      name: 'integration',
      include: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
      pool: 'forks',
      isolate: true,           // each file gets its own module registry
      fileParallelism: false,  // serialize to avoid DB contention
    },
  },
]);
```

**Tradeoff:** Use per-project `isolate: false` for pure-function unit suites where all shared module state is readonly (constants, pure utilities, value objects). Do NOT set `isolate: false` on any project containing modules with module-level `let` or `var` that tests mutate — you will get test-order-dependent failures that only surface under parallel execution. Named alternative: `pool: 'vmThreads'` with `isolate: true` (default) achieves isolation at a lower speed cost than `forks`; a middle ground between maximum speed and maximum isolation. [official]

---

### Pattern 238: Jest `fakeTimers.enableGlobally` + `doNotFake` — project-wide timer isolation with explicit allowlist  [official]

Setting `fakeTimers: { enableGlobally: true }` in `jest.config.ts` makes fake timers the default for every test file, eliminating the need to call `jest.useFakeTimers()` in each `beforeEach`. The `doNotFake` array specifies real APIs that must not be intercepted (e.g., `nextTick`, `queueMicrotask`) to avoid breaking test frameworks that rely on them for internal scheduling.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    enableGlobally: true,        // fake timers on by default in all test files
    doNotFake: [
      'nextTick',                // Node.js process.nextTick — used by many libraries
      'queueMicrotask',          // microtask queue — do not intercept
      'performance',             // performance.now() — used by some test reporters
    ],
    timerLimit: 50_000,          // guard against infinite recursive timer loops
    now: new Date('2025-01-01'), // project-wide fixed "now" time
  },
  restoreMocks: true,            // pair with fake timers for clean mock state
});

// tests/debounce.test.ts — no need for jest.useFakeTimers()
import { test, expect, jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { debounce } from '../src/debounce';

test('debounce delays callback by specified ms', () => {
  const fn = jest.fn();
  const debounced = debounce(fn, 300);

  debounced('call1');
  debounced('call2');
  expect(fn).not.toHaveBeenCalled();

  jest.advanceTimersByTime(300);
  expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledWith('call2');
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `fakeTimers.enableGlobally` when the majority of test files need fake timers and you want to enforce consistent timer behavior across the project. Do NOT use `enableGlobally` if any test file intentionally uses real timers without explicitly opting out via `jest.useRealTimers()` — forgetting that global fake timers are active is a common source of confusion for new team members. Named alternative: a shared `beforeEach` in a `setupFilesAfterFramework` file that calls `jest.useFakeTimers()` and an `afterEach(() => jest.useRealTimers())`; more explicit and visible per file. [official]

---

### Pattern 239: Vitest `vi.mockObject()` with `{ spy: true }` — selective spy wrapping for sociable test isolation  [official]

`vi.mockObject(instance, { spy: true })` (Vitest 3.2+) recursively wraps every method of an object with a spy that delegates to the real implementation by default. Unlike `vi.spyOn()` on individual methods, `vi.mockObject()` intercepts ALL methods in one call and works on nested objects. The `{ spy: true }` mode is ideal for sociable tests where you want to verify which methods were called without replacing their logic.

```typescript
// src/orderService.ts
export class OrderService {
  constructor(
    private readonly inventory: InventoryClient,
    private readonly payments: PaymentGateway,
  ) {}

  async placeOrder(userId: string, items: CartItem[]): Promise<OrderResult> {
    const available = await this.inventory.checkAvailability(items);
    if (!available) throw new Error('Out of stock');
    const charge = await this.payments.charge(userId, items);
    return { orderId: charge.transactionId, items };
  }
}

// tests/orderService.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { OrderService } from '../src/orderService';
import { InventoryClient } from '../src/inventoryClient';
import { PaymentGateway } from '../src/paymentGateway';

test('placeOrder charges payment after checking inventory', async () => {
  const inventory = new InventoryClient({ host: 'localhost:3001' });
  const payments = new PaymentGateway({ apiKey: 'test-key' });

  // Wrap ALL methods with spies; real implementations still run
  const inventorySpy = vi.mockObject(inventory, { spy: true });
  const paymentsSpy = vi.mockObject(payments, { spy: true });

  // Override only the methods whose real implementations call a network
  inventorySpy.checkAvailability.mockResolvedValue(true);
  paymentsSpy.charge.mockResolvedValue({ transactionId: 'txn-123' });

  const svc = new OrderService(inventory, payments);
  const result = await svc.placeOrder('user-1', [{ sku: 'A', qty: 1 }]);

  expect(result.orderId).toBe('txn-123');
  expect(inventorySpy.checkAvailability).toHaveBeenCalledBefore(paymentsSpy.charge);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `vi.mockObject({ spy: true })` when you want to verify call ordering and arguments across the entire surface of a collaborator while preserving real logic for methods you do not explicitly override. Do NOT use it when the real implementations have side effects (DB writes, HTTP calls) that you do not want executing during the test — use a full stub object instead. Named alternative: `vi.spyOn(obj, 'method')` per method; more surgical but verbose for objects with many methods. [official]

---

### Pattern 240: Playwright `test.abort()` from route handlers — fail-fast isolation when network invariants are violated mid-test  [official]

Playwright v1.60 introduced `test.abort()`, callable from inside `page.route()` handlers and fixtures. If a test's network invariants are violated (e.g., a call to a production API endpoint is detected during a test run that should only hit mocks), the route handler can call `test.abort()` to immediately fail the test with a clear message — preventing the test from silently passing with degraded data.

```typescript
// tests/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow uses only mock endpoints', async ({ page }) => {
  const ALLOWED_HOSTS = new Set(['localhost', 'api-mock.test']);

  // Guard: abort immediately if any request hits a real external host
  await page.route('**/*', async (route, request) => {
    const url = new URL(request.url());
    if (!ALLOWED_HOSTS.has(url.hostname)) {
      await test.abort(`Unexpected external request to: ${url.hostname}`);
      await route.abort();
      return;
    }
    await route.continue();
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4242424242424242');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText('Payment successful')).toBeVisible();
  // If any request leaked to a real host, test.abort() already failed the test
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `test.abort()` in route handlers as a production-network guard for integration tests that must remain hermetic — it turns silent data contamination into a loud, immediate failure. Do NOT use `test.abort()` as normal test assertion logic — it bypasses the normal pass/fail mechanism and skips cleanup hooks; reserve it for invariant violations where continuing the test is meaningless. Named alternative: `expect(requestUrl).toMatch(allowedPattern)` assertions in an `afterEach` that checks recorded requests; softer but does not fail fast mid-test. [official]

---

### Pattern 241: Vitest `vi.hoisted()` + factory pattern — ESM-safe mock variable initialization without temporal dead zone errors  [official]

Vitest performs compile-time hoisting of `vi.mock()` calls above `import` statements. If the mock factory references a variable declared with `let` or `const`, the variable is in the temporal dead zone when the factory executes, causing `ReferenceError`. `vi.hoisted()` wraps initialization logic that should be hoisted alongside `vi.mock()`, allowing the mock factory to safely reference the variable.

```typescript
// tests/apiClient.test.ts
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

// vi.hoisted() runs at hoist time (before imports); safe to reference in vi.mock()
const { mockGet, mockPost } = vi.hoisted(() => ({
  mockGet: vi.fn(),
  mockPost: vi.fn(),
}));

// vi.mock() is also hoisted; it safely references mockGet/mockPost from vi.hoisted()
vi.mock('../src/httpClient', () => ({
  httpClient: {
    get: mockGet,
    post: mockPost,
  },
}));

// Regular imports resolve after hoisting
import { fetchUser, createUser } from '../src/apiClient';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.clearAllMocks(); // reset call history; implementations preserved
});

test('fetchUser calls GET /users/:id', async () => {
  mockGet.mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: '1', name: 'Alice' });
  const user = await fetchUser('1');
  expect(mockGet).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/users/1');
  expect(user.name).toBe('Alice');
});

test('createUser calls POST /users with body', async () => {
  mockPost.mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: '2', name: 'Bob' });
  const user = await createUser({ name: 'Bob' });
  expect(mockPost).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/users', { name: 'Bob' });
  expect(mockGet).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); // clearAllMocks worked
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Use `vi.hoisted()` whenever a `vi.mock()` factory needs to reference a variable that will later be used in test assertions (the common case when you need both a module mock and the ability to call `.mockReturnValue` in each test). Do NOT initialize stateful objects inside `vi.hoisted()` that have side effects at construction time (e.g., opening a DB connection) — hoisted code runs before test framework setup. Named alternative: inline `vi.fn()` directly inside the `vi.mock()` factory with no external variable; simpler but you lose the ability to reconfigure the mock per-test. [official]

---

## Real-World Gotchas — Cycle 34

223. **Vitest `aroundEach` teardown (the code after `await use()`) does NOT run when a setup step throws before `use()` is called — if the database connection in the setup phase is refused, the teardown code is skipped entirely, leaving any partially-created resources open.** [community]
    WHY: The `aroundEach` pattern relies on the `use()` call acting as the suspension point between setup and teardown. If the code before `use()` throws (e.g., database connection refused), `use()` is never reached and the code below it never executes. This is the same semantics as a `try {} finally {}` where the `try` block throws before reaching the `finally` boundary — but developers expect "setup threw, so teardown should still clean up." Fix: wrap the post-`use()` teardown in its own `try/finally`, or use `await using` on the resource object (which ensures disposal via `Symbol.asyncDispose` regardless of where the throw occurred in the `aroundEach` body).

224. **Jest `fakeTimers.enableGlobally: true` causes `async/await` to hang indefinitely in tests that use `Promise`-based APIs when `doNotFake` does not include `'nextTick'` — microtask scheduling is silently blocked.** [community]
    WHY: When `enableGlobally: true` is set without `doNotFake: ['nextTick']`, Jest replaces `process.nextTick` with its fake scheduler. Many `Promise` resolution cycles internally schedule microtask continuations via `process.nextTick`. If fake timers are installed but `jest.runAllTimers()` or `jest.runAllTicks()` is never called in the test, `Promise` continuations are queued on the fake tick scheduler and never resolved — causing every `await` expression to hang indefinitely. The test eventually times out with no indication that fake timers are the cause. Fix: always include `'nextTick'` in `doNotFake`, or call `jest.runAllTicks()` after any operation that returns a `Promise` when fake timers are globally enabled.

225. **Vitest `isolate: false` + `fileParallelism: true` causes module-level `let` variables initialized in one file's `beforeAll` to hold the previous file's value when the second file runs — because the module registry is shared, the module is NOT re-evaluated between files.** [community]
    WHY: With `isolate: false`, Vitest caches the compiled module in a shared registry. Module-level `let db: Db | null = null` is only evaluated once when the module is first imported. File A's `beforeAll` assigns `db = await connect()`. File B also has a `beforeAll` that assigns `db = await connect()`. Under parallel execution, file B may read `db` before its own `beforeAll` completes, seeing File A's connection. Fix: always use factory functions (`export function getDb() { return db; }`) or a `beforeAll` that creates a local-scoped variable inside the test closure rather than writing to a module-level export; ensure `beforeAll` assignments complete before any test in the same file reads the variable.

226. **Playwright `storageState` loaded from a JSON fixture generated by Playwright older than v1.46 silently omits `httpOnly` cookies, causing authenticated API calls to return 401 without any error message about missing cookies.** [community]
    WHY: Playwright's `storageState({ path })` captures the browser cookie jar via the CDP `Network.getAllCookies` response. The Chrome DevTools Protocol includes `httpOnly: true` in the response, but the Playwright serialization layer in versions before v1.46 stored cookies in a format that omitted the `httpOnly` field entirely. When such a fixture is loaded in a newer Playwright version, the `httpOnly` cookies are absent from the browser context, causing session tokens stored as `httpOnly` cookies to be missing. The resulting 401 does not mention cookies; developers chase the wrong root cause. Fix: regenerate all `storageState` fixture files after upgrading Playwright past v1.46; add a CI step that validates the fixture JSON schema includes `httpOnly` fields.

227. **Vitest `vi.mock()` called inside a `describe` block does NOT scope the mock to that block — `vi.mock()` is hoisted to file scope at compile time regardless of nesting depth, so it silently applies to every test in the entire file.** [community]
    WHY: Vitest processes `vi.mock()` calls at compile time using Vite's transform pipeline, similar to how Babel hoists `jest.mock()`. The hoisting is a static analysis pass that moves ALL `vi.mock()` calls to the top of the file, above all `import` statements, regardless of their syntactic nesting inside `describe`, `if`, or function bodies. A developer who writes `describe('with mock', () => { vi.mock('./foo'); test(...) })` expecting the mock to only apply inside that describe block will be surprised to find it affects tests in a sibling `describe('without mock', ...)` block. Fix: use separate test files for tests that need conflicting module implementations, or use `vi.doMock()` (which is NOT hoisted) with `vi.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` for per-describe scoping.

228. **Jest `jest.resetModules()` clears the module registry but does NOT clear the mock registry — modules re-imported after `resetModules()` will still be intercepted by an earlier `jest.mock('./foo')` call, silently returning the mock instead of the real module.** [community]
    WHY: Jest maintains two separate internal caches: the module registry (which compiled module instances are cached) and the mock registry (which module paths have been registered as mocked). `jest.resetModules()` only clears the module registry. A `jest.mock('./db')` call at file scope remains in the mock registry even after `jest.resetModules()`, so any subsequent `require('./db')` or `await import('./db')` returns a fresh instance of the MOCK, not the real module. Developers who use `resetModules()` expecting a "clean slate" are surprised that the real module does not run. Fix: call `jest.unmock('./db')` before `jest.resetModules()` to explicitly remove the mock registry entry, then re-import.

229. **Vitest `test.concurrent` tests that use the globally imported `expect` (not the context-bound `expect` from the test callback parameter) corrupt each other's snapshot files — parallel tests write to the same `.snap` file offset simultaneously, producing interleaved or truncated snapshot content.** [community]
    WHY: Vitest's snapshot system is file-local: all tests in a file share a single `.snap` file. Under `test.concurrent`, multiple tests race to write their snapshots to the same file. The globally imported `expect` does not carry per-test snapshot tracking context, so concurrent writes interleave or truncate each other's entries. The context-bound `expect` from the test callback parameter (`test('name', ({ expect }) => { ... })`) carries a per-test snapshot tracker that serializes writes correctly via Vitest's internal snapshot manager. Fix: always destructure `expect` from the test callback parameter in all `test.concurrent` tests; never use the globally imported `expect` for snapshot assertions in concurrent contexts.

230. **Playwright worker-scoped fixtures whose teardown depends on another worker fixture being alive can crash when the dependency fixture closes its resource early — because worker fixture teardown executes in reverse dependency order, and a premature `close()` call before `await use()` violates the expected lifecycle.** [community]
    WHY: Playwright's fixture engine resolves the dependency graph and runs teardown (the code after `await use()`) in reverse dependency order. If fixture B depends on fixture A, A tears down last and B tears down first — this is correct. However, if a developer accidentally calls `a.resource.close()` BEFORE `await use()` inside fixture A's body (a mistake: closing the resource during setup), A's resource is closed while B is still being set up or used. B's teardown then calls methods on a closed/destroyed resource. Fix: NEVER close or release a fixture's resource before `await use()`. The split at `await use()` is the contract: setup above, teardown below. Any `close()` call belongs after `await use()`.

---

## Quick Reference — Cycle 34

| Problem | Symptom | Solution | Framework |
|---------|---------|----------|-----------|
| `aroundEach` setup throws before `use()` | Teardown code never runs; resource leak | Wrap post-`use()` teardown in `try/finally` or use `await using` | Vitest |
| `enableGlobally: true` hangs `async/await` | Tests timeout — `Promise` callbacks never resolve | Add `'nextTick'` to `doNotFake` | Jest |
| `isolate: false` + parallel files + module-level `let` | File B reads File A's partially-assigned state | Replace exported mutable vars with factory functions | Vitest |
| `storageState` fixture missing `httpOnly` cookies → 401 | Authenticated requests return 401 silently | Regenerate fixture files with Playwright ≥ v1.46 | Playwright |
| `vi.mock()` inside `describe` not scoped | Mock leaks to all tests in file | Use separate files or `vi.doMock()` + `resetModules()` | Vitest |
| `resetModules()` does not clear mock registry | Re-imported module still returns mock | Call `jest.unmock()` before `jest.resetModules()` | Jest |
| `test.concurrent` global `expect` corrupts snapshots | Interleaved `.snap` file content | Destructure `expect` from test callback parameter | Vitest |
| Worker fixture resource closed before `use()` | Dependency fixture teardown crashes | Never close fixture resources before `await use()` | Playwright |
| `viteModuleRunner: false` crashes component tests | Import fails — Vite transform not applied | Keep `viteModuleRunner: true` (default) for UI component tests | Vitest |
| `vi.hoisted()` with side-effectful construction | DB connection opened before test setup | Only initialize inert mocks in `vi.hoisted()`; defer side effects | Vitest |

### Pattern 242: Jest `jest.onGenerateMock()` — intercept and patch auto-generated mocks at creation time  [official]

**Description:** `jest.onGenerateMock(callback)` registers a project-level callback that is invoked every time Jest generates a new automatic mock via `jest.createMockFromModule()` or `jest.mock()` without an explicit factory. The callback receives the module path and the freshly-generated mock object and must return the (possibly modified) mock. This lets you enforce domain conventions — for example, adding a `.validate()` stub to every mocked service class — without repeating setup code in every test file. Because the callback runs before the mock is cached, every test file that mocks the same module gets the same baseline, preventing per-file drift.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts (referenced in jest.config.ts's setupFilesAfterFramework)
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

jest.onGenerateMock((modulePath: string, moduleMock: Record<string, unknown>) => {
  // Enforce that every mocked "Service" class exposes a typed .validate fn
  if (modulePath.includes('/services/') && typeof moduleMock === 'object') {
    const mock = moduleMock as Record<string, jest.Mock>;
    if (!mock['validate']) {
      mock['validate'] = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ ok: true });
    }
    if (!mock['dispose']) {
      mock['dispose'] = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
    }
  }
  return moduleMock;
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** you have many test files that auto-mock the same family of modules and each file independently adds the same boilerplate stubs; centralising into `onGenerateMock` eliminates the drift.
- **Do NOT use when** the mock shape varies significantly per test file — the centrally-added stub may mask intentional per-file overrides or hide that a test was never actually configured its mock.
- **Alternative:** Per-file `jest.mock('./service', () => ({ validate: jest.fn() }))` factory keeps each file self-contained and more reviewable; prefer this until two or more files share identical boilerplate.

---

### Pattern 243: Jest `using` keyword spy auto-restoration — lexical scope disposal of spies without `afterEach`  [official]

**Description:** The JavaScript Explicit Resource Management proposal (TC39 stage 3, TypeScript >= 5.2) allows `using spy = jest.spyOn(target, 'method')`. When the enclosing block exits — whether normally or via exception — `spy[Symbol.dispose]()` is automatically invoked, which internally calls `spy.mockRestore()`. This eliminates the classic `afterEach(() => spy.mockRestore())` pattern and ensures restoration even when the test throws before the assertion. Jest 30 ships `MockInstance` with `[Symbol.dispose]` support. The `await using` variant works with async teardown.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';

test('console.warn is isolated to this test block', () => {
  // `using` calls spy.mockRestore() when this test block exits
  using warnSpy = jest.spyOn(console, 'warn').mockImplementation(() => {});
  using errorSpy = jest.spyOn(console, 'error').mockImplementation(() => {});

  triggerDeprecationWarning();

  expect(warnSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  expect(warnSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.stringContaining('deprecated')
  );
  // Both spies automatically restored here — no afterEach needed
});

test('console.warn is real again in this test', () => {
  // Proves isolation: previous test's spy did not leak
  expect(() => console.warn('hello')).not.toThrow();
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** you need bulletproof spy restoration inside a single test body and want to eliminate `afterEach` boilerplate; especially valuable in tests with multiple early-exit paths.
- **Do NOT use when** targeting Node.js < 22 or TypeScript < 5.2 without a `Symbol.dispose` polyfill — the `using` keyword is a syntax error in older environments.
- **Alternative:** `try/finally` with `spy.mockRestore()` in the `finally` block achieves the same result without requiring TypeScript 5.2+.

---

### Pattern 244: Jest `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` — `requestAnimationFrame` isolation in fake-timer suites  [official]

**Description:** `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` drains all callbacks queued via `requestAnimationFrame` up to the next animation frame boundary (~16 ms). Before Jest 30 / `@sinonjs/fake-timers` v13, the only way to flush rAF callbacks was to call `jest.advanceTimersByTime(16)` — a brittle magic number. The new API is semantically correct regardless of the host timer resolution. This is essential for testing animation-driven or scroll-driven UI code that relies on `requestAnimationFrame` timing without flakiness from timer drift.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

// Component under test schedules a DOM write via rAF
function scheduleColorChange(el: HTMLElement, color: string): void {
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    el.style.color = color;
  });
}

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

test('color change applies only after the next animation frame', () => {
  const el = document.createElement('div');
  document.body.appendChild(el);

  scheduleColorChange(el, 'red');
  expect(el.style.color).toBe(''); // rAF not yet fired

  jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // flush exactly one rAF cycle
  expect(el.style.color).toBe('red');

  document.body.removeChild(el);
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** any code path schedules work with `requestAnimationFrame` and you need deterministic frame-by-frame assertions.
- **Do NOT use when** using `@jest/legacy-fake-timers` — the `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` method is only available with the `@sinonjs/fake-timers` modern timer implementation (the default).
- **Alternative:** `jest.advanceTimersByTime(16)` still works but breaks when the environment's rAF budget differs; prefer the semantic API.

---

### Pattern 245: Vitest `test.extend()` `scope: 'file'` fixtures — share expensive resources within a file without global state  [official]

**Description:** Vitest 3.2 formalized the `scope` option on fixture initializers in `test.extend()`. Setting `scope: 'file'` causes the fixture to be created once per test file (not once per test), enabling shared-but-isolated resources such as an in-process server instance or a seeded database connection. Unlike module-level singletons, a file-scoped fixture is created fresh for every test file, so files are still isolated from each other. The fixture teardown (code after `await use()`) runs once after the last test in the file completes, even on failure.

```typescript
// fixtures/server.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { createTestServer } from '../src/testServer';
import type { TestServer } from '../src/testServer';

interface ServerFixtures {
  server: TestServer;
  serverUrl: string;
}

export const test = base.extend<ServerFixtures>({
  // scope:'file' — created once per file, not once per test
  server: [async ({}, use) => {
    const srv = await createTestServer({ port: 0 });
    await srv.start();
    await use(srv);
    await srv.stop(); // called once after last test in file
  }, { scope: 'file' }],

  // Test-scoped URL derived from the file-scoped server
  serverUrl: async ({ server }, use) => {
    await use(`http://localhost:${server.port}`);
  },
});

// product.test.ts
import { test } from './fixtures/server';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

test('GET /products returns 200', async ({ serverUrl }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${serverUrl}/products`);
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** starting or seeding a resource is slow (> 100 ms) and all tests in a file can share the same initial state without contamination; saves significant wall time in files with many tests.
- **Do NOT use when** any test mutates the shared resource in a way that cannot be rolled back — use test-scoped fixtures in that case.
- **Alternative:** Worker-scoped fixtures (`scope: 'worker'`) allow sharing across files within the same worker, but eliminate file-level isolation boundaries entirely.

---

### Pattern 246: Node.js `node:test` `isolation: 'none'` mode — fast in-process test execution with manual module isolation  [official]

**Description:** Node.js 22.8.0 added an `isolation` option to `node:test`'s `run()` function. The default `'process'` isolation spawns each test file in a separate child process, ensuring full OS-level isolation. Setting `isolation: 'none'` runs all test files in the same process, eliminating process-spawn overhead — a measurable benefit in large suites where dozens of small utility modules are tested. The trade-off is that module-level state is shared, so tests must explicitly clean up globals. This mode is appropriate for pure function suites with no side effects.

```typescript
// test-runner.ts — custom runner for fast in-process execution
import { run } from 'node:test';
import path from 'node:path';
import { glob } from 'node:fs/promises';

const files: string[] = [];
for await (const f of glob('src/**/*.test.ts')) {
  files.push(path.resolve(f));
}

const runner = run({
  files,
  isolation: 'none',        // All files run in THIS process — no child spawning
  concurrency: true,        // Enable file-level parallelism within the process
  timeout: 5000,            // Per-test timeout (Node.js 24: per-test, not suite-wide)
});

runner.on('test:fail', ({ name, details }: { name: string; details: { error?: Error } }) => {
  console.error(`FAIL: ${name}`, details.error?.message);
});

runner.pipe(process.stdout);
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** the test suite consists of pure function or utility tests with no global state mutations, and spawn-overhead is a bottleneck (especially in CI where Node.js startup time adds up).
- **Do NOT use when** any test relies on fresh module state (e.g., tests that check `require.cache` or module-level singleton initialisation) — use the default `'process'` isolation.
- **Alternative:** `isolation: 'process'` (default) requires zero discipline about state cleanup and is the safe baseline; switch to `'none'` only after confirming tests pass with it.

---

### Pattern 247: Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks` — pinpoint leaked async handle sources at test boundaries  [official]

**Description:** Vitest 4.1's `detectAsyncLeaks: true` configuration option hooks into Node.js's `async_hooks` to detect still-open async handles after each test completes. When a leaked handle is found, Vitest reports the source location where it was created (e.g., a `setTimeout` never cleared, a `setInterval` in a module-level initializer, or an unresolved `Promise`) rather than the generic "open handle" message from Jest. This makes async resource leaks actionable rather than mysterious. Unlike Jest's `--detectOpenHandles`, Vitest's implementation works at per-test granularity, not just at suite end.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,  // requires Node.js async_hooks — not supported in vmThreads pool
    pool: 'forks',           // recommended with detectAsyncLeaks (threads pool limitations)
  },
});

// leaky-service.test.ts — demonstrates detectAsyncLeaks catching a stray interval
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { startPollingService } from '../src/pollingService';

// NOTE: intentionally missing pollingService.stop() to demonstrate the leak detection
test('polling service initializes correctly', () => {
  const svc = startPollingService({ intervalMs: 100 });
  expect(svc.isRunning).toBe(true);
  // detectAsyncLeaks will report the setInterval handle with source location:
  // pollingService.ts:12 — so you know exactly where to add the cleanup
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** debugging flaky tests caused by async resource leaks (timers, intervals, open TCP connections) — the source-location reporting saves hours of investigation.
- **Do NOT use when** running tests in the `vmThreads` pool — `async_hooks` is not available in the VM sandbox; switch to `forks` pool first.
- **Alternative:** Jest's `--detectOpenHandles` flag reports open handles at suite-end with no per-test granularity; useful as a fallback but less precise.

---

### Pattern 248: Vitest `viteModuleRunner: false` — production-faithful ESM resolution without Vite sandboxing  [official]

**Description:** Vitest 4.1 introduced the experimental `viteModuleRunner: false` option that disables the Vite-based module sandbox and resolves modules using native Node.js. Normally Vitest wraps every module in Vite's module runner, which applies HMR transforms, path aliases, and `define` replacements. Disabling it lets tests run with the same module graph as production Node.js, catching ESM interop bugs, missing `exports` map entries, and CJS/ESM boundary issues that Vite silently papers over. The primary use case is library packages that ship as pure ESM and must be tested against actual Node.js resolution.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — production-faithful resolution for library packages
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    experimental: {
      viteModuleRunner: false,  // disable Vite sandbox; use native Node.js resolution
    },
    // viteModuleRunner:false incompatibilities:
    // - Vite plugins (e.g. @vitejs/plugin-react) will NOT run
    // - Path aliases from vite.config.ts resolve option will NOT apply
    // - `define` replacements will NOT apply in tests
    // Ensure tsconfig paths and package.json exports are explicitly set up
  },
});

// exports-check.test.ts — verify library ESM exports are resolvable natively
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

test('package main export resolves correctly under Node.js native ESM', async () => {
  // If exports map is misconfigured, this import fails under viteModuleRunner:false
  // but would silently succeed under the Vite sandbox
  const { createClient } = await import('../dist/index.js');
  expect(typeof createClient).toBe('function');
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** developing library packages that ship as pure ESM and need to validate that the `package.json` `exports` map, `main`, and `module` fields are correct for actual consumers.
- **Do NOT use when** the project uses Vite-specific features in tests (path aliases, Vite plugins, CSS modules, `import.meta.env`) — these all break without the Vite sandbox.
- **Alternative:** Run `node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/.bin/jest` with Jest's native ESM mode for an alternative production-faithful ESM check.

---

### Pattern 249: Jest `globalsCleanup` + `protectProperties` — automatic global state enforcement between test files  [official]

**Description:** Jest 30 added `testEnvironmentOptions.globalsCleanup` to detect and optionally remove global properties that test files attach to `globalThis` but never clean up. In `'soft'` mode (default) Jest warns; in `'on'` mode it automatically deletes the leaked properties before the next file runs. For properties that are intentionally shared (e.g., polyfills or constants set by `globalSetup`), the `protectProperties(target)` helper from `jest-util` marks them as exempt from cleanup. This eliminates a whole class of cross-file pollution bugs where a test file sets `globalThis.myService = ...` and a later file accidentally reads the polluted global.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';
export default defineConfig({
  testEnvironmentOptions: {
    globalsCleanup: 'on',  // auto-delete unprotected globals after each file
  },
  setupFiles: ['./jest.globalSetup.ts'],
});

// jest.globalSetup.ts — protect legitimate globals from automatic cleanup
import { protectProperties } from 'jest-util';

// Polyfills and constants that should survive across all test files
protectProperties(globalThis['ResizeObserver'] as object);
protectProperties(globalThis['IntersectionObserver'] as object);

// DO NOT protect singletons that should be re-created per file:
// (e.g., DB connections, event emitters, server instances)
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** a large codebase has accumulated subtle cross-file global leaks that are hard to locate manually; `'on'` mode acts as an automated guardrail.
- **Do NOT use when** the test suite relies on globals deliberately shared across files (e.g., a global test database injected in `globalSetup`) without properly protecting them — `globalsCleanup: 'on'` will delete them.
- **Alternative:** ESLint's `no-global-assign` rule catches some leaks at lint time, but only for named globals; `globalsCleanup` catches dynamic property assignments.

---

### Pattern 250: Vitest `test.signal` AbortSignal — cancel in-flight async resources on test timeout or bail  [official]

**Description:** Vitest 3.2 added a `signal` property to every test's context object — an `AbortSignal` that becomes aborted when the test times out, when the user presses Ctrl+C, when `vitest.cancelCurrentRun()` is called programmatically, or when another test fails under `bail: 1`. Passing this signal to `fetch`, `EventSource`, WebSocket constructors, or database query methods ensures those operations are immediately cancelled and their underlying handles closed, preventing the test from hanging at the timeout boundary and suppressing the "open handles" warning.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

// Utility that accepts a cancellation signal
async function queryUserDatabase(
  params: { userId: string; includeHistory: boolean },
  options: { signal?: AbortSignal }
): Promise<{ userId: string; name: string }> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${params.userId}`, {
    signal: options.signal,  // fetch is aborted when signal fires
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json() as Promise<{ userId: string; name: string }>;
}

test('slow database query is cancelled on timeout', async ({ signal }) => {
  // signal is already wired to Vitest's timeout/bail/cancel system
  const result = await queryUserDatabase(
    { userId: '42', includeHistory: true },
    { signal }  // propagate Vitest's cancellation signal directly
  );
  expect(result.userId).toBe('42');
}, { timeout: 3000 });
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** tests call slow I/O operations (HTTP, DB, gRPC) that can hang after a timeout; the signal prevents open-handle warnings and ensures the worker process exits cleanly.
- **Do NOT use when** the test intentionally needs to verify timeout/cancellation behavior — in that case, create your own `AbortController` so you control exactly when the signal fires.
- **Alternative:** `afterEach` with a local `AbortController.abort()` call works but is boilerplate-heavy and does not fire on bail from another test.

---

### Pattern 251: Playwright v1.57 `browserContext.route()` for service worker network interception — isolate SW fetch handlers in tests  [official]

**Description:** Playwright v1.57 extended `BrowserContext.route()` to intercept network requests issued by service workers, with opt-out via the `SW_DISABLE_ROUTING` environment variable. Before this change, requests dispatched by a registered service worker bypassed Playwright's network interception layer entirely, making it impossible to assert on or stub API calls made during SW background sync, push notification handling, or offline fallback logic. With the new routing, you can `context.route('/api/**', handler)` and have it apply uniformly to both page and SW fetch calls within the context.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('service worker handles offline mode correctly', async ({ context, page }) => {
  // context.route intercepts BOTH page and service-worker fetch requests (v1.57+)
  await context.route('/api/products', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify([{ id: 1, name: 'Widget', cached: true }]),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/');
  // Wait for service worker to be ready before going offline
  await page.evaluate(() => navigator.serviceWorker.ready);

  // Simulate offline by blocking all other network requests
  await context.route('**/*', (route) => route.abort());

  // Service worker's cache-first strategy should serve the routed response
  const productsText = await page.locator('[data-testid="product-list"]').textContent();
  expect(productsText).toContain('Widget');
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** the application registers a service worker that makes background API calls (sync, push, background fetch) and you need deterministic test control over those requests.
- **Do NOT use when** the test must verify actual SW registration or the SW install/activate lifecycle — routing stubs the network but does not affect SW lifecycle events.
- **Alternative:** Disable service workers entirely with `browser.newContext({ serviceWorkers: 'block' })` when you only want to test the page without SW interference.

---

### Pattern 252: Vitest `watchTriggerPatterns` — invalidate test files when non-imported assets change  [official]

**Description:** Vitest 3.2's `watchTriggerPatterns` config option maps glob patterns of non-test, non-source files (e.g., SQL migration files, JSON fixtures, `.env` templates, code-generation outputs) to test file glob patterns that should re-run when those assets change. Without this option, editing a SQL migration never triggers the corresponding integration test re-run in watch mode because Vitest only tracks `import()` graph edges. This closes the gap for database fixture files, OpenAPI spec files, and code-generator outputs that tests depend on but do not `import` directly.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    watchTriggerPatterns: [
      // When any SQL migration changes, re-run all DB integration tests
      {
        pattern: 'db/migrations/**/*.sql',
        testsToRun: ['src/**/*.integration.test.ts'],
      },
      // When the OpenAPI spec changes, re-run the contract test suite
      {
        pattern: 'openapi/schema.yaml',
        testsToRun: ['src/api/**/*.contract.test.ts'],
      },
      // When fixture JSON changes, re-run snapshot tests
      {
        pattern: 'fixtures/**/*.json',
        testsToRun: ['src/**/*.snapshot.test.ts'],
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** watch mode feedback is incomplete because critical test inputs (migrations, specs, fixtures) are not imported by any test file and so never trigger re-runs.
- **Do NOT use when** the non-imported files change very frequently (e.g., a build output directory) — overly broad trigger patterns cause the entire test suite to re-run on every build, negating watch mode's incremental benefit.
- **Alternative:** Structure tests to `import` their fixtures directly (e.g., `import fixture from '../fixtures/users.json' assert { type: 'json' }`) — Vitest will then track the dependency automatically.

---

### Pattern 253: Node.js 24 `node:test` JSON module mocking — isolate tests from static data files without file system manipulation  [official]

**Description:** Node.js 24 added `t.mock.module()` support for JSON modules in `node:test`, allowing tests to replace a `.json` file's exported content with a test-controlled value without touching the file system or module registry globally. This is particularly useful for testing code paths that branch on configuration values, feature flags, or locale bundles loaded as JSON. The mock is scoped to the test and its subtests, auto-restored after the test ends, and works with native ESM `import` assertions.

```typescript
import { test, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('feature flag routing uses json config correctly', async (t) => {
  // Scope the JSON mock to this test and its subtests only
  t.mock.module('./config/feature-flags.json', {
    defaultExport: {
      newCheckoutFlow: true,
      darkMode: false,
      betaSearch: true,
    },
  });

  // Re-import the module under test AFTER the mock is installed
  const { getFeatureFlags } = await import('./src/featureService.ts');

  const flags = getFeatureFlags();
  assert.strictEqual(flags.newCheckoutFlow, true);
  assert.strictEqual(flags.darkMode, false);
  // After test ends, real feature-flags.json is automatically restored
});

test('feature flags use real json config by default', async () => {
  const { getFeatureFlags } = await import('./src/featureService.ts');
  // Real config — no mock installed in this test
  const flags = getFeatureFlags();
  assert.ok(typeof flags.newCheckoutFlow === 'boolean');
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** code reads JSON configuration files at module load time and you need per-test control over those config values without mutating the file system.
- **Do NOT use when** the JSON file is loaded lazily via `fs.readFileSync` at call time rather than via `import` — module mocking only intercepts the ESM module graph.
- **Alternative:** Abstract JSON loading behind a function (`getConfig()`) and use dependency injection or environment variables to control values; avoids module mocking entirely.

---

### Pattern 254: Vitest test tags + conditional fixture initialization — selective resource allocation by test category  [official]

**Description:** Vitest 4.1 introduced `test.tag` (individual tag) and `test.tags` (array) annotations alongside the `--tags-filter` CLI flag for filtering test runs. Tags integrate with the test's `TaskContext` object inside fixture factories, allowing fixture creators to check whether the current test is tagged with e.g. `database` or `integration` before spinning up expensive resources. Combined with `test.extend`, this enables a single fixture definition that conditionally allocates real vs. mock resources based on tags without maintaining separate fixture files.

```typescript
// fixtures/db.ts
import { test as base, type TaskContext } from 'vitest';
import { createRealDb, createMockDb } from '../src/db';
import type { Database } from '../src/db';

interface DbFixture { db: Database }

export const test = base.extend<DbFixture>({
  db: async ({}, use, ctx: TaskContext) => {
    // Check if the current test is tagged as an integration test
    const isIntegration = (ctx.task.tags ?? []).includes('integration');

    const db = isIntegration
      ? await createRealDb({ url: process.env['TEST_DATABASE_URL']! })
      : createMockDb();

    await use(db);
    await db.close();
  },
});

// user.test.ts
import { test } from './fixtures/db';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

// Unit test: gets a mock DB (fast, no external deps)
test('createUser validates email format', async ({ db }) => {
  await expect(db.createUser({ email: 'bad' })).rejects.toThrow('Invalid email');
});

// Integration test: gets a real DB connection (run with vitest --tags-filter=integration)
test.tag('integration')('createUser inserts a real record', async ({ db }) => {
  const user = await db.createUser({ email: 'alice@example.com' });
  expect(user.id).toMatch(/^[0-9a-f-]{36}$/);
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** a single test file contains both unit tests (fast, mocked) and integration tests (slow, real resources), and you want a single fixture definition to handle both cases.
- **Do NOT use when** the conditional logic inside the fixture makes it hard to reason about what a test actually receives — prefer separate fixture files for very different resource types.
- **Alternative:** Separate `vitest.integration.config.ts` and `vitest.unit.config.ts` project configurations with entirely different fixture sets are more explicit but require running two separate commands.

---

### Pattern 255: Playwright `browser.on('context')` — intercept newly-created browser contexts for universal isolation enforcement  [official]

**Description:** Playwright v1.59 added `browser.on('context', cb)` — an event that fires whenever any new `BrowserContext` is created on the browser instance, including contexts opened by popup windows and `page.context()` calls from within tests. This allows test infrastructure to automatically apply isolation rules (network route stubs, auth state, cookie blocklists) to every context that is ever created, rather than applying them only to the fixture-provided context. It is especially valuable in tests that trigger OAuth redirects, file-download dialogs, or extension popups that open their own contexts.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect, type BrowserContext, type Browser } from '@playwright/test';

interface BrowserFixture { browser: Browser }

// Extended test fixture: intercept ALL contexts created during the test
export const test = base.extend<BrowserFixture>({
  browser: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const contexts: BrowserContext[] = [];

    // Fires for EVERY new context — popup, extension, OAuth redirect window, etc.
    browser.on('context', (ctx: BrowserContext) => {
      contexts.push(ctx);
      // Apply the same network isolation to every new context automatically
      void ctx.route('**/analytics/**', (route) => route.abort());
      void ctx.route('**/ads/**', (route) => route.abort());
    });

    await use(browser);

    // Tear down any contexts the test opened but did not close
    for (const ctx of contexts) {
      if (!ctx.isClosed()) await ctx.close();
    }
  },
});

test('OAuth popup does not leak analytics traffic', async ({ browser }) => {
  const page = await browser.newPage();
  await page.goto('https://app.example.com/login');
  // Clicking triggers a popup — browser.on('context') fires and installs routes on it
  const [popup] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('popup'),
    page.click('[data-testid="google-login"]'),
  ]);
  await expect(popup).toHaveURL(/accounts\.google\.com/);
  await popup.close();
  await page.close();
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** tests trigger popup flows, OAuth redirects, or window.open() calls that create new browser contexts that would otherwise escape the standard route/intercept configuration.
- **Do NOT use when** the test only uses a single context created by the standard `page`/`context` fixture — the standard fixture's `context.route()` already covers that case.
- **Alternative:** `page.on('popup', cb)` handles page-level popup events but only fires for popups opened by that specific page, not for contexts opened via other means.

---

### Pattern 256: Vitest 4.0 unified `maxWorkers` pool configuration — deterministic parallelism control across pool types  [official]

**Description:** Vitest 4.0's pool architecture rewrite consolidated the separate `poolOptions.threads.maxThreads` and `poolOptions.forks.maxForks` options into a single top-level `maxWorkers` setting that applies uniformly to all pool types (`threads`, `forks`). The `vmMemoryLimit` option similarly moved from `poolOptions.vmThreads.memoryLimit` to a top-level option. This means existing configs that set per-pool limits in nested `poolOptions` objects silently lose the limit after upgrading, causing unexpected full-CPU parallelism in CI environments. Migration requires explicitly moving limits to the top-level field.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — BEFORE Vitest 4.0 (nested config — silently ignored in v4)
// export default defineConfig({
//   test: {
//     pool: 'forks',
//     poolOptions: {
//       forks: { maxForks: 4 },              // BROKEN in v4 — silently ignored
//       vmThreads: { memoryLimit: '512mb' }, // BROKEN in v4 — silently ignored
//     },
//   },
// });

// vitest.config.ts — AFTER Vitest 4.0 (correct top-level placement)
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    pool: 'forks',
    maxWorkers: 4,           // top-level — applies to ALL pool types in v4+
    vmMemoryLimit: '512mb',  // moved from poolOptions.vmThreads.memoryLimit
    // Non-unified per-pool options still go in poolOptions:
    poolOptions: {
      forks: {
        singleFork: false,   // non-unified option — still pool-specific
      },
    },
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:**
- **Use when** upgrading from Vitest 3.x to 4.x — audit every `poolOptions.threads.maxThreads` and `poolOptions.forks.maxForks` usage and migrate to top-level `maxWorkers`.
- **Do NOT use when** running Vitest 3.x — `maxWorkers` at top-level is only available from Vitest 4.0 onwards.
- **Alternative:** Leave `maxWorkers` unset and rely on Vitest's default heuristic (half the available CPU cores) if CI machines have consistent core counts.

## Real-World Gotchas — Cycle 35

231. **Jest `jest.retryTimes(n, { retryImmediately: true })` runs the retry within the same test file execution, meaning any module-level state mutated by the first attempt is still dirty when the retry runs — the retry is NOT isolated from the previous attempt's side effects.** [community]
    WHY: `jest.retryTimes()` instructs jest-circus to re-run the test function callback if the assertion fails, but it does NOT reset the module registry, `beforeEach` hooks, or any module-level variables between attempts. If the first attempt sets a module-level flag (`attemptedOnce = true`) and the test logic branches on that flag, the retry will see `true` rather than the clean initial state. `retryImmediately: true` exacerbates this because there is not even a full re-run of `beforeEach` in between. Fix: use `retryImmediately: false` (which does re-run `beforeEach` before each retry) and ensure any state mutated by the test body is reset in `beforeEach`, not just at module load time.

232. **Vitest's `test.tag()` annotation does NOT filter tests at collection time — tagged tests are still collected and counted in the total, then skipped during execution, which inflates the "skipped" count and makes CI reports misleading when `--tags-filter` is used.** [community]
    WHY: Vitest processes tags as a runtime filter: all test files are loaded (paying their full import cost), all tests are registered, and then tests that do not match the tag filter are marked as skipped rather than excluded from the plan. Projects with expensive module-level initialization in test files (e.g., a global `beforeAll` that connects to a database) pay that cost even for entirely-skipped files. Fix: structure test projects so that database-heavy integration tests live in separate files from unit tests, and use separate `vitest --project=integration` invocations rather than relying on tag filtering to avoid the initialization cost.

233. **Node.js 24 automatic subtest completion changes isolation timing — if a subtest allocates a resource and the parent test's outer `afterEach` cleanup runs before the subtest finishes, the resource is destroyed while the subtest is still using it.** [community]
    WHY: Before Node.js 24, `t.test()` returned a Promise that callers had to explicitly `await`, making resource lifetimes explicit. Node.js 24 automatically awaits subtests — but only within the parent test's body. If cleanup is registered at the `describe` level via `afterEach` and runs concurrently with automatic subtest completion, the cleanup may fire before the subtest's async code finishes. This surfaces as `ECONNRESET` errors or "use after free" behavior with database connections. Fix: register cleanup inside the parent test body using `t.after()` (the test-context-scoped teardown) rather than an outer `afterEach`.

234. **Playwright `page.route()` handlers registered in `beforeAll` do NOT apply to pages created inside worker-scoped fixtures — the route is installed on a specific `Page` object, not on the browser context, so pages opened by worker-scoped fixtures bypass the route entirely.** [community]
    WHY: `page.route()` scopes route handlers to the `Page` object. Worker-scoped fixtures that create their own pages via `browser.newPage()` create a fresh `Page` with no inherited route handlers. Only `context.route()` (installing on the `BrowserContext`) applies universally to all pages within that context. In multi-page tests (OAuth popups, file downloads, multi-tab workflows), `page.route()` installs handlers on a specific page while the popup's page has none. Fix: install all network isolation rules via `context.route()` to ensure all pages within the test's context inherit them.

235. **Jest `jest.onGenerateMock()` callback is NOT invoked when a module is mocked with an explicit factory function — `jest.mock('./db', () => ({ connect: jest.fn() }))` bypasses `onGenerateMock` entirely, so any convention-enforcement code in the callback silently has no effect for factory-mocked modules.** [community]
    WHY: `jest.onGenerateMock(cb)` hooks into the auto-mock generation path, which only runs when Jest inspects the real module and generates mock stubs automatically. When a factory function is provided to `jest.mock()`, Jest uses the factory directly and never calls the auto-mock generator. A team that writes `jest.onGenerateMock` to add a `.dispose` stub to all service mocks will not see the stub on any module that uses an explicit factory, silently violating the convention. Fix: document this limitation at the project level; consider a lint rule or a shared factory wrapper function instead of relying on `onGenerateMock` for universal coverage.

236. **Vitest `scope: 'file'` fixtures whose teardown code follows `await use()` does NOT run when the worker process is forcibly killed by `--bail=1` mid-file — database rows, temp files, and open connections from the file-scoped fixture are permanently leaked.** [community]
    WHY: Vitest's `bail` mechanism terminates the worker process after a configurable number of test failures. Process termination bypasses the fixture teardown queue entirely — there is no graceful shutdown hook that flushes pending `scope: 'file'` teardowns. The teardown code after `await use()` relies on the process running to completion. Fix: for resources that must be cleaned up even on process death (database rows, temp files), pair the file-scoped fixture with `onWorkerCleanup(() => cleanupFn())` which registers a process-level `beforeExit` handler that runs even under bail.

237. **Playwright `context.setStorageState()` (added in v1.59) clears cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB for ALL origins within the context — calling it mid-test to switch user sessions also clears storage for any third-party origins already authenticated (e.g., a CDN auth cookie or subdomain session token), causing cascading 401s.** [community]
    WHY: `setStorageState()` is a bulk-replace operation: it sets storage for the listed origins and clears everything else. If the test page loaded resources from `cdn.example.com` that set their own session cookies, those cookies are not included in the new `storageState` object and are deleted by `setStorageState()`. The subsequent request to `cdn.example.com` receives a 401, which may manifest only as a broken image or silent API failure rather than an obvious test error. Fix: capture the full `storageState` (including all origins) immediately before calling `setStorageState()` and merge the third-party origin cookies into the new state; alternatively, use separate browser contexts per user session instead of in-context state swapping.

---

## Quick Reference — Cycle 35

| Problem | Symptom | Solution | Framework |
|---------|---------|----------|-----------|
| Auto-mock missing domain conventions | Stubs inconsistent across test files | Use `jest.onGenerateMock(cb)` to patch all generated mocks | Jest |
| Spy not restored after test throws | Console/method leak to next test | Use `using spy = jest.spyOn(...)` (TypeScript 5.2+) | Jest |
| `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks not flushed | Animation state assertions fail | Call `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` | Jest |
| Server start overhead on every test | Slow file with 50+ tests | Use `scope: 'file'` fixture — one server instance per file | Vitest |
| `node:test` file parallelism spawn overhead | Slow CI for pure-function suites | Set `isolation: 'none'` in `run()` options | Node.js |
| Async handle leak source unknown | "open handles" warning, no location | Enable `detectAsyncLeaks: true` + `pool: 'forks'` | Vitest |
| ESM exports map bug invisible in tests | Test passes, production import fails | Use `viteModuleRunner: false` to test with native Node.js | Vitest |
| Cross-file global state contamination | Order-dependent test failures | Enable `globalsCleanup: 'on'` + `protectProperties()` | Jest |
| Async resource hangs on test timeout | Worker process stalls at timeout | Pass `test.signal` to `fetch`/DB query options | Vitest |
| Service worker requests bypass route handlers | SW fetches not intercepted | Upgrade to Playwright >= v1.57; use `context.route()` | Playwright |
| Watch mode misses non-imported asset changes | Stale results after migration edit | Add `watchTriggerPatterns` mapping | Vitest |
| JSON config untestable without FS mutation | Config branching hard to test | Use `t.mock.module('./config.json', ...)` (Node.js 24) | Node.js |
| Expensive fixtures wasted for tag-filtered tests | High CI time even for unit-only runs | Use separate project configs instead of tag filtering | Vitest |
| Popup contexts bypass network isolation | OAuth/download contexts not stubbed | Use `browser.on('context', cb)` to install routes on all contexts | Playwright |
| `poolOptions.forks.maxForks` silently ignored | Full CPU usage after Vitest 4 upgrade | Move limit to top-level `maxWorkers` | Vitest |
| `retryImmediately` retry sees dirty module state | Flaky retry passes on polluted state | Use `retryImmediately: false`; reset state in `beforeEach` | Jest |
| Subtest resource freed before subtest finishes | ECONNRESET mid-subtest (Node.js 24) | Use `t.after()` not outer `afterEach` for subtest resources | Node.js |
| `page.route()` missing on popup pages | Popup requests not intercepted | Use `context.route()` instead of `page.route()` | Playwright |
| `onGenerateMock` not called for factory mocks | Convention-enforcement silently bypassed | Document limitation; use shared factory wrappers instead | Jest |
| `bail` kills worker before `scope:'file'` teardown | Resource leak on bail | Pair with `onWorkerCleanup()` for process-level cleanup | Vitest |
| `setStorageState()` clears third-party cookies | CDN/subdomain 401 after user switch | Capture full state; merge third-party origins before replacing | Playwright |
