## Community Gotchas — Cycle 37

244. **Vitest `vi.mockObject(obj, { spy: true })` wraps only methods present at mock-creation time — methods added to the object prototype *after* the spy-mode mock is created are NOT tracked, causing `expect(spied.lateMethod).toHaveBeenCalled()` to throw `TypeError: spied.lateMethod is not a function`.** [community]
    WHY: `vi.mockObject` iterates the object's own enumerable properties and prototype chain at the moment it is called and creates spy wrappers for each function it finds. Prototype methods added after `vi.mockObject()` runs (e.g., by a mixin applied in `beforeEach`) are invisible to the wrapper and remain as plain non-spy functions on the returned proxy. Fix: call `vi.mockObject()` *after* all prototype augmentation is complete, or use individual `vi.spyOn()` calls for dynamically added methods.

245. **Jest 30 `resetModules: true` clears the module *require cache* between tests but does NOT clear the `jest.mock()` auto-mock registry — reimporting a module after `jest.resetModules()` returns a fresh instance but still applies the factory registered at the top of the file, so `jest.resetModules()` alone cannot give you the real (un-mocked) module.** [community]
    WHY: `jest.resetModules()` and `resetModules: true` clear the resolved module instances (the require cache) but the list of mocked module specifiers is separate state tracked by Jest's runtime. The mock factory registration survives module resets. A test that calls `jest.resetModules()` hoping to get a "real" `./db` module will still get the mocked version because the top-of-file `jest.mock('./db')` registration is never undone. Fix: call `jest.unmock('./db')` before `jest.resetModules()`, then re-import to get the real module — or restructure using `jest.isolateModules()` which runs a fresh registry without inheriting the mock registrations from the outer scope.

246. **Playwright worker-scoped fixtures that create a `BrowserContext` during worker setup share that context across ALL tests in the worker — cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB set by one test persist into the next test in the same worker, silently contaminating its starting state.** [community]
    WHY: Playwright's worker-scoped fixtures are initialised once per worker process and shared across all tests assigned to that worker. If a `BrowserContext` is created in a worker-scoped fixture and tests call `page.goto()` (which can set cookies), `localStorage.setItem()`, or execute JavaScript that writes IndexedDB, those side-effects accumulate in the shared context. A later test in the same worker sees the dirty context state. Fix: create the `BrowserContext` in a *test-scoped* fixture (the default) so each test gets a fresh context; or call `context.clearCookies()`, `context.clearPermissions()`, and `page.evaluate(() => localStorage.clear())` in the worker fixture's teardown.

247. **Node.js `--test-global-setup` runs the setup module in the parent process — any in-memory singletons created there (e.g., a Prisma client that opens a connection pool) live only in the parent heap and are NOT visible in child worker processes, leading to duplicate connection pools when each worker re-imports the module.** [community]
    WHY: With `isolation: 'process'` (the default), each test file runs in a child process forked from the parent. The child inherits `process.env` but NOT the parent's heap — in-memory objects, open sockets, and module-level singletons in the parent are not transferred. A `PrismaClient` instantiated in the global setup creates a pool in the parent and then each child process creates another pool when it imports Prisma for the first time. Fix: the global setup should only set `process.env` values (database URL, port numbers, test tokens) and spawn external processes. All in-process singletons must be created inside the test workers where they will actually be used.

248. **Vitest `aroundEach` does NOT run for tests marked `test.skip()` or `test.todo()` — cleanup-only logic at the end of the `aroundEach` block is never reached for skipped tests, which surprises teams who expect `aroundEach` to behave like `afterEach` (which also skips, but whose mental model is "always clean up after each test slot").** [community]
    WHY: `aroundEach` is only invoked for tests that are actually *executed*. Skipped and todo tests are never run, so their `aroundEach` wrapper is never called. The teardown code after `await runTest()` is never reached. The confusion arises when teams use `aroundEach` for resources pre-allocated in a `beforeAll` and expect `aroundEach` to always release them. Fix: use `afterAll` (not `aroundEach`) for resources allocated before any test runs and that must always be released regardless of skip status.

249. **Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks: true` reports false-positive leaked handles for `node:http` `Agent` keep-alive sockets created by `axios` or `node-fetch` — the TCP socket established during a test HTTP call may remain in TIME_WAIT state at the test boundary and be reported as an open handle, even though it will be closed by the OS within the keep-alive timeout.** [community]
    WHY: `detectAsyncLeaks` uses `node:async_hooks` to track open handles at test boundaries. HTTP keep-alive sockets remain in the Node.js event loop until the keep-alive timeout expires (default 5 seconds for `http.Agent`). Even though the test has logically finished and all assertions have passed, the underlying TCP socket is still an active handle. Fix: pass `{ keepAlive: false }` to the axios/fetch client under test so connections close immediately after each request, or call `agent.destroy()` in `afterEach` to force-close the pool.

250. **Jest 30 removed the deprecated `toBeCalled()`, `toBeCalledWith()`, `toReturn()`, and `toReturnWith()` matcher aliases — existing test suites that used these aliases throw `TypeError: expect(...).toBeCalled is not a function` at *runtime*, not at TypeScript compile time, because the types were updated in Jest 29 but the runtime enforcement was deferred until Jest 30.** [community]
    WHY: The deprecated aliases were removed from `jest-circus`'s matcher registration in Jest 30. Because the aliases were not part of the `@types/jest` type stubs for years, many codebases had already migrated their TypeScript but left the runtime usage in `.js` test files or JS-based config helpers untouched. The TypeScript compiler silently accepted the calls but the runtime error only surfaces when Jest 30 actually runs the tests. Fix: run `npx jest-codemods` or a project-wide search-and-replace for `toBeCalled(`, `toBeCalledWith(`, `toReturn(`, `toReturnWith(`, `toThrowError(` before upgrading to Jest 30.

## Quick Reference — Cycle 37

| Problem | Symptom | Solution | Framework |
|---------|---------|----------|-----------|
| Spy on all methods of an object at once | N separate `vi.spyOn()` calls, verbose | Use `vi.mockObject(obj, { spy: true })` | Vitest |
| In-flight async resource leaks on test timeout | `detectAsyncLeaks` warns after each test | Pass `test.signal` (AbortSignal) to fetch/stream | Vitest |
| `afterEach` spy cleanup skipped on assertion throw | Next test inherits spy from failed test | Use `using spy = vi.spyOn(...)` (TS 5.2+) | Vitest |
| `beforeEach`/`afterEach` can't share local variables | DB client allocated in one, released in other | Replace with `aroundEach` single-closure pattern | Vitest |
| Mock error stack trace points into helper internals | Hard to find the failing test line | Wrap helper with `vi.defineHelper()` | Vitest |
| Mock throw needs verbose `mockImplementation` wrapper | Noisy error-path test setup | Use `mock.mockThrowOnce(error)` / `mock.mockThrow(error)` | Vitest |
| `objectContaining` assertion drifts from production schema | Schema and assertion diverge silently | Use `expect.schemaMatching(zodSchema)` | Vitest |
| Config file accepts unknown keys silently | Typos in config not caught until runtime | Use `defineConfig()`; `mergeConfig()` for composition | Jest |
| `jest.mock()` passes locally, fails in Linux CI | Case mismatch on macOS HFS+ filesystem | Jest 30 enforces exact-case paths; fix casing | Jest |
| Only re-run failing tests after flaky CI failure | Full suite re-run wastes CI budget | Use `--test-rerun-failures=state.json` | Node.js |
| Known bug silently suppressed with `test.skip` | Bug fix not noticed when it ships | Replace with `it.expectFailure({ label, match })` | Node.js |
| Order-dependent tests pass in declaration order only | Hidden shared state not detected | Use `--test-randomize` nightly; replay with `--test-random-seed` | Node.js |
| Integration and unit tests compete for DB connections | High peak memory/connection count in CI | Use `sequence.groupOrder: 'sequential'` for integration project | Vitest |
| `page.clock.install()` breaks CSS transitions/debounce | UI components freeze during test | Use `page.clock.setFixedTime()` for date-only isolation | Playwright |
| Different environments need different setup files | Single `setupFiles` array can't branch | Use inline `projects` array in `vitest.config.ts` | Vitest |

### Pattern 287: Vitest `vi.doMock()` with `using` for inline ESM isolation without manual `vi.doUnmock()`  [official]

`vi.doMock()` is the non-hoisted counterpart to `vi.mock()` — it runs at the call site rather than being lifted to the top of the file, which means it can close over variables already in scope. In Vitest 4.1, `vi.doMock()` was updated to return a disposable object so the TC39 Explicit Resource Management `using` keyword automatically calls `vi.doUnmock()` when the block exits, eliminating the need for a separate cleanup call in `afterEach`. This pattern is particularly valuable when a test needs a different mock variant per test case: each `test()` block declares `using _m = vi.doMock(...)` and the mock is reverted the moment the test ends, regardless of whether it passes or throws.

```typescript
import { vi, test, expect } from "vitest";

// Module under test dynamically imports its config dependency.
// We need a different value per test without global vi.mock() overhead.

test("feature flag ON — renders premium UI", async () => {
  using _mockConfig = vi.doMock("../config", () => ({
    featureFlags: { premium: true },
  }));
  // Static import was already evaluated; re-import to pick up the mock.
  const { render } = await import("../feature-widget");
  const html = render();
  expect(html).toContain("premium");
  // vi.doUnmock('../config') called automatically here
});

test("feature flag OFF — renders standard UI", async () => {
  using _mockConfig = vi.doMock("../config", () => ({
    featureFlags: { premium: false },
  }));
  const { render } = await import("../feature-widget");
  const html = render();
  expect(html).toContain("standard");
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.doMock()` only affects modules imported *after* the call — static top-level imports in the test file itself are already resolved and remain un-mocked. For modules imported at the top of the test file you must use `vi.mock()` (hoisted) or dynamically re-import inside the test body. The `using` syntax requires TypeScript 5.2+ and a tsconfig `target` of ES2022 or later with `lib: ["ES2022"]`. [official]

---

### Pattern 288: Vitest `vi.hoisted()` to declare shared mock state before ESM import hoisting  [official]

ESM's static import evaluation occurs before any executable code runs. This means that the variables you define at the top of a test file are not yet assigned when `vi.mock()` factories execute — a classic "temporal dead zone" problem. `vi.hoisted()` solves this by running its callback in the same pre-import phase as `vi.mock()` factories, returning a value that both factory closures and test bodies can reference. This allows a shared `mockFn` to be created once, used inside the mock factory, and then have its implementation changed per test via `.mockImplementation()`.

```typescript
import { vi, beforeEach, test, expect } from "vitest";
import { processOrder } from "../order-service";

// vi.hoisted runs BEFORE ESM imports are resolved.
const { mockPayment, mockInventory } = vi.hoisted(() => ({
  mockPayment: vi.fn(),
  mockInventory: vi.fn(),
}));

// vi.mock factories execute in the same pre-import phase.
vi.mock("../payment-gateway", () => ({ charge: mockPayment }));
vi.mock("../inventory", () => ({ reserve: mockInventory }));

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.resetAllMocks(); // clear call counts between tests
});

test("successful order commits inventory and charges payment", async () => {
  mockInventory.mockResolvedValueOnce({ reservationId: "R1" });
  mockPayment.mockResolvedValueOnce({ transactionId: "T1" });

  const result = await processOrder({ itemId: "SKU1", quantity: 2 });

  expect(mockInventory).toHaveBeenCalledWith("SKU1", 2);
  expect(mockPayment).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.objectContaining({ amount: expect.any(Number) }));
  expect(result.status).toBe("confirmed");
});

test("payment failure rolls back inventory reservation", async () => {
  mockInventory.mockResolvedValueOnce({ reservationId: "R2" });
  mockPayment.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error("card declined"));

  await expect(processOrder({ itemId: "SKU1", quantity: 1 })).rejects.toThrow("card declined");
  // Inventory rollback should be called
  expect(mockInventory).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2); // reserve + release
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.hoisted()` is a Vitest-only API — there is no equivalent in Jest or `node:test`. Code that uses it cannot be shared with Jest test suites. If your project runs both frameworks, consider abstracting the shared mock references into a dedicated setup file that uses `jest.fn()` / `vi.fn()` conditionally, though this adds complexity. [official]

---

### Pattern 289: Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` for per-test ESM module-registry sandboxing  [official]

`jest.isolateModules()` only supports CommonJS synchronous `require()`. For ESM modules that use top-level `await` or that must be `import()`-ed dynamically, Jest provides `jest.isolateModulesAsync()`. This wraps a callback in a temporary module registry: every `require()` or dynamic `import()` inside the callback gets a fresh module instance, completely independent of the outer registry. Combined with `jest.doMock()` (non-hoisted) inside the callback, each test can assert against a module variant configured specifically for that test without leaking module state to siblings.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect } from "@jest/globals";

test("DB service uses connection string from environment", async () => {
  await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
    // Set env BEFORE importing the module so its top-level initializer picks it up.
    process.env.DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://localhost/test_a";

    // Non-hoisted mock: executes here, inside the sandbox.
    jest.doMock("../logger", () => ({ info: jest.fn(), error: jest.fn() }));

    const { DbService } = await import("../db-service");
    const svc = new DbService();

    expect(svc.connectionString).toBe("postgresql://localhost/test_a");
  });
});

test("DB service handles missing DATABASE_URL at import time", async () => {
  await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
    delete process.env.DATABASE_URL;

    jest.doMock("../logger", () => ({ info: jest.fn(), error: jest.fn() }));

    // Module that throws if DATABASE_URL is absent at init time.
    await expect(import("../db-service")).rejects.toThrow("DATABASE_URL is required");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Each `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` call re-evaluates all imported modules, including their dependency trees, so cold-import-heavy modules (e.g., Prisma client, large config validators) make per-test sandboxing slow. Benchmark with `--verbose` timing output before applying this pattern globally. The callback executes serially — concurrent isolation requires multiple top-level test bodies, not parallel `Promise.all()` calls inside one `isolateModulesAsync()`. [official]

---

### Pattern 290: Node.js `context.mock.timers` with `[Symbol.dispose]` for guaranteed timer teardown  [official]

The `node:test` built-in runner's `MockTimers` class gained `[Symbol.dispose]()` support, enabling the TC39 `using` keyword for deterministic timer restoration. Without explicit teardown, fake timers left active in one test silently affect all subsequent tests in the same process when running with `isolation: 'none'`. The `using` pattern eliminates this class of leak: the timer mock is restored immediately when the `using` binding goes out of scope, whether the test passes, throws, or is explicitly aborted. The pattern also works with `timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'Date'], now: specificTimestamp })` for fixed-time testing of date-sensitive logic.

```typescript
import { test, mock } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";

test("retry logic backs off exponentially", (context) => {
  // 'using' guarantees timers.reset() + original timer restoration on scope exit.
  using timers = context.mock.timers;
  timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "Date"], now: 0 });

  const attemptTimes: number[] = [];
  let callCount = 0;

  function retryableOperation(): Promise<void> {
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const attempt = () => {
        callCount++;
        attemptTimes.push(Date.now());
        if (callCount < 3) {
          setTimeout(attempt, 2 ** callCount * 100); // 200ms, 400ms
          reject(new Error("transient"));
        } else {
          resolve();
        }
      };
      attempt();
    });
  }

  const p = retryableOperation();
  // Tick through both retry delays
  timers.tick(200);
  timers.tick(400);
  timers.runAll();

  assert.deepEqual(attemptTimes, [0, 200, 600]);
});
// timers automatically restored here — no afterEach needed
```

**Tradeoff:** `using` is a TypeScript 5.2+ / Node.js 22+ language feature. Projects targeting older Node.js must fall back to manual `context.mock.timers.reset()` in `after()` hooks or a `try/finally` block. The `Symbol.dispose` method resets the timer state but does not execute pending timers — if your teardown logic relies on timer callbacks firing during cleanup, call `timers.runAll()` before the `using` scope exits. [official]

---

### Pattern 291: Playwright `test.use({ storageState })` per-describe-block for multi-role isolation  [official]

Playwright's `test.use()` call at the `describe` level overrides fixture configuration for all tests within that block without needing separate config files or conditional logic in a worker fixture. For applications with multiple user roles (admin, editor, viewer), each describe block can declare `test.use({ storageState: './fixtures/admin.json' })` and all tests inside run with that pre-authenticated context. Because `storageState` is baked into the context before the first navigation, there is no per-test authentication round trip — the browser starts in the authenticated state. This also prevents cookie leakage between roles: each describe block's fixture is fully isolated from siblings.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

// Admin role block — all tests start as admin
test.describe("Admin dashboard", () => {
  test.use({ storageState: "e2e/fixtures/admin-storage.json" });

  test("can delete any user", async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto("/admin/users");
    const row = page.getByRole("row", { name: "alice@example.com" });
    await row.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete" }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText("User deleted")).toBeVisible();
  });

  test("can promote editor to admin", async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto("/admin/users");
    await page.getByRole("row", { name: "bob@example.com" })
      .getByRole("button", { name: "Promote" }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText("Role updated")).toBeVisible();
  });
});

// Viewer role block — completely isolated storage state
test.describe("Viewer access control", () => {
  test.use({ storageState: "e2e/fixtures/viewer-storage.json" });

  test("cannot access admin panel", async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto("/admin");
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `storageState` files must be generated in advance (e.g., via `playwright/auth` setup scripts and `page.context().storageState({ path })`) and checked into version control or generated in CI global setup. If the application's authentication mechanism changes (e.g., new cookie names, token rotation), all storage state files must be regenerated. For applications with dynamic session tokens that expire quickly, combine with `test.beforeAll()` to refresh the storage state before the describe block runs. [official]

### Pattern 292: Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` with `isolate: true` per-project for C-addon singleton isolation  [official]

Native Node.js addons (`.node` binaries compiled from C/C++) and ORM clients that maintain process-level connection pools are notoriously difficult to isolate because they store state in C heap memory that is invisible to the JavaScript garbage collector and module registry. Vitest's `vmForks` pool combines two layers of isolation: each worker runs in a separate child process (fork isolation) AND inside a V8 `vm.Context` sandbox (module isolation). This ensures that the C-addon's `dlopen`-loaded library is unloaded when the worker exits, so the next test file gets a clean native state. Set this only for projects that import native addons to avoid the performance cost for pure-JS tests.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — targeted pool isolation for native-addon tests
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        test: {
          name: "pure-unit",
          include: ["src/**/*.unit.test.ts"],
          pool: "threads", // fast, low overhead
          isolate: false,  // share module registry within project for speed
        },
      },
      {
        test: {
          name: "db-integration",
          include: ["src/**/*.db.test.ts"],
          // vmForks = subprocess + V8 vm.Context sandbox
          pool: "vmForks",
          isolate: true,
          poolOptions: {
            vmForks: {
              // Limit concurrent subprocesses to cap DB connection count
              maxForks: 2,
            },
          },
          globalSetup: ["./vitest.db-setup.ts"],
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vmForks` has the highest per-test startup cost of all Vitest pool types: each fork spawns a new Node.js process AND initialises a new V8 context. On a suite of 500 integration tests, this overhead can add 10-30 seconds compared to `forks` pool. Use `maxForks` to cap memory usage at the cost of wall-clock time. Inspect native-addon isolation needs with `vitest --reporter=verbose` to confirm that state from test N is not visible in test N+1 before committing to `vmForks` for the entire integration project. [official]

### Pattern 293: Jest `jest.onGenerateMock()` callback for intercepting and augmenting auto-mock generation  [official]

Jest 30 introduced `jest.onGenerateMock(modulePath, mock)` as a programmatic hook that fires every time Jest generates an automatic mock for a module. This enables centralised mock augmentation: instead of copy-pasting `mockReturnValue(undefined)` defaults across dozens of test files, a single `setupFilesAfterEnv` entry can register a callback that injects sensible defaults into every auto-generated mock matching a pattern. This is especially useful for SDK clients where auto-mock returns `undefined` for all methods but production code asserts on the return value, causing cryptic `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` failures.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts — registered in jest.config.ts setupFilesAfterEnv
import { jest } from "@jest/globals";

jest.onGenerateMock((modulePath: string, mock: Record<string, unknown>) => {
  // Add safe default return values for Stripe SDK auto-mocks.
  if (modulePath.includes("stripe")) {
    const customers = mock.customers as Record<string, jest.Mock> | undefined;
    customers?.create?.mockResolvedValue({ id: "cus_test", object: "customer" });
    customers?.retrieve?.mockResolvedValue({ id: "cus_test", object: "customer" });

    const charges = mock.charges as Record<string, jest.Mock> | undefined;
    charges?.create?.mockResolvedValue({ id: "ch_test", status: "succeeded" });
  }
  return mock; // return (possibly modified) mock
});

// In test file — just call jest.mock; defaults are injected automatically.
jest.mock("stripe");
import Stripe from "stripe";

test("checkout creates customer then charge", async () => {
  const stripe = new Stripe("sk_test");
  const customer = await stripe.customers.create({ email: "a@example.com" });
  expect(customer.id).toBe("cus_test"); // default from onGenerateMock
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `jest.onGenerateMock()` runs for every auto-mock generation in the process, including modules you did not intend to customise. Guard the augmentation with a `modulePath.includes(...)` check. The callback receives the mock object *after* Jest's auto-mock generation but *before* the test file imports it, so overrides are always applied. Callbacks registered in `setupFilesAfterEnv` are global; callbacks registered via `jest.onGenerateMock()` inside individual test files only apply within that file's worker process. [official]

### Pattern 294: Node.js `--test-shard` combined with `--test-random-seed` for reproducible parallel CI partitioning  [official]

`node:test`'s `--test-shard=<index>/<total>` flag partitions the test file list across CI nodes deterministically. Combined with `--test-random-seed=<N>` (which shuffles execution order within each shard), this gives both horizontal scale-out and order-sensitivity detection in a single CI pass. The seed is printed in the test summary and can be passed to `--test-random-seed` on a subsequent run to reproduce a specific shard's execution order exactly. This removes the need for a separate nightly randomisation job: every CI run is both sharded and randomised.

```typescript
// package.json scripts — pass SHARD and SEED as env vars from CI matrix
// "test:ci": "node --test --test-shard=$SHARD_INDEX/$SHARD_TOTAL --test-random-seed=$RANDOM_SEED src/**/*.test.ts"

// vitest.workspace equivalent for reference:
// vitest run --shard=1/4

// Example GitHub Actions matrix
// strategy:
//   matrix:
//     shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
//     seed: [42]  # fixed seed so all shards share the same randomisation epoch

// Helper to assert shard coverage in CI
import { run } from "node:test";
import path from "node:path";
import glob from "node:fs/promises";

const shardIndex = parseInt(process.env.SHARD_INDEX ?? "1", 10);
const shardTotal = parseInt(process.env.SHARD_TOTAL ?? "1", 10);
const seed      = parseInt(process.env.RANDOM_SEED   ?? "0", 10);

const allFiles = (await glob.readdir("./src", { recursive: true }))
  .filter(f => f.endsWith(".test.ts"))
  .map(f => path.resolve("./src", f))
  .sort(); // deterministic sort before sharding

const shardFiles = allFiles.filter((_, i) => i % shardTotal === shardIndex - 1);

await run({ files: shardFiles, concurrency: 4, seed });
```

**Tradeoff:** `--test-shard` in `node:test` is a file-level partition — it does not shard within a single large test file. A test file with 500 tests always runs entirely on one shard. If your test suite has a few very large files that dominate runtime, sharding by file count does not balance wall-clock time. Consider splitting large files or using `--test-concurrency` in combination with sharding. The `seed` must be identical across all shards for the CI run to be reproducible from the printed summary. [official]

### Pattern 295: Playwright `page.routeFromHAR()` for hermetic network replay isolation  [official]

Playwright's `page.routeFromHAR(harFile, options)` replays previously recorded HTTP responses from a HAR archive, giving E2E tests a hermetic network layer without running a real API server or maintaining a full MSW handler suite. Unlike MSW, HAR replay works at the browser network layer, so it captures binary responses (images, PDFs, fonts) and non-JSON content types that are tedious to stub by hand. The `{ update: false, notFound: 'abort' }` option pair causes any unrecorded request to abort immediately rather than silently fall through to the real network, surfacing missing coverage early.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";
import path from "node:path";

const HAR_PATH = path.join(__dirname, "fixtures", "dashboard-api.har");

test.describe("Dashboard (offline replay)", () => {
  test("renders KPI tiles from recorded API responses", async ({ page }) => {
    // Serve network from HAR; abort any request not in the archive.
    await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH, {
      update: false,
      notFound: "abort",
      // Only intercept calls to our API domain; pass CDN assets through.
      url: "**/api/**",
    });

    await page.goto("/dashboard");
    await expect(page.getByTestId("kpi-revenue")).toHaveText("$1,234,567");
    await expect(page.getByTestId("kpi-users")).toHaveText("42,000");
  });

  test("handles empty state when HAR returns 204 for empty dataset", async ({ page }) => {
    await page.routeFromHAR(HAR_PATH, {
      update: false,
      notFound: "abort",
      url: "**/api/**",
    });

    // Override just one route inside HAR replay for the empty-state variant.
    await page.route("**/api/metrics", route =>
      route.fulfill({ status: 204, body: "" })
    );

    await page.goto("/dashboard");
    await expect(page.getByTestId("empty-state")).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** HAR files must be periodically regenerated when the API changes, and they can become large (megabytes) for pages with many API calls, increasing git repository size. Use `.gitattributes` to mark HAR files as binary to avoid line-ending noise in diffs. The `{ url: "**/api/**" }` filter prevents the HAR layer from intercepting CDN assets that the real browser should load, but means tests still need a network connection for non-API resources unless you also serve static assets locally. [official]

---

### Pattern 296: Vitest `test.override()` for fixture value overrides without a new `test.extend()` chain  [official]

Vitest 4.1 replaced the deprecated `test.scoped()` with `test.override()`, which overrides a fixture value for a specific test without requiring a new `test.extend()` declaration. This fills the gap between global fixture defaults and per-test inline setup: a describe block can declare a default database fixture returning a read-write client, while a specific test inside the block calls `test.override({ db: readOnlyDb })` to receive a read-only variant — all without modifying the fixture definition file or creating a new fixture layer. Unlike `test.use()` (which applies to all tests in a describe block), `test.override()` is scoped to the single test that declares it.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from "vitest";
import { createReadWriteDb, createReadOnlyDb } from "../test-helpers/db";

// Base fixture — defaults to read-write DB
const test = base.extend<{ db: ReturnType<typeof createReadWriteDb> }>({
  db: async ({}, use) => {
    const db = createReadWriteDb();
    await use(db);
    await db.close();
  },
});

test("write operation succeeds", async ({ db }) => {
  await db.insert("users", { name: "Alice" });
  const user = await db.findOne("users", { name: "Alice" });
  expect(user).toBeDefined();
});

// This single test gets a read-only variant — no new extend() needed.
test.override({ db: createReadOnlyDb() })(
  "write on read-only DB throws PermissionError",
  async ({ db }) => {
    await expect(
      db.insert("users", { name: "Bob" })
    ).rejects.toThrow("PermissionError");
  }
);

test("read-back works after write", async ({ db }) => {
  await db.insert("items", { sku: "ABC" });
  const item = await db.findOne("items", { sku: "ABC" });
  expect(item?.sku).toBe("ABC");
  // db here is the default read-write client, unaffected by the override above
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `test.override()` was introduced in Vitest 4.1; older Vitest versions throw `TypeError: test.override is not a function`. Pin `vitest` to `>=4.1.0` in `package.json` if you adopt this pattern. The override applies to the fixture value *instance* for that test only — it does not change setup/teardown logic. If the overridden fixture requires custom teardown (e.g., closing a DB connection), manage it manually inside the test or wrap in a `using` disposable. [official]

---

### Pattern 297: Jest `jest.replaceProperty()` with `jest.Replaced<T>` for type-safe non-configurable property isolation  [official]

`jest.spyOn()` cannot intercept non-configurable properties (e.g., `process.env.NODE_ENV`, readonly getters on built-in objects) because it needs to redefine the property descriptor. `jest.replaceProperty()` bypasses this by directly assigning the new value and recording the original for later restoration via `.restore()`. Jest 30 introduced the `jest.Replaced<T>` type to give TypeScript-level awareness that the returned handle is a replacement token (not a mock function), preventing `mockReturnValue` call errors that appear at compile time rather than runtime.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect, afterEach } from "@jest/globals";

// Type-safe handle: jest.Replaced<string> (not jest.SpyInstance)
let replacedEnv: jest.Replaced<string>;

afterEach(() => {
  replacedEnv?.restore(); // revert to original value
});

test("analytics disabled in development mode", () => {
  replacedEnv = jest.replaceProperty(process.env, "NODE_ENV", "development");
  // Module re-evaluated with development env
  jest.resetModules();
  const { Analytics } = require("../analytics");
  expect(new Analytics().isEnabled()).toBe(false);
});

test("analytics enabled in production mode", () => {
  replacedEnv = jest.replaceProperty(process.env, "NODE_ENV", "production");
  jest.resetModules();
  const { Analytics } = require("../analytics");
  expect(new Analytics().isEnabled()).toBe(true);
});

// Attempting this would be a TypeScript error with jest.Replaced<T>:
// replacedEnv.mockReturnValue('staging'); // TS Error: Property 'mockReturnValue' does not exist
```

**Tradeoff:** `jest.replaceProperty()` only works with own enumerable properties and some built-in read-only values. It cannot override non-configurable, non-writable properties whose `writable: false` descriptor is enforced by the runtime (e.g., `Object.freeze()`-d objects). For those cases, `vi.stubGlobal()` in Vitest has broader coverage because it stores and restores the original descriptor rather than directly assigning. Verify your target property is replaceable with `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(target, key)` before committing to this pattern. [official]

---

### Pattern 298: MSW `http.passthrough()` in `beforeAll` handler for selective API isolation in integration tests  [community]

MSW v2's `http.passthrough()` return value instructs the service worker or server to forward the matched request to the real network, bypassing all other handlers. This enables an inversion of the usual MSW isolation model: instead of mocking specific endpoints and letting everything else through, you can install a catch-all handler that blocks all traffic by default, then selectively `passthrough()` requests to real backend endpoints that must remain live for the current test suite. This is the correct pattern for integration test environments where most third-party calls should be blocked but one real service (e.g., a local database REST API) must remain accessible.

```typescript
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";
import { beforeAll, afterAll, afterEach, test, expect } from "vitest";
import { fetchDashboardData } from "../api-client";

const server = setupServer(
  // 1. Allow the local test DB API through on all methods.
  http.all("http://localhost:5433/*", () => http.passthrough()),

  // 2. Mock the external payment processor — never hit real Stripe in tests.
  http.post("https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges", () =>
    HttpResponse.json({ id: "ch_test", status: "succeeded" }, { status: 200 })
  ),

  // 3. Block everything else with a 503 to surface unexpected external calls.
  http.all("*", ({ request }) => {
    console.warn(`[MSW] Blocked unhandled request: ${request.method} ${request.url}`);
    return HttpResponse.json({ error: "blocked by MSW" }, { status: 503 });
  })
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: "bypass" }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test("dashboard aggregation calls local DB and mocked Stripe", async () => {
  const data = await fetchDashboardData();
  expect(data.revenue).toBeDefined(); // from local DB passthrough
  expect(data.lastCharge).toEqual({ id: "ch_test", status: "succeeded" });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The catch-all blocking handler makes MSW configuration order-sensitive: handlers are matched in insertion order and the first match wins. The `passthrough()` handler must appear before the catch-all blocker or it will never be reached. Use `server.use(overrideHandler)` in individual tests to override the default block for specific routes during that test only, and call `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` to remove those overrides. [community]

---

### Pattern 299: Vitest `aroundAll` with fixture context for shared resource setup with per-suite teardown  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduced a breaking change to `aroundAll`: it now receives the *fixture context* as its first argument rather than executing bare. This enables resource allocation inside `aroundAll` that is wired through the same fixture dependency graph as individual tests, eliminating the need to store resource handles in closure variables or module-level state. A file-scoped database migration can be seeded once in `aroundAll`, exposed via the fixture context, and consumed by individual tests through the standard fixture mechanism — with guaranteed teardown even if tests throw.

```typescript
import { test as base, aroundAll, expect } from "vitest";
import { migrate, seedTestData, rollbackMigration } from "../test-helpers/db-lifecycle";

interface TestFixtures {
  dbVersion: string;
}

const test = base.extend<TestFixtures>({
  dbVersion: async ({}, use) => {
    // Fixture provides current migration version to tests that request it.
    const version = process.env.DB_VERSION ?? "latest";
    await use(version);
  },
});

// aroundAll receives fixture context — access fixtures here in Vitest 4.1+
aroundAll(async ({ dbVersion }, runSuite) => {
  await migrate({ version: dbVersion });
  await seedTestData();
  try {
    await runSuite();
  } finally {
    await rollbackMigration({ version: dbVersion });
  }
});

test("finds seeded admin user", async ({ dbVersion }) => {
  const { queryUser } = await import("../user-repository");
  const admin = await queryUser({ role: "admin" });
  expect(admin).toBeDefined();
  expect(admin?.dbVersion).toBe(dbVersion);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** In Vitest 4.0 and earlier, `aroundAll` received no arguments. Code that was written before the 4.1 breaking change either ignores the first argument (safe) or will need to be updated to destructure `{ fixtureKey }` from it. Like `aroundEach`, `aroundAll` is skipped entirely when all tests in the suite are `.skip()` or `.todo()` — teardown after `runSuite()` is only guaranteed when the suite actually runs. Combine with `afterAll` for resources that must be released even for empty suites. [official]

---

### Pattern 300: Node.js `AsyncLocalStorage` with `defaultValue` option for zero-`undefined` per-test context stores  [official]

Node.js 24 added an optional `defaultValue` parameter to `AsyncLocalStorage` that is returned when `.getStore()` is called outside an active `.run()` context. Before this, any utility function that read from an `AsyncLocalStorage` store and was called from outside a test had to handle `undefined`, cluttering TypeScript codebases with non-null assertions and optional chaining. With `defaultValue`, a per-test trace context store can expose a safe empty object that downstream utilities consume without null checks, while each test's `aroundEach` or `beforeEach` establishes a proper run context that overrides the default.

```typescript
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from "node:async_hooks";
import { aroundEach, test, expect } from "vitest";

interface TraceContext {
  traceId: string;
  spanId: string;
  testName: string;
}

// Safe default — never undefined, eliminates null checks in utilities.
const traceStore = new AsyncLocalStorage<TraceContext>({
  defaultValue: { traceId: "00000000", spanId: "00000000", testName: "<none>" },
});

// Utility that reads from the store — no undefined check needed.
export function currentTraceId(): string {
  return traceStore.getStore().traceId;
}

aroundEach(async (task, runTest) => {
  const context: TraceContext = {
    traceId: crypto.randomUUID().replace(/-/g, "").slice(0, 8),
    spanId:  crypto.randomUUID().replace(/-/g, "").slice(0, 8),
    testName: task.name,
  };
  // Wrap each test in an ALS context — store is populated during the test.
  await traceStore.run(context, runTest);
});

test("trace ID is available inside test execution", () => {
  const id = currentTraceId();
  // Not the default value — we are inside aroundEach's ALS.run() context.
  expect(id).not.toBe("00000000");
  expect(id).toHaveLength(8);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `defaultValue` option is Node.js 24+. On Node.js 22 and earlier, `AsyncLocalStorage` constructor accepts no options argument and `getStore()` returns `undefined` outside a `run()` context. For cross-version compatibility, implement a thin `getTraceStore()` wrapper that falls back to a static default object: `const s = traceStore.getStore(); return s ?? DEFAULT_CONTEXT;`. [official]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 38

251. **Vitest `vi.mock()` with a factory cannot reference variables declared in the test file's module scope because the factory is hoisted above the import declarations — the variable is in the temporal dead zone at factory execution time, causing a `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'X' before initialization` that only appears at runtime, not at TypeScript compile time.** [official]
    WHY: ESM hoisting moves `vi.mock()` calls (and their inline factory functions) to execute before the file's `import` statements are resolved. Any `const`/`let`/`class` declarations in the test file are hoisted *as bindings* but remain uninitialised until the line where they are declared — which is after the factory has already run. The fix is `vi.hoisted()`: call `vi.hoisted(() => vi.fn())` to create the shared reference in the same pre-import phase as the factory, then close over the returned value inside the factory. Using `var` instead of `const` is a workaround but is a code-smell and breaks TypeScript strict mode.

252. **Jest `jest.useFakeTimers()` also replaces the `Date` constructor globally — test code that creates a `new Date()` inside a module imported after `useFakeTimers()` is called will get the fake date, but if the module was *already in the require cache*, its constructor reference points to the real `Date`, causing `instanceof Date` checks to fail on objects created by the cached module.** [community]
    WHY: `jest.useFakeTimers()` replaces `global.Date` with a fake implementation. Modules that were already loaded and assigned `const D = Date` at module-init time hold a reference to the original `Date` constructor. An object created by such a module via `new D()` fails `x instanceof Date` because the left-hand `Date` is the fake replacement while the right-hand prototype chain traces back to the original. Fix: combine `jest.useFakeTimers()` with `jest.resetModules()` and re-import the module, or move the `const D = Date` assignment inside the function that creates the date so it picks up the current (fake) `Date` at call time.

253. **Node.js `t.mock.module()` (per-test ESM isolation in `node:test`) only intercepts `import()` calls made *inside the test callback* — static top-level imports in the test file are already resolved before the test runs and are not affected by `t.mock.module()`, silently leaving the real module active for those import paths.** [official]
    WHY: `TestContext.mock.module()` creates a mock that is active for the lifetime of the test callback. By the time the test callback begins executing, all static imports at the top of the file have already been evaluated and their bindings are set. Only subsequent `import()` calls (dynamic imports) within the test callback pick up the mock. Test authors who see the Jest `jest.mock()` (which is hoisted) pattern and apply `t.mock.module()` at the top of a `test()` callback expecting the same effect will find their statically imported module unchanged. Fix: restructure code to use dynamic `import()` inside the test callback, or use file-level `mock.module()` from the `node:test` module-level API rather than `t.mock.module()`.

254. **Playwright worker-scoped fixtures whose teardown calls `await context.close()` receive a `TargetClosedError` if any test in the worker crashed the browser process — the browser is already gone, so `context.close()` throws, and this error supersedes the original test failure, hiding the root cause in CI logs.** [community]
    WHY: Playwright worker-scoped fixtures share a single browser process across all tests in the worker. If a test triggers a browser crash (e.g., navigating to a `chrome://crash` URL, or an unhandled fatal JS error in an extension context), the browser process is terminated. The shared `BrowserContext` becomes invalid, and subsequent `context.close()` calls in the worker fixture teardown throw `TargetClosedError`. Because the fixture teardown exception occurs after the failing test completes, it may appear as a separate error in the reporter that obscures the original crash message. Fix: wrap `await context.close()` in a try/catch that logs but swallows `TargetClosedError` in the worker fixture teardown, and emit a warning with the test name so the crash is visible without blocking teardown of the worker.

255. **Vitest `restoreMocks: true` in `vitest.config.ts` calls `vi.restoreAllMocks()` automatically after each test, but this does NOT restore mocks created with `vi.mock()` (module-level mocks) — only `vi.spyOn()` mocks and mocks created via the `spy: true` option of `vi.mockObject()` are restored, leaving module mock implementations active across tests.** [official]
    WHY: `vi.restoreAllMocks()` (like Jest's `jest.restoreAllMocks()`) iterates the list of spies registered via `vi.spyOn()` and calls `.mockRestore()` on each. Module-level mocks registered via `vi.mock()` are a different code path — they replace the module in the module registry and are not tracked in the spy list. Restoring them requires `vi.unmock()` (hoisted) or `vi.doUnmock()` (runtime) followed by `vi.resetModules()`. A common bug: `restoreMocks: true` passes in CI because module mock implementations happen to be idempotent, then a refactor makes them stateful and the suite becomes order-dependent overnight. Fix: use `vi.clearAllMocks()` / `vi.resetAllMocks()` for module mock call-count resets, and explicitly call `vi.doUnmock()` + `vi.resetModules()` in the test body when you need the real module back.

256. **MSW v2 `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` removes *runtime* handlers added via `server.use()` during a test, but it does NOT remove handlers passed to `setupServer(handlers...)` at construction time — calling `resetHandlers()` after a test that pushed a new handler does not revert to a "clean slate" if the initial handler list itself contains a bug or stale mock.** [community]
    WHY: MSW distinguishes between "initial handlers" (the list passed to `setupServer()` or `setupWorker()`) and "runtime handlers" (added via `server.use()`). `resetHandlers()` pops all runtime handlers back to the initial list. If you accidentally add a handler to the initial list during a refactor (e.g., moving a `server.use()` call to the `setupServer()` invocation), `resetHandlers()` will never remove it, and tests will continue to receive its mocked response even when they don't expect it. Fix: inspect the initial handler list with `server.listHandlers()` when debugging unexpected mock responses after `resetHandlers()` has been called. Use `server.close()` + `server.listen()` in a `beforeAll`/`afterAll` pair if you need a fully clean state between suites.

257. **Playwright `page.route()` handlers registered inside a test are NOT automatically removed after the test ends when using the built-in `page` fixture — if the test fails before `page.unroute()` is called, the route handler accumulates on the page object and the next test (if the `page` fixture is worker-scoped) receives a page with stale handlers that intercept requests unexpectedly.** [community]
    WHY: Route handlers registered with `page.route()` persist on the `Page` object until explicitly removed with `page.unroute()` or the page is closed. The built-in Playwright `page` fixture is test-scoped by default (a new page per test), so this is usually not a problem. But teams that override `page` with a worker-scoped fixture to share a page across tests (for performance) expose themselves to handler accumulation: a route added in test 3 is still active in test 4. Fix: either keep `page` test-scoped (the default and recommended approach), or call `page.unrouteAll()` in the worker fixture's teardown block before closing the context.

258. **Jest `jest.resetModules()` inside a `beforeEach` combined with `import` (ES module static syntax) at the top of the test file does NOT give you a fresh module per test — the top-level `import` is a static binding that is evaluated once when the file loads, and `jest.resetModules()` only affects subsequent `require()` or dynamic `import()` calls made after it runs.** [community]
    WHY: Jest's `resetModules: true` config option and `jest.resetModules()` API clear the CommonJS require cache (and the ESM module registry for files transformed by Babel/ts-jest). However, static `import` declarations at the top of a test file create permanent bindings at file evaluation time. The binding variable `myModule` is permanently linked to the first-loaded instance of the module — `jest.resetModules()` cannot rebind it. Developers who write `import { svc } from '../service'` at the top and then call `jest.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` are surprised when `svc` still refers to the same instance. Fix: remove top-level imports for modules you want to re-instantiate per test and replace them with `const { svc } = require('../service')` inside `beforeEach`, or use `jest.isolateModules()` with a synchronous `require()` callback.

## Cycle 39 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 301: Jest 30 `globalsCleanup: 'on'` for automatic post-file global leak detection  [official]

Jest 30 added `testEnvironmentOptions.globalsCleanup: 'on'` which causes Jest to compare the set of global properties before and after each test file runs and warn about any new properties that were not cleaned up. This eliminates an entire class of subtle isolation failures where a library installed a global (e.g. `window.__chartInstances`, `global.__openHandles`) and left it for subsequent test files to inherit. The check fires at the file boundary rather than the test boundary, so it catches leaks caused by module-level side effects that no per-test teardown can reach. Combine it with `protectProperties(globalThis['my-lib-key'])` for third-party globals you intend to share across files.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "jest";

export default defineConfig({
  testEnvironment: "jsdom",
  testEnvironmentOptions: {
    // Detect un-cleaned globals after every test file.
    globalsCleanup: "on",
  },
});

// In setup-globals.ts — protect an intentional shared global from the cleanup warning
import { protectProperties } from "jest-util";

// My app seeds a global feature-flag store at module init time.
// Tell Jest this is intentional and should not be flagged as a leak.
protectProperties((globalThis as Record<string, unknown>)["__featureFlags"]);
```

**Tradeoff:** `globalsCleanup: 'on'` adds a small but measurable overhead to each test file teardown because Jest must diff the global property set. On codebases with thousands of test files this can add several seconds to total run time. The `'soft'` value logs warnings rather than hard-failing, giving teams a migration path: start with `'soft'` to inventory existing leaks, then graduate to `'on'` once the inventory is clean. Third-party libraries that legitimately install globals (e.g. Sentry's `window.__SENTRY__`) must be allowlisted via `protectProperties` or the warning becomes noise. [official]

### Pattern 302: Jest 30 `jest.spyOn()` with `using` keyword for automatic spy restoration via explicit resource management  [official]

Jest 30 added support for the TC39 Explicit Resource Management proposal on spy objects: a value returned by `jest.spyOn()` now implements `Symbol.dispose`, so wrapping it in a `using` declaration guarantees the spy is restored when the enclosing block exits — even if the test throws. This removes the pattern of pairing every `jest.spyOn()` with a manual `afterEach(() => jest.restoreAllMocks())` or a manual `spy.mockRestore()` call. The spy is scoped precisely to the block it is declared in, enabling granular sub-test scoping that lifecycle hooks cannot express.

```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, jest } from "@jest/globals";
import { logger } from "../src/logger";
import { processOrder } from "../src/order-service";

describe("order processing", () => {
  test("logs a warning for back-ordered items", () => {
    // Spy is automatically restored when this block exits.
    using warnSpy = jest.spyOn(logger, "warn").mockImplementation(() => {});

    processOrder({ itemId: "BACKORDER-001", quantity: 5 });

    expect(warnSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(warnSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.stringContaining("back-ordered")
    );
    // No afterEach needed — Symbol.dispose restores logger.warn here.
  });

  test("does not warn for in-stock items", () => {
    // The spy from the previous test is already fully restored here.
    processOrder({ itemId: "IN-STOCK-001", quantity: 1 });
    // logger.warn is the real implementation — would throw if spy leaked.
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `using` keyword requires TypeScript 5.2+ (for type-checking) and a runtime that supports the TC39 proposal — Node.js 18.20+ / Node.js 20+. Projects still on Node.js 16 or TypeScript 5.1 cannot use this pattern and must fall back to explicit `spy.mockRestore()` or `restoreMocks: true` in config. Unlike `restoreMocks: true`, block-scoped `using` spies do not rely on Jest's internal spy registry, so they are restored even if `jest.clearAllMocks()` or `jest.resetAllMocks()` is called mid-test without `restore`. [official]

---

### Pattern 303: Jest 30 `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` for `requestAnimationFrame` isolation  [official]

Jest 30 introduced `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` which advances fake timers until the next `requestAnimationFrame` callback fires, mirroring the browser's 16.67 ms frame boundary. Before this API, testing `rAF`-driven animations or render loops required calling `jest.advanceTimersByTime(16)` with a magic constant, or faking `requestAnimationFrame` manually. The new method advances time by exactly the correct frame interval and fires all pending `rAF` callbacks without requiring you to know or hardcode the milliseconds-per-frame value. It is safe to call in loops to step through multi-frame animations deterministically.

```typescript
import { test, expect, jest, beforeEach, afterEach } from "@jest/globals";
import { AnimationController } from "../src/animation-controller";

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
});

test("animates through three frames and reaches final position", () => {
  const controller = new AnimationController({
    from: 0,
    to: 300,
    durationFrames: 3,
  });

  controller.start();

  // Advance one frame at a time — no magic 16ms constant needed.
  jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // frame 1
  expect(controller.currentPosition).toBeCloseTo(100, 0);

  jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // frame 2
  expect(controller.currentPosition).toBeCloseTo(200, 0);

  jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // frame 3
  expect(controller.currentPosition).toBeCloseTo(300, 0);

  expect(controller.isComplete).toBe(true);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` is only available when `jest.useFakeTimers()` is active with the modern timer implementation (`legacyFakeTimers: false`, which is the default in Jest 30). Calling it with legacy timers throws an error. The method advances the fake clock but does not simulate the browser's rendering pipeline — callbacks that rely on actual layout measurements (e.g. `element.getBoundingClientRect()`) inside a `rAF` callback will still receive the jsdom stubs, not real layout values. [official]

---

### Pattern 304: Node.js 24 `--test-global-setup` for process-level shared resource lifecycle  [official]

Node.js 24 added `--test-global-setup=<file>` support, allowing a dedicated module to export `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` async functions that bracket the entire test run in a single coordinated lifecycle. This is the Node.js test runner equivalent of Jest's `globalSetup`/`globalTeardown` config and Vitest's `globalSetup` option. Resources that are expensive to create (database connections, Docker containers, compiled Wasm modules) can be provisioned once in `globalSetup`, stored in a file or environment variable, consumed by individual tests via `process.env`, and cleanly destroyed in `globalTeardown` regardless of test outcome.

```typescript
// test-global-setup.ts  (passed via --test-global-setup=./test-global-setup.ts)
import { startTestDatabase } from "./helpers/test-database";
import type { TestDatabaseHandle } from "./helpers/test-database";

let dbHandle: TestDatabaseHandle;

export async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  dbHandle = await startTestDatabase({ migrations: true });
  // Expose connection URL for all test files via env variable.
  process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL = dbHandle.connectionUrl;
  console.log(`[global-setup] Test DB ready at ${dbHandle.connectionUrl}`);
}

export async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  if (dbHandle) {
    await dbHandle.stop();
    console.log("[global-teardown] Test DB stopped");
  }
  delete process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL;
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `--test-global-setup` runs the setup module in the main process, not in the test worker processes. Data passed from `globalSetup` to tests must flow through side channels (environment variables, temporary files, sockets) because there is no shared memory between the main process and worker test threads. This makes the pattern straightforward for connection URLs and flags but awkward for complex object graphs. Unlike Vitest's `globalSetup`, the Node.js version does not support returning a teardown function from `globalSetup` — teardown must be in the separately exported `globalTeardown` function. [official]

---

### Pattern 305: Node.js test runner `run({ isolation: 'process' })` with `rerunFailuresFilePath` for deterministic re-runs  [official]

Node.js 24.7+ added `rerunFailuresFilePath` to the programmatic `run()` API, which persists the set of failed test locations to a file after a run. Passing the same file path on a subsequent `run()` invocation causes the runner to re-execute only the tests that failed, skipping all passing tests. Combined with `isolation: 'process'` (the default), each re-run still gets a clean subprocess, making the combination suitable for CI workflows that need to retry flaky tests without re-running the full suite. The file is overwritten on each run, so a passing retry produces an empty state file that correctly causes the next run to execute nothing.

```typescript
import { run } from "node:test";
import { createWriteStream } from "node:fs";

const STATE_FILE = "/tmp/test-failures.json";

// First pass: run everything, persist failures.
const firstPass = run({
  files: ["./tests/**/*.test.ts"],
  isolation: "process",
  rerunFailuresFilePath: STATE_FILE,
  concurrency: 4,
});

firstPass.compose(createWriteStream("/dev/null"));

await new Promise<void>((resolve) => firstPass.on("close", resolve));

// Second pass: only re-run what failed — clean slate per test via isolation.
const retryPass = run({
  files: ["./tests/**/*.test.ts"],
  isolation: "process",
  rerunFailuresFilePath: STATE_FILE,
  concurrency: 1, // Serial for easier debugging on retry.
});

retryPass.pipe(process.stdout);
await new Promise<void>((resolve) => retryPass.on("close", resolve));
```

**Tradeoff:** `rerunFailuresFilePath` is a Node.js 24.7+ feature. On older Node.js versions the option is silently ignored and all tests run on every pass. The state file path must be writable from the test runner process and stable across runs (e.g. a consistent `/tmp/` path or a project-relative path). If the file is deleted between the first and second `run()` calls, the second pass will run the full suite again. The feature does not currently support filtering by test name within a file — it retries the entire test file that contained the failure. [official]

---

### Pattern 306: Playwright `browserContext.storageState({ indexedDB: true })` for Firebase-auth test isolation  [official]

Playwright 1.51 added an `indexedDB: true` option to `browserContext.storageState()`, enabling IndexedDB contents to be captured alongside cookies and localStorage in the saved state snapshot. Applications that use Firebase Authentication, PouchDB, or Dexie.js store authentication tokens and user data exclusively in IndexedDB — prior to this addition, `storageState` silently omitted that data and login fixtures built with those libraries were broken after serialization. With `indexedDB: true`, a one-time login setup can now capture the full client-side auth state including IndexedDB, and that complete snapshot can be restored in subsequent tests via `test.use({ storageState })`, achieving the same zero-login-per-test speed that cookie-based auth fixtures have always provided.

```typescript
// global-setup.ts
import { chromium, FullConfig } from "@playwright/test";

export default async function globalSetup(config: FullConfig): Promise<void> {
  const browser = await chromium.launch();
  const context = await browser.newContext();
  const page = await context.newPage();

  // Perform the Firebase login flow once.
  await page.goto(`${config.projects[0].use.baseURL}/login`);
  await page.fill('[name="email"]', process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!);
  await page.fill('[name="password"]', process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.click('button[type="submit"]');
  await page.waitForURL("**/dashboard");

  // Capture state INCLUDING IndexedDB (required for Firebase auth tokens).
  await context.storageState({
    path: "playwright/.auth/user.json",
    indexedDB: true,          // New in Playwright 1.51
  });

  await browser.close();
}
```

**Tradeoff:** `indexedDB: true` captures a point-in-time snapshot of the entire IndexedDB for the origin. If the IndexedDB contains large amounts of cached data (e.g. an offline-first app with megabytes of cached records), the storage state file can become very large, slowing fixture setup and commit history if the file is checked in. Scope the login page to a clean origin or clear non-auth IndexedDB stores before calling `storageState()`. Additionally, Firefox's IndexedDB serialization format is not identical to Chromium's — a state file captured in Chromium may not restore correctly in Firefox fixtures. [official]

---

### Pattern 307: Playwright `page.routeWebSocket()` for deterministic WebSocket test isolation  [official]

Playwright 1.48 introduced `page.routeWebSocket()` (and `browserContext.routeWebSocket()`) which intercepts WebSocket connections matching a URL glob and provides a handler to fully control the bidirectional communication. Before this API, isolating WebSocket-dependent tests required either running a real mock server process or patching the global `WebSocket` constructor, both of which introduce coordination complexity. With `routeWebSocket()`, the test can respond to messages without a real server, inject server-originated messages at any point in the test, and verify that specific messages were sent by the client — all within the same test process. Use `ws.connectToServer()` for partial interception when you want to pass most messages through but intercept a specific command.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("chat widget receives and displays a server push message", async ({
  page,
}) => {
  // Intercept all connections to the chat WebSocket endpoint.
  await page.routeWebSocket("wss://chat.example.com/ws", (ws) => {
    ws.onMessage((message) => {
      // Echo client messages back with a confirmation prefix.
      if (typeof message === "string") {
        ws.send(`ack:${message}`);
      }
    });

    // Simulate a server push 500 ms after the connection opens.
    setTimeout(() => {
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "push", text: "You have a new message" }));
    }, 500);
  });

  await page.goto("/chat");
  await page.waitForSelector(".chat-connected");

  // Trigger a client send.
  await page.fill(".message-input", "hello");
  await page.click(".send-button");

  // Verify the pushed message appeared in the UI.
  await expect(page.locator(".message-list")).toContainText(
    "You have a new message"
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `page.routeWebSocket()` intercepts at the network level — the `WebSocket` object in the page behaves normally from the application's perspective, so production code does not need to be changed for tests. However, the handler runs in the Node.js test process, not in the browser page's context, which means you cannot access page-scoped variables (e.g. `window.currentUser`) directly inside the handler. Pass any test-specific data to the handler via closure variables captured at route registration time. Routes registered with `page.routeWebSocket()` are not automatically cleared between tests when using a worker-scoped `page`; call `page.unrouteAll()` in the fixture teardown. [official]

---

### Pattern 308: Playwright `browserContext.clearCookies({ name, domain })` for targeted pre-test cookie hygiene  [official]

Playwright 1.43 added `name` and `domain` filter options to `browserContext.clearCookies()`, enabling surgical removal of a single cookie without wiping all cookies in the context. This is valuable in tests that need to verify the app's behaviour when a specific session cookie is absent while preserving other cookies (e.g. a consent banner state, a language preference, a CSRF token). Before the filter options, achieving this required reading all cookies, filtering them in JS, clearing everything, then re-setting the retained cookies — a fragile multi-step process that could race with background requests. The new syntax expresses the intent directly in a single call.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test.use({
  storageState: "playwright/.auth/user.json",
});

test("shows session expired banner when auth cookie is removed mid-session", async ({
  context,
  page,
}) => {
  await page.goto("/dashboard");
  await expect(page.locator("h1")).toContainText("Dashboard");

  // Remove only the auth session cookie — leave CSRF and preference cookies.
  await context.clearCookies({ name: "session_token" });

  // Trigger a navigation that requires the auth cookie.
  await page.click(".refresh-data-button");

  // App should detect the missing session and show the expiry banner.
  await expect(page.locator(".session-expired-banner")).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator(".session-expired-banner")).toContainText(
    "Your session has expired"
  );
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `name` filter performs an exact string match — it does not support glob or regex patterns. If the session cookie name is dynamic (e.g. `session_<hash>`), you must first call `context.cookies()` to discover the full name, then pass it to `clearCookies`. The `domain` filter is also an exact match and is case-sensitive in most browsers. Clearing a cookie with `clearCookies({ name: 'session' })` does not clear `session_v2` or any other cookie with a different but similar name — be precise. [official]

---

### Pattern 309: Vitest browser mode iframe isolation and mutable barrel wrapper for sealed ESM namespace  [official]

Vitest's browser mode runs each test file in a dedicated iframe sandbox, which provides DOM and global isolation but introduces a restriction: the ESM module namespace object is sealed and cannot be reconfigured using `vi.spyOn(module, 'export')` the way Node.js-mode tests can. The standard workaround is to author all modules that need to be spied on through a re-export barrel that explicitly wraps exports in a plain object, then spy on the wrapper object rather than the sealed namespace. This approach works in both Node.js mode and browser mode, making it a portable pattern. The barrel object is mutable because it is a plain JS object — only the ESM namespace `Module` object returned by `import *` is sealed.

```typescript
// src/analytics/tracker.ts — the actual implementation
export function trackEvent(name: string, payload: object): void {
  navigator.sendBeacon("/api/analytics", JSON.stringify({ name, payload }));
}

// src/analytics/index.ts — mutable wrapper barrel for browser-mode spying
import * as tracker from "./tracker";

export const analytics = {
  trackEvent: tracker.trackEvent,
};

// tests/analytics.browser.test.ts
import { test, expect, vi } from "vitest";
import { analytics } from "../src/analytics";
import { UserInteractionComponent } from "../src/components/UserInteractionComponent";

test("tracks a button click event in browser mode", async () => {
  // Spy on the mutable wrapper — works in browser mode (sealed namespace workaround).
  const trackSpy = vi
    .spyOn(analytics, "trackEvent")
    .mockImplementation(() => {});

  await UserInteractionComponent.mount({ target: document.body });
  document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>(".cta-button")!.click();

  expect(trackSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith("cta_click", expect.any(Object));
  vi.restoreAllMocks();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The barrel wrapper pattern adds an indirection layer that can mislead tree-shaking — bundlers may not be able to statically eliminate `trackEvent` if it is always imported through the wrapper object rather than the original module. During production builds, ensure the analytics barrel is only imported in test code (or that the barrel is a pure re-export with no side effects so dead-code elimination can still function). The sealed namespace restriction is a browser ESM spec requirement, not a Vitest limitation — any tool that runs tests in a real browser will face the same constraint. [official]

---

### Pattern 310: Vitest `vi.setConfig({ fakeTimers })` per-file to override global timer fake configuration  [official]

Vitest 4.x added `vi.setConfig()` as a runtime API that allows individual test files to override any configuration that would otherwise apply globally from `vitest.config.ts`. For timer isolation this means a test file that needs fake timers with a specific `toFake` list (e.g. only faking `Date` but not `setTimeout`) can call `vi.setConfig({ fakeTimers: { toFake: ['Date'] } })` at the top of the file without needing a separate Vitest project configuration entry. This is more targeted than calling `vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: [...] })` before every test because `vi.setConfig()` applies to the entire file scope, including `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks that run before the first test body.

```typescript
// payments.test.ts
import { vi, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from "vitest";

// Override fake timer config for this file only.
// We only want to fake Date (for timestamp assertions),
// not setTimeout/setInterval (which the payment retry logic uses for real delays).
vi.setConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    toFake: ["Date"],
    now: new Date("2026-01-15T12:00:00.000Z").getTime(),
  },
});

beforeAll(() => vi.useFakeTimers());
afterAll(() => vi.useRealTimers());

test("payment record is stamped with the frozen test timestamp", async () => {
  const { createPaymentRecord } = await import("../src/payment-service");
  const record = createPaymentRecord({ amount: 999, currency: "USD" });

  // Date is faked — we get the frozen time.
  expect(record.createdAt).toBe("2026-01-15T12:00:00.000Z");
});

test("retry mechanism uses real setTimeout delays (not faked)", async () => {
  // setTimeout is NOT faked — this resolves at real speed in tests.
  const { retryPayment } = await import("../src/payment-service");
  const result = await retryPayment({ paymentId: "pay_test_001" });
  expect(result.status).toBe("succeeded");
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.setConfig()` mutations persist for the life of the file unless explicitly reversed with another `vi.setConfig()` call. If the global `vitest.config.ts` already has `fakeTimers` configured and a test file calls `vi.setConfig({ fakeTimers: { toFake: ['Date'] } })`, the file-level config is a full replacement — it does not merge with the global config. Test files that need to restore the global config at teardown should cache the initial config with `vi.getConfig()` (if available) or document the mutation explicitly. [official]
