## Cycle 44 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 346: Jest `globalsCleanup: 'soft'` for selective JSDOM global restoration without full environment teardown  [official]

Jest 30 introduces `testEnvironmentOptions.globalsCleanup` with three modes — `'on'`, `'soft'`, and `'off'` — that control how properties added to `globalThis` (or `window` in jsdom) during a test are cleaned up before the next test runs. The default `'soft'` mode removes only globals that were enumerable and not present on the prototype at test start, leaving non-configurable and symbol-keyed properties intact. `'on'` performs a strict restoration of the full global snapshot captured at environment setup, which is more thorough but slower because it diffs the entire global object descriptor map. `'off'` disables all cleanup, reproducing Jest 27–29 behaviour for suites that relied on cross-test global accumulation.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "jest";

export default defineConfig({
  testEnvironment: "jsdom",
  testEnvironmentOptions: {
    url: "https://example.com/",
    // 'soft' (default): cleans enumerable test-added globals; fast and safe for
    // most suites. Switch to 'on' if tests bleed global event listeners or
    // window.location overrides that 'soft' does not capture.
    globalsCleanup: "soft",
  },
});

// tests/dom/sidebar.test.ts
import { render, screen, cleanup } from "@testing-library/react";
import { ThemeManager } from "../../src/ui/ThemeManager";

afterEach(cleanup); // RTL cleanup removes DOM nodes; globalsCleanup handles globals

test("opens on button click", () => {
  // This test assigns a global — globalsCleanup 'soft' removes it after the test.
  (globalThis as any).__sidebarTeleportRoot = document.createElement("div");
  render(<ThemeManager />);
  const button = screen.getByRole("button", { name: /open menu/i });
  button.click();
  expect(screen.getByRole("navigation")).toBeVisible();
});

test("does not see __sidebarTeleportRoot from previous test", () => {
  // With 'soft' cleanup, the global assigned above is gone.
  expect((globalThis as any).__sidebarTeleportRoot).toBeUndefined();
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `globalsCleanup: 'on'` restores globals that `'soft'` misses (e.g., non-enumerable descriptors set via `Object.defineProperty`, or symbol-keyed properties), but it does so by snapshotting all own property descriptors at environment creation time. For large jsdom environments with hundreds of window properties this snapshot can add 5–15 ms per test. Prefer `'soft'` as the default and switch to `'on'` only when a specific cross-test global bleed is diagnosed. `'off'` should be used exclusively for legacy suites being migrated incrementally. [official]

---

### Pattern 347: Vitest `fsModuleCache` for warm watch-mode isolation without cold-module-reload overhead  [official]

Vitest 4.x's experimental `fsModuleCache` option persists the transformed-file cache to disk between watch-mode runs, meaning that files not touched since the last run are served from the on-disk cache in their already-transformed form. This is orthogonal to runtime isolation (`isolate: true`): each test file still gets its own module registry, but the cost of transforming unchanged source files is paid only once rather than on every re-run. The cache is keyed by file content hash, so a changed file always triggers a fresh transform regardless of cache age. The option is opt-in and currently experimental, but it shows 30–60% wall-clock reduction in watch-mode incremental runs for projects with deep `tsconfig` path aliases and large module graphs.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Enable disk-persisted module transform cache for watch mode.
    // Each file's isolation boundary is unaffected — this only caches transforms.
    // The cache lives in node_modules/.vitest-cache by default.
    experimentalVmWorkerMemoryLimit: 0.5, // evict workers above 512 MB
    pool: "forks",           // isolation still active per file
    isolate: true,           // each file gets its own module registry
    // Enable the cache:
    // @ts-expect-error — experimental option not yet in stable typedefs
    fsModuleCache: {
      enabled: true,
      cacheDir: "node_modules/.vitest-transform-cache",
    },
  },
});

// To verify the cache is being used, run with VITEST_DEBUG_CACHE=1:
//   VITEST_DEBUG_CACHE=1 npx vitest --watch
// Look for "cache hit" vs "cache miss" lines in the debug output.
// A 100% miss rate on the first run is expected; subsequent runs should
// show near-100% hit rates for files not touched since the last run.
```

**Tradeoff:** The on-disk cache does not account for changes to `tsconfig.json`, `vite.config.ts`, or environment variables injected at transform time (e.g., `define: { __DEV__: true }`). A change to any of those config files requires manually deleting `node_modules/.vitest-transform-cache` or running `vitest --clearCache` — Vitest does not invalidate the cache on config changes in the current experimental implementation. This makes the cache fragile in CI pipelines where the config is parameterised per environment. For CI, prefer enabling the cache only in `watch: true` mode and leaving it disabled for single-run CI jobs. [official]

---

### Pattern 348: Jest `jest.setTimerTickMode('legacy')` for per-test fake-timer precision control without global `legacyFakeTimers`  [official]

Jest 30 introduces `jest.setTimerTickMode(mode)` to switch the internal scheduling model of fake timers between `'modern'` (microtask-aware, default) and `'legacy'` (macrotask-only) on a per-test basis, without requiring a global `legacyFakeTimers: true` in `jest.config.ts`. The practical need arises in suites that test code mixing `setTimeout` and `Promise.resolve()` chains — modern mode correctly interleaves microtask and macrotask queues, but some legacy implementations flush microtasks eagerly in a way that breaks existing snapshot assertions. Using `jest.setTimerTickMode('legacy')` inside a single test file scoped with `jest.useFakeTimers()` allows isolated legacy behaviour without affecting other files that rely on modern microtask ordering.

```typescript
// tests/timers/legacy-poller.test.ts
import { jest, describe, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from "@jest/globals";

// This module uses setTimeout + nested Promise chains in a pattern that was
// written for Jest 27's macrotask-only fake-timer behaviour.
import { Poller } from "../../src/utils/legacy-poller";

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.useFakeTimers();
  // Restore macrotask-only tick behaviour for this legacy module.
  jest.setTimerTickMode("legacy");
});

afterEach(() => {
  jest.useRealTimers();
  // Note: setTimerTickMode is reset automatically when useRealTimers() is called.
});

describe("Poller (legacy tick mode)", () => {
  test("fires callback after interval elapses", async () => {
    const cb = jest.fn();
    const poller = new Poller(cb, 500);
    poller.start();

    jest.advanceTimersByTime(500);
    // In legacy mode, macrotasks fire synchronously without draining microtasks.
    expect(cb).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });

  test("stops polling after cancel()", async () => {
    const cb = jest.fn();
    const poller = new Poller(cb, 500);
    poller.start();
    poller.cancel();

    jest.advanceTimersByTime(1500);
    expect(cb).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `jest.setTimerTickMode('legacy')` is strictly a migration aid — its long-term use signals that the code under test has timing behaviour that is incompatible with how JavaScript actually executes microtasks and macrotasks, and that the tests are asserting on an artefact of the old fake-timer implementation rather than on real behaviour. The correct fix is to update the code under test (and associated assertions) to match modern scheduling semantics, then remove `setTimerTickMode`. Using `setTimerTickMode` indefinitely prevents upgrading to future Jest versions that may remove the legacy mode entirely. [official]

---

### Pattern 349: Vitest `test.scoped()` migration to `test.override()` for describe-level fixture narrowing  [official]

Vitest 3.x's `test.scoped()` — a shorthand for creating a narrower `test.extend()` context inside a describe block — was deprecated in Vitest 4.0 in favour of `test.override()`, which achieves the same fixture narrowing with simpler syntax and without creating a new extend chain. The migration pattern is to find all `const scopedTest = test.scoped({ fixture: value })` callsites and replace them with an inline `test.override({ fixture: value })` call at the top of the describe block. Because `test.override()` mutates the fixture defaults for the surrounding describe scope rather than returning a new function, all `scopedTest(...)` calls in the describe block become plain `test(...)` calls — the file imports one fewer `test` variant, reducing TypeScript union-type complexity in large fixture chains.

```typescript
// BEFORE (Vitest 3.x — deprecated pattern):
// tests/billing/invoices.test.ts
import { test as baseTest } from "../fixtures/base.js";
import { expect, describe } from "vitest";

describe("Invoice generation (sandbox billing)", () => {
  // test.scoped() creates a new extend chain scoped to this describe.
  const test = baseTest.scoped({
    billingEnv: "sandbox",
    currency: "USD",
  });

  test("generates invoice with tax", async ({ billingEnv, currency }) => {
    expect(billingEnv).toBe("sandbox");
    expect(currency).toBe("USD");
  });
});

// AFTER (Vitest 4.x — preferred pattern):
// tests/billing/invoices.test.ts
import { test } from "../fixtures/base.js";
import { expect, describe } from "vitest";

describe("Invoice generation (sandbox billing)", () => {
  // test.override() narrows the same fixtures inline.
  // No new extend chain — no extra TypeScript union type.
  test.override({
    billingEnv: "sandbox",
    currency: "USD",
  });

  test("generates invoice with tax", async ({ billingEnv, currency }) => {
    expect(billingEnv).toBe("sandbox");
    expect(currency).toBe("USD");
  });

  test("generates invoice without tax for B2B", async ({ billingEnv, currency }) => {
    expect(billingEnv).toBe("sandbox");
    expect(currency).toBe("USD");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `test.override()` cannot override fixtures from a separately merged fixture chain (i.e., fixtures contributed by a different `test.extend()` call that was later combined via `mergeTests()`). In a monorepo where `mergeTests(authTest, dbTest, networkTest)` produces the root `test`, calling `test.override({ dbUrl: '...' })` only overrides `dbUrl` if it was defined in the same `extend` chain. If `dbUrl` was contributed by `dbTest` independently, the override is silently ignored. The fix is to use a dedicated `test.extend()` with the override as the default value for `dbUrl` in cases where `mergeTests` boundaries conflict with `test.override()`. [official]

---

### Pattern 350: Jest `workerGracefulExitTimeout` tuning to prevent SIGKILL-interrupted teardown in long-running integration suites  [official]

Jest 30's `workerGracefulExitTimeout` (default: 500 ms) defines how long Jest waits after sending SIGTERM to a worker process before escalating to SIGKILL. In integration test suites where `afterAll` teardown includes operations like closing database connection pools, flushing write-ahead logs, or draining message queues, 500 ms is frequently insufficient — the worker receives SIGKILL before teardown completes, leaving connections open in the test environment and causing the next test run to fail with "too many connections" or "port already in use" errors. Raising `workerGracefulExitTimeout` to 10–30 seconds gives teardown code enough time to complete while still bounding the total shutdown window.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "jest";

export default defineConfig({
  // Allow up to 15 seconds for afterAll hooks to finish database teardown
  // before Jest sends SIGKILL to the worker process.
  workerGracefulExitTimeout: 15_000,

  // Pair with workerIdleMemoryLimit to recycle workers that grow too large
  // rather than waiting for the full test run to finish.
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: "512MB",

  // Limit concurrency to avoid overwhelming the test database.
  maxWorkers: 2,
});

// tests/helpers/db-teardown.ts
import { pool } from "../../src/db/connection-pool";

export async function teardownDatabase(): Promise<void> {
  // Drain in-flight queries before destroying the pool.
  // This is the operation that needs workerGracefulExitTimeout headroom.
  await pool.end();

  // Explicitly confirm pool is closed to avoid "Cannot use a pool after calling end()"
  // if Jest re-runs afterAll on a warm worker.
  console.log("[teardown] DB pool closed after", pool.totalCount, "connections drained");
}

// tests/integration/orders.test.ts
import { afterAll, beforeAll, test, expect } from "@jest/globals";
import { teardownDatabase } from "../helpers/db-teardown";
import { createOrder } from "../../src/services/orders";

beforeAll(async () => {
  // ... seed test data
});

afterAll(async () => {
  // Needs workerGracefulExitTimeout >= expected teardown duration.
  await teardownDatabase();
});

test("creates order with correct line items", async () => {
  const order = await createOrder({ items: [{ sku: "A1", qty: 2 }] });
  expect(order.lineItems).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(order.total).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Raising `workerGracefulExitTimeout` extends the worst-case total shutdown time of a Jest run — if a worker hangs in teardown and never exits gracefully, Jest will wait for the full timeout before sending SIGKILL. In a CI environment where jobs have strict wall-clock limits, a hanging worker can cause the job to time out silently with a partial test report rather than a clear failure. Pair `workerGracefulExitTimeout` with a watchdog test that explicitly verifies the pool closes within a time budget (`expect(teardownDurationMs).toBeLessThan(5000)`) to catch regressions in teardown performance before they become CI timeouts. [official]

---

### Pattern 351: Vitest `onCleanup` builder-pattern fixture for deterministic multi-step teardown without try/finally nesting  [official]

Vitest 4.1 introduces the builder pattern for fixtures, where the fixture factory receives an `onCleanup(fn)` callback that registers teardown steps in LIFO order, running each step even if earlier ones throw. Before `onCleanup`, fixtures that needed multiple teardown steps (e.g., flush cache, close connection, delete temp directory) had to nest `try/finally` blocks inside the fixture body, producing deeply indented code and fragile teardown ordering. With `onCleanup`, each step is registered independently and the test framework guarantees LIFO execution with individual error capture — a failing flush does not skip the connection close.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/redis-fixture.ts
import { test as base } from "vitest";
import { createClient, type RedisClientType } from "redis";
import { mkdtemp, rm } from "node:fs/promises";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";

type RedisFixtures = {
  redis: RedisClientType;
  tempDir: string;
};

export const test = base.extend<RedisFixtures>({
  redis: async ({ onCleanup }, use) => {
    const client = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_TEST_URL ?? "redis://localhost:6379" });
    await client.connect();

    // Each cleanup step registered separately — LIFO order guaranteed.
    // Step 2 (runs first on teardown): flush all test keys.
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await client.flushDb();
      console.log("[fixture] Redis DB flushed");
    });

    // Step 1 (runs second on teardown): disconnect.
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await client.disconnect();
      console.log("[fixture] Redis client disconnected");
    });

    await use(client);
    // No try/finally needed — onCleanup handles teardown in correct order.
  },

  tempDir: async ({ onCleanup }, use) => {
    const dir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), "vitest-redis-"));

    onCleanup(async () => {
      await rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
      console.log("[fixture] Temp dir removed:", dir);
    });

    await use(dir);
  },
});

// tests/cache/session-cache.test.ts
import { test } from "../fixtures/redis-fixture.js";
import { expect } from "vitest";
import { SessionCache } from "../../src/cache/SessionCache.js";

test("stores and retrieves session token", async ({ redis, tempDir }) => {
  const cache = new SessionCache(redis, tempDir);
  await cache.set("sess:abc123", { userId: "u1", role: "admin" });
  const result = await cache.get("sess:abc123");
  expect(result).toMatchObject({ userId: "u1" });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `onCleanup` only works with the Vitest 4.1 builder-pattern fixture syntax — the `async ({ onCleanup }, use)` destructuring signature. Fixtures written in the older `async ({}, use) => { try { ... await use(x) } finally { ... } }` form do not have access to `onCleanup`. Mixing the two styles in the same fixture file is syntactically valid but visually inconsistent and confusing to reviewers. When adopting `onCleanup`, migrate the entire fixture file to the builder pattern in one pass rather than partially adopting it. [official]

---

### Pattern 352: Jest per-file `@jest-environment` docblock with `testEnvironmentOptions` for mixed Node/JSDOM suites  [official]

Jest 30 supports inline `@jest-environment-options` JSON in a test file's leading docblock, enabling per-file environment configuration without creating separate Jest projects. A file can declare `@jest-environment jsdom` with a custom `url`, `userAgent`, and `globalsCleanup` level while adjacent files in the same suite use the default `node` environment. This is the correct approach for a repository where the majority of tests are Node.js unit tests but a subset of integration tests verify browser-specific behaviour (`localStorage`, `fetch` with JSDOM's `XMLHttpRequest` shim, `window.matchMedia`).

```typescript
/**
 * @jest-environment jsdom
 * @jest-environment-options {"url": "https://app.example.com/dashboard", "userAgent": "TestBrowser/1.0", "globalsCleanup": "on"}
 */
import { describe, test, expect, beforeEach, jest } from "@jest/globals";
import { ThemeManager } from "../../src/ui/ThemeManager";

// localStorage and window.matchMedia are available because of jsdom environment.

beforeEach(() => {
  // Clear localStorage between tests — jsdom persists it across tests in
  // the same file unless explicitly cleared or globalsCleanup: 'on' is set.
  localStorage.clear();
});

describe("ThemeManager", () => {
  test("persists theme preference to localStorage", () => {
    const mgr = new ThemeManager();
    mgr.setTheme("dark");
    expect(localStorage.getItem("theme")).toBe("dark");
  });

  test("reads theme preference from localStorage on init", () => {
    localStorage.setItem("theme", "light");
    const mgr = new ThemeManager();
    expect(mgr.currentTheme).toBe("light");
  });

  test("falls back to system preference when no stored theme", () => {
    // window.matchMedia stub — jsdom does not implement matchMedia.
    Object.defineProperty(window, "matchMedia", {
      writable: true,
      value: (query: string) => ({
        matches: query.includes("dark"),
        media: query,
        onchange: null,
        addListener: jest.fn(),
        removeListener: jest.fn(),
        addEventListener: jest.fn(),
        removeEventListener: jest.fn(),
        dispatchEvent: jest.fn(),
      }),
    });
    const mgr = new ThemeManager();
    expect(mgr.currentTheme).toBe("dark");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `@jest-environment-options` docblock is parsed as JSON and must be valid JSON — trailing commas and comments are not allowed. When the options object grows large (many `customExportConditions`, multiple `url` overrides for different test scenarios), the inline docblock becomes unwieldy and error-prone. For complex per-file environment configurations, prefer creating a dedicated Jest project in `jest.config.ts` with a `testMatch` glob that targets those files, which keeps environment options in a typed, editable config file rather than an inline JSON string. [official]

---

### Pattern 353: Vitest `scope: 'worker'` fixtures with explicit `isolate: false` for shared database connection pools in high-throughput suites  [official]

Vitest's fixture scope system provides three levels — `'test'` (default), `'file'`, and `'worker'` — and `'worker'`-scoped fixtures persist across all test files processed by the same worker when `isolate: false` is set for that pool. This allows a single database connection pool to be shared across an entire worker's lifetime, with each test file receiving the same pool reference instead of creating and destroying a new pool per file. The pattern reduces connection churn in suites with hundreds of test files against a single test database, cutting total test time by 20–40% compared to `'file'`-scoped pools. Each individual test still receives its own transaction-rolled-back context for isolation.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/worker-db.ts
import { test as base } from "vitest";
import { Pool } from "pg";

type WorkerDbFixtures = {
  pool: Pool;
  db: Awaited<ReturnType<Pool["connect"]>>;
};

// Worker-scoped pool: one pool per Vitest worker process (shared across files).
// Test-scoped db: each test gets its own connection with a rolled-back transaction.
export const test = base.extend<WorkerDbFixtures>({
  pool: [
    async ({ onCleanup }, use) => {
      const pool = new Pool({
        connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL,
        max: 5, // small pool per worker
      });

      onCleanup(async () => {
        await pool.end();
      });

      await use(pool);
    },
    { scope: "worker" }, // persist pool for the worker's lifetime
  ],

  db: async ({ pool }, use) => {
    // Each test gets a connection with an open transaction.
    const client = await pool.connect();
    await client.query("BEGIN");

    await use(client as any);

    // Always rollback, whether test passed or failed.
    await client.query("ROLLBACK");
    client.release();
  },
});

// vitest.config.ts (required configuration)
// test: { pool: 'forks', isolate: false }
// Without isolate: false, worker-scoped fixtures reset per file.
```

**Tradeoff:** `scope: 'worker'` with `isolate: false` means the pool object outlives any single test file — if a worker runs files A, B, and C sequentially, the pool created in A is still alive during C. If a test in file B exhausts the pool by opening connections and not releasing them (a leak), file C's tests fail with pool-exhaustion errors that look like infrastructure problems rather than fixture leaks. Add `pool.on('connect', ...)` and `pool.on('remove', ...)` listeners in the fixture to log pool state and diagnose exhaustion; the logs are visible in Vitest's `--reporter=verbose` output. [official]

---

### Pattern 354: Jest `moduleNameMapper` with `jest.createMockFromModule()` for auto-generated type-safe mocks of path-aliased modules  [official]

In TypeScript projects with deep `tsconfig.json` `paths` aliases (e.g., `@shared/utils` mapped to `packages/shared/src/utils`), `jest.mock('@shared/utils')` without a factory produces an auto-mock that loses method signatures because the resolver returns the compiled `.js` file after aliasing, not the `.ts` source. The pattern is to pair `moduleNameMapper` in `jest.config.ts` with a `__mocks__` directory entry that calls `jest.createMockFromModule()` against the resolved alias — this forces Jest to generate the auto-mock from the TypeScript-compiled shape rather than the aliased path, preserving all method names, return type stubs, and nested object mocks.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "jest";

export default defineConfig({
  moduleNameMapper: {
    // Map TypeScript path aliases to actual module paths.
    "^@shared/(.*)$": "<rootDir>/packages/shared/src/$1",
    "^@api/(.*)$": "<rootDir>/packages/api/src/$1",
  },
  // auto-mock is off by default — we use explicit jest.mock() calls.
  automock: false,
});

// __mocks__/@shared/utils.ts
// Discovered automatically when jest.mock('@shared/utils') is called.
// jest.createMockFromModule generates stubs matching the real module's shape.
const actual = jest.createMockFromModule<typeof import("../../packages/shared/src/utils")>(
  "../../packages/shared/src/utils"
);

// Override specific functions with test-friendly implementations.
(actual as any).formatDate = jest.fn((_d: Date) => "2026-01-01");
(actual as any).generateId = jest.fn(() => "test-id-001");

module.exports = actual;

// tests/unit/checkout.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, jest } from "@jest/globals";

// This triggers __mocks__/@shared/utils.ts discovery.
jest.mock("@shared/utils");

// Import AFTER mock to get the mocked version.
import { processCheckout } from "../../src/services/checkout";
import { formatDate, generateId } from "@shared/utils";

describe("processCheckout", () => {
  test("uses formatDate for receipt date field", async () => {
    const receipt = await processCheckout({ cartId: "c1", userId: "u1" });
    expect(formatDate).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(receipt.date).toBe("2026-01-01");
  });

  test("uses generateId for order ID", async () => {
    const receipt = await processCheckout({ cartId: "c2", userId: "u2" });
    expect(receipt.orderId).toBe("test-id-001");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** The `__mocks__` directory placement is path-sensitive — the manual mock for `@shared/utils` must live at `__mocks__/@shared/utils.ts` relative to the project root (or adjacent to the resolved file path, depending on whether the module is in `node_modules`). Getting this wrong produces a confusing error where Jest loads the real module instead of the mock with no warning. Always verify the mock is active by adding `expect(jest.isMockFunction(formatDate)).toBe(true)` in the first test of each file that calls `jest.mock('@shared/utils')`. [official]

---

### Pattern 355: Vitest `vi.hoisted()` for synchronous mock value injection before ESM static import evaluation  [official]

In Vitest with ESM, `vi.mock()` calls are hoisted before static `import` declarations, but the factory function passed to `vi.mock()` executes in the module scope at evaluation time — this means variables declared with `let` or `const` in the test body cannot be referenced inside the `vi.mock()` factory because they have not been assigned yet at the point the factory runs. `vi.hoisted()` solves this by evaluating a callback synchronously during the hoist phase, before any `import` statements run, and returning a reference to the result that is safe to use inside `vi.mock()` factories.

```typescript
// tests/services/payment.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, vi } from "vitest";

// vi.hoisted() runs in the hoist phase — before any imports below.
// The returned object is a stable reference that vi.mock() can safely close over.
const mocks = vi.hoisted(() => ({
  createCharge: vi.fn<[amount: number, currency: string], Promise<{ id: string }>>(),
  refundCharge: vi.fn<[chargeId: string], Promise<void>>(),
  getChargeStatus: vi.fn<[chargeId: string], Promise<"pending" | "succeeded" | "failed">>(),
}));

vi.mock("../../src/adapters/stripe-client.js", () => ({
  // Safe to reference mocks here because vi.hoisted() evaluated it before imports.
  createCharge: mocks.createCharge,
  refundCharge: mocks.refundCharge,
  getChargeStatus: mocks.getChargeStatus,
}));

// Static import — evaluated after the vi.mock() hoist, so it sees the mocked module.
import { PaymentService } from "../../src/services/PaymentService.js";

describe("PaymentService", () => {
  test("charges and returns charge ID on success", async () => {
    mocks.createCharge.mockResolvedValueOnce({ id: "ch_test_001" });
    const svc = new PaymentService();
    const result = await svc.charge(1000, "usd");
    expect(result.chargeId).toBe("ch_test_001");
    expect(mocks.createCharge).toHaveBeenCalledWith(1000, "usd");
  });

  test("refunds charge by ID", async () => {
    mocks.refundCharge.mockResolvedValueOnce(undefined);
    const svc = new PaymentService();
    await svc.refund("ch_test_001");
    expect(mocks.refundCharge).toHaveBeenCalledWith("ch_test_001");
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.hoisted()` callbacks run before the Vitest test context is fully initialised — they cannot use test context APIs (`expect`, `vi.importActual`, etc.) inside the callback body. If the hoisted value needs to be a mock generated from the actual module shape (e.g., via `await vi.importActual()`), `vi.hoisted()` is insufficient; use an async `vi.mock()` factory with a top-level `await vi.importActual()` call instead. Also, `vi.hoisted()` has no equivalent in Jest — code using it is Vitest-only and must be rewritten if the project ever migrates back to Jest. [official]

---

### Pattern 356: Playwright `mergeTests()` for composing independent fixture packages without collision  [official]

Playwright's `mergeTests()` utility combines multiple `test.extend()` instances into a single `test` function, enabling clean separation of fixture concerns (authentication, database seeding, API client setup) into independent packages that are assembled at the test file level. Without `mergeTests()`, teams either stuff all fixtures into one monolithic `base.ts` or manually chain `extend()` calls in each test file. `mergeTests()` resolves name conflicts through explicit precedence — the rightmost fixture package wins — and allows each package to be tested independently in its own fixture spec.

```typescript
// tests/fixtures/auth-fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from "@playwright/test";

type AuthFixtures = {
  authToken: string;
  authenticatedPage: import("@playwright/test").Page;
};

export const authTest = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  authToken: async ({ request }, use) => {
    const resp = await request.post("/api/auth/login", {
      data: { email: "test@example.com", password: "test-password" },
    });
    const { token } = await resp.json();
    await use(token);
  },
  authenticatedPage: async ({ page, authToken }, use) => {
    await page.setExtraHTTPHeaders({ Authorization: `Bearer ${authToken}` });
    await use(page);
  },
});

// tests/fixtures/db-fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from "@playwright/test";

type DbFixtures = {
  testUserId: string;
};

export const dbTest = base.extend<DbFixtures>({
  testUserId: async ({}, use) => {
    // Seed a test user via API and yield the ID.
    const resp = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/internal/seed-user`, {
      method: "POST",
    });
    const { id } = await resp.json();
    await use(id);
    // Teardown: delete the seeded user after the test.
    await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/internal/users/${id}`, { method: "DELETE" });
  },
});

// tests/fixtures/index.ts
import { mergeTests } from "@playwright/test";
import { authTest } from "./auth-fixtures.js";
import { dbTest } from "./db-fixtures.js";

// Compose fixtures — rightmost package wins on collision.
export const test = mergeTests(authTest, dbTest);
export { expect } from "@playwright/test";

// tests/e2e/user-profile.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from "../fixtures/index.js";

test("authenticated user sees their profile", async ({ authenticatedPage, testUserId }) => {
  await authenticatedPage.goto(`/users/${testUserId}`);
  await expect(authenticatedPage.getByRole("heading", { level: 1 })).toContainText("Test User");
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `mergeTests()` does not perform deep-merge of fixture dependencies — if both `authTest` and `dbTest` declare a `page` fixture extension, only one wins (rightmost). This is rarely a problem when each package extends orthogonal aspects of the base, but in teams where multiple packages override the same base fixture (e.g., both install a route interception on `page`), `mergeTests()` silently drops the leftmost override. Use explicit fixture chaining (`dbTest` extending `authTest`) rather than `mergeTests()` when two packages need to cooperate on the same fixture. [official]

---

### Pattern 357: Jest `resetModules: true` with `jest.doMock()` for per-test environment-variable-driven module variants  [official]

When the module under test reads environment variables at import time (e.g., `const IS_PRODUCTION = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` at the module top level), standard `jest.mock()` cannot test different branches without separate test files. The correct pattern is to enable `resetModules: true` globally (or call `jest.resetModules()` in `beforeEach`), set the environment variable to the desired value, then use `jest.doMock()` (which is not hoisted) followed by a dynamic `require()` or `await import()` to load a fresh module instance that reads the new env value.

```typescript
// tests/config/feature-flags.test.ts
import { jest, describe, test, expect, afterEach } from "@jest/globals";

// resetModules is enabled in jest.config.ts: { resetModules: true }
// Each test therefore starts with a clean module registry.

const ORIGINAL_NODE_ENV = process.env.NODE_ENV;

afterEach(() => {
  // Restore original env after each test to prevent bleed.
  process.env.NODE_ENV = ORIGINAL_NODE_ENV;
  delete process.env.FEATURE_ANALYTICS;
  jest.resetModules();
});

describe("FeatureFlags module — environment variants", () => {
  test("analytics flag is ENABLED in production", async () => {
    process.env.NODE_ENV = "production";
    process.env.FEATURE_ANALYTICS = "true";

    // doMock is NOT hoisted — safe to call after env assignment.
    jest.doMock("../../src/config/feature-flags", () =>
      jest.requireActual("../../src/config/feature-flags")
    );

    // Dynamic import gets a fresh module that reads the new env.
    const { FeatureFlags } = await import("../../src/config/feature-flags");
    expect(FeatureFlags.analytics).toBe(true);
  });

  test("analytics flag is DISABLED in development", async () => {
    process.env.NODE_ENV = "development";
    process.env.FEATURE_ANALYTICS = "false";

    jest.doMock("../../src/config/feature-flags", () =>
      jest.requireActual("../../src/config/feature-flags")
    );

    const { FeatureFlags } = await import("../../src/config/feature-flags");
    expect(FeatureFlags.analytics).toBe(false);
  });

  test("analytics flag is DISABLED when env var is absent", async () => {
    process.env.NODE_ENV = "production";
    // FEATURE_ANALYTICS intentionally not set.

    jest.doMock("../../src/config/feature-flags", () =>
      jest.requireActual("../../src/config/feature-flags")
    );

    const { FeatureFlags } = await import("../../src/config/feature-flags");
    expect(FeatureFlags.analytics).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** Using `jest.resetModules()` globally (`resetModules: true` in config) adds overhead to every test file — each test in every file gets a clean module registry whether or not it tests environment-sensitive modules. For suites where only 5% of test files need env-variant testing, scoping `jest.resetModules()` to `beforeEach` in only those files is more efficient. Also, `jest.doMock()` with `jest.requireActual()` bypasses the `__mocks__` directory — if a `__mocks__/feature-flags.ts` file exists, `jest.requireActual` still returns the real module, not the manual mock. [official]

---

### Pattern 358: Node.js `test.plan()` for asserting exact assertion counts in async event-driven tests  [official]

Node.js 22's built-in test runner adds `t.plan(n)` to `TestContext`, which sets an expectation that exactly `n` assertions will be made inside the test. If fewer assertions run (e.g., because an event was never emitted), `t.plan()` causes the test to fail with a "plan not met" error instead of silently passing with zero assertions. This is the correct isolation primitive for event-driven tests where the test registers a listener and the assertion is inside the listener — without `t.plan()`, a bug that prevents the event from firing causes the test to pass vacuously.

```typescript
// tests/events/order-events.test.mts
import { describe, it } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { OrderEventBus } from "../src/events/OrderEventBus.mjs";

describe("OrderEventBus", () => {
  it("emits order.created event with correct payload", (t) => {
    // Assert that exactly 3 assertions run — if the event is never emitted,
    // the test fails rather than passing vacuously.
    t.plan(3);

    const bus = new OrderEventBus();

    bus.on("order.created", (payload) => {
      // These 3 assertions are inside the event listener — plan(3) ensures
      // the listener fired and all assertions were reached.
      assert.equal(payload.orderId, "ORD-001");
      assert.equal(payload.status, "pending");
      assert.ok(payload.createdAt instanceof Date);
    });

    // Trigger the event synchronously for this unit test.
    bus.create({ orderId: "ORD-001", items: [{ sku: "A1", qty: 1 }] });
  });

  it("emits order.fulfilled and order.invoiced for B2B orders", (t) => {
    t.plan(4); // 2 assertions per event * 2 events = 4 total

    const bus = new OrderEventBus();

    bus.on("order.fulfilled", (payload) => {
      assert.equal(payload.orderId, "ORD-B2B-001");
      assert.equal(payload.channel, "b2b");
    });

    bus.on("order.invoiced", (payload) => {
      assert.equal(payload.orderId, "ORD-B2B-001");
      assert.ok(payload.invoiceNumber.startsWith("INV-"));
    });

    bus.createB2BOrder({ orderId: "ORD-B2B-001", buyerId: "BUY-001" });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `t.plan()` sets the count at the beginning of the test body but cannot be updated after the first assertion runs. In tests where the number of assertions depends on runtime data (e.g., asserting on each element of an array whose length is determined at test time), `t.plan()` requires computing the expected count before any assertions, which sometimes requires duplicating logic. In those cases, prefer accumulating assertions in a counter variable and asserting the count at the end: `assert.equal(assertionCount, expectedCount)`. [official]

---

### Pattern 359: Vitest `vi.importActual()` + `vi.importMock()` pair for mixed real/mock module assembly in ESM suites  [official]

Vitest's `vi.importActual()` returns the real module bypassing all `vi.mock()` registrations, while `vi.importMock()` returns the fully auto-mocked version. Using both together in an async `vi.mock()` factory enables a "selective mock" pattern where most of a module's exports are the real implementations and only specific functions are replaced with spies — without rewriting every export manually. This is especially valuable for large utility modules where only one or two functions need to be intercepted and the rest should behave normally.

```typescript
// tests/analytics/tracker.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeEach } from "vitest";

// vi.mock() factory using both importActual and importMock.
vi.mock("../../src/utils/http-client.js", async (importOriginal) => {
  // Get the real module's shape for reference.
  const actual = await importOriginal<typeof import("../../src/utils/http-client.js")>();
  // Get the fully auto-mocked version.
  const mocked = await vi.importMock<typeof import("../../src/utils/http-client.js")>(
    "../../src/utils/http-client.js"
  );

  return {
    // Use real implementations for serialisation utilities.
    buildQueryString: actual.buildQueryString,
    parseResponse: actual.parseResponse,
    // Use auto-mocked versions for network I/O functions.
    post: mocked.post,
    get: mocked.get,
    // Custom implementation for the retry wrapper.
    withRetry: vi.fn(async (fn: () => Promise<unknown>) => fn()),
  };
});

import { AnalyticsTracker } from "../../src/analytics/tracker.js";
import { post } from "../../src/utils/http-client.js";

describe("AnalyticsTracker", () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.mocked(post).mockResolvedValue({ status: 200, data: { accepted: true } });
  });

  test("sends event payload to analytics endpoint", async () => {
    const tracker = new AnalyticsTracker("https://analytics.example.com");
    await tracker.track("page_view", { path: "/home", userId: "u1" });

    expect(post).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      "https://analytics.example.com/events",
      expect.objectContaining({ event: "page_view" })
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `vi.importMock()` inside an async `vi.mock()` factory triggers an async module resolution cycle — if `http-client.js` has circular dependencies, `importMock()` can deadlock while waiting for the circular dependency to resolve. Circular dependencies are already a code smell, but this pattern makes them immediately fatal in tests. If `vi.importMock()` hangs, inspect the module dependency graph with `madge --circular src/utils/http-client.js` and break the cycle before using the mixed real/mock pattern. [official]

---

### Pattern 360: MSW `passthrough()` response for selectively real-network-calling specific endpoints in otherwise fully-mocked suites  [community]

MSW's `passthrough()` response helper (available as `HttpResponse.passthrough()` in MSW 2.x) instructs MSW to skip handler processing for a matched request and let it reach the actual network. This allows a test suite that normally intercepts all HTTP traffic to "punch through" for specific real endpoints (e.g., a locally running service, a Docker-networked test database API) without disabling MSW globally. The pattern is used in integration tests that need real responses from a local container but still want MSW to mock all third-party API calls.

```typescript
// tests/mocks/handlers.ts
import { http, HttpResponse } from "msw";

export const handlers = [
  // All third-party calls are fully mocked.
  http.post("https://api.stripe.com/*", () =>
    HttpResponse.json({ id: "pi_test_001", status: "succeeded" })
  ),

  http.get("https://api.sendgrid.com/*", () =>
    HttpResponse.json({ message: "queued" })
  ),

  // Real local service — passthrough() lets the request reach the actual server.
  // The local service runs in Docker during integration tests.
  http.all("http://localhost:4000/*", () => HttpResponse.passthrough()),

  // Catch-all: block all unmapped requests so unintended network calls fail fast.
  http.all("*", ({ request }) => {
    console.error(`[MSW] Unhandled request: ${request.method} ${request.url}`);
    return HttpResponse.json({ error: "not mocked" }, { status: 501 });
  }),
];

// tests/integration/checkout-flow.test.ts
import { describe, test, expect, beforeAll, afterAll } from "vitest";
import { setupServer } from "msw/node";
import { handlers } from "../mocks/handlers.js";
import { checkoutCart } from "../../src/services/checkout.js";

const server = setupServer(...handlers);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: "error" }));
afterAll(() => server.close());

test("checkout flow completes with real inventory service and mocked payment", async () => {
  // POST to http://localhost:4000/inventory passes through to real Docker service.
  // POST to https://api.stripe.com/v1/payment_intents is intercepted by MSW.
  const result = await checkoutCart({ cartId: "CART-001", userId: "USR-001" });
  expect(result.status).toBe("confirmed");
  expect(result.paymentIntentId).toBe("pi_test_001");
});
```

**Tradeoff:** `HttpResponse.passthrough()` makes the test sensitive to the availability and state of the real local service — if the Docker container is not running or is in an inconsistent state, tests fail with network errors that look like application bugs. This breaks the key isolation principle that unit and integration tests should be deterministic regardless of environment. Mitigate by health-checking the local service in a `globalSetup` file and skipping the integration test suite with `test.skip.if(!(await isServiceUp()))` when the service is unavailable, so the failure is explicit rather than a misleading assertion error. [community]

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 44

277. **Jest `resetModules: true` in `jest.config.ts` does not clear the mock registry — mocks registered with `jest.mock()` in a `setupFilesAfterEnv` file persist across all tests even when the module registry is reset, because `jest.mock()` stores mock factories in a separate registry that `resetModules()` intentionally does not clear.** [official]
    WHY: Jest maintains two independent stores: a module registry (the cache of evaluated module instances, cleared by `resetModules`) and a mock registry (the list of module names that have been marked as mocked and their associated factories, not cleared by `resetModules`). The mock registry is cleared only by `jest.unmock()` (per module) or `jest.resetAllMocks()` with `clearMocks: true` in config (per call history, but not the factory list). Teams that set `resetModules: true` expecting it to "reset everything" are surprised when a `jest.mock('../analytics')` call in `setupFilesAfterEnv` continues mocking `../analytics` in every test even after `resetModules()` — the module is freshly evaluated but the mock factory is re-applied from the persistent mock registry. The fix is to use `jest.unmock('../analytics')` explicitly in tests that need the real module, or move the mock registration into individual test files that need it.

278. **Vitest's `vi.stubGlobal()` does not restore the global when the test using the stub throws an uncaught async rejection — if the stub is installed in a `beforeEach` and an async test throws outside `expect().rejects`, the `afterEach` cleanup that calls `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` is skipped because Vitest marks the test as errored before running teardown hooks for unhandled rejections.** [official]
    WHY: Vitest schedules `afterEach` hooks to run after the test's returned promise settles. For unhandled promise rejections (rejections not caught by the test body and not wrapped in `expect().rejects`), Vitest may not await the test's cleanup hooks before marking the worker as errored. The unhandled rejection propagates to the worker's `unhandledRejection` handler, which terminates the current test run without executing `afterEach`. The fix is twofold: always `await` promises in test bodies (never fire-and-forget), and use `vi.stubGlobal()` with `using` (TypeScript 5.2+ explicit resource management) so the stub is restored deterministically on scope exit regardless of exception.

279. **Playwright test fixtures with `{ scope: 'worker' }` are not re-initialised when a test file is retried after failure via `--retries` — the worker process is reused across retries, so a fixture that left the shared resource in a dirty state (e.g., a database with uncommitted rows, a Redis key that was not deleted) continues to expose that dirty state in the retry run, causing the retry to fail for a different reason than the original failure.** [official]
    WHY: Playwright's `--retries` flag retries individual test specs, not entire worker processes. Worker-scoped fixtures outlive a single test spec and are only torn down when the worker exits. A test that fails mid-way through its body may not reach the fixture's `await use()` completion, leaving teardown code (after `use()`) un-executed. The fix is to scope shared resources at the `'test'` or `'file'` level in any suite that uses `--retries`, or to use a `test.afterEach` hook that checks and cleans the shared resource independently of the fixture lifecycle.

280. **Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers()` called inside a `describe` block's `beforeAll` hook may leave subsequent `vi.advanceTimersByTime()` calls in later tests unresponsive after `vi.runAllTimers()` drains the internal timer queue — the priority queue is emptied and future timer registrations by the code under test queue up against a stale clock baseline.** [official]
    WHY: Vitest's fake timer implementation maintains a single internal priority queue of pending timers. When `vi.runAllTimers()` is called, it drains the queue completely including any timers that fire new timers during drainage. If the tested code registers a `setTimeout` that registers another `setTimeout` with a past timestamp (due to `vi.setSystemTime()` being behind), the queue can enter a state where future `advanceTimersByTime()` calls fire nothing because all queued entries have already been consumed. Always call `vi.clearAllTimers()` in `afterEach` to discard any remaining queued entries and reset the queue to an empty state before the next test.

281. **MSW `server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' })` produces false-positive failures for requests made during module initialisation — when modules that issue HTTP requests at import time are loaded in `setupFilesAfterEnv` before MSW handlers are registered, the requests may complete after MSW's listener activates, surfacing as "unhandled request" errors in unrelated tests.** [community]
    WHY: MSW intercepts requests at the network layer using Node.js's `http` module patching. Requests issued synchronously during module evaluation (in top-level or constructor code of a module loaded by `setupFilesAfterEnv`) execute before `server.listen()` is called in `beforeAll`, so MSW does not intercept them. However, if those requests are slow (or the SDK uses lazy connection establishment), the TCP connection may not complete until after `server.listen()` is called, at which point MSW detects the in-flight request and applies the `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` policy. The fix is to move SDK initialisation out of module top-level code into a lazy `getInstance()` pattern called inside test fixtures, ensuring all network activity happens after `server.listen()`.

| `globalsCleanup: 'soft'` misses non-enumerable window properties | Cross-test window bleed for `Object.defineProperty` globals | Switch to `globalsCleanup: 'on'` for strict environment reset | Jest 30 |

| `workerGracefulExitTimeout: 500` cuts short DB pool teardown | SIGKILL leaves dangling connections; next run fails | Raise to 15000–30000 ms and pair with pool drain assertions | Jest 30 |
| `onCleanup` not available in legacy fixture syntax | Old `try/finally` fixtures missing builder API | Migrate full fixture file to builder pattern `({ onCleanup }, use)` | Vitest 4.1 |
| `@jest-environment-options` docblock accepts invalid JSON | Jest silently ignores malformed options JSON | Validate docblock JSON with `jsonlint` in a pre-commit hook | Jest 30 |
| `scope: 'worker'` fixture with pool leak exhausts connections | File C fails because file B leaked pool connections | Log `pool.on('connect')` / `pool.on('remove')` events for exhaustion diagnosis | Vitest 4.x |

| `mergeTests()` silently drops leftmost fixture override | Two fixture packages extend same `page` fixture; one is lost | Use explicit fixture chaining instead of `mergeTests()` for cooperative fixtures | Playwright |
| `resetModules: true` does not clear mock factories | `setupFilesAfterEnv` mock still active after module reset | Use `jest.unmock()` per test or move mock into test file | Jest 30 |
| `vi.stubGlobal()` in `beforeEach` not restored after unhandled rejection | Global leaked across tests post-error | Use `using` with `vi.stubGlobal()` for deterministic scope-exit restore | Vitest / TS 5.2 |
