| `fakeTimers.enableGlobally` in jsdom breaks `await` | Promises never resolve; test hangs | Add `'queueMicrotask'` to `doNotFake` when using jsdom + globalFakeTimers | Jest |

| `context.mock.timers.setTime()` doesn't fire past timers | Timer callback never runs; test hangs | Use `tick(delta)` to fire timers; use `setTime()` only for repositioning `Date.now()` | Node 22 |
| `snapshot.setResolveSnapshotPath()` called twice | Second resolver silently overwrites first | Call resolver exactly once in the earliest-executing global setup file | Node 22 |
| `test.step()` errors point into fixture internals | Hard to map failure to test line in reporter | Add `{ box: true }` to infrastructure steps to redirect error to call site | Playwright |
| Worker-scoped fixture dirty state on retry | Retry fails for different reason than original | Use ROLLBACK/DELETE at start of fixture `use()` block, or switch to test-scoped fixture | Playwright |
| `sequence.shuffle` doesn't detect between-describe leakage | Describe-level singleton bleed survives shuffling | Split each describe into its own file for inter-describe isolation testing | Vitest |
| `runAll()` with async timer callbacks misses side effects | Assertions pass before async body completes | `await Promise.resolve()` after `runAll()` to flush microtask queue | Node 22 |
| `http.all('*')` placed first in handler array | All feature handlers unreachable; silent 200s | Always place catch-all handler last in `setupServer()` array | MSW 2.x |
| `resetMocks: true` doesn't clear inline `jest.fn(() => value)` | Mock still returns value after reset | Use `jest.fn()` with no argument; add implementation via `mockReturnValue()` | Jest |
| `test.fail()` marks entire test; misses post-error assertions | Only first assertion tracked as known failure | Scope known-broken assertion in `test.step()` with TODO comment | Playwright |
| `moduleNameMapper` CSS proxy echoes property name not hash | Snapshot tests diverge between Jest and browser | Assert on `data-testid`/ARIA roles not CSS class names in snapshot tests | Jest |
| Benchmarks with `vmThreads` always get fresh VM context | Cold-start overhead inflates warm-path benchmark results | Use `pool: 'threads'` with `isolate: false` + `singleThread: true` for benchmarks | Vitest |

## Cycle 47 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 391 — Node.js `run({ isolation: 'none' })` for in-process test execution when child-process overhead dominates suite time [official]

Node.js 22.8.0 introduced an explicit `isolation` option on the programmatic `run()` API, letting you opt all test files into the current process rather than spawning a child per file. When a suite contains hundreds of micro-benchmark files or fast unit files that each take under 10 ms to execute, the per-process spawn cost (typically 80–200 ms on Node 22) can dwarf the actual test time, producing misleadingly slow CI runs. Setting `isolation: 'none'` eliminates that overhead but requires that every test file is genuinely side-effect-free — no module-level singletons, no `process.env` mutations without cleanup, and no `globalThis` writes. Use this pattern only after confirming with `--test-concurrency=1` + `isolation: 'none'` that all files pass in sequence; if any order-dependent failures appear, revert to `isolation: 'process'`.

```typescript
// run-fast-tests.mts
import { run } from 'node:test';
import { glob } from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';

// Collect all unit test files — fast micro-tests only
const files: string[] = [];
for await (const f of glob('src/**/*.unit.test.ts')) {
  files.push(path.resolve(f));
}

// isolation: 'none' skips child-process spawn per file.
// env option is intentionally absent — incompatible with isolation: 'none'.
const stream = run({
  files,
  isolation: 'none',
  concurrency: 1,        // serial within-process to surface order bugs first
});

stream.on('test:fail', (data) => {
  console.error(`FAIL: ${data.name} — ${data.details?.error?.message}`);
});

await new Promise<void>((resolve) => stream.on('close', resolve));
```

**Tradeoff.** `isolation: 'none'` cannot be combined with the `env` option (passing custom environment variables per run) — Node throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` at startup. Additionally, any test that mutates `process.env` without restoring it will silently pollute subsequent tests that share the same process, which is undetectable unless you run with `isolation: 'none'` + `concurrency: 1` and cross-check against the `isolation: 'process'` results in CI.

---

### Pattern 392 — Node.js `t.mock.module()` for per-test module isolation with automatic cache restoration [official]

The Node.js built-in test runner's `t.mock.module(specifier, options)` method (added in Node 22) registers a replacement for a CommonJS or ESM module within the current test's module registry and automatically calls `ctx.restore()` when the test finishes, ensuring the real module is back in the cache before the next test runs. This is the correct alternative to Jest's `jest.mock()` in the native runner: unlike the global `mock.module()` (which must be cleaned up manually with `mock.restore()`), context-bound `t.mock.module()` participates in the test's lifecycle and cannot leak across tests. The specifier must be the same string that the system-under-test uses at its own `import` site — relative paths are resolved from the test file's location, not from the module being mocked.

```typescript
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('fetchUser returns shaped user object from mocked HTTP module', async (t) => {
  // Replace the built-in https module for this test only.
  // t.mock.module() restores the original after the test, automatically.
  t.mock.module('node:https', {
    namedExports: {
      get: (_url: string, cb: (res: unknown) => void) => {
        const res = {
          on(event: string, handler: (chunk?: Buffer) => void) {
            if (event === 'data') handler(Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' })));
            if (event === 'end') handler();
          },
        };
        cb(res);
        return { on: () => {} };
      },
    },
  });

  // Import AFTER mocking so the module resolver sees the mock
  const { fetchUser } = await import('../src/fetchUser.js');
  const user = await fetchUser(1);

  assert.deepEqual(user, { id: 1, name: 'Alice' });
  // 'node:https' is automatically restored here — no afterEach needed
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `t.mock.module()` works on the module cache that was in effect when the test started. If the system-under-test was already `import`-ed at the top of the test file (outside the `test()` call), Node has already resolved and cached it against the real module — the mock is registered too late. Always `await import()` the system-under-test _inside_ the `test()` callback, after `t.mock.module()`, to guarantee the mock is in place when the target module resolves its own imports.

---

### Pattern 393 — Vitest `vi.mock()` hoisting awareness: placing mock factory above imports using `vi.hoisted()` to share variables [official]

Vitest transforms test files so that every `vi.mock()` call is hoisted to the top of the module, before any `import` statement, to ensure that when the module-under-test is loaded its dependencies are already replaced. This hoisting means that ordinary `const` variables declared before `vi.mock()` in the source text are not yet initialised when the factory executes — accessing them produces `undefined`, which silently makes your mock return `undefined` for every call. The `vi.hoisted()` helper solves this by running its callback during the hoisting phase itself, returning a reference that is safe to share between the hoisted factory and the rest of the test body. Wrap any variable the mock factory needs — spy references, return-value holders, configuration objects — inside `vi.hoisted()`.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';

// vi.hoisted() runs at hoist-time, before all imports.
// The returned object is safe to reference inside vi.mock() factories.
const mocks = vi.hoisted(() => ({
  sendEmail: vi.fn<[string, string], Promise<void>>(),
}));

vi.mock('../src/emailService.js', () => ({
  sendEmail: mocks.sendEmail,
}));

// Import under test AFTER vi.mock() — Vitest hoisting guarantees this order.
import { registerUser } from '../src/userService.js';

describe('userService.registerUser', () => {
  it('sends a welcome email after successful registration', async () => {
    mocks.sendEmail.mockResolvedValueOnce(undefined);

    await registerUser({ email: 'alice@example.com', name: 'Alice' });

    expect(mocks.sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(mocks.sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      'alice@example.com',
      expect.stringContaining('Welcome'),
    );
  });

  it('does not send email when registration fails', async () => {
    // mocks.sendEmail is a fresh vi.fn() — no mockReturnValue set
    await expect(registerUser({ email: '', name: '' })).rejects.toThrow();
    expect(mocks.sendEmail).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.hoisted()` produces a shared mutable object that is re-used across every test in the file. If one test calls `mocks.sendEmail.mockImplementation(...)` without a `Once` variant, that implementation persists into subsequent tests even with `clearMocks: true` (which only clears call records, not implementation). Always pair `vi.hoisted()` with `restoreMocks: true` in `vitest.config.ts` or call `vi.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach` to wipe implementations between tests.

---

### Pattern 394 — Vitest browser mode `{ spy: true }` in `vi.mock()` for observable-but-unmodified module exports in a sealed namespace [official]

In Vitest's browser mode the module namespace object returned by `import *` is a sealed ES Module namespace — you cannot assign properties onto it, so `vi.spyOn(module, 'exportedFn')` throws `TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property`. Passing `{ spy: true }` to `vi.mock()` instructs Vitest to generate a module wrapper that re-exports every original implementation while wrapping each export in a `vi.fn()` spy, preserving runtime behaviour while making calls observable. This is the canonical browser-mode substitute for `vi.spyOn()` on an ESM export and is the only pattern that survives Vitest's browser namespace sealing without either replacing the implementation or rewriting the module under test.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts  — assumes browser: { provider: 'playwright' } is set
// Test file: src/analytics/tracker.browser.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';

// { spy: true } wraps every export in a vi.fn() that delegates to the original.
// No implementation is replaced — the real code still runs.
vi.mock('../src/analytics/events.js', { spy: true });

import * as events from '../src/analytics/events.js';
import { trackPageView } from '../src/analytics/tracker.js';

describe('tracker (browser mode)', () => {
  it('calls logEvent with the correct page name', async () => {
    await trackPageView('/dashboard');

    // logEvent ran its real implementation AND was recorded as a spy call
    expect(events.logEvent).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ page: '/dashboard' }),
    );
  });

  it('logEvent spy call count resets between tests', async () => {
    // clearMocks: true (vitest.config.ts) resets spy call records
    expect(events.logEvent).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Because `{ spy: true }` leaves the original implementation intact, a failing test causes the real side-effect (network call, DOM mutation, localStorage write) in addition to the spy assertion failure. If you need to suppress side effects in browser tests, you must use a full `vi.mock()` factory with explicit stub implementations — `{ spy: true }` is purely observational and unsuitable when the real implementation is expensive or has external dependencies.

---

### Pattern 395 — Jest `resetModules: true` combined with `jest.isolateModules()` for per-test singleton re-initialisation [official]

Jest's global `resetModules: true` config option resets the module registry before every test, ensuring that `require()`/`import()` calls inside a test always see a freshly initialised module. However, the global flag applies to every test in the suite and can produce misleading errors when a test file legitimately depends on a shared singleton initialised at the top of the file (e.g., a database client created via a top-level `import`). `jest.isolateModules(fn)` provides surgical per-test scope: only the modules loaded inside its callback get a fresh registry; modules loaded outside the callback share the file-level cache as normal. Use `isolateModules` for the minority of tests that need singleton re-initialisation while leaving `resetModules: false` globally to avoid unexpected re-initialisation in tests that share an intentional singleton.

```typescript
// config.test.ts — tests a module whose singleton reads process.env at load time
import { jest, describe, it, expect, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

const ORIGINAL_ENV = { ...process.env };

afterEach(() => {
  Object.assign(process.env, ORIGINAL_ENV);
  // Remove keys that were not in the original snapshot
  for (const key of Object.keys(process.env)) {
    if (!(key in ORIGINAL_ENV)) delete process.env[key];
  }
});

describe('AppConfig singleton', () => {
  it('reads DATABASE_URL from env at module load time', async () => {
    process.env.DATABASE_URL = 'postgres://test-db:5432/mydb';

    let config!: { databaseUrl: string };
    jest.isolateModules(() => {
      // A fresh copy of config.ts is evaluated inside this scope only
      config = require('../src/config') as { databaseUrl: string };
    });

    expect(config.databaseUrl).toBe('postgres://test-db:5432/mydb');
  });

  it('uses a different URL when env changes', async () => {
    process.env.DATABASE_URL = 'postgres://other-db:5432/otherdb';

    let config!: { databaseUrl: string };
    jest.isolateModules(() => {
      config = require('../src/config') as { databaseUrl: string };
    });

    expect(config.databaseUrl).toBe('postgres://other-db:5432/otherdb');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `jest.isolateModules()` is synchronous in its execution scope — you cannot `await` inside the callback in the standard API. Modules with top-level `await` (ESM native async modules) cannot be fully initialised inside `isolateModules()` because Node's ESM loader does not honour synchronous registry snapshots for async module graphs. For those cases, set `resetModules: true` globally and restructure the test file so every test is self-contained, or use Vitest's `vi.resetModules()` which has fewer restrictions on async ESM.

---

### Pattern 396 — Playwright `mergeTests()` for composing domain-specific fixture sets without cross-contamination [official]

Large Playwright suites typically accumulate multiple independent fixture sets — one for authenticated HTTP sessions, one for database seeding, one for feature-flag overrides. Merging these with `mergeTests()` produces a single `test` function whose types and setup/teardown are fully composable, with no risk of one fixture set's setup polluting another's teardown. Each fixture in the merged set retains its own scope (test vs. worker) and its own `await use()` barrier, so teardown order is still governed by the dependency graph rather than by merge order. This is preferable to extending a single base `test` object multiple times, which forces a strict inheritance chain and makes it difficult to share fixture combinations across projects.

```typescript
// fixtures/auth.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
export type AuthFixtures = { authToken: string };

export const authTest = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  authToken: async ({}, use) => {
    const token = await obtainTestToken();
    await use(token);
    await revokeTestToken(token);
  },
});

// fixtures/db.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
export type DbFixtures = { seedId: string };

export const dbTest = base.extend<DbFixtures>({
  seedId: async ({}, use) => {
    const id = await seedDatabase();
    await use(id);
    await deleteDbSeed(id);
  },
});

// fixtures/index.ts — merge without inheritance chain
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { authTest } from './auth.js';
import { dbTest } from './db.js';

export const test = mergeTests(authTest, dbTest);
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// tests/dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/index.js';

test('authenticated user sees seeded data', async ({ page, authToken, seedId }) => {
  await page.setExtraHTTPHeaders({ Authorization: `Bearer ${authToken}` });
  await page.goto(`/items/${seedId}`);
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `mergeTests()` performs a shallow merge of fixture registrations: if both input `test` objects define a fixture with the same name, the last one in the argument list wins silently without a runtime error. Teams that grow fixture libraries organically across multiple files can accidentally create silent override bugs — the first fixture's setup never runs, its teardown never runs, and no warning appears in the reporter. Enforce unique fixture names with a lint rule or CI check that scans all `base.extend()` calls for duplicate keys before merging.

---

### Pattern 397 — Playwright `{ auto: true }` fixture for capturing verbose debug logs on every test without opt-in boilerplate [official]

Automatic Playwright fixtures run their setup and teardown for every test in a worker, regardless of whether the test function declares the fixture in its parameter list. This is the correct pattern for cross-cutting infrastructure like debug-log collectors, performance-mark recorders, and per-test network trace archivers: the test author writes only business assertions, while the infrastructure fixture silently captures context before `await use()` and persists it (or discards it on pass) after `await use()`. Without `{ auto: true }`, teams either add the fixture to every test signature (fragile — easy to forget) or use a `beforeEach` at the global level (which cannot access test metadata such as `testInfo.title` or `testInfo.status`).

```typescript
// fixtures/debugCapture.ts
import { test as base, TestInfo } from '@playwright/test';
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';

type DebugFixtures = { _debugCapture: void };

export const test = base.extend<DebugFixtures>({
  _debugCapture: [
    async ({ page }, use, testInfo: TestInfo) => {
      const logs: string[] = [];

      // Capture all browser console output before the test body runs
      page.on('console', (msg) => logs.push(`[${msg.type()}] ${msg.text()}`));

      await use(); // test body executes here

      // Only write logs to disk when the test fails — no noise on passing runs
      if (testInfo.status !== 'passed') {
        const logPath = path.join(
          testInfo.outputDir,
          `console-${testInfo.workerIndex}.log`,
        );
        await fs.writeFile(logPath, logs.join('\n'), 'utf8');
        testInfo.attachments.push({ name: 'console-log', path: logPath, contentType: 'text/plain' });
      }
    },
    { auto: true, scope: 'test' }, // runs for every test automatically
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Automatic fixtures with `scope: 'test'` re-run their setup and teardown for every single test in the worker — even tests that have nothing to do with the domain the fixture covers. A `{ auto: true }` fixture that opens a database connection, initialises a file watcher, or performs network I/O on every test will multiply its overhead by the total test count. Reserve `{ auto: true }` for genuinely zero-cost or near-zero-cost setup (event listener registration, in-memory log buffer allocation) and prefer explicit fixture parameters for anything with measurable I/O.

---

### Pattern 398 — Jest `injectGlobals: false` with explicit `@jest/globals` imports for type-safe, IDE-resolvable test APIs in monorepos [official]

Jest injects `describe`, `it`, `expect`, `jest`, `beforeEach` etc. as implicit globals in every test file by default. In a TypeScript monorepo with multiple Jest configs, this creates ambiguity: the `@types/jest` package adds these symbols to the global `lib.dom.d.ts` namespace, which can conflict with `@types/mocha`, `@types/jasmine`, or Vitest's type declarations when multiple test frameworks coexist. Setting `injectGlobals: false` removes Jest's implicit globals, forcing each test file to `import { test, expect, jest } from '@jest/globals'`. The import makes the Jest version explicit, eliminates type conflicts, and enables tree-shaking of unused test globals in test bundles.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import type { Config } from 'jest';

const config: Config = {
  preset: 'ts-jest',
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  injectGlobals: false,          // Disable implicit global injection
  // ...other config
};

export default config;

// src/__tests__/calculator.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, jest, beforeEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { add, divide } from '../calculator.js';

describe('calculator', () => {
  let consoleSpy: ReturnType<typeof jest.spyOn>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    consoleSpy = jest.spyOn(console, 'warn').mockImplementation(() => {});
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    consoleSpy.mockRestore();
  });

  it('adds two positive numbers', () => {
    expect(add(2, 3)).toBe(5);
  });

  it('emits a console.warn when dividing by zero', () => {
    divide(10, 0);
    expect(consoleSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(expect.stringContaining('division by zero'));
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `injectGlobals: false` breaks every existing test file in the project simultaneously — there is no gradual migration path unless you wrap the change in a per-directory Jest config with `projects`. Additionally, third-party test helper libraries that rely on Jest globals being present in `globalThis` (e.g., some versions of `@testing-library/jest-dom` that call `expect.extend` in a setup file) may fail silently or emit `expect is not defined` errors at setup time rather than at assertion time. Audit all `setupFilesAfterFramework` entries before enabling this flag.

---

### Pattern 399 — Node.js `run({ isolation: 'process' })` with `--test-global-setup` for shared server startup isolated from per-test module caches [official]

Node.js 24.0.0 introduced `--test-global-setup=<module>` (and the corresponding `globalSetup` / `globalTeardown` exports) to run one-time infrastructure — servers, database containers, shared auth tokens — before any test process spawns. Combined with the default `isolation: 'process'` mode, this creates a clean two-layer isolation model: the global setup runs once in the parent process, its outputs are passed to child processes via environment variables, and each child process has its own isolated module cache with no access to the parent's in-memory state. This is the native-runner equivalent of Jest's `globalSetup` / `globalTeardown` and eliminates the need to start test servers inside `beforeAll` blocks (which are per-file and re-run for every isolated child).

```typescript
// test-global-setup.mts  (referenced by --test-global-setup flag)
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

let server: ReturnType<typeof createServer>;

export async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  server = createServer((req, res) => {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
    res.end(JSON.stringify({ stub: true, path: req.url }));
  });

  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', resolve));

  const addr = server.address() as { port: number };
  // Expose to all child test processes via environment variable
  process.env.TEST_SERVER_PORT = String(addr.port);
}

export async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) =>
    server.close((err) => (err ? reject(err) : resolve())),
  );
}

// test/api.test.ts — reads the env var set by globalSetup
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('stub server returns 200 for /health', async () => {
  const port = process.env.TEST_SERVER_PORT!;
  const res = await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/health`);
  assert.equal(res.status, 200);
  const body = await res.json() as { stub: boolean };
  assert.equal(body.stub, true);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** If `globalSetup` throws, Node skips all tests and does **not** call `globalTeardown`. This means servers or database containers started partway through a failing `globalSetup` are orphaned — their ports remain bound or their containers remain running — until the CI runner's timeout kills them. Always structure `globalSetup` to clean up partial initialisation on error (try/catch + explicit cleanup before re-throwing), or use a process-exit hook (`process.on('exit', ...)`) as a last-resort safety net inside the setup module itself.

---

### Pattern 400 — Vitest `poolOptions.threads.isolate: false` with `singleThread: true` for deterministic benchmark baselines that require a warm JIT [official]

Vitest's default thread pool creates a fresh worker thread per test file and runs each file in isolation. For micro-benchmarks this means the V8 JIT never reaches its optimised tier within a single file run — the benchmark measures JIT warm-up cost rather than the hot-path throughput the author intended to quantify. Setting `isolate: false` within `poolOptions.threads` allows multiple benchmark files to share the same worker thread, and adding `singleThread: true` constrains all files to a single thread to eliminate cross-thread scheduling jitter. The result is that V8 has time to tier-up through Ignition → Sparkplug → Maglev → Turbofan across repeated `bench()` iterations, producing stable, reproducible baseline numbers.

```typescript
// vitest.config.benchmark.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    include: ['benchmarks/**/*.bench.ts'],
    pool: 'threads',
    poolOptions: {
      threads: {
        isolate: false,      // Reuse the worker between files — no fresh VM per file
        singleThread: true,  // One thread total — eliminates cross-thread jitter
      },
    },
    benchmark: {
      reporter: 'verbose',
      // Warm-up rounds so V8 tiers up before measurement begins
      warmupTime: 1000,
      warmupIterations: 5,
    },
  },
});

// benchmarks/string-utils.bench.ts
import { bench, describe } from 'vitest';
import { camelToSnake } from '../src/stringUtils.js';

describe('camelToSnake', () => {
  bench('short string (10 chars)', () => {
    camelToSnake('myVarName');
  });

  bench('long string (100 chars)', () => {
    camelToSnake('thisIsAVeryLongVariableNameThatExceedsATypicalIdentifierLengthForBenchmarkingPurposes');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** With `isolate: false` + `singleThread: true`, a benchmark file that accidentally mutates a module-level singleton (e.g., caching a computed value after the first `bench()` run) will carry that mutation into every subsequent `bench()` call in the same worker session, making later iterations artificially faster. This is the desired behaviour for benchmarking (it mirrors how the code behaves in production after warm-up), but it makes the benchmark useless for measuring first-call latency. Add a separate benchmark suite with `isolate: true` (the default) if you need cold-start measurements alongside warm-path measurements.

---

### Pattern 401 — Node.js `context.mock.module()` with `namedExports` for ESM-compatible module boundary mocking without loader hooks [official]

The Node.js test runner's `mock.module()` API introduced in Node 22 provides ESM-aware module mocking without requiring `--experimental-vm-modules`, `--loader`, or any other experimental flag. Passing `namedExports` replaces specific exports while leaving the module's default export and other named exports untouched, which is the correct granularity for mocking a single function in a utility module without accidentally nullifying the rest of the module's API. The mock is scoped to the test context (`t.mock`) and is automatically removed from the module cache when the test ends, making it safe to use in concurrent tests that import the same module path through different entry points.

```typescript
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

describe('notificationService', () => {
  test('sends push notification via mocked transport layer', async (t) => {
    // Mock only the sendPush export; other exports (sendSMS, sendEmail) remain real
    t.mock.module('../src/transport.js', {
      namedExports: {
        sendPush: async (deviceToken: string, payload: object): Promise<{ id: string }> => {
          // Record the call in a closure variable for assertion
          calls.push({ deviceToken, payload });
          return { id: 'mock-notification-id' };
        },
      },
    });

    const calls: Array<{ deviceToken: string; payload: object }> = [];

    // Import AFTER mock registration — critical for ESM cache bypass
    const { notify } = await import('../src/notificationService.js');
    await notify({ userId: 'u-001', message: 'Your order shipped' });

    assert.equal(calls.length, 1);
    assert.equal(calls[0].deviceToken, 'device-token-for-u-001');
    assert.deepEqual(calls[0].payload, { message: 'Your order shipped' });
    // t.mock automatically restores transport.js to its real implementation here
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `t.mock.module()` operates on Node's internal module registry and requires the mock to be set up **before** the system-under-test is imported for the first time in the current process. If a top-level `import` at the top of the test file already caused Node to resolve and cache the real module, registering a mock with `t.mock.module()` inside the test body has no effect — the system-under-test holds a reference to the already-cached real dependency. Always use dynamic `await import()` inside the test body, after the mock is registered, and avoid top-level static imports of the system-under-test in test files that need per-test module mocking.

---

### Pattern 402 — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` scoped to individual tests with `unstubAllEnvs()` backstop for hermetic environment variable isolation [official]

`vi.stubEnv(key, value)` replaces a single `process.env` key with a test-controlled value and records the original so `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` can restore it. Unlike directly assigning `process.env.KEY = 'value'` (which requires a manual teardown that test authors frequently forget), `vi.stubEnv()` integrates with Vitest's automatic cleanup lifecycle: setting `unstubEnvs: true` in `vitest.config.ts` calls `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` automatically after every test, preventing any env variable set in one test from leaking into the next. This is the idiomatic Vitest pattern for testing code that branches on environment variables (feature flags, environment names, API endpoints) without modifying the shell environment that CI uses for other processes.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    unstubEnvs: true,  // Auto-call vi.unstubAllEnvs() after every test
  },
});

// src/__tests__/featureFlag.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { isFeatureEnabled } from '../src/featureFlags.js';

describe('isFeatureEnabled', () => {
  it('returns true when FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD env is "1"', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD', '1');

    expect(isFeatureEnabled('NEW_DASHBOARD')).toBe(true);
    // unstubEnvs: true restores process.env.FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD after this test
  });

  it('returns false when FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD env is absent', () => {
    // FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD is already restored to its original value
    vi.stubEnv('FEATURE_NEW_DASHBOARD', undefined as unknown as string);

    expect(isFeatureEnabled('NEW_DASHBOARD')).toBe(false);
  });

  it('returns false by default when env is unset', () => {
    // No stubbing needed — original env is clean after previous tests
    expect(isFeatureEnabled('NONEXISTENT_FEATURE')).toBe(false);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.stubEnv()` stubs at the `process.env` object level — it does not reach into modules that have already read `process.env.KEY` at load time and stored the value in a module-level constant (e.g., `const ENDPOINT = process.env.API_ENDPOINT ?? 'https://prod.example.com'`). For those modules, `vi.stubEnv()` after the module is loaded has no effect because the constant has already been captured. The only solution is to reset the module registry (`vi.resetModules()`) and re-import the module after stubbing, accepting the cold-import overhead for each test that exercises env-dependent module initialisation.

---

### Pattern 403 — Jest `isolateModulesAsync()` for per-test ESM singleton re-initialisation in projects using `--experimental-vm-modules` [official]

`jest.isolateModules()` is synchronous and cannot handle ES modules that use top-level `await`. Jest 29.4+ ships `jest.isolateModulesAsync(fn)`, which accepts an async callback and runs it inside a fresh module registry that includes proper ESM async initialisation support under `--experimental-vm-modules`. This enables per-test re-initialisation of ESM singletons — database pool initialisers, configuration loaders, event emitter bootstrappers — that would otherwise share a single cached instance across every test in the file, producing cross-test state leakage that the standard `resetModules: true` flag would fix at the file level but not the individual test level.

```typescript
// users.test.ts  (run with --experimental-vm-modules)
import { jest, describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';

describe('UserRepository ESM singleton isolation', () => {
  it('initialises with a pool size of 5 when DB_POOL_SIZE is 5', async () => {
    process.env.DB_POOL_SIZE = '5';

    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      // Top-level await in db.ts is handled correctly by the async version
      const { db } = await import('../src/db.js');
      const { UserRepository } = await import('../src/userRepository.js');

      const repo = new UserRepository(db);
      expect(repo.poolSize).toBe(5);
    });

    delete process.env.DB_POOL_SIZE;
  });

  it('initialises with a pool size of 1 when DB_POOL_SIZE is absent', async () => {
    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      const { db } = await import('../src/db.js');
      const { UserRepository } = await import('../src/userRepository.js');

      const repo = new UserRepository(db);
      expect(repo.poolSize).toBe(1); // default
    });
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` creates a brand-new module registry per call, which means every module in the dependency graph (not just the module being tested) is re-evaluated — including heavy transitive dependencies like ORMs, HTTP clients, and crypto libraries. In a test suite with dozens of calls to `isolateModulesAsync()`, this can inflate test suite wall time by seconds. Profile with `--verbose` and `--detectOpenHandles` to confirm that the registry teardown correctly closes any asynchronous resources (timers, open sockets, file watchers) that the re-initialised modules create, since Jest's normal `--forceExit` may mask leaked handles.

---

### Pattern 404 — Playwright `storageState` fixture override for test-scoped authentication session isolation [official]

Playwright's `storageState` built-in option accepts a path to a JSON file containing cookies and `localStorage` values and applies them to each new `BrowserContext`. Overriding the `storageState` fixture at the test level — returning dynamically constructed cookie objects rather than a static file path — ensures that every test starts with a cryptographically distinct session token, preventing the scenario where two concurrently running Playwright workers share the same session and one test's logout action invalidates the session mid-flight for another test running in a different worker. This is especially important in suites with `--workers > 1` and a real authentication backend that enforces single-session-per-user rules.

```typescript
// fixtures/authSession.ts
import { test as base, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import { issueTestSessionToken, revokeToken } from '../helpers/authHelper.js';

type AuthFixtures = {
  authenticatedContext: BrowserContext;
};

export const test = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  authenticatedContext: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    // Issue a unique per-test session token from the test auth helper
    const { token, userId } = await issueTestSessionToken();

    const context = await browser.newContext({
      storageState: {
        cookies: [
          {
            name: 'session',
            value: token,
            domain: 'localhost',
            path: '/',
            httpOnly: true,
            secure: false,
            sameSite: 'Lax',
          },
        ],
        origins: [
          {
            origin: 'http://localhost:3000',
            localStorage: [{ name: 'userId', value: userId }],
          },
        ],
      },
    });

    await use(context);

    // Teardown: revoke the unique token so it cannot be replayed
    await revokeToken(token);
    await context.close();
  },
});

// tests/profile.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/authSession.js';

test('authenticated user can update display name', async ({ authenticatedContext }) => {
  const page = await authenticatedContext.newPage();
  await page.goto('/profile');
  await page.getByLabel('Display name').fill('New Name');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Profile updated')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Issuing a real session token per test via `issueTestSessionToken()` couples the Playwright suite to the availability of the authentication backend. If the auth service is down or slow, every test fails with a fixture initialisation error rather than a test logic error, masking the actual problem. Mitigate by adding a health-check step at the start of the worker-scoped global setup so that authentication backend failures produce a single clear error at the suite level, not a waterfall of per-test fixture timeouts.

---

### Pattern 405 — Vitest `vi.mock()` with a factory that reads `vi.importActual()` for partial module mocks that preserve unmodified exports [official]

When a test needs to replace one function in a module but leave all other exports intact, `vi.mock()` with a factory that calls `vi.importActual()` is the canonical Vitest pattern. Without `importActual`, the factory must manually enumerate every export to preserve — a maintenance burden that causes silent test breakage whenever the real module adds a new export that the test's mock factory omits (the omitted export becomes `undefined` in the test). Using `await vi.importActual()` inside the factory fetches the real module implementation and spreads it as the mock's base, so only the explicitly overridden exports differ from reality.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

vi.mock('../src/dateUtils.js', async (importActual) => {
  // Fetch the real module implementation as the base
  const actual = await importActual<typeof import('../src/dateUtils.js')>();
  return {
    ...actual, // All real exports preserved
    getCurrentDate: vi.fn(() => new Date('2026-01-15T12:00:00.000Z')), // Only this one is replaced
  };
});

import { formatRelativeDate, getCurrentDate } from '../src/dateUtils.js';

describe('formatRelativeDate', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.mocked(getCurrentDate).mockReturnValue(new Date('2026-01-15T12:00:00.000Z'));
  });

  it('returns "today" for the current date', () => {
    // getCurrentDate is mocked; formatRelativeDate uses it internally
    const result = formatRelativeDate(new Date('2026-01-15T08:00:00.000Z'));
    expect(result).toBe('today');
  });

  it('returns "yesterday" for one day prior', () => {
    const result = formatRelativeDate(new Date('2026-01-14T08:00:00.000Z'));
    expect(result).toBe('yesterday');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `importActual` parameter inside the `vi.mock()` factory is an async function, meaning the factory itself must be `async`. Vitest supports async mock factories, but this means the mock is registered asynchronously during the hoisting phase — Vitest must resolve the factory Promise before any test in the file runs, adding a microtask-queue round-trip to the file's startup time. In files with many `vi.mock()` calls that each use `importActual`, this accumulates into a measurable startup delay. If startup time is a concern, consider caching the `importActual` result in a module-level variable via `vi.hoisted()` and reusing it across all factories in the file.

---

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 47

294. **Node.js `run({ isolation: 'none', env: { KEY: 'value' } })` throws `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` at startup rather than at test execution time — the `env` option is silently incompatible with `isolation: 'none'` because there is no child process to pass environment variables to, but the error message says "invalid option combination" rather than naming the two conflicting options, making it hard to diagnose from logs alone.** [official]
    WHY: When `isolation: 'none'` is active, all test files run in the current parent process. Passing `env` would require the test runner to mutate `process.env` for the parent process itself, which would leak the env values into the runner's own internals (reporters, coverage tools, CLI flags) and is therefore prohibited. The Node.js test runner validates the combination eagerly at `run()` call time, before any file discovery, so the error is thrown synchronously even if no test files match the `files` glob — a source of confusion for teams that first encounter the error in CI without a matching test run log to contextualise it.

295. **Vitest `vi.mock()` with an async factory that calls `vi.importActual()` does not work in browser mode — the browser runtime cannot execute the factory during Vitest's static analysis / transform phase because `vi.importActual()` in browser mode issues a real network request to the dev server, and the hoisting transform runs before the browser network stack is available, silently making the factory return `undefined` for all exports.** [community]
    WHY: Vitest's browser mode uses a Vite transform plugin to hoist `vi.mock()` calls at bundle time. In Node mode, `vi.importActual()` is resolved by the module system synchronously during the factory call because the file is already in the require cache. In browser mode, the equivalent operation requires a dynamic `import()` over the browser's HTTP channel to the Vite dev server, which is not available during the transform phase. The workaround is to avoid `importActual` in browser-mode mock factories and instead manually import the real module's types for spreading, using static type assertions rather than runtime value spreading.

296. **Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` does not close asynchronous handles opened by the re-initialised modules — if the freshly loaded module starts a `setInterval`, opens a `net.Socket`, or creates a database connection pool with a keep-alive timer, Jest's `--detectOpenHandles` flag will report those handles as leaked after the test, but only if `--forceExit` is not set; with `--forceExit` (the common CI default) the handles are silently orphaned and the process exit masks the leak entirely.** [official]
    WHY: `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` creates an isolated module registry that lives for the duration of the async callback. When the callback completes, Jest drops the registry reference and lets the garbage collector reclaim module instances. However, Node.js does not garbage-collect objects that have live handle references (sockets, timers, file descriptors) until those handles are explicitly closed. The isolated module instance is unreachable from application code, but its handles keep the event loop alive. The only robust fix is to design modules that `isolateModulesAsync` is used against to expose an explicit `close()` or `destroy()` method, call it before the async callback returns, and verify with `--detectOpenHandles` in a CI job that never sets `--forceExit`.

297. **Playwright's `mergeTests()` does not validate fixture name collisions at call time — if two merged `test` objects both define a fixture named `page` (e.g., one overrides `page` to auto-navigate and another overrides `page` to set viewport), the last argument's fixture silently wins, the first fixture's setup and teardown code never execute, and there is no warning in the test output or in the TypeScript types.** [official]
    WHY: `mergeTests()` performs a plain key-merge of the fixture maps from all arguments, applying them left-to-right so later entries overwrite earlier ones with the same key. TypeScript's type system cannot detect this collision because both inputs have the same type for the `page` fixture (they are both valid `Locator`-returning fixtures), so the merged type looks identical to either individual input type. The collision manifests at runtime as mysteriously missing behaviour (the auto-navigation never happens, or the viewport is never set) rather than as an error. A lint rule or a runtime check in the fixture infrastructure that asserts uniqueness across all merged fixture names is the only reliable guard.

298. **Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` does not affect `import.meta.env` in browser mode — `vi.stubEnv('VITE_API_URL', 'http://test')` mutates `process.env.VITE_API_URL` on the server side, but in browser mode the system-under-test reads `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`, which is statically replaced by Vite's transform at bundle time and is no longer a runtime lookup — meaning the stubbed value is never seen by the browser-mode test.** [community]
    WHY: Vite processes `import.meta.env.*` references at build/transform time by substituting the actual environment variable values into the bundle as string literals. In browser mode, by the time the test module runs in the browser, all `import.meta.env.VITE_*` references have been replaced by their compile-time values and there is no runtime object to intercept. `vi.stubEnv()` operates on `process.env` in the Node.js server context, which is entirely disconnected from the already-transformed browser bundle. The correct approach for browser-mode env testing is to configure Vite's `define` option in `vitest.config.ts` to inject a test-specific value at transform time, or to mock the module that consumes `import.meta.env` entirely with `vi.mock()`.

299. **Node.js `--test-global-setup` module's `globalTeardown` is NOT called when `globalSetup` throws — teams that start a database container or bind a port inside `globalSetup` and rely on `globalTeardown` to stop it will leak the resource every time the setup phase fails, including on the first CI run of a new branch where the setup logic has a bug.** [official]
    WHY: The Node.js test runner exits with a non-zero code immediately when `globalSetup` throws, skipping the `globalTeardown` call entirely. This is documented behaviour mirroring Jest's `globalSetup` contract, but teams migrating from Jest often assume the teardown is called as a finally-style cleanup. The reliable mitigation is a two-part defence: (1) wrap the entire `globalSetup` body in try/catch and run an inline cleanup in the catch block before re-throwing, and (2) register a `process.on('exit', emergencyCleanup)` listener inside `globalSetup` as a last-resort guard that runs even when the process is killed with `SIGTERM` (e.g., by a CI timeout), preventing dangling containers from persisting across CI runs.

---

| Problem | Symptom | Solution | Framework |
|---------|---------|----------|-----------|
| `run({ isolation: 'none', env: {...} })` throws at startup | `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` before any test runs | Remove `env` option; set vars on `process.env` directly before calling `run()` | Node 22+ |
| `t.mock.module()` has no effect when module was already imported at file top level | System-under-test uses real dependency despite mock | Use dynamic `await import()` inside test body, after `t.mock.module()` | Node 22+ |
| `vi.mock()` factory returns `undefined` for all exports in browser mode with `importActual` | Tests see `undefined` for mocked module members | Avoid `importActual` in browser-mode factories; manually spread types | Vitest browser |
| `vi.stubEnv()` doesn't affect `import.meta.env.VITE_*` in browser mode | Stubbed value never seen by browser-mode test | Use Vite `define` config for test env values; or mock the consuming module | Vitest browser |
| `mergeTests()` silently drops first fixture when names collide | Auto-navigation or viewport override never runs | Enforce unique fixture names with lint rule; check for same-key warnings | Playwright |
| `mergeTests()` TypeScript types look correct despite fixture collision | No compile error, silent runtime failure | Assert fixture name uniqueness in test infrastructure setup code | Playwright |
| `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` leaks handles with `--forceExit` | Open handles masked in CI | Expose `close()` on isolated modules; verify with `--detectOpenHandles` in CI (no `--forceExit`) | Jest |
| `globalTeardown` not called when `globalSetup` throws | Database container / port leaked on setup failure | Wrap globalSetup in try/catch with inline cleanup; add `process.on('exit', ...)` guard | Node 24+ |
| `vi.hoisted()` shared mock mutated by `mockImplementation()` leaks to next test | Test B sees implementation left by test A | Use `restoreMocks: true` in config, or call `vi.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach` | Vitest |
| `injectGlobals: false` breaks third-party setup files calling `expect.extend` globally | `expect is not defined` at setup time, not assertion time | Audit all `setupFilesAfterFramework` entries before enabling; patch helpers to import from `@jest/globals` | Jest |
| `poolOptions.threads.isolate: false` + benchmarks inflate cold-start cost | Benchmark numbers include JIT warm-up | Use `singleThread: true` + `warmupTime: 1000` to tier up V8 before measurement | Vitest |
| Worker-scoped auth session shared across parallel workers causes mid-test invalidation | Logout in worker A kills session used by worker B | Issue unique per-test tokens from `storageState` fixture; revoke in teardown | Playwright |
| `resetModules: true` globally breaks files with shared intentional singletons | Singleton re-initialised unexpectedly; test fails for wrong reason | Use `jest.isolateModules()` surgically per test; leave global `resetModules: false` | Jest |
| `vi.mock()` with async factory causes measurable startup delay per file | File init slow when many `vi.mock` calls use `importActual` | Cache `importActual` result in `vi.hoisted()` and reuse across factories | Vitest |
| `isolation: 'none'` with `process.env` mutations leaks to later test files | Test N+1 sees env value set by test N | Snapshot and restore `process.env` in `beforeEach`/`afterEach` for every test that mutates it | Node 22+ |
