## Quick Reference — Cycle 51

| Problem | Symptom | Solution | Framework |
|---------|---------|----------|-----------|
| `vi.waitFor()` with `timeout: 0` — no retries | Immediate failure despite correct system state | Use positive timeout (default 1000ms); `timeout: 0` = single synchronous check | Vitest |
| `jest.advanceTimersByTime()` — async callback not fully executed | Assertion sees pre-await state | Follow with `await Promise.resolve()` to drain microtask queue | Jest |
| `test.use({ storageState })` in describe — `beforeAll` uses wrong user | Setup navigates as admin; 403 errors misattributed | Move auth-sensitive setup to `beforeEach` or pass credentials explicitly | Playwright |
| `vi.hoisted()` TDZ error in mock factory | "Cannot access before initialization" | Declare all `vi.hoisted()` bindings before their consuming `vi.mock()` calls | Vitest |
| `t.mock.timers.tick()` — async callbacks interleave unexpectedly | Second async timer callback sees pre-await state of first | Insert `await new Promise(setImmediate)` between `tick()` calls | Node.js |
| `doNotFake: ['performance']` — `performance.now() - Date.now()` produces absurd value | Billion-magnitude diff; asserts explode | Never cross-compare real monotonic and fake epoch clocks; use one or the other | Jest |
| `vi.mock('x', { spy: true })` — real side effects still fire | Unexpected DB writes or network calls in unit test | Use `{ spy: true }` only for observation; use factory mock to suppress side effects | Vitest |
| `jest.resetModules()` overhead per test — slow suite | Each test takes 200+ ms due to full re-evaluation | Use Construct-with-Collaborators DI pattern; inject config at construction time instead | Jest |
| `vi.waitUntil()` — intermittent exception aborts polling prematurely | Test fails on transient error before state resolves | Use `vi.waitFor()` when transient errors are expected; `vi.waitUntil()` for binary readiness | Vitest |
| `@jest-environment-options` docblock — changing app origin requires updating many files | URL drift across test files | Centralise URL in `setupFiles` constant; reference via env var in docblocks | Jest |
| `node:test mock.module()` partial export shape — un-listed exports are `undefined` | Production code throws "X is not a function" | Enumerate all required named exports in `namedExports` shape | Node.js |
| Vitest `scope: 'file'` DB fixture + ROLLBACK — test cannot see committed state | Trigger/constraint assertions fail | Use savepoints for sub-transaction isolation or switch to per-test connection | Vitest |
| `setupFiles` contains `expect.extend()` — crashes with `injectGlobals: false` | `ReferenceError: expect is not defined` | Move `expect.extend()` to `setupFilesAfterEnv`; keep polyfills in `setupFiles` | Jest |
| `vi.mock(importOriginal)` spread — new exports are `undefined` after module update | Silent "method not found" failures | Always spread `importOriginal` in factories for growing module boundaries | Vitest |
| `customExportConditions: ['browser']` in Node env — window globals missing | `ReferenceError: window is not defined` | Stub browser globals explicitly in `setupFiles` when using browser export conditions | Jest |

## Cycle 53 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 481 — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` + `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` for per-test environment variable isolation [official]

Use `vi.stubEnv(name, value)` to temporarily override `process.env` and `import.meta.env` simultaneously for a single test, then call `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` in `afterEach` to restore every stubbed variable to its original value in one call. Unlike direct assignment (`process.env.X = 'y'`), `vi.stubEnv` records the original value at first call so that even if a test throws before its own cleanup the `afterEach` hook restores the correct baseline. The paired `vi.stubGlobal` / `vi.unstubAllGlobals` API follows the identical contract for `globalThis` properties.

```typescript
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { createDbConnection } from './db';

describe('createDbConnection — env-driven config', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Override both process.env AND import.meta.env in one call
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://test-host/ci_db');
    vi.stubEnv('DB_POOL_SIZE', '2');
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    // Restore all stubs to their pre-test originals
    vi.unstubAllEnvs();
  });

  it('uses the stubbed DATABASE_URL', () => {
    const conn = createDbConnection();
    expect(conn.url).toBe('postgres://test-host/ci_db');
    expect(conn.poolSize).toBe(2);
  });

  it('falls back to default pool size when env is absent', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DB_POOL_SIZE', undefined); // explicitly unset
    const conn = createDbConnection();
    expect(conn.poolSize).toBe(10); // default
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `vi.stubEnv` is synchronous and has negligible overhead. Its main limitation is that it patches `import.meta.env` shallowly — nested objects like `import.meta.env.VITE_CONFIG` must be fully replaced rather than mutated in place. Avoid mixing direct `process.env.X =` assignments and `vi.stubEnv` in the same test file; direct assignments bypass the stub registry and will not be unwound by `vi.unstubAllEnvs()`. [official]

---

### Pattern 482 — Vitest `vi.stubGlobal()` for DOM API shimming in jsdom-free environments [official]

When running Vitest in the default `node` environment without jsdom, browser globals like `window`, `navigator`, `IntersectionObserver`, or `ResizeObserver` do not exist. Use `vi.stubGlobal(name, value)` to attach a minimal stub to `globalThis` for the duration of the test, then call `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in `afterEach` to remove it. This avoids the overhead of a full jsdom environment for tests that only need one or two globals, while still ensuring isolation between tests that might assert on the presence or absence of that global.

```typescript
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';
import { createObserver } from './intersection-tracker';

// Running in 'node' environment — IntersectionObserver does not exist by default
describe('createObserver — browser global shimming', () => {
  const MockIntersectionObserver = vi.fn().mockImplementation((callback) => ({
    observe: vi.fn(),
    unobserve: vi.fn(),
    disconnect: vi.fn(),
    _trigger: (entries: object[]) => callback(entries),
  }));

  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.stubGlobal('IntersectionObserver', MockIntersectionObserver);
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.unstubAllGlobals();
    MockIntersectionObserver.mockClear();
  });

  it('constructs an IntersectionObserver with the provided threshold', () => {
    createObserver(document.createElement('div'), { threshold: 0.5 });
    expect(MockIntersectionObserver).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.any(Function),
      expect.objectContaining({ threshold: 0.5 }),
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Stubbing individual globals is much faster than switching the environment to `jsdom` but requires manually enumerating every missing global the module under test accesses. For components that depend on more than 3–4 browser APIs, switching to `jsdom` or `happy-dom` per file (via `@vitest-environment jsdom` docblock) is more maintainable than maintaining a growing list of `vi.stubGlobal` calls. [official]

---

### Pattern 483 — Vitest `onTestFinished` / `onTestFailed` context hooks for conditional test-scoped teardown [official]

Vitest's test context exposes `onTestFinished(fn)` and `onTestFailed(fn)` as in-test registration points for teardown logic that must run unconditionally after the test body, or only when the test fails. These are particularly useful inside helpers and custom fixtures where `afterEach` is not accessible, and where the cleanup is tightly coupled to a resource created during the test body rather than during fixture setup. Unlike `afterEach`, `onTestFinished` fires even when the test was skipped.

```typescript
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { acquireLock, releaseLock } from './distributed-lock';

async function withExclusiveLock(
  resourceId: string,
  fn: () => Promise<void>,
  ctx: { onTestFinished: (fn: () => void | Promise<void>) => void },
): Promise<void> {
  const lockToken = await acquireLock(resourceId);

  // Register teardown directly in the test context — no afterEach needed
  ctx.onTestFinished(async () => {
    await releaseLock(resourceId, lockToken);
  });

  await fn();
}

it('modifies shared resource under exclusive lock', async (ctx) => {
  await withExclusiveLock('resource:42', async () => {
    // test body — lock is released in onTestFinished even if this throws
    expect(true).toBe(true);
  }, ctx);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `onTestFinished` is scoped to the individual test invocation and runs before the next test starts — it does not replace `afterAll` for suite-level teardown. In concurrent suites, multiple `onTestFinished` handlers from different tests may interleave; ensure handlers are idempotent and operate only on resources owned by that specific test to prevent races. [official]

---

### Pattern 484 — Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` for per-test ESM singleton isolation without `jest.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` [official]

`jest.isolateModulesAsync(fn)` creates a completely fresh module registry inside the async callback, allowing a test to `await import('module')` and receive a pristine singleton instance that is independent of the main test file's module registry. Unlike calling `jest.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` (which resets the global registry and forces every subsequent `require` to re-evaluate), `isolateModulesAsync` is scoped to the callback and leaves the outer registry intact, making it safe to use in individual tests without affecting test helpers loaded at file scope.

```typescript
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

describe('AppConfig singleton — per-test isolation', () => {
  it('returns fresh singleton when FEATURE_FLAG=on', async () => {
    let config!: Awaited<typeof import('./app-config')>;

    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      // Set env BEFORE dynamic import so module-level init sees it
      process.env.FEATURE_FLAG = 'on';
      config = await import('./app-config');
    });

    expect(config.isFeatureEnabled()).toBe(true);
    delete process.env.FEATURE_FLAG;
  });

  it('returns fresh singleton when FEATURE_FLAG=off', async () => {
    let config!: Awaited<typeof import('./app-config')>;

    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      process.env.FEATURE_FLAG = 'off';
      config = await import('./app-config');
    });

    expect(config.isFeatureEnabled()).toBe(false);
    delete process.env.FEATURE_FLAG;
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `isolateModulesAsync` has a non-trivial overhead because it creates a new module registry for each invocation — avoid calling it in tight loops or for modules without singleton initialization state. For modules that are pure functions with no module-level side effects, prefer `jest.mock()` factories instead. [official]

---

### Pattern 485 — Jest `jest.onGenerateMock()` for cross-cutting auto-mock post-processing [official]

`jest.onGenerateMock(callback)` registers a function that receives every auto-generated mock object before it is returned to the test, allowing centralized post-processing such as injecting default return values, attaching shared spies, or replacing specific method implementations. Multiple callbacks are chained — each callback receives the output of the previous — so this is safe to call in `setupFilesAfterEnv` without overwriting previous registrations. Unlike `jest.mock()` factories (which apply to a specific module path), `onGenerateMock` operates on all auto-mocked modules.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts (setupFilesAfterEnv)
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

jest.onGenerateMock((modulePath, moduleMock) => {
  // Inject a default resolved promise for every auto-mocked async method
  for (const key of Object.keys(moduleMock)) {
    const val = (moduleMock as Record<string, unknown>)[key];
    if (jest.isMockFunction(val)) {
      // If the original was async (returns Promise), keep it resolvable
      if (modulePath.includes('service') || modulePath.includes('repository')) {
        (val as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValue(undefined);
      }
    }
  }
  return moduleMock;
});

// In test file — no per-test setup needed; service methods resolve by default
jest.mock('./user-service');
import { UserService } from './user-service';

test('getAllUsers returns empty array by default', async () => {
  (UserService.prototype.getAll as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValue([]);
  const svc = new UserService();
  await expect(svc.getAll()).resolves.toEqual([]);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `onGenerateMock` runs only for auto-mocked modules (those mocked without a factory); modules with explicit factory functions are not processed. Overusing it leads to implicit global behaviour that is hard to trace. Reserve it for truly universal conventions (e.g., "all service auto-mocks have resolved-by-default async methods") and document the registration in a top-level `setupFilesAfterEnv` comment. [official]

---

### Pattern 486 — Playwright `page.routeFromHAR()` for deterministic network replay in isolation-sensitive E2E tests [official]

`page.routeFromHAR(harFile, options)` replays pre-recorded HTTP Archive (HAR) responses for matching URLs, completely replacing live network calls during a test. The `update: false` mode (default) enforces deterministic replay — any request not present in the HAR file can be configured to throw, fall through, or be blocked, making network state fully reproducible across CI runs. Recording is done with `update: true` locally and the `.har` file committed to version control alongside the test.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

test.use({
  // All tests in this file use HAR replay — no live network
});

test('checkout flow renders correctly with pre-recorded API data', async ({ page }) => {
  const harPath = path.join(__dirname, 'fixtures', 'checkout.har');

  await page.routeFromHAR(harPath, {
    url: '*/**/api/**',         // only intercept API calls
    update: false,               // replay mode — fail if request not in HAR
    updateContent: 'embed',      // content stored inline in HAR
    notFound: 'abort',           // block any API call missing from the HAR
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Summary' })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.getByText('$99.00')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** HAR files must be regenerated when API contracts change; stale HAR files cause subtle failures where the UI silently uses outdated response shapes. Keep HAR files focused by scoping `url` patterns tightly to the service under test, and use `notFound: 'abort'` rather than `notFound: 'fallback'` in CI to surface unmocked requests immediately as test failures rather than intermittent flakiness. [official]

---

### Pattern 487 — Node.js `node:test` `t.mock` per-test automatic restore for deterministic method isolation [official]

When using the built-in `node:test` module, mocks registered via `t.mock.method(object, 'methodName', implementation)` are automatically restored to their original values after the test completes — no `afterEach` cleanup is required. This per-test automatic restore model contrasts with Jest's `jest.spyOn` which requires explicit `mockRestore()` or `restoreMocks: true` in config. The scoped `t.mock` is tied to the test's `MockTracker` instance; subtests receive their own tracker and do not inherit parent mocks.

```typescript
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

const db = {
  query: async (sql: string) => ({ rows: [] }),
};

describe('UserRepository', () => {
  test('findById returns user row', async (t) => {
    // t.mock.method auto-restores after THIS test only
    t.mock.method(db, 'query', async (_sql: string) => ({
      rows: [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }],
    }));

    const { UserRepository } = await import('./user-repository.js');
    const repo = new UserRepository(db as any);
    const user = await repo.findById(1);

    assert.strictEqual(user?.name, 'Alice');
    assert.strictEqual(db.query.mock.callCount(), 1);
    // db.query is restored to original after this test
  });

  test('findById with real db returns empty', async (_t) => {
    // db.query is back to the real implementation here
    const { UserRepository } = await import('./user-repository.js');
    const repo = new UserRepository(db as any);
    const user = await repo.findById(999);
    assert.strictEqual(user, undefined);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The per-test auto-restore guarantee only applies to mocks registered through the test's `t.mock` tracker. Global stubs (e.g., direct `originalMethod = obj.method; obj.method = () => {}`) are not tracked and must be cleaned up manually. For module-level mocking (`t.mock.module()`), each call creates a new cached version — call `mock.restore()` explicitly if you need to re-mock the same specifier with a different implementation in a later test. [official]

---

### Pattern 488 — Playwright `auto: true` worker-scoped fixture for single-sign-on authentication state isolation [official]

Defining a `storageState`-loading fixture with `scope: 'worker'` and `auto: true` ensures each worker process initialises its own browser session from a pre-recorded auth storage state file exactly once, then reuses that session for all tests in the worker. This avoids per-test login flows while keeping session state isolated across workers. If a test corrupts the session (e.g., by calling a logout endpoint), subsequent tests in the same worker start from a poisoned state — the fixture should verify session health and re-authenticate if necessary.

```typescript
// fixtures.ts
import { test as base, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

type WorkerFixtures = { authedContext: BrowserContext };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  authedContext: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      const storageStatePath = path.join(
        __dirname,
        '.auth',
        `worker-${process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX ?? '0'}.json`,
      );

      const context = await browser.newContext({ storageState: storageStatePath });

      // Health-check: verify session is still valid
      const page = await context.newPage();
      const resp = await page.request.get('/api/me');
      if (!resp.ok()) {
        // Re-authenticate if session expired mid-worker-run
        await page.goto('/login');
        await page.fill('[name=email]', process.env.TEST_EMAIL!);
        await page.fill('[name=password]', process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
        await page.click('[type=submit]');
        await context.storageState({ path: storageStatePath });
      }
      await page.close();

      await use(context);
      await context.close();
    },
    { scope: 'worker', auto: true },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped auth fixtures share session state across all tests in a worker. Tests that mutate auth state (role changes, MFA enrolment, logout) must restore it before returning, or the test must be tagged with `test.use({ storageState: freshStateFile })` to opt into a private session. Never use worker-scoped auth fixtures for tests that intentionally test session invalidation behaviour. [official]

---

### Pattern 489 — Vitest `test.extend()` `injected: true` fixture for project-level fixture override without wrapper re-export [official]

Marking a fixture as `injected: true` in a `test.extend()` definition makes it overridable per Vitest project via the `provide` config option in `vitest.config.ts`, without requiring test files to import from a different test wrapper. This is the canonical way to vary a fixture value across environments (e.g., a different `apiBaseUrl` per CI project) without maintaining multiple test wrapper modules. The fixture must be exported from the test wrapper; calling `test.extend({ fixtureKey: [defaultFn, { injected: true }] })` marks the slot.

```typescript
// fixtures/base.ts
import { test as vitest } from 'vitest';

export const test = vitest.extend<{ apiBaseUrl: string }>({
  apiBaseUrl: [
    // Default implementation — used unless overridden by project config
    async ({}, use) => {
      await use('http://localhost:3000');
    },
    { injected: true }, // project can override via provide: { apiBaseUrl: '...' }
  ],
});

// vitest.config.ts (staging project)
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        test: {
          name: 'staging',
          include: ['**/*.e2e.ts'],
          provide: {
            apiBaseUrl: 'https://staging.example.com',
          },
        },
      },
    ],
  },
});

// In test file — no import change needed; apiBaseUrl comes from project provide
import { test } from '../fixtures/base';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

test('health endpoint responds', async ({ apiBaseUrl }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/api/health`);
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `injected: true` is a compile-time contract — the `provide` key must exactly match the fixture name, and TypeScript will not catch mismatches between the `provide` object keys and the declared fixture types unless the project config is also typed. Use the `InferProvide<typeof test>` utility type from Vitest to derive the expected shape and pass it to the config's `provide` option for end-to-end type safety. [official]

---

### Pattern 490 — Jest `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` for `requestAnimationFrame` isolation in UI animation tests [official]

`jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` advances fake timers by exactly 16 ms (one 60 fps animation frame) and executes any pending `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks scheduled for that frame boundary. Unlike `jest.runAllTimers()` which runs all pending timers recursively, `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` stops at exactly one frame boundary, allowing per-frame assertion checkpoints without triggering the entire animation sequence at once. This is essential for testing animation state machines where intermediate frames must be asserted.

```typescript
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { Animator } from './animator';

jest.useFakeTimers();

describe('Animator — per-frame isolation', () => {
  let animator: Animator;

  beforeEach(() => {
    animator = new Animator({ duration: 300 }); // 300ms = ~18 frames
    animator.start();
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    jest.clearAllTimers();
    jest.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('is at 0% progress before any frames advance', () => {
    expect(animator.progress).toBe(0);
  });

  it('is at ~5% after first frame (16ms / 300ms)', () => {
    jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame(); // advance exactly one rAF frame
    expect(animator.progress).toBeCloseTo(0.053, 2);
  });

  it('is at 100% after all frames complete', () => {
    // Advance ~19 frames to cover 300ms (19 * 16 = 304ms)
    for (let i = 0; i < 19; i++) {
      jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame();
    }
    expect(animator.progress).toBe(1);
    expect(animator.isComplete).toBe(true);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` is only available when `requestAnimationFrame` is included in the fake timer scope (it is faked by default in jsdom environments; in Node environments you must pass `{ now: ... }` or polyfill `requestAnimationFrame` on `global` before calling `jest.useFakeTimers()`). If the animation logic mixes `rAF` callbacks with `setTimeout` callbacks, use `jest.advanceTimersByTime(16)` instead, which fires both timer types at the 16 ms boundary. [official]

### Pattern 491 — Vitest `vi.doMock()` for within-file per-test module variant switching without factory hoisting [official]

`vi.doMock(path, factory)` is the non-hoisted equivalent of `vi.mock()` — it registers a mock factory that takes effect on the next `import()` call, rather than being hoisted to the top of the file. This allows a single test file to test the same module under multiple configurations by calling `vi.doMock()` with different factories before each dynamic import, preceded by `vi.resetModules()` to clear the module registry cache. Without `vi.resetModules()`, the second import returns the already-cached module from the first test rather than re-evaluating with the new factory.

```typescript
import { beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';

describe('FeatureFlag — per-variant module switching', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.resetModules(); // clear cache so doMock factory re-runs on next import
  });

  it('renders new UI when FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=true', async () => {
    vi.doMock('./config', () => ({
      getConfig: () => ({ featureNewCheckout: true }),
    }));
    const { renderCheckout } = await import('./checkout-page');
    const html = renderCheckout();
    expect(html).toContain('new-checkout-flow');
  });

  it('renders legacy UI when FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=false', async () => {
    vi.doMock('./config', () => ({
      getConfig: () => ({ featureNewCheckout: false }),
    }));
    const { renderCheckout } = await import('./checkout-page');
    const html = renderCheckout();
    expect(html).toContain('legacy-checkout');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Every test that calls `vi.resetModules()` pays the cost of re-evaluating all transitively imported modules on the next import — this can be 50–200 ms per test in large module graphs. Limit `vi.doMock`/`vi.resetModules` to tests that genuinely require module-level variant switching; prefer constructor injection or `vi.stubEnv` for config variants that don't require different module-level initialization. [official]

---

### Pattern 492 — Node.js `node:test` `context.mock.timers.enable({ apis })` selective timer mocking for per-test clock control [official]

The `node:test` built-in test runner's `context.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'Date'] })` enables fake timers scoped to the current test's `MockTracker`. The `apis` array specifies which timer APIs to intercept — unspecified APIs remain real. When both `setTimeout` and `Date` are faked, `context.mock.timers.tick(n)` advances both clocks together, ensuring `Date.now()` inside a timer callback returns the simulated timestamp rather than the real wall clock. Each test gets its own timer registry, so there is no cross-test timer leakage when using the `context.mock` API.

```typescript
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

interface CacheEntry { value: unknown; expiresAt: number }
function createTtlCache(ttlMs: number) {
  const store = new Map<string, CacheEntry>();
  return {
    set(key: string, value: unknown) {
      store.set(key, { value, expiresAt: Date.now() + ttlMs });
    },
    get(key: string): unknown | undefined {
      const entry = store.get(key);
      if (!entry || Date.now() > entry.expiresAt) return undefined;
      return entry.value;
    },
  };
}

describe('TtlCache', () => {
  test('returns value before TTL expires', (context) => {
    context.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['Date'], now: 1_000_000 });
    const cache = createTtlCache(5_000);
    cache.set('k', 'v');
    context.mock.timers.tick(4_999); // advance 4.999 s — still within TTL
    assert.strictEqual(cache.get('k'), 'v');
  });

  test('returns undefined after TTL expires', (context) => {
    context.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ['Date'], now: 1_000_000 });
    const cache = createTtlCache(5_000);
    cache.set('k', 'v');
    context.mock.timers.tick(5_001); // advance past TTL
    assert.strictEqual(cache.get('k'), undefined);
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `context.mock.timers` restores automatically at test end, but only for APIs that were in the `apis` array. If you add a third-party library that calls `setInterval` and `setTimeout` is not in the `apis` list, those calls are real and may fire during later tests. When in doubt, enumerate all timer APIs explicitly; omitting one is a common source of test flakiness that is hard to reproduce because it only appears when two tests run in the same process sequentially. [official]

---

### Pattern 493 — Jest snapshot `toMatchInlineSnapshot()` with `propertyMatchers` for deterministic volatile-field isolation [official]

`toMatchInlineSnapshot(propertyMatchers, snapshot)` allows key fields that change on every run (timestamps, UUIDs, generated IDs) to be replaced by asymmetric matchers before the snapshot comparison, while all remaining fields are verified verbatim against the inline snapshot string. This eliminates the need to mock `Date.now()` or UUID generators just to produce a stable snapshot, keeping the test focused on structural correctness rather than value determinism for volatile fields.

```typescript
import { describe, expect, it, jest } from '@jest/globals';
import { createUser } from './user-factory';

describe('createUser — snapshot isolation', () => {
  it('produces the expected user shape', () => {
    const user = createUser({ name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' });

    expect(user).toMatchInlineSnapshot(
      // Property matchers replace non-deterministic fields
      {
        id: expect.stringMatching(/^usr_[a-z0-9]{16}$/),
        createdAt: expect.any(String),
        updatedAt: expect.any(String),
      },
      // Remaining fields are exact — snapshot updated by jest --updateSnapshot
      `
      Object {
        "createdAt": Any<String>,
        "id": StringMatching /^usr_[a-z0-9]{16}$/,
        "name": "Alice",
        "role": "admin",
        "updatedAt": Any<String>,
      }
      `,
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Inline snapshots are automatically updated in-place by Jest's `--updateSnapshot` flag, which modifies source files during CI if the test environment allows writes. Configure `ci: true` (or rely on `--ci` flag) to prevent silent snapshot updates in pull request builds — `--ci` causes snapshot mismatches to fail rather than auto-update, ensuring snapshot changes require an intentional developer action. [official]

---

### Pattern 494 — Vitest `vi.mock()` returning a tracked class constructor for instance-level isolation verification [official]

When the module under test `new`s a dependency class, use `vi.mock()` with a factory that returns a mock class whose constructor and prototype methods are all `vi.fn()` instances. Access `MockClass.mock.instances[0]` to retrieve the instance created during the test and assert on the methods called on that specific instance. This avoids the common anti-pattern of asserting on the class constructor's call count without verifying which methods were invoked on the resulting instance.

```typescript
import { beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';

vi.mock('./email-sender', () => {
  const MockEmailSender = vi.fn().mockImplementation(() => ({
    send: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'msg-123' }),
    connect: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
    disconnect: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  }));
  return { EmailSender: MockEmailSender };
});

import { EmailSender } from './email-sender';
import { NotificationService } from './notification-service';

describe('NotificationService — constructor isolation', () => {
  let service: NotificationService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
    service = new NotificationService();
  });

  it('connects on init and sends welcome email', async () => {
    await service.init();
    await service.sendWelcome('alice@example.com');

    // Assert on the instance created during NotificationService construction
    const emailSenderInstance = (EmailSender as ReturnType<typeof vi.fn>).mock.instances[0];
    expect(emailSenderInstance.connect).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(emailSenderInstance.send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'alice@example.com', subject: 'Welcome' }),
    );
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `MockClass.mock.instances[0]` is only populated when the mock class is called with `new`; direct factory function calls do not create entries in `instances`. If the module under test conditionally instantiates the class (e.g., lazy-loading), `instances[0]` will be `undefined` until the first instantiation — guard the assertion with `expect(instances).toHaveLength(1)` before accessing `instances[0]` to avoid confusing `undefined` access errors. [official]

### Pattern 495 — Community pattern: `vi.mock()` factory closure over mutable `let` binding for per-test mock value switching [community]

A common community pattern for changing mock return values across tests without calling `vi.doMock()` + `vi.resetModules()` is to declare a `let` binding above the `vi.mock()` factory that closes over the variable, then reassign the binding in `beforeEach`. Since the mock factory runs once at module load time and the mock function reads the closed-over variable at call time, each test can set a different value by updating the `let` binding without re-evaluating the module graph. This is especially effective for config-flag-controlled code paths.

```typescript
import { beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';

// Mutable binding — reassigned per test to switch mock behaviour
let mockFeatureFlags: Record<string, boolean> = {};

vi.mock('./feature-flags', () => ({
  // Factory runs ONCE; the function reads the binding at call time
  getFlags: vi.fn(() => mockFeatureFlags),
  isEnabled: vi.fn((flag: string) => mockFeatureFlags[flag] ?? false),
}));

import { renderDashboard } from './dashboard';

describe('Dashboard — feature flag switching via closure', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    // Reset to safe defaults before each test
    mockFeatureFlags = {};
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it('renders new analytics widget when flag is on', () => {
    mockFeatureFlags = { 'analytics-v2': true };
    const html = renderDashboard();
    expect(html).toContain('analytics-v2-widget');
  });

  it('renders classic widget when flag is off', () => {
    mockFeatureFlags = { 'analytics-v2': false };
    const html = renderDashboard();
    expect(html).toContain('classic-analytics-widget');
  });

  it('renders nothing for unknown flags', () => {
    // mockFeatureFlags is {} — flag is absent
    const html = renderDashboard();
    expect(html).not.toContain('analytics-v2-widget');
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff.** This pattern requires the `let` binding to be declared in module scope above the `vi.mock()` call, which means Vitest's hoisting transform will see it before the factory. The critical gotcha is that the binding must be a `let` (not `const`) and must not be declared inside the factory itself — factory-internal variables are scoped to the factory closure and cannot be mutated from `beforeEach`. The pattern does not work across worker boundaries in `pool: 'forks'` mode because each forked worker has an independent copy of the module-scope binding. [community]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 53

326. **Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` does NOT affect environment variables read at module evaluation time — if a module executes `const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL` at import time (outside any function), `vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgres://...')` called in `beforeEach` has no effect on `dbUrl` because the assignment already happened when the module was first loaded, before any test ran; the test reads the stubbed value correctly via `process.env.DATABASE_URL` but the module-level constant retains its original value.** [official]
    WHY: JavaScript modules are evaluated once when first imported, and module-level `const`/`let` declarations that read `process.env` are evaluated at that single point. `vi.stubEnv()` modifies the `process.env` object in place, which is visible to future property reads but cannot retroactively change the value already captured in a module-level variable. To test code that reads config at evaluation time, combine `vi.stubEnv()` with `vi.resetModules()` and a dynamic `await import()` inside the test body so the module is re-evaluated with the new environment value.

327. **Jest `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` calls `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks but does NOT drain the microtask queue after each callback — an `async` `rAF` callback that `await`s a Promise will be suspended at the first `await` and its continuation will not run until the test explicitly yields to the microtask queue with `await Promise.resolve()` or `await new Promise(queueMicrotask => queueMicrotask(undefined))`, causing assertions made immediately after `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` to see pre-await state.** [official]
    WHY: `jest.advanceTimersToNextFrame()` is synchronous — it invokes the queued `rAF` callbacks and then returns. When a `rAF` callback is `async`, the function starts executing synchronously up to its first `await`, then suspends and queues a microtask continuation. `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` returns before those continuations run. This is identical to the `advanceTimersByTime()` / async-callback interaction (Gotcha 317) but affects `requestAnimationFrame` specifically. The fix is to await a microtask drain (`await Promise.resolve()`) after each `advanceTimersToNextFrame()` call when the callback contains async logic.

328. **Node.js `node:test` `t.mock.module()` caches the mocked version for the lifetime of the module cache — if two tests in the same file call `t.mock.module('./dep', { namedExports: ... })` with different shapes, the second call receives the FIRST cached mock because `t.mock.module()` does not invalidate the existing module cache entry; the second test sees the first test's mock implementation, leading to assertion failures that are difficult to diagnose because the mock appears to have been "registered" by the second test.** [official]
    WHY: Node.js's `node:test` module mocking uses the same module loader cache as `require`/`import`. When `t.mock.module(specifier)` is first called, it inserts a synthetic entry into the cache. Subsequent calls to `t.mock.module()` with the same specifier in the same process check the cache, find the existing synthetic entry, and return it rather than creating a new one. The fix is to call `mock.restore()` on the mock returned by the first `t.mock.module()` call before the second test registers its version, or to use `t.mock.method()` on the already-loaded module object instead of re-mocking at the module level.

329. **Playwright `test.use({ storageState })` fixture override does NOT propagate into worker-scoped fixtures defined in the same `test.extend()` — the worker fixture is initialized once at worker startup before any `test.use()` calls are processed, so a `browserContext` fixture with `scope: 'worker'` that reads `storageState` during its setup will always see the project-level default, not the per-describe override registered by `test.use()`.** [official]
    WHY: Playwright resolves worker-scoped fixtures at worker initialization time, which occurs before any test files are parsed or `test.use()` calls are evaluated. The `scope: 'worker'` contract means the fixture value is fixed for the worker's entire lifetime. `test.use()` fixture overrides are test-scoped (they apply per test invocation), so they cannot retroactively change a worker fixture that was already initialized. If you need per-describe `storageState` isolation, the browser context must be test-scoped (`scope: 'test'`), accepting the per-test setup overhead in exchange for isolation correctness.

330. **Vitest `vi.mock()` closure over a `let` binding that is reassigned to an object reference in `beforeEach` will NOT see the new object's properties if the mock function captures the INITIAL object reference — `vi.fn(() => mockConfig.flag)` correctly re-reads the binding's current value because it dereferences `mockConfig` at call time, but `vi.fn().mockReturnValue(mockConfig.flag)` captures the VALUE of `flag` at the time `mockReturnValue` is called and will NOT update when `mockConfig` is reassigned or mutated in a later `beforeEach`.** [community]
    WHY: `vi.fn().mockReturnValue(x)` stores `x` by value at the time of the call — it does not close over the variable `x`. When `mockConfig.flag` evaluates to `true` at file load time and is passed to `mockReturnValue`, the mock permanently returns `true` regardless of later mutations to `mockConfig`. The fix is to use `vi.fn(() => mockConfig.flag)` (factory form) instead, which evaluates the expression at call time. This is a subtle but common mistake when migrating `jest.fn().mockReturnValue(...)` patterns to per-test-variant patterns where the factory-closure approach is required.

### New Patterns

**Pattern 496: Vitest `test.signal` AbortController integration for long-lived resource cleanup** [official]
Vitest 3.2+ exposes `context.signal` — an `AbortSignal` that fires on test timeout, bail, or Ctrl-C. Wiring async resources to that signal guarantees teardown even when `afterEach` never runs (e.g., in a bail scenario). This is strictly stronger than a plain `afterEach` for I/O-holding resources.

```typescript
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createWebSocketClient } from './ws-client';

it('streams events until assertion or timeout', async ({ signal }) => {
  // Pass the test's own AbortSignal to the resource constructor
  const client = createWebSocketClient('wss://localhost:8080', { signal });

  const events: string[] = [];
  client.on('message', (msg: string) => events.push(msg));

  await client.connect();
  // signal.aborted becomes true on test timeout → client auto-closes
  await client.send('{"type":"subscribe","channel":"prices"}');

  await vi.waitFor(() => expect(events.length).toBeGreaterThan(0), {
    timeout: 3000,
  });

  expect(events[0]).toContain('"channel":"prices"');
  // No explicit close needed: signal fires → client's internal AbortController listener calls close()
});
```

Tradeoff: The resource constructor must accept an `AbortSignal` option. Adapting legacy libraries requires a thin wrapper that calls `resource.destroy()` inside `signal.addEventListener('abort', ...)`. If the underlying resource ignores the signal the cleanup is silently skipped — always verify teardown in a first test that intentionally times out during development.

---

**Pattern 497: Jest `defineConfig` + `mergeConfig` for type-safe multi-project isolation** [official]
Jest 30 introduced `defineConfig` and `mergeConfig` helpers that replace the untyped `Config` import pattern. Using them to compose a base config with per-project overrides gives TypeScript compile-time guarantees on every isolation option (testEnvironment, resetModules, setupFilesAfterEnv) across a monorepo.

```typescript
// jest.config.base.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export const baseConfig = defineConfig({
  resetMocks: true,
  restoreMocks: true,
  clearMocks: true,
  testTimeout: 10_000,
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
});

// packages/api/jest.config.ts
import { mergeConfig } from 'jest';
import { baseConfig } from '../../jest.config.base';

export default mergeConfig(baseConfig, {
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  resetModules: true,           // API package uses module-level singletons
  globalSetup: '<rootDir>/global-setup.ts',
  globalTeardown: '<rootDir>/global-teardown.ts',
});

// packages/ui/jest.config.ts
import { mergeConfig } from 'jest';
import { baseConfig } from '../../jest.config.base';

export default mergeConfig(baseConfig, {
  testEnvironment: 'jsdom',
  testEnvironmentOptions: { url: 'http://localhost:3000' },
  // No resetModules: UI components do not hold singleton state
});
```

Tradeoff: `mergeConfig` performs a shallow merge for arrays (e.g., `setupFilesAfterEnv` is concatenated, not replaced). If a package must override rather than extend an array option, assign the array in the `defineConfig` call directly and avoid specifying it in the base. For `transform` maps the merge is additive — later keys win, so base transforms are preserved unless a project explicitly shadows the same key.

---

**Pattern 498: Playwright `{ timeout }` per-fixture timeout allocation for slow provisioning** [official]
Playwright allows each fixture to declare its own timeout budget via the `{ timeout: ms }` option in the tuple syntax. Slow database provisioning or container startup that would otherwise blow the per-test timeout can be isolated to the fixture, keeping per-test timeout values tight.

```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { PgContainer } from './test-infra/pg-container';

type Fixtures = { db: PgContainer };

const test = base.extend<Fixtures>({
  db: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Container startup can take 20–30 s; isolate cost to the fixture budget
      const container = await PgContainer.start({ schema: 'test_schema' });
      await container.migrate();
      await use(container);
      await container.stop();
    },
    { scope: 'worker', timeout: 45_000 }, // 45 s fixture budget, not charged to each test
  ],
});

test('inserts a row and retrieves it', async ({ db }) => {
  await db.query(`INSERT INTO users(name) VALUES ('alice')`);
  const { rows } = await db.query(`SELECT name FROM users`);
  expect(rows).toEqual([{ name: 'alice' }]);
});
```

Tradeoff: The fixture timeout is consumed once per worker (scope: 'worker') or once per test (scope: 'test'). A 45 s worker-scoped fixture budget is cheap when 50 tests share the worker; it becomes expensive if combined with `fullyParallel: true` and many workers, each paying the startup cost independently. Profile worker count × fixture cost before choosing scope.

---

**Pattern 499: Vitest `vi.mock(import(...))` type-safe dynamic module promise** [official]
Vitest supports passing a dynamic `import()` expression directly to `vi.mock()` to give the mock factory full TypeScript types for `importOriginal`. This eliminates the `as typeof import(...)` cast that was previously required when extending the real module.

```typescript
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';

vi.mock(import('./analytics-client'), async (importOriginal) => {
  // importOriginal is typed as () => Promise<typeof import('./analytics-client')>
  const real = await importOriginal();
  return {
    ...real,
    // Override only the side-effectful method; keep pure helpers real
    track: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ queued: true }),
    flush: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ sent: 0 }),
  };
});

import { track, flush, buildEventPayload } from './analytics-client';

describe('analytics isolation', () => {
  it('calls track with correct event shape', async () => {
    const payload = buildEventPayload('page_view', { path: '/home' });
    await track(payload);
    expect(track).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ event: 'page_view' }),
    );
  });

  it('real buildEventPayload logic is preserved', () => {
    const p = buildEventPayload('click', { target: 'cta' });
    expect(p).toHaveProperty('timestamp');
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: The `import(...)` form requires Vitest's Vite plugin to be configured; it does not work in plain Node.js or Jest. If your monorepo uses both Jest and Vitest, the import-expression syntax must be guarded by project boundaries. The factory still runs at module evaluation time (hoisted), so top-level `await` inside it is safe but adds startup latency.

---

**Pattern 500: Jest `setupFilesAfterEnv` global `afterEach` for guaranteed mock restoration** [official]
Rather than relying on every test file to call `jest.restoreAllMocks()`, register a global `afterEach` in `setupFilesAfterEnv`. This gives a single, project-wide safety net that fires even if a test file's own `afterEach` throws, preventing spy/mock leak across files.

```typescript
// jest.setup.ts  (referenced by setupFilesAfterEnv)
import { afterEach, beforeEach } from '@jest/globals';

// Restore all spies after every test — prevents bleed between test files
afterEach(() => {
  jest.restoreAllMocks();
});

// Reset module registry if a test called jest.resetModules() mid-test
afterEach(() => {
  // No-op when resetModules is not called; safe to call unconditionally
  // jest.resetModules() is idempotent
});

// Warn on leaked real timers — catches tests that call useFakeTimers without cleanup
afterEach(() => {
  // Check if fake timers are still active after test completes
  const timerState = (jest as any)._fakeTimersAreEnabled?.();
  if (timerState) {
    console.warn(
      `[jest.setup] Fake timers still active after test: "${expect.getState().currentTestName}". ` +
      `Call jest.useRealTimers() in afterEach or add restoreMocks: true to jest.config.`,
    );
    jest.useRealTimers();
  }
});
```

Tradeoff: Global teardown hooks in `setupFilesAfterEnv` run in every test file, including files where the cleanup is unnecessary. On a 10 000-test suite the extra `restoreAllMocks()` call costs ~0.1 ms per test — negligible. The real cost is discoverability: developers reading a test file won't see the restoration hook and may not realize why mocks are clean at each test boundary. Document in CLAUDE.md or a `jest.setup.ts` header comment.

---

**Pattern 501: Vitest `aroundEach` + database transaction rollback for hermetic integration tests** [official]
Vitest 4.1 introduced `aroundEach`, a hook that wraps each test in a single try/finally closure with guaranteed teardown. This is stronger than the `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pair for transaction rollback: even if `afterEach` would be skipped by an unhandled throw, `aroundEach`'s `finally` branch always runs.

```typescript
import { aroundEach, describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { pool } from './db';

describe('Order repository — isolated transactions', () => {
  // aroundEach provides a `use` callback: call it once inside the hook body
  aroundEach(async (use) => {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    // Inject the transactional client into the test context
    (globalThis as any).__txClient = client;

    try {
      await use();           // run the test inside the transaction
    } finally {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      client.release();
      delete (globalThis as any).__txClient;
    }
  });

  it('creates an order row visible within the transaction', async () => {
    const client = (globalThis as any).__txClient;
    await client.query(
      `INSERT INTO orders(id, status) VALUES ('ord-1', 'pending')`,
    );
    const { rows } = await client.query(
      `SELECT status FROM orders WHERE id = 'ord-1'`,
    );
    expect(rows[0].status).toBe('pending');
  });

  it('sees an empty orders table — previous test rolled back', async () => {
    const client = (globalThis as any).__txClient;
    const { rows } = await client.query(`SELECT * FROM orders`);
    expect(rows).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `aroundEach` calls `use()` exactly once. If you accidentally call it zero or twice Vitest throws a `FixtureUsageError`. Also, `aroundEach` receives the fixture context only in Vitest 4.1+; earlier versions pass no arguments. The `globalThis` injection pattern used above is pragmatic but couples tests to a global; prefer Vitest `test.extend()` fixture injection for cleaner API boundaries.

---

**Pattern 502: Playwright `page.clock.install()` before `page.goto()` for deterministic time-travel in E2E tests** [official]
Calling `await page.clock.install({ time: fixedMs })` before `goto()` ensures the page's `Date`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, and `performance.now()` are all frozen at the specified instant from the very first script execution. Any code that reads the clock at module-evaluation time (e.g., session expiry computed at page load) will see the deterministic value.

```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('session-expiry banner appears 5 minutes before token expires', async ({ page }) => {
  // Pin clock to a known instant — token issued "55 minutes ago" (expires in 5 min)
  const baseTime = new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00Z').getTime();
  await page.clock.install({ time: baseTime });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Advance clock by 4 minutes — banner should not yet appear
  await page.clock.fastForward(4 * 60_000);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).not.toBeVisible();

  // Advance one more minute — now inside the 5-minute warning window
  await page.clock.fastForward(60_000);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /session expiring/i })).toBeVisible();

  // Advance to actual expiry — redirect to login
  await page.clock.fastForward(5 * 60_000);
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
});
```

Tradeoff: `page.clock.install()` must be called before any page navigation; calling it after `goto()` will not affect scripts that already evaluated. The clock is per-page, not per-browser-context — each new `page` fixture instance starts with the real system clock unless `install` is re-called. For worker-scoped pages shared across tests, install the clock inside an `aroundEach` or `beforeEach` to ensure each test gets a fresh time origin.

---

**Pattern 503: Node.js `node:test` `t.mock.module()` with `mock.restore()` for per-test ESM re-mocking** [official]
`node:test` `t.mock.module()` returns a `MockModuleContext` with a `.restore()` method. Calling `restore()` removes the synthetic cache entry so the next test can register a different factory for the same specifier — enabling per-test ESM module variant switching without forking processes.

```typescript
import { describe, it, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

describe('feature flag driven behaviour', () => {
  it('renders premium UI when flag is on', async (t) => {
    const flagMock = t.mock.module('./flags', {
      namedExports: { isPremium: () => true },
    });

    const { renderHeader } = await import('./header');
    assert.match(renderHeader(), /premium-header/);

    flagMock.restore(); // evict from module cache before next test
  });

  it('renders standard UI when flag is off', async (t) => {
    // Can now re-register the same specifier with a different factory
    const flagMock = t.mock.module('./flags', {
      namedExports: { isPremium: () => false },
    });

    const { renderHeader } = await import('./header');
    assert.match(renderHeader(), /standard-header/);

    flagMock.restore();
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `mock.restore()` must be called before the next `import()` of the target module, otherwise the stale cached module is returned. The call order matters: restore the mock from test N before test N+1 begins. In `node:test` this is safest done at the end of each test body (not in `afterEach`) because `afterEach` in `node:test` runs after the test's assertions but its timing relative to the next test's `import()` is not guaranteed in all Node.js versions.

---

**Pattern 504: Vitest `vi.stubGlobal` + `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` for browser-API shimming in Node environment** [official]
Vitest's `vi.stubGlobal(name, value)` registers a replacement for any `globalThis` property and tracks it for automatic restoration. `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in `afterEach` (or via `unstubGlobals: true` in vitest.config) restores all stubs atomically, preventing global pollution between tests when shimming browser APIs like `fetch`, `crypto`, `matchMedia`, or `ResizeObserver`.

```typescript
import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from 'vitest';

describe('useGeolocation hook — browser API isolation', () => {
  let geolocationMock: { getCurrentPosition: ReturnType<typeof vi.fn> };

  beforeEach(() => {
    geolocationMock = {
      getCurrentPosition: vi.fn((success) =>
        success({ coords: { latitude: 48.8566, longitude: 2.3522 } }),
      ),
    };
    vi.stubGlobal('navigator', {
      ...globalThis.navigator,
      geolocation: geolocationMock,
    });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    vi.unstubAllGlobals(); // atomically removes every stubGlobal registration
  });

  it('resolves coordinates from geolocation API', async () => {
    const { getLocation } = await import('./geolocation-service');
    const coords = await getLocation();
    expect(coords).toEqual({ lat: 48.8566, lng: 2.3522 });
    expect(geolocationMock.getCurrentPosition).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });

  it('throws when geolocation is denied', async () => {
    geolocationMock.getCurrentPosition.mockImplementation((_s, error) =>
      error({ code: 1, message: 'User denied Geolocation' }),
    );
    const { getLocation } = await import('./geolocation-service');
    await expect(getLocation()).rejects.toThrow('User denied Geolocation');
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `vi.stubGlobal('navigator', ...)` replaces the entire `navigator` object. If the code under test reads other `navigator` properties (e.g., `userAgent`, `onLine`), the spread `...globalThis.navigator` must include them or they will be `undefined`. A safer approach for partial shimming is `vi.spyOn(globalThis.navigator, 'geolocation', 'get')` when the property is configurable, which avoids replacing unrelated navigator fields.

---

**Pattern 505: MSW v2 `server.boundary()` per-render handler scoping for React component tests** [official]
MSW v2's `server.boundary()` wraps a React render in a per-render handler scope. Handlers registered inside the boundary are isolated to that render and do not affect other concurrent renders or tests. This is the canonical MSW pattern for component tests that need different API response shapes.

```typescript
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import { server } from '../mocks/server';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { UserProfile } from './UserProfile';

describe('UserProfile — MSW boundary isolation', () => {
  it('displays user name on success', async () => {
    await server.boundary(async () => {
      server.use(
        http.get('/api/user/:id', () =>
          HttpResponse.json({ id: '1', name: 'Alice', role: 'admin' }),
        ),
      );
      render(<UserProfile userId="1" />);
      await waitFor(() =>
        expect(screen.getByText('Alice')).toBeInTheDocument(),
      );
    });
  });

  it('displays error state on 404', async () => {
    await server.boundary(async () => {
      server.use(
        http.get('/api/user/:id', () =>
          HttpResponse.json({ error: 'not found' }, { status: 404 }),
        ),
      );
      render(<UserProfile userId="99" />);
      await waitFor(() =>
        expect(screen.getByRole('alert')).toHaveTextContent('User not found'),
      );
    });
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `server.boundary()` requires MSW v2.4+. It does not support handler persistence across `boundary()` calls — each invocation gets a fresh handler stack derived from the `server.use()` calls made inside. Handlers registered outside the boundary (at `beforeAll` level) are inherited as defaults and can be overridden inside the boundary. If a handler needs to track call counts across tests, use `server.use()` at describe-scope outside a boundary and check `handler.mock` after all tests finish.

---

**Pattern 506: Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks` for surfacing leaked timer and promise handles** [official]
Vitest 4.1 introduced `detectAsyncLeaks: true` in `vitest.config`. When enabled, Vitest instruments `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Promise`, and `queueMicrotask` to detect handles that are still open when a test completes. Leaked handles surface as test warnings rather than silent flakiness in later tests.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,    // warn on open handles after test completion
    pool: 'forks',             // required: async leak detection works in forks pool
    poolOptions: {
      forks: { singleFork: false },
    },
  },
});

// Test that previously leaked silently — now surfaces a warning
it('polls until condition — must cancel on completion', async () => {
  let tick = 0;
  const intervalId = setInterval(() => tick++, 100);

  await vi.waitFor(() => expect(tick).toBeGreaterThan(2), { timeout: 500 });

  // WITHOUT this line, detectAsyncLeaks emits: "Async resource leaked: Timeout"
  clearInterval(intervalId);

  expect(tick).toBeGreaterThan(2);
});
```

Tradeoff: `detectAsyncLeaks` requires `pool: 'forks'`; it is incompatible with `pool: 'threads'` because V8 worker threads do not expose the async hooks needed for handle tracking. Enabling it adds ~5–15% overhead per test due to async hook instrumentation. On a suite with intentionally long-lived background tasks (e.g., keep-alive health pings), the warnings become noise — suppress per-file with `// @vitest-leak-allowed` or exclude specific handles by passing a filter function to `detectAsyncLeaks`.

---

**Pattern 507: Playwright `mergeTests()` for compositional fixture isolation across concerns** [official]
`mergeTests()` combines fixture sets from independent `test.extend()` calls without coupling them. Each concern (auth, database, accessibility, network mocking) lives in its own file, and tests pull in only what they need. Merging preserves fixture scope, teardown ordering, and TypeScript types.

```typescript
// fixtures/auth.ts
export const authTest = base.extend<{ userSession: Session }>({
  userSession: async ({}, use) => {
    const session = await createTestSession({ role: 'admin' });
    await use(session);
    await session.revoke();
  },
});

// fixtures/db.ts
export const dbTest = base.extend<{ db: TestDatabase }>({
  db: [async ({}, use) => {
    const database = await TestDatabase.spin({ schema: 'isolated' });
    await use(database);
    await database.drop();
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],
});

// fixtures/a11y.ts
export const a11yTest = base.extend<{ axe: AxeBuilder }>({
  axe: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await use(new AxeBuilder({ page }));
  },
});

// tests/admin-dashboard.spec.ts
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { authTest } from '../fixtures/auth';
import { dbTest } from '../fixtures/db';
import { a11yTest } from '../fixtures/a11y';

const test = mergeTests(authTest, dbTest, a11yTest);

test('admin dashboard is accessible with seeded data', async ({
  page, userSession, db, axe,
}) => {
  await db.seed('dashboard-fixtures.sql');
  await page.goto(`/admin?token=${userSession.token}`);
  const results = await axe.analyze();
  expect(results.violations).toHaveLength(0);
});
```

Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` does not detect fixture name collisions at compile time — if two merged fixtures export the same name, the last one wins silently at runtime. Use TypeScript's intersection type to surface collisions (`type Merged = AuthFixtures & DbFixtures` will error on duplicate keys). Also, fixture teardown order in merged sets follows reverse dependency order, not merge order; if cleanup B must run before cleanup A, express that dependency explicitly via fixture injection.

---

**Pattern 508: Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` + `resetModules: true` for memory-isolated test workers** [official]
Jest's `workerIdleMemoryLimit` recycles a worker when its idle memory footprint exceeds the threshold. Combined with `resetModules: true`, each recycled worker gets a fresh module registry, breaking singleton state that accumulates across test files without requiring `--runInBand` or manual `jest.resetModules()` calls.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Recycle workers whose idle memory exceeds 400 MB
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '400MB',

  // Reset module registry before every test file — fresh singleton state
  resetModules: true,

  // Each worker handles at most 50 test files before forced recycle
  maxWorkers: '50%',

  // Setup runs after module reset — re-registers matchers and globals
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],

  testEnvironment: 'node',

  // Randomize order to smoke-test for hidden singleton dependencies
  randomize: true,
});

// jest.setup.ts — must be idempotent: runs in every recycled worker context
import { expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { toBeWithinRange } from './custom-matchers';

expect.extend({ toBeWithinRange });

afterEach(() => {
  jest.clearAllTimers();
  jest.restoreAllMocks();
});
```

Tradeoff: `resetModules: true` prevents test files from sharing a compiled module across the suite — every `require`/`import` re-executes the module factory per test file. This catches singleton bugs but increases startup latency for files that import large dependency trees. Benchmark before enabling globally; selectively apply via `jest.resetModules()` inside only the files that exercise singleton-heavy code paths.

---

**Pattern 509: Vitest `test.extend()` `injected: true` + `provide()` for project-level fixture value injection** [official]
Vitest's `injected: true` fixture option defers the fixture value to the project config's `provide` map. This lets a single fixture definition serve multiple projects (e.g., staging vs. production API endpoints) without forking test files — the project config injects the right value and the fixture exposes it with full TypeScript types.

```typescript
// fixtures/api-context.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';

interface ApiFixtures {
  apiBaseUrl: string;
  apiTimeout: number;
}

export const test = base.extend<ApiFixtures>({
  apiBaseUrl: [
    'http://localhost:3000', // fallback default
    { injected: true },
  ],
  apiTimeout: [5_000, { injected: true }],
});

// vitest.config.ts — project-level injection
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    projects: [
      {
        name: 'staging',
        provide: {
          apiBaseUrl: 'https://staging.api.example.com',
          apiTimeout: 15_000,
        },
      },
      {
        name: 'local',
        // uses defaults declared in the fixture
      },
    ],
  },
});

// test file — same file runs in both projects with injected values
import { test } from '../fixtures/api-context';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

test('health check responds 200', async ({ apiBaseUrl, apiTimeout }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/health`, {
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(apiTimeout),
  });
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
});
```

Tradeoff: `injected: true` fixtures cannot have teardown logic (there is no `use()` callback form for injected values). If the injected resource requires cleanup (e.g., an HTTP client with a connection pool), wrap it in a non-injected fixture that reads the injected scalar value and constructs the resource with proper teardown. Also, the fallback default in `base.extend` is used when no project `provide` entry matches — ensure it points to a valid local environment to avoid silent test skips in plain `vitest run` mode.

---

**Pattern 510: Playwright `auto: true` worker-scoped fixture for session auth initialization** [official]
A worker-scoped automatic fixture initializes once per Playwright worker and is shared across all tests in that worker without being listed as a test parameter. Combined with `storageState` export, it enables a single login per worker while keeping per-test pages fully isolated — the canonical pattern for authenticated E2E suites.

```typescript
// fixtures/auth-worker.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

const STORAGE_PATH = path.join(process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_OUTPUT_DIR ?? '.', `auth-worker-${process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX ?? '0'}.json`);

export const test = base.extend({
  // Auto worker-scoped: runs once per worker, no need to list in test params
  workerAuth: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      // Create a temporary context for login — not the test page
      const ctx = await browser.newContext();
      const page = await ctx.newPage();

      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.fill('[name=email]', `worker-${process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX}@test.com`);
      await page.fill('[name=password]', process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
      await page.click('[type=submit]');
      await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');

      // Persist auth state so per-test contexts can reuse it
      await ctx.storageState({ path: STORAGE_PATH });
      await ctx.close();

      await use(undefined); // signal setup is complete
      // Teardown: clean up the stored state file
    },
    { scope: 'worker', auto: true },
  ],

  // Per-test page uses the stored auth state
  page: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ storageState: STORAGE_PATH });
    const page = await ctx.newPage();
    await use(page);
    await ctx.close();
  },
});
```

Tradeoff: Worker-index-scoped storage files prevent workers from overwriting each other's auth state, but require `process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX` to be set by the Playwright runner (it is set automatically in v1.44+). If session expiry is shorter than the worker lifetime, add a health-check inside the `workerAuth` fixture that re-authenticates when the session is about to expire. Note that `auto: true` + `scope: 'worker'` fixtures cannot access test-scoped fixtures — `browser` (worker-scoped) is available but `page` (test-scoped) is not.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G331: Vitest `vi.resetModules()` clears the module cache but does NOT reset the mock registry**
If you call `vi.resetModules()` between tests to force module re-evaluation, the mock registry (populated by previous `vi.mock()` calls) is NOT cleared. On re-import, Vitest re-evaluates the module factory but immediately re-applies all mocks still registered in the mock registry, giving you a freshly evaluated but still fully mocked module — which may or may not be what you intended. Tests that call `vi.resetModules()` expecting a "real" re-import of a previously mocked module will silently continue to receive the mock.
WHY: Vitest intentionally separates the module evaluation cache (cleared by `resetModules()`) from the mock intent registry (cleared by `vi.unmock(specifier)` or `vi.restoreAllMocks()`). The design allows you to force re-evaluation of a module's factory function while keeping its mock declaration intact. The fix is to call `vi.unmock('./target-module')` before `vi.resetModules()` when you need a genuinely clean re-import.
Fix: Call `vi.unmock('./module')` before `vi.resetModules()`, then `await import('./module')` inside the test body to get a real, freshly evaluated module instance.

---

**Gotcha G332: Playwright `test.use({ storageState })` does NOT affect worker-scoped fixtures already initialized**
Calling `test.use({ storageState: 'path/to/state.json' })` inside a `describe` block overrides the storage state option for test-scoped browser contexts in that describe group — but any worker-scoped `browserContext` fixture that already initialized at worker startup retains its original storage state. This causes the describe-level `test.use()` override to be silently ignored for worker-scoped contexts, producing puzzling behavior where authenticated tests run as anonymous users.
WHY: Worker-scoped fixtures are initialized before any test file is parsed, so `test.use()` declarations (which are evaluated during file parsing) cannot retroactively mutate an already-running worker fixture. The Playwright documentation states this constraint in the fixture scopes section, but the error manifests silently rather than as an exception. The fix is to define the browser context as test-scoped (`scope: 'test'`) when per-describe storage state variation is required.
Fix: Change the `browserContext` fixture to `scope: 'test'` to allow `test.use({ storageState })` to take effect, accepting the per-test context creation cost.

---

**Gotcha G333: Jest `jest.useFakeTimers()` called in `beforeAll` leaks into sibling `describe` blocks when `restoreMocks` is `false`**
When `jest.useFakeTimers()` is called inside a `beforeAll` and the matching `jest.useRealTimers()` is in an `afterAll`, Jest restores real timers only after the enclosing `describe` block finishes. However, sibling `describe` blocks that run in the same file share the same Jest environment, so if the `afterAll` teardown in block A fails or is omitted, `describe` block B inherits fake timers. Tests in block B that use real `setTimeout` for retry logic or debounce will then hang indefinitely waiting for timers that never advance.
WHY: Jest's fake timer state is attached to the JavaScript environment (a `vm` context), which is shared within a test file. `describe` blocks are lexical groupings, not separate environments. The `afterAll` only restores timers after the describe block's last test and `afterAll` hooks have all run — if any of those throw and the `afterAll` is not wrapped in try/finally, the restoration is skipped. The global `restoreMocks: true` config option restores spy implementations but does NOT restore real timers; `useRealTimers` must be called explicitly.
Fix: Move `jest.useFakeTimers()` / `jest.useRealTimers()` to `beforeEach` / `afterEach` (not `beforeAll`/`afterAll`) so timer state is fully scoped to each test and sibling describes cannot inherit it.

---

**Gotcha G334: Vitest `onCleanup()` inside a fixture can only be called once — registering it twice throws `FixtureUsageError`**
Vitest 4.1 enforces that `onCleanup()` within a single fixture invocation can be called at most once. If a fixture conditionally calls `onCleanup()` in an early-return branch AND the happy path also calls it, the second call throws `FixtureUsageError: onCleanup was already registered`. This typically appears when adding error-handling cleanup to an existing fixture that already has a happy-path `onCleanup`.
WHY: Vitest's fixture engine models cleanup as a single deferred callback per fixture activation. Multiple cleanup registrations would require the engine to compose them, introducing ordering ambiguity. The design decision is that each fixture is responsible for exactly one cleanup registration; complex teardown logic must be expressed as a single async function that handles all branches. The error only surfaces in Vitest 4.1+; earlier versions silently ignored the second registration, which could cause resource leaks when the first cleanup was conditional.
Fix: Extract all cleanup branches into a single `onCleanup(async () => { /* all cleanup logic */ })` call. Use a `let resource: Resource | null = null` pattern so the single cleanup function can guard against resources that were never allocated.

---

**Gotcha G335: Node.js `--test-global-setup` module runs in the same process as tests — module-level singletons are shared with all tests and cannot be cleared between test files**
Unlike Jest's `globalSetup` which runs in a subprocess with no shared module cache, Node.js `--test-global-setup` evaluates in the same Node.js process that runs the tests. Any module-level singleton created during global setup (e.g., a database connection pool, a Redis client, an HTTP server) is reachable from every test file via the module cache. Tests that accidentally import the same module as the global setup will receive the already-initialized singleton, violating isolation for tests that expect a fresh instance.
WHY: Node.js's `node:test` global setup feature was designed for lightweight process-level setup (e.g., setting environment variables, creating temp directories) rather than long-lived resource management. The Jest subprocess model provides stronger isolation but adds IPC overhead. In Node.js the tradeoff was intentionally made toward performance (no subprocess fork cost) at the expense of the singleton isolation guarantee. The workaround is to scope shared resources to named globals (`globalThis.__testDb = pool`) and check for their presence in each test file rather than re-requiring the module.
Fix: Store shared resources on `globalThis` with a test-prefixed key and check `globalThis.__testDb` in tests rather than re-importing the module. For tests requiring fresh instances, call the resource constructor directly and manage teardown locally.
