## Cycle 55 — 2026-05-14

<!-- Sources: vitest.dev/guide/test-context, jestjs.io/docs/configuration, playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures,
     vitest.dev/guide/mocking, nodejs.org/docs/latest/api/test.html, mswjs.io/docs/api/setup-server,
     vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4-1, community production experience 2025-2026 -->

### New Patterns

**Pattern 511: Vitest `test.extend()` builder-pattern chaining for composable fixture trees** [official]
Extending `test` multiple times in a chain produces a single fixture namespace where each layer can depend on fixtures declared in an earlier layer. This eliminates the flat `beforeAll` + `afterAll` soup that accumulates in integration test suites.

```typescript
// test-utils/fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { createPool, type Pool } from '../src/db.js';
import { buildHttpClient, type HttpClient } from '../src/http.js';

// Layer 1 — infrastructure fixtures
const withDb = base.extend<{ pool: Pool }>({
  pool: async ({}, use) => {
    const p = await createPool({ url: process.env.TEST_DB_URL! });
    await use(p);
    await p.end();
  },
});

// Layer 2 — service fixtures that depend on layer 1
export const test = withDb.extend<{ http: HttpClient }>({
  http: async ({ pool }, use) => {
    // pool is injected from layer 1 automatically — Vitest resolves the graph
    const client = buildHttpClient({ pool });
    await use(client);
    await client.destroy();
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/orders.test.ts
import { test } from '../test-utils/fixtures.js';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

test('creates order via HTTP layer', async ({ http }) => {
  const res = await http.post('/orders', { item: 'widget', qty: 3 });
  expect(res.status).toBe(201);
  expect(res.body.id).toBeDefined();
});

test('pool is independent per test', async ({ pool, http }) => {
  // Both pool AND http are available in the same test body
  const { rows } = await pool.query('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders');
  expect(Number(rows[0].count)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0);
});
```

Tradeoff: The builder chain must be consistent — if `withDb` is imported in multiple files, each file gets an independent chain root, meaning `test.extend()` cannot share instance state across files unless the fixture is `scope: 'worker'`. Keep the shared `pool` in a worker-scoped fixture and the per-test `http` in the default test scope.

---

**Pattern 512: Vitest `injected: true` + `provide` in project config for multi-environment fixture injection** [official]
`injected: true` marks a fixture as overridable from outside the test file — the actual value is supplied by the Vitest project config's `provide` map. This is the idiomatic way to parameterize the same test file across dev/staging/prod environments without `process.env` branching inside tests.

```typescript
// test-utils/fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';

interface EnvFixtures {
  baseUrl: string;
  authToken: string;
}

export const test = base.extend<EnvFixtures>({
  // injected: true — actual value comes from vitest project config's `provide` map
  baseUrl: [async ({}, use) => { await use('http://localhost:3000'); }, { injected: true }],
  authToken: [async ({}, use) => { await use('dev-token'); }, { injected: true }],
});
```

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    test: {
      name: 'local',
      include: ['tests/**/*.test.ts'],
      provide: {
        baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
        authToken: process.env.DEV_TOKEN ?? 'dev-token',
      },
    },
  },
  {
    test: {
      name: 'staging',
      include: ['tests/**/*.test.ts'],
      provide: {
        baseUrl: 'https://staging.example.com',
        authToken: process.env.STAGING_TOKEN ?? '',
      },
    },
  },
]);
```

```typescript
// tests/api.test.ts
import { test } from '../test-utils/fixtures.js';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

test('GET /health returns 200', async ({ baseUrl, authToken }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/health`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${authToken}` },
  });
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
});
```

Tradeoff: `injected: true` fixtures must declare a default value (the second arg to `extend()`). That default is only used when no `provide` key is present in the project config — it is NOT the fixture value during normal runs. If `provide` is omitted entirely, the default silently applies and tests may pass locally against the wrong environment. Document the `provide` requirement in the test file header.

---

**Pattern 513: Playwright `test.use()` `storageState` override per describe-block for multi-role isolation** [official]
`test.use()` inside a `describe` block scopes the storageState override to that block's test-scoped browser contexts. This avoids maintaining separate fixture files per role — a single spec file can exercise admin, member, and guest paths with zero shared state.

```typescript
// tests/permissions.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Admin describe block
test.describe('Admin role', () => {
  test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' });

  test('can delete any user', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/admin/users');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete user-42' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('User deleted')).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('can see audit log', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/admin/audit-log');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('audit-table')).toBeVisible();
  });
});

// Guest describe block — separate storage state, no admin cookies
test.describe('Guest role', () => {
  test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } }); // blank slate

  test('cannot access admin panel', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/admin/users');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `test.use()` only affects test-scoped fixtures (`page`, `context`). Worker-scoped fixtures that were already initialized at worker startup are not re-initialized when `test.use()` is evaluated. If you have a worker-scoped `browserContext`, this pattern silently does nothing for that context (see Gotcha G332). Use only when all browser contexts in the describe block are test-scoped.

---

**Pattern 514: Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` + `resetModules: true` combination for memory-leak isolation in long test suites** [official]
`workerIdleMemoryLimit` recycles worker processes that exceed a memory threshold between test files. Pairing it with `resetModules: true` ensures the new worker starts with a clean module registry rather than inheriting cached module state that may contain open handles or large data structures.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Reset module registry before each test file — fresh require cache per file
  resetModules: true,

  // Recycle workers whose idle RSS exceeds 512 MB
  // Prevents progressive memory growth in suites with 500+ test files
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '512MB',

  // Graceful exit: give workers 2 s to flush any pending async operations
  workerGracefulExitTimeout: 2000,

  // Flag leaked async operations that keep the event loop alive
  openHandlesTimeout: 1000,

  // Reinforce: clear mock state on the fresh registry
  clearMocks: true,
  restoreMocks: true,
});
```

```typescript
// tests/report-generator.test.ts
// This module creates a 50 MB in-memory PDF buffer during its tests.
// With workerIdleMemoryLimit, Jest recycles the worker after this file
// completes — the buffer is freed and the next file starts fresh.
import { describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { generatePdfReport } from '../src/report-generator.js';

describe('ReportGenerator', () => {
  it('generates a valid PDF buffer', async () => {
    const buffer = await generatePdfReport({ rows: 10_000 });
    expect(buffer.byteLength).toBeGreaterThan(1024);
    expect(buffer.slice(0, 4)).toEqual(Buffer.from('%PDF'));
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `workerIdleMemoryLimit` measures RSS after the test file finishes — not peak usage during the file. A single test that allocates 2 GB and then frees it will not trigger recycling (RSS returns to baseline). For large-allocation tests, pair with `--runInBand` for the specific suite or increase the limit. The memory check adds ~1 ms overhead per test file.

---

**Pattern 515: Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` + `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` for per-test environment variable isolation** [official]
`vi.stubEnv()` sets a specific `process.env` key and registers it for restoration. Combined with the `unstubEnvs: true` config option (auto-restores between tests), this is a fully declarative environment variable isolation pattern that avoids the fragile `const original = process.env.X; afterEach(() => process.env.X = original)` anti-pattern.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    // Auto-call vi.unstubAllEnvs() before each test — no manual afterEach needed
    unstubEnvs: true,
    // Also auto-restore globals stubbed with vi.stubGlobal
    unstubGlobals: true,
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/config-loader.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi } from 'vitest';
import { loadConfig } from '../src/config-loader.js';

describe('ConfigLoader', () => {
  it('uses DATABASE_URL from environment', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgresql://test:test@localhost/testdb');
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'test');

    const config = loadConfig();

    expect(config.databaseUrl).toBe('postgresql://test:test@localhost/testdb');
    expect(config.isTest).toBe(true);
    // vi.unstubAllEnvs() fires automatically before next test (unstubEnvs: true)
  });

  it('throws when DATABASE_URL is missing', () => {
    // vi.stubEnv restores previous value on unstub; delete achieves absence
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', '');
    expect(() => loadConfig()).toThrow('DATABASE_URL is required');
  });

  it('uses default port 5432 when DB_PORT is unset', () => {
    // No stub needed — previous stubs were already cleared by unstubEnvs: true
    vi.stubEnv('DATABASE_URL', 'postgresql://host/db');
    vi.stubEnv('DB_PORT', undefined as any);
    const config = loadConfig();
    expect(config.dbPort).toBe(5432);
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv(key, undefined)` sets the key to the string `'undefined'` in some Vitest versions — to truly unset a key, call `delete process.env.KEY` after `stubEnv`, or use `vi.stubEnv(key, '')` and check for empty string in the module. The `unstubEnvs: true` config restores to the value at the time of stubbing, not to the process's original env; if a previous test deleted the key outright, restoration sets it back to `undefined` (the string).

---

**Pattern 516: MSW `server.boundary()` per-component handler scoping for React Testing Library isolation** [official]
MSW v2.4+ introduced `server.boundary()` which wraps a subtree with its own handler stack. Handlers registered inside the boundary are active only for fetch calls made within that render scope, preventing handler bleed between sibling components rendered in the same test.

```typescript
// tests/checkout.test.tsx
import { render, screen, waitFor } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import { server } from '../mocks/server.js';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { CheckoutForm } from '../src/CheckoutForm.js';
import { OrderSummary } from '../src/OrderSummary.js';

test('CheckoutForm and OrderSummary use independent handlers', async () => {
  // CheckoutForm boundary: POST /api/checkout returns success
  const CheckoutBoundary = server.boundary(() => (
    <CheckoutForm />
  ));

  // OrderSummary boundary: GET /api/cart returns different data
  const SummaryBoundary = server.boundary(() => (
    <OrderSummary />
  ));

  // Register handler INSIDE the boundary scope
  server.use(
    http.post('/api/checkout', () =>
      HttpResponse.json({ orderId: 'ord-001', status: 'confirmed' })
    )
  );

  render(
    <div>
      <CheckoutBoundary />
      <SummaryBoundary />
    </div>
  );

  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i }));

  await waitFor(() => {
    expect(screen.getByText('Order ord-001 confirmed')).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `server.boundary()` requires MSW v2.4+ and the `msw/browser` or `msw/node` server to be in scope. In Node.js (Jest/Vitest), `boundary()` is a higher-order component concept that wraps an async context — it works with React's async context propagation but does NOT work for plain fetch calls made outside React's render tree. For non-React isolation, `server.use()` + `server.resetHandlers()` remains the correct pattern.

---

**Pattern 517: Playwright `page.route()` per-test network mock for API call isolation without MSW** [official]
`page.route()` intercepts network calls at the browser level and is automatically scoped to the `page` fixture lifetime — when the test ends and the page is closed, all routes are torn down. No `afterEach` registration is required.

```typescript
// tests/product-detail.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows out-of-stock badge when inventory is zero', async ({ page }) => {
  // Route is scoped to this page instance — cleared automatically on page.close()
  await page.route('/api/inventory/*', async (route, request) => {
    const productId = request.url().split('/').pop();
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ productId, quantity: 0, inStock: false }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/products/widget-42');

  await expect(page.getByTestId('stock-badge')).toHaveText('Out of Stock');
  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i })).toBeDisabled();
});

test('shows add-to-cart button when inventory is available', async ({ page }) => {
  // Different route, completely independent of the previous test's page
  await page.route('/api/inventory/*', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ quantity: 42, inStock: true }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/products/widget-42');

  await expect(page.getByRole('button', { name: /add to cart/i })).toBeEnabled();
});
```

Tradeoff: `page.route()` handlers match URL patterns, not request method + URL combinations. If two handlers match the same URL pattern, the last registered one wins. For API endpoints that behave differently on GET vs POST, use `route.request().method()` inside the handler to branch, rather than registering two routes for the same URL glob.

---

**Pattern 518: Vitest `vi.mock()` with `importOriginal` + partial spy for tree-shaken module isolation** [official]
When only one export of a large module needs to be replaced, using `importOriginal` to spread the real module and override only the target export maintains the rest of the module's behavior — preventing the "every import returns undefined" failure that occurs with a full empty mock factory.

```typescript
// tests/email-service.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

// Mock only the send function; keep formatMessage, validateAddress, etc. real
vi.mock(import('../src/email-transport.js'), async (importOriginal) => {
  const real = await importOriginal();
  return {
    ...real,
    send: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'test-msg-001', accepted: ['to@example.com'] }),
  };
});

// Static import is safe here — vi.mock() is hoisted above all imports
import { send } from '../src/email-transport.js';
import { EmailService } from '../src/email-service.js';

describe('EmailService', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it('calls send with formatted subject and body', async () => {
    const service = new EmailService({ from: 'no-reply@example.com' });
    await service.notify('user@example.com', { type: 'order-confirmed', orderId: 'ord-1' });

    expect(send).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({
        to: 'user@example.com',
        subject: expect.stringContaining('Order Confirmed'),
        html: expect.stringContaining('ord-1'),
      })
    );
  });

  it('does not send when notifications are disabled', async () => {
    const service = new EmailService({ from: 'no-reply@example.com', disabled: true });
    await service.notify('user@example.com', { type: 'order-confirmed', orderId: 'ord-2' });
    expect(send).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: The `importOriginal` spread must be shallow — any exported class or function that closes over module-internal state will still reference the original module's internal scope, not the mocked one. For modules with internal cross-dependencies (i.e., `funcA` calls `funcB` and you mock `funcB`), Vitest's hoisted `vi.mock()` replaces the module binding at the import site but not at the call site inside the module. Use `vi.spyOn` on the exported object after import for intra-module call patching.

---

**Pattern 519: Node.js `node:test` `context.mock.timers` with `tick()` for async timer drain** [official]
Node.js's built-in `MockTimers` class (available via `context.mock.timers` in `node:test`) provides `tick(ms)` to advance the fake clock and drain all pending timers synchronously. Unlike Jest's `advanceTimersByTime`, `tick()` in `node:test` resolves Promise microtasks inline with each timer callback, making it safe to `await` after `tick()`.

```typescript
// tests/retry-policy.test.mts
import { describe, it, mock, before, after } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { RetryPolicy } from '../src/retry-policy.js';

describe('RetryPolicy', () => {
  let timers: ReturnType<typeof mock.timers>;

  before(() => {
    // Enable fake timers for Date, setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate
    timers = mock.timers;
    timers.enable({ apis: ['setTimeout', 'Date'] });
  });

  after(() => {
    // Restore real timers after the describe block finishes
    timers.reset();
  });

  it('retries 3 times with exponential backoff', async () => {
    const action = mock.fn(() => Promise.reject(new Error('transient')));
    const policy = new RetryPolicy({ maxRetries: 3, baseDelayMs: 100 });

    const promise = policy.run(action);

    // Tick 100ms — first retry fires
    timers.tick(100);
    // Tick 200ms — second retry fires (100 * 2^1)
    timers.tick(200);
    // Tick 400ms — third retry fires (100 * 2^2), then exhausted
    timers.tick(400);

    await assert.rejects(promise, /transient/);
    assert.strictEqual(action.mock.callCount(), 4); // 1 initial + 3 retries
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `mock.timers.tick()` in `node:test` is synchronous but returns a Promise when timer callbacks themselves return Promises — the returned Promise must be awaited to allow microtask queues to drain. In Jest, `advanceTimersByTime` is synchronous and does NOT await async callbacks; use `jest.runAllTimersAsync()` when timer callbacks are async. The APIs are superficially similar but have different semantics for async callbacks.

---

**Pattern 520: Vitest `vi.defineHelper()` for stack-trace-clean test utility functions** [official]
`vi.defineHelper()` marks a utility function so that Vitest strips its frames from assertion stack traces. This means when a shared helper like `expectApiResponse()` fails, the stack trace points to the test body line — not the internal line inside the helper — making test failures faster to diagnose.

```typescript
// test-utils/api-helpers.ts
import { expect, vi } from 'vitest';

// Frames from this function are hidden in Vitest failure output
export const expectApiResponse = vi.defineHelper(
  function expectApiResponse<T>(
    actual: Response,
    expectedStatus: number,
    expectedBody?: Partial<T>
  ) {
    // This expect() failure will show the CALLER's location, not line 12 here
    expect(actual.status).toBe(expectedStatus);

    if (expectedBody !== undefined) {
      expect(actual.json()).resolves.toMatchObject(expectedBody);
    }
  }
);

export const expectEmpty = vi.defineHelper(
  function expectEmpty(collection: unknown[]) {
    expect(collection).toHaveLength(0);
    expect(collection).toEqual([]);
  }
);
```

```typescript
// tests/users-api.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { expectApiResponse, expectEmpty } from '../test-utils/api-helpers.js';
import { handler } from '../src/users-handler.js';

test('GET /users returns empty list for new tenant', async () => {
  const res = await handler(new Request('http://localhost/users'));

  // Stack trace on failure: points to THIS line, not to api-helpers.ts
  expectApiResponse(res, 200, { users: [] });
  // Also: points to THIS line
  expectEmpty(await res.clone().json().then((b: any) => b.users));
});
```

Tradeoff: `vi.defineHelper()` is a Vitest-only API — there is no Jest equivalent. In mixed Jest/Vitest monorepos, guard the import with a runtime check or duplicate the helper without the wrapper. The helper name must be a named function expression (not an arrow function) for the stack-frame stripping to work correctly — arrow functions do not have a `.name` property Vitest can use to identify the frame.

---

**Pattern 521: Playwright `page.clock.pauseAt()` for event-sequence isolation in multi-step UI tests** [official]
`page.clock.pauseAt(time)` suspends time at a specific instant, preventing any background timers (polling, session refresh, toasts) from firing while the test interacts with the UI. This gives deterministic control over which timers fire explicitly, avoiding race conditions from autosave or debounce timers running between user actions.

```typescript
// tests/form-autosave.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows saving indicator exactly once during autosave debounce', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install clock and immediately pause it — no timers will fire without explicit advance
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-05-14T09:00:00Z') });
  await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('2026-05-14T09:00:00Z'));

  await page.goto('/editor');
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /document title/i }).fill('My Report');

  // At T+0: saving indicator should NOT be visible (debounce not triggered)
  await expect(page.getByTestId('saving-indicator')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Advance by 500ms — debounce threshold reached, autosave fires
  await page.clock.tickFor(500);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('saving-indicator')).toBeVisible();

  // Advance by 1000ms — save completes, indicator hides
  await page.clock.tickFor(1000);
  await expect(page.getByTestId('saving-indicator')).not.toBeVisible();

  // Verify no spurious second save was triggered
  const saveCalls = await page.evaluate(() => window.__testSaveCallCount ?? 0);
  expect(saveCalls).toBe(1);
});
```

Tradeoff: `pauseAt()` combined with `tickFor()` is a manual-mode clock — every timer advance must be explicit. Background polls (health-check pings, analytics beacons) are completely frozen, which can break page initialization if those polls are load-blocking. If the page's initial paint depends on a polling sequence, call `tickFor(initialPollInterval)` before any user interactions to let the page settle.

---

**Pattern 522: Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` for single-test async ESM isolation without `resetModules` side-effects** [official]
`jest.isolateModulesAsync()` runs a callback in an isolated module registry — modules imported with dynamic `import()` inside the callback get fresh instances, but the isolation is local to the callback. Unlike `resetModules: true` in `beforeEach`, `isolateModulesAsync` does not affect modules loaded before or after the isolated block.

```typescript
// tests/singleton-logger.test.ts
import { describe, it, expect, jest } from '@jest/globals';

describe('Logger singleton isolation', () => {
  it('two isolated imports create independent instances', async () => {
    // Each call to isolateModulesAsync creates its own registry bubble
    let instance1: any;
    let instance2: any;

    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      // Dynamic import inside the bubble — fresh module evaluation
      const { Logger } = await import('../src/logger.js');
      instance1 = new Logger({ name: 'service-a' });
      instance1.log('init');
    });

    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      const { Logger } = await import('../src/logger.js');
      instance2 = new Logger({ name: 'service-b' });
    });

    // Same constructor but different instances — singleton registry was reset per bubble
    expect(instance1).not.toBe(instance2);
    expect(instance1.getLogs()).toEqual(['init']);
    expect(instance2.getLogs()).toHaveLength(0);
  });

  it('outer module registry is unchanged — top-level imports are unaffected', async () => {
    // This import is OUTSIDE the isolateModulesAsync bubble — uses the main registry
    const { Logger: OuterLogger } = await import('../src/logger.js');
    const outer = new OuterLogger({ name: 'outer' });

    await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      const { Logger: InnerLogger } = await import('../src/logger.js');
      // Different registry — different class object
      expect(InnerLogger).not.toBe(OuterLogger);
    });

    // Outer registry unchanged
    expect(new OuterLogger({ name: 'outer2' })).toBeInstanceOf(OuterLogger);
  });
});
```

Tradeoff: `isolateModulesAsync` creates a temporary module registry that is discarded after the callback returns. Modules imported inside the bubble cannot be referenced after the bubble closes except via values assigned to outer-scope variables. If the module uses `top-level await`, the async evaluation happens inside the bubble — this is the primary advantage of `isolateModulesAsync` over `resetModules` + `doMock`.

---

**Pattern 523: Vitest `scope: 'worker'` fixture with `onCleanup` for expensive singletons shared across a worker's test files** [official]
Worker-scoped fixtures initialize exactly once per Vitest worker process, regardless of how many test files run in that worker. Combining them with `onCleanup` (the fixture-local teardown hook) ensures the singleton is closed only after the last test in the worker finishes, not after each file.

```typescript
// test-utils/fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { createRedisClient, type RedisClient } from '../src/redis.js';

export const test = base.extend<{}, { redis: RedisClient }>({
  // Note: worker-scoped fixtures are in the second type parameter
  redis: [
    async ({}, use, { onCleanup }) => {
      // Runs ONCE per worker — shared across all test files in the worker
      const client = await createRedisClient({
        url: process.env.REDIS_TEST_URL ?? 'redis://localhost:6379/15',
      });
      await client.flushDb(); // clear test DB at start of worker run

      onCleanup(async () => {
        await client.flushDb(); // final cleanup
        await client.quit();
      });

      await use(client);
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});
```

```typescript
// tests/cache-service.test.ts
import { test } from '../test-utils/fixtures.js';
import { expect } from 'vitest';
import { CacheService } from '../src/cache-service.js';

// redis fixture is shared with every test in this worker — startup cost paid once
test('stores and retrieves a value', async ({ redis }) => {
  const svc = new CacheService(redis);
  await svc.set('greeting', 'hello', { ttl: 60 });
  expect(await svc.get('greeting')).toBe('hello');
});

test('returns null for expired keys', async ({ redis }) => {
  await redis.set('expiring', 'value', 'EX', 1);
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 1100)); // let Redis expire the key
  expect(await redis.get('expiring')).toBeNull();
});
```

Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures cannot access test-scoped context data (e.g., the test name or task object) because they initialize before any specific test runs. If the fixture needs test metadata, downgrade to `scope: 'file'`. Also, worker-scoped teardown failure (an `onCleanup` that throws) silently swallows errors in some Vitest versions — wrap teardown in a `try/catch` with explicit error logging to avoid silent resource leaks.

---

**Pattern 524: Playwright `mergeTests()` for orthogonal concern isolation without fixture name collisions** [official]
`mergeTests()` composes two independently maintained fixture modules into one `test` object. Each module owns its own fixtures; concerns do not bleed into each other. When the same fixture name appears in both modules, the last module wins — so deliberate naming discipline is required.

```typescript
// fixtures/db-fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { createTestDb, type TestDb } from '../test-infra/db.js';

export const dbTest = base.extend<{ testDb: TestDb }>({
  testDb: async ({}, use) => {
    const db = await createTestDb();
    await use(db);
    await db.teardown();
  },
});
```

```typescript
// fixtures/auth-fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { loginAs, type AuthSession } from '../test-infra/auth.js';

export const authTest = base.extend<{ session: AuthSession }>({
  session: async ({ page }, use) => {
    const s = await loginAs('test-admin@example.com');
    await page.context().addCookies(s.cookies);
    await use(s);
  },
});
```

```typescript
// fixtures/index.ts
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { dbTest } from './db-fixture.js';
import { authTest } from './auth-fixture.js';

// Merged fixture: testDb + session + all Playwright built-ins
export const test = mergeTests(dbTest, authTest);
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';
```

```typescript
// tests/admin-dashboard.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '../fixtures/index.js';

test('admin sees all pending orders', async ({ page, testDb, session }) => {
  await testDb.seed('orders', [
    { id: 'ord-1', status: 'pending', tenant: session.tenantId },
  ]);

  await page.goto('/admin/orders');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-ord-1')).toBeVisible();
});
```

Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` merges at the fixture registry level — TypeScript type inference for merged fixtures requires explicit generic parameters if fixture types clash. If `dbTest` and `authTest` both extend from different `base` objects (e.g., one is `@playwright/test`, one is a custom subclass), `mergeTests` may emit a TypeScript type error. Always use `@playwright/test`'s `base.extend()` as the common root for all modules that will be merged.

---

**Pattern 525: Vitest `test.override()` for per-suite fixture value replacement without a full fixture chain rebuild** [official]
`test.override()` injects a new value for an existing fixture within a `describe` block without requiring a new `test.extend()` call. It is the correct API when a small subset of tests needs a different fixture variant — replacing `beforeEach` hacks that mutate shared state.

```typescript
// test-utils/fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';

export const test = base.extend<{ config: { env: string; logLevel: string } }>({
  config: async ({}, use) => {
    await use({ env: 'development', logLevel: 'debug' });
  },
});
```

```typescript
// tests/feature-toggle.test.ts
import { test } from '../test-utils/fixtures.js';
import { expect, describe } from 'vitest';
import { FeatureToggle } from '../src/feature-toggle.js';

// Default tests — use development config
test('debug logging is enabled in development', ({ config }) => {
  const toggle = new FeatureToggle(config);
  expect(toggle.isDebugEnabled()).toBe(true);
});

// Production suite — override config fixture for this block only
describe('production mode', () => {
  test.override('config', { env: 'production', logLevel: 'error' });

  test('debug logging is disabled in production', ({ config }) => {
    expect(config.env).toBe('production');
    const toggle = new FeatureToggle(config);
    expect(toggle.isDebugEnabled()).toBe(false);
  });

  test('error logging still active in production', ({ config }) => {
    expect(config.logLevel).toBe('error');
    const toggle = new FeatureToggle(config);
    expect(toggle.isErrorEnabled()).toBe(true);
  });
});

// Tests AFTER the describe block revert to the original fixture value
test('development config is restored after describe block', ({ config }) => {
  expect(config.env).toBe('development');
});
```

Tradeoff: `test.override()` is a Vitest 4.1+ API that replaced the deprecated `test.scoped()`. It overrides fixture values at the suite boundary — tests outside the describe block that declared `override` are unaffected. The override applies only to fixture values, not to fixture factories: if you need a different initialization logic (not just a different value), use `test.extend()` with a new scope.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G336: Vitest `vi.mock(import(...))` hoisting only works when the `import()` path is a string literal — dynamic path expressions are silently not hoisted**
If the path passed to `vi.mock(import(...))` is constructed at runtime (e.g., from a variable or template literal), Vitest's static analysis cannot hoist the call and the mock is registered AFTER module evaluation, so the `import` at the top of the file uses the real module. Symptom: the mock appears to have no effect but no error is thrown.
WHY: Vitest's hoisting transform (powered by `vite-plugin-hoisting`) performs static AST analysis to lift `vi.mock()` calls above `import` declarations. The analysis can only identify string literals as the import path — any dynamic expression defeats the AST transform and the call is left in place. The module has already been evaluated by the time the dynamic `vi.mock()` executes.
Fix: Always use a static string literal in `vi.mock(import('./path'))`. If the path must vary between tests, use `vi.doMock()` (not hoisted) combined with `vi.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` and dynamic `import()` inside the test body.

---

**Gotcha G337: Playwright `page.route()` handlers registered with `page.route('**', ...)` intercept ALL requests including static assets — navigation can hang if the handler doesn't call `route.fulfill()` or `route.continue()`**
A catch-all `'**'` glob in `page.route()` intercepts every network request from the page — not just API calls but also fonts, images, CSS, and JavaScript bundles. If the handler conditionally calls `fulfill()` or `continue()` based on the URL and misses some URLs (e.g., static asset paths), those requests are silently dropped, causing the page to load partially or time out.
WHY: Playwright's route interception is a complete network intercept — intercepted requests are held until the handler resolves them. An unresolved handler (one that neither fulfills, continues, nor aborts) leaves the request pending forever. This is different from MSW which only intercepts requests explicitly matched by a handler; unmatched requests pass through by default.
Fix: Use specific URL patterns (e.g., `'/api/**'`) instead of `'**'`. If a catch-all is required, always include a terminal `await route.continue()` in the else branch of the condition.

---

**Gotcha G338: Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` callback must not import the same specifier that was imported before the call — the outer registry takes precedence and the inner bubble sees the cached outer instance**
When a module is imported at the top of a test file (`import { Foo } from './foo'`) and then `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` attempts to re-import the same specifier, the inner bubble receives the already-cached module from the outer registry. The isolation does not apply retroactively to modules already evaluated in the test file's scope.
WHY: Jest's module registry is a two-level structure: the outer file-level registry and the temporary isolated-modules registry created by `isolateModulesAsync`. When a dynamic `import('./foo')` is evaluated inside the bubble, Jest first checks the isolated registry (empty), then falls through to the outer file registry (hit — already evaluated). The "isolation" only applies to modules NOT yet in the outer registry.
Fix: Do not add static top-level imports for modules you intend to isolate. Import them only via dynamic `import()` inside `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` callbacks. If legacy code requires a top-level import, move the test to a separate file where the module is only imported inside the bubble.

---

**Gotcha G339: Vitest `scope: 'worker'` fixture teardown runs AFTER the worker closes its last test file — if `--bail` is triggered mid-suite, worker teardown may not run at all**
When Vitest's `--bail` flag terminates the run after N failures, worker processes are force-terminated immediately after the bail threshold is hit. The `onCleanup` callback registered for worker-scoped fixtures is part of the graceful shutdown sequence, but a SIGKILL sent to the worker process (Vitest's behavior on bail) bypasses the cleanup path. Resources held by worker-scoped fixtures (database connections, Redis clients, HTTP servers) may not be closed.
WHY: Worker-scoped fixtures are designed for the "normal run completes" path. Vitest's bail implementation sends `SIGTERM` with a grace period configured by `bail.gracefulShutdownTimeout` (default: 5000 ms), but if the worker has open handles that prevent `process.exit`, the runner falls back to `SIGKILL`. Any `onCleanup` or `afterAll` logic that was pending at the time of the signal is lost.
Fix: For any external resource opened in a worker-scoped fixture, also register a `process.on('SIGTERM', cleanup)` handler in the fixture body. This handler fires during the graceful period before SIGKILL escalation. Alternatively, use a `scope: 'file'` fixture instead of `scope: 'worker'` for resources where teardown reliability is critical.

---

**Gotcha G340: MSW `server.use()` called inside a `beforeAll` whose test suite imports MSW handlers from a shared module runs the handlers in the WRONG order — shared handlers always have lower priority than per-suite handlers, but only if `server.use()` is called AFTER `server.listen()`**
When `server.listen()` is called in a global `beforeAll` and the shared handler module is initialized at import time (before the test file's `beforeAll` runs), the shared handlers are already in the stack. A per-suite `server.use()` in `beforeAll` pushes its handlers ABOVE the shared ones — correct. But if a shared handler module calls `server.use()` at module evaluation time (not inside a `beforeAll`), those handlers are registered at `import` evaluation time, which is BEFORE `server.listen()` and BEFORE any per-suite `server.use()`. MSW silently accepts pre-listen `server.use()` calls, but handler order relative to per-suite handlers becomes undefined.
WHY: MSW's handler stack is a mutable array. `server.use()` prepends to the stack (highest priority first). The order of `server.use()` calls determines priority, not the order of `beforeAll` execution. Module-level `server.use()` calls in shared modules run at import time, which is before any test-level `beforeAll`, placing those handlers at an arbitrary position in the stack relative to per-suite additions.
Fix: Never call `server.use()` at module evaluation time in shared handler modules. Always wrap `server.use()` calls in `beforeAll` or `beforeEach`. The single entry point for initial handlers is `setupServer(...handlers)`, which is the correct place for baseline handlers.

## Cycle 56 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 526: Vitest `test.extend()` fixture lazy initialization guard** [official]
Vitest only initializes a fixture when its name appears in the test's destructured argument list. If a fixture performs expensive I/O (database connection, HTTP server spin-up), it is safe to define it globally — it will never run for tests that don't request it. Combine with `scope: 'file'` to share one instance across an entire spec file while still paying zero cost in unrelated files.
```typescript
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { createTestDb, destroyTestDb } from './helpers/db';

export const test = base.extend<{ db: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof createTestDb>> }>({
  db: [
    async ({}, use, testContext) => {
      // Only runs when a test actually destructures `db`
      const db = await createTestDb(`test_${testContext.task.id}`);
      await use(db);
      await destroyTestDb(db);
    },
    { scope: 'file' }, // one connection per file, not one per test
  ],
});

// This test DOES pay the setup cost:
test('inserts a record', async ({ db }) => {
  await db.query('INSERT INTO items VALUES (1, "hello")');
  const rows = await db.query('SELECT * FROM items');
  expect(rows).toHaveLength(1);
});

// This test pays ZERO cost — `db` is never mentioned:
test('pure unit logic', () => {
  expect(2 + 2).toBe(4);
});
```
Tradeoff: Lazy initialization is a powerful optimization but it means the fixture factory is only type-checked if at least one test in the file uses it. Add a dedicated smoke-test file that exercises every fixture to catch factory regressions at CI time.

---

**Pattern 527: Vitest `onCleanup` inside `aroundEach` for single-closure transaction rollback** [official]
`aroundEach` wraps each test with a generator-style hook, enabling setup and teardown to share local variables in a single closure. This is stronger than a `beforeEach`/`afterEach` pair because the cleanup code always runs even if the test throws, and the shared variable needs no outer `let` binding.
```typescript
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { pool } from './db/pool';

export const test = base.extend({
  isolatedTx: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Nothing here — the aroundEach hook manages state
      await use(undefined);
    },
    { scope: 'test' },
  ],
});

test.extend({
  // aroundEach takes a generator; yield resumes inside the test body
  isolatedTx: async ({}, use, { onCleanup }) => {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await client.query('ROLLBACK');
      client.release();
    });
    await use(client);
  },
})('rolls back insert after test', async ({ isolatedTx: client }) => {
  await client.query("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('alice', 100)");
  const res = await client.query("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE name='alice'");
  expect(res.rows[0].balance).toBe(100);
  // ROLLBACK fires in onCleanup — no trace left for next test
});
```
Tradeoff: `onCleanup` can only be called once per fixture invocation (Vitest 4.1 constraint). If you need two teardown steps, chain them inside a single `onCleanup` callback rather than calling `onCleanup` twice.

---

**Pattern 528: Playwright `test.use({ storageState })` per-`describe` block for multi-role E2E isolation** [official]
Playwright's `test.use()` applies configuration overrides scoped to the nearest enclosing `describe` block. Setting `storageState` at the describe level lets you colocate role-specific tests without creating separate project configurations or duplicating `page.goto('/login')` boilerplate in every test.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Admin panel', () => {
  test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/admin.json' });

  test('can delete a user', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/admin/users');
    await page.locator('[data-testid="delete-user-1"]').click();
    await expect(page.locator('.toast')).toContainText('User deleted');
  });
});

test.describe('Regular user view', () => {
  test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' });

  test('cannot see admin panel link', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/dashboard');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="admin-link"]')).not.toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `storageState` files must be generated by a global setup script (e.g., `playwright/auth.setup.ts` in `projects[].dependencies`) and committed or stored in CI cache. If the auth flow changes, all stale `.json` files produce silent false-passes — add an expiry assertion to the setup script.

---

**Pattern 529: Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` + `unstubEnvs: true` in `vitest.config` for zero-ceremony environment variable isolation** [official]
`vi.stubEnv(key, value)` overrides a `process.env` key for the duration of a test and registers the original value for automatic restoration. When `unstubEnvs: true` is set in `vitest.config`, all stubs are unstubbed after every test automatically — no `afterEach(() => vi.unstubAllEnvs())` boilerplate required.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    unstubEnvs: true,   // auto-restore after every test
    unstubGlobals: true, // same for vi.stubGlobal()
  },
});

// payment.test.ts
import { vi, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { getStripeKey } from './payment';

test('returns live key in production', () => {
  vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'production');
  vi.stubEnv('STRIPE_KEY', 'sk_live_abc123');
  expect(getStripeKey()).toBe('sk_live_abc123');
});

test('returns test key outside production', () => {
  vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'test');
  vi.stubEnv('STRIPE_KEY', 'sk_test_xyz789');
  expect(getStripeKey()).toBe('sk_test_xyz789');
});

// No afterEach needed — config handles cleanup
```
Tradeoff: `unstubEnvs: true` is a global setting. If you intentionally carry a stubbed env across multiple tests inside a `describe` block (for performance), you must reset the global setting to `false` and manage stubs manually or use `test.scoped()`/`test.override()` at the suite boundary instead.

---

**Pattern 530: Playwright `page.clock.install()` before `page.goto()` for deterministic time-dependent UI** [official]
Playwright's `page.clock.install()` installs a fake `Date`/`setTimeout`/`setInterval` in the browser context before the page loads. Calling it before `goto()` ensures every timer and date object created during page initialization uses the fake clock — there is no race window where real timers fire before the fake clock takes over.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('banner shows "Offer expires in 2 days"', async ({ page }) => {
  // Freeze time at a known date BEFORE the page loads
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-06-01T12:00:00Z') });
  await page.goto('/promotions');

  // Promotion ends 2026-06-03 — with fake clock, "2 days" is deterministic
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="countdown"]')).toContainText('2 days');

  // Advance clock to near expiry — no real waiting
  await page.clock.fastForward('1d 23h');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="countdown"]')).toContainText('1 hour');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install()` replaces the browser's `Date` globally for that page context. If the page uses a service worker with independent timer logic, the service worker's clock is NOT faked — you must also route and mock any time-sensitive service worker responses separately.

---

**Pattern 531: Vitest `scope: 'worker'` fixture for expensive singleton (ORM connection pool) shared across all tests in a worker process** [official]
Worker-scoped fixtures are initialized once per Vitest worker process and torn down when the worker shuts down. This is the correct scope for database connection pools, compiled WASM modules, or any resource whose initialization cost (>100ms) would make per-file or per-test scoping unacceptably slow.
```typescript
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { DataSource } from 'typeorm';
import { entities } from '../src/entities';

export const test = base.extend<object, { dataSource: DataSource }>({
  dataSource: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      const ds = new DataSource({
        type: 'postgres',
        url: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL,
        entities,
        synchronize: false,
      });
      await ds.initialize();
      await use(ds);
      await ds.destroy(); // runs once when the worker exits
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('finds user by email', async ({ dataSource }) => {
  const repo = dataSource.getRepository('User');
  const user = await repo.findOneBy({ email: 'alice@example.com' });
  expect(user).not.toBeNull();
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures are shared across all test files assigned to that worker. If one test mutates shared state (e.g., inserts a row without cleanup), subsequent tests in the same worker see the dirty state. Always pair a worker-scoped pool with a test-scoped transaction fixture (see Pattern 527) that rolls back after each test.

---

**Pattern 532: Vitest `test.extend()` fixture dependency chain for composable multi-layer isolation** [official]
Fixtures can depend on other fixtures — Vitest resolves the dependency graph automatically, initializing dependencies before dependents and tearing them down in reverse order. This composes independent concerns (DB connection, transaction, seeded data) without coupling their implementations.
```typescript
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { pool } from './db/pool';
import { seedUsers } from './fixtures/seed';

const withDb = base.extend({
  client: async ({}, use) => {
    const client = await pool.connect();
    await use(client);
    client.release();
  },
});

const withTx = withDb.extend({
  tx: async ({ client }, use) => {
    await client.query('BEGIN');
    await use(client);
    await client.query('ROLLBACK');
  },
});

export const test = withTx.extend({
  seededUsers: async ({ tx }, use) => {
    const users = await seedUsers(tx);
    await use(users);
    // No teardown needed — tx ROLLBACK removes seed data
  },
});

test('returns seeded users from repo', async ({ seededUsers, tx }) => {
  const repo = new UserRepository(tx);
  const found = await repo.findAll();
  expect(found).toHaveLength(seededUsers.length);
});
```
Tradeoff: Deep fixture chains increase initialization time and make teardown order harder to reason about. Keep chains to 3-4 levels maximum. For complex domain setups, prefer a single "scenario fixture" that bundles multiple concerns internally rather than a deep chain of single-concern fixtures.

---

**Pattern 533: Playwright `mergeTests()` for orthogonal fixture namespaces without coupling** [official]
`mergeTests()` combines custom `test` objects from multiple modules, merging their fixture namespaces into a single callable. This allows DB helpers, accessibility utilities, and auth fixtures to evolve independently with zero coupling — each module exports its own typed `test` object and they are composed at the suite level.
```typescript
// fixtures/db.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
export const dbTest = base.extend({ db: async ({}, use) => { /* ... */ await use(db); } });

// fixtures/a11y.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
export const a11yTest = base.extend({ a11y: async ({}, use) => { /* ... */ await use(axe); } });

// fixtures/auth.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
export const authTest = base.extend({ authUser: async ({}, use) => { /* ... */ await use(user); } });

// e2e/user-profile.spec.ts
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { dbTest } from '../fixtures/db';
import { a11yTest } from '../fixtures/a11y';
import { authTest } from '../fixtures/auth';

const test = mergeTests(dbTest, a11yTest, authTest);

test('profile page is accessible for authenticated user',
  async ({ page, db, a11y, authUser }) => {
    await db.seedProfile(authUser.id);
    await page.goto(`/profile/${authUser.id}`);
    const results = await a11y.run(page);
    expect(results.violations).toHaveLength(0);
  },
);
```
Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` performs a shallow merge of fixture definitions. If two source `test` objects define a fixture with the same name, the rightmost definition wins silently. Always use distinct fixture names per domain module to avoid shadowing. TypeScript will surface type conflicts if both sources define the same name with different types.

---

**Pattern 534: Playwright `{box: true}` fixture option to hide implementation details from test traces** [official]
Marking a fixture with `{ box: true }` causes Playwright's trace viewer and UI Mode to collapse the fixture's internals into a single opaque node. This reduces trace noise for frequently-used utility fixtures (e.g., login helpers, seed data loaders) that would otherwise produce dozens of trace entries per test.
```typescript
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend({
  loggedInPage: [
    async ({ page, baseURL }, use) => {
      // These internal steps are hidden in traces when box: true
      await page.goto(`${baseURL}/login`);
      await page.fill('[name="email"]', 'admin@example.com');
      await page.fill('[name="password"]', 'secret');
      await page.click('[type="submit"]');
      await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard');
      await use(page);
    },
    { box: true, scope: 'test' },
  ],
});

test('dashboard loads after login', async ({ loggedInPage }) => {
  // Trace shows "loggedInPage setup" as one step, not 6 steps
  await expect(loggedInPage.locator('h1')).toContainText('Dashboard');
});
```
Tradeoff: `{ box: true }` intentionally obscures fixture internals from developers investigating failures. Do not box fixtures that are actively being debugged or that contain complex logic likely to be the source of failures. Use `{ box: false }` (the default) during development and add `box: true` only to fully stable, well-tested fixture code.

---

**Pattern 535: Vitest `vi.defineHelper()` for stack-trace-clean test utility functions** [official]
Functions created with `vi.defineHelper()` are marked as framework internals and are excluded from Vitest's stack-trace trimming. This means assertion errors thrown inside helper functions show the caller's line in the error, not the helper's line — dramatically improving the actionability of failure messages.
```typescript
import { vi, expect, test } from 'vitest';

// Without vi.defineHelper: stack trace points to this file, not the caller
const assertUserShape = vi.defineHelper((user: unknown) => {
  expect(user).toMatchObject({
    id: expect.any(Number),
    email: expect.stringContaining('@'),
    createdAt: expect.any(Date),
  });
});

test('createUser returns a well-formed user', async () => {
  const user = await createUser({ email: 'alice@example.com' });
  assertUserShape(user); // Failure here shows THIS line, not assertUserShape's body
});

test('updateUser preserves shape', async () => {
  const user = await updateUser(1, { email: 'new@example.com' });
  assertUserShape(user); // Each callsite shows its own line number in failures
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.defineHelper()` is a Vitest 4.1+ API with no equivalent in Jest. If you maintain a codebase that runs tests under both Jest and Vitest (e.g., during a migration), wrap the helper in a compat shim that falls back to a plain function when running under Jest. The fallback produces slightly noisier stack traces but does not break functionality.

---

**Pattern 536: Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks: true` for surfacing un-awaited timers and open handles** [official]
Enabling `detectAsyncLeaks: true` in `vitest.config` causes Vitest to report any async handles (timers, open sockets, unresolved promises) still alive after a test completes. This surfaces the most common cause of flaky tests — fire-and-forget async work that finishes in a later test — without requiring manual `--detectOpenHandles` investigation loops.
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectAsyncLeaks: true, // Report lingering handles after each test
    pool: 'forks',          // Works best with forks pool (full process isolation)
  },
});

// leaky.test.ts — Vitest will flag the test below
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

test('fires analytics without awaiting (LEAK)', () => {
  // This unhandled promise outlives the test and may resolve during a later test
  fetch('/analytics/event', { method: 'POST', body: '{"event":"click"}' });
  expect(true).toBe(true);
  // detectAsyncLeaks will report: "Test left 1 pending fetch handle"
});

test('correct: awaits all async work', async () => {
  await fetch('/analytics/event', { method: 'POST', body: '{"event":"click"}' });
  expect(true).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: `detectAsyncLeaks` adds a small overhead per test (~0.5ms) to snapshot the async handle table before and after execution. In suites with thousands of tests this adds up to seconds. Disable it in fast unit-test suites and enable it only in integration test projects where async leaks are more likely.

---

**Pattern 537: Playwright `page.routeWebSocket()` for WebSocket connection isolation** [official]
`page.routeWebSocket(url, handler)` intercepts WebSocket connections matching a URL pattern and exposes a mock `ws` object for controlling messages in both directions. Tests that exercise real-time UI features (chat, live dashboards) can simulate any server message sequence without running a real WebSocket server.
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('dashboard updates when server pushes a price tick', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://prices.example.com/feed', (ws) => {
    // Immediately send a connected message then a price update
    ws.onopen = () => {
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'connected' }));
      setTimeout(() => {
        ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'tick', symbol: 'AAPL', price: 182.50 }));
      }, 100);
    };
    // Echo client pings back as pongs for keepalive
    ws.onmessage = (msg) => {
      const data = JSON.parse(msg as string);
      if (data.type === 'ping') ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'pong' }));
    };
  });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-symbol="AAPL"] .price')).toContainText('182.50');
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.routeWebSocket()` is available from Playwright v1.48+. The mock `ws` object uses the WebSocket protocol but runs in-process — it does not exercise TLS handshake, WebSocket upgrade negotiation, or proxy behavior. For tests that must verify those aspects, use a real lightweight WebSocket server (e.g., `ws` npm package) started in `beforeAll`.

---

**Pattern 538: Node.js `node:test` `t.mock.module()` per-test ESM isolation without Jest** [official]
Node.js v22.3+ ships `t.mock.module()` on the test context object, enabling ESM module mocking that is automatically restored after each test without any test runner plugin or Babel transform. This is the native alternative to Vitest's `vi.mock()` / Jest's `jest.unstable_mockModule()` for projects that run tests directly under `node --test`.
```typescript
import { test, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('sendEmail uses the mock transport', async (t) => {
  // Mock is scoped to this test and auto-restored afterward
  const mockTransport = t.mock.module('./transport', {
    namedExports: {
      send: t.mock.fn(async () => ({ messageId: 'mock-001' })),
    },
  });

  // Dynamic import picks up the mocked module
  const { sendEmail } = await import('./emailService.js');
  const result = await sendEmail('alice@example.com', 'Hello');

  assert.equal(result.messageId, 'mock-001');
  assert.equal(mockTransport.namedExports.send.mock.callCount(), 1);
  // No afterEach needed — mock is torn down with the test context
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.mock.module()` requires the tested module to be imported via dynamic `import()` AFTER the mock is registered — static top-level imports from the same file have already been evaluated and will not see the mock. This is the same constraint as Vitest's `vi.doMock()`. Plan module boundaries accordingly.

---

**Pattern 539: Jest `jest.replaceProperty()` for non-configurable property isolation** [official]
`jest.replaceProperty(obj, key, value)` replaces a property on an object (including non-configurable and read-only properties) for the duration of a test, with automatic restoration via `jest.restoreAllMocks()` or `afterEach`. This is the correct tool for isolating constants, version strings, or frozen config objects that `jest.spyOn()` cannot replace.
```typescript
import { jest, test, expect, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { APP_VERSION } from './version';
import { getVersionBanner } from './banner';

afterEach(() => {
  jest.restoreAllMocks();
});

test('banner includes version number', () => {
  // APP_VERSION is a const exported string — spyOn cannot intercept it
  // replaceProperty works because it targets the module namespace object
  jest.replaceProperty(
    require('./version'), // the module namespace
    'APP_VERSION',
    '9.9.9-test',
  );

  const banner = getVersionBanner();
  expect(banner).toContain('9.9.9-test');
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.replaceProperty()` uses `Object.defineProperty` under the hood and only works when the property is writable on the module namespace (CJS modules: yes; ESM via Jest's experimental ESM: namespace properties are read-only and this fails silently). For ESM, use `jest.unstable_mockModule()` with a factory that returns the desired value.

---

**Pattern 540: Vitest `vi.mock(import(...))` type-safe module promise pattern for ESM isolation** [official]
Passing an `import()` promise to `vi.mock()` instead of a string path gives TypeScript full type inference over the factory's return type — the factory's return must match the module's exported interface, surfacing mock shape errors at compile time rather than at runtime.
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { sendNotification } from './notifier';

// Type-safe: factory return type is checked against the real module shape
vi.mock(import('./emailClient'), async (importOriginal) => {
  const real = await importOriginal();
  return {
    ...real,
    // TypeScript errors here if `sendEmail` doesn't exist on the real module
    sendEmail: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ status: 'sent', id: 'mock-id' }),
  };
});

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.clearAllMocks();
});

test('sendNotification delegates to emailClient.sendEmail', async () => {
  const { sendEmail } = await import('./emailClient');
  await sendNotification({ to: 'bob@example.com', subject: 'Hi' });
  expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({ to: 'bob@example.com' }),
  );
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.mock(import(...))` is hoisted by Vitest's transform — the `import()` inside the call is NOT a real dynamic import at runtime; it is transformed into a string path during compilation. This means you cannot compute the path dynamically (see Gotcha G336). The benefit of this syntax is purely TypeScript ergonomics; the runtime behavior is identical to `vi.mock('./emailClient', factory)`.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G341: Vitest `scope: 'file'` fixture does not reset between `describe` blocks in the same file — shared mutable state persists across all blocks**
A `scope: 'file'` fixture is initialized once when the first test in the file that requests it runs, and torn down after the last test in the file completes. Any mutable state on the fixture object (e.g., an in-memory array, a counter, a Map) persists across all `describe` blocks without reset.
WHY: Vitest's fixture scoping model maps directly to worker lifetime (worker scope), file lifetime (file scope), and test lifetime (test scope). "File" scope means one instance per file — there is no "describe-block scope" in the hierarchy. Developers expecting `beforeEach` semantics within describes are surprised that the fixture object is the same reference throughout the file.
Fix: For mutable fixture state that must reset between `describe` blocks, use `scope: 'test'` (default) and accept the per-test initialization cost, or use `beforeEach` to call a `.reset()` method on the file-scoped fixture explicitly.

---

**Gotcha G342: Playwright `test.use()` inside a `describe` block only applies to tests defined IN that block — dynamically generated tests added via `for` loops or `test.describe.configure()` outside the block are unaffected**
`test.use()` configures the test context for the enclosing `describe` block. Tests generated dynamically (e.g., `roles.forEach(role => test(...))`) that are defined outside the describe block do not inherit the configuration even if they logically belong to the same group.
WHY: Playwright's fixture override system is based on lexical nesting — `test.use()` applies to tests that are syntactically inside the `describe()` callback at parse time. Dynamic test generation patterns that iterate outside a describe block bypass the lexical boundary, so the override is never applied.
Fix: Move the dynamic test generation loop INSIDE the `describe` block that calls `test.use()`, or create a helper function that accepts the configured `test` object as a parameter and calls it to generate tests.

---

**Gotcha G343: Node.js `t.mock.module()` mock is not visible to modules that were already cached in the module registry before the test ran**
When `t.mock.module('./dep')` is called, Node.js installs the mock into the ESM module map for the current test context. However, if `./dep` was already imported by another module that was loaded before the test context was established (e.g., imported at the top of the test file itself), the cached binding is not updated.
WHY: ESM live bindings are resolved at module link time. Once a module is linked with the real `./dep`, that link is permanent for the lifetime of the module in the cache. `t.mock.module()` inserts a new entry into the module map, but it cannot retroactively update already-linked bindings from previously evaluated modules.
Fix: Ensure the module under test is imported via dynamic `import()` AFTER `t.mock.module()` is called. Do not import the module under test (or any module that transitively imports the dependency being mocked) at the top-level of the test file.

---

**Gotcha G344: Vitest `aroundEach` hook that throws before the `yield` prevents the test from running AND prevents the post-yield cleanup from executing — resources allocated pre-yield leak**
If an `aroundEach` hook throws an error before the `yield` (the point at which the test executes), both the test body and all post-`yield` cleanup code in the same hook are skipped. Any resources allocated before the throw (database transactions, open file handles) are not released.
WHY: `aroundEach` is implemented as an async generator. A `throw` before the `yield` statement causes the generator to terminate in an error state. The generator's `finally` block (if any) still runs, but any code written after the `yield` in a `try/finally`-less generator body is dead code from the perspective of the error path. This mirrors the semantics of `async function*` in JavaScript.
Fix: Always wrap the pre-yield setup and post-yield teardown in `try/finally` inside `aroundEach`:
```typescript
test.extend({}).aroundEach(async function* ({ onCleanup }) {
  const resource = await acquire(); // May throw
  try {
    yield; // Test runs here
  } finally {
    await release(resource); // Always runs, even if acquire() or test() throws
  }
});
```

---

**Gotcha G345: Jest `jest.resetModules()` clears the module registry but does NOT clear `jest.mock()` registrations — re-imported modules after `resetModules()` are still mocked**
A common misconception is that `jest.resetModules()` "resets all mocking state." It only resets the module instance cache (so the next `require()` or `import()` re-evaluates the module file). The mock registry (which modules are stubbed and with what factory) is separate and is unaffected by `resetModules()`. Modules re-imported after `resetModules()` will use the mock factory if one was registered.
WHY: Jest maintains two independent data structures: the module registry (instance cache keyed by resolved path) and the mock registry (set of mocked modules with optional factory functions). `resetModules()` clears the instance cache. `clearAllMocks()` clears mock call state. `restoreAllMocks()` restores spies. None of these operations affect the mock registry entries created by `jest.mock()`. Only `jest.unmock(path)` removes a specific entry.
Fix: If you want a module to be re-imported as its real implementation after a test that used `jest.mock()`, explicitly call `jest.unmock('./the-module')` before the dynamic re-import. If you need per-test real/mock switching, use `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` with conditional `jest.mock()` inside each bubble.

## Cycle 57 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 541** — Vitest `test.extend()` with `injected: true` for per-project fixture value overrides without test-file edits
```typescript
import { test as base } from 'vitest';

// Define the configurable fixture in a shared setup file
export const test = base.extend<{ apiBaseUrl: string }>({
  apiBaseUrl: [
    async ({ }, use) => {
      // Default value — overridden per Vitest project config via `provide`
      await use('http://localhost:3000');
    },
    { injected: true },
  ],
});

// In vitest.config.ts (project-level override):
// export default defineConfig({
//   test: { provide: { apiBaseUrl: 'https://staging.example.com' } },
// });

test('fetches user from configured base', async ({ apiBaseUrl }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${apiBaseUrl}/users/1`);
  expect(res.ok).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: `injected: true` fixtures require the `provide` key in the Vitest project config to match the fixture name exactly (case-sensitive). Typos in `provide` silently fall back to the fixture default, making misconfiguration hard to detect without an explicit assertion that the injected value was applied.

---

**Pattern 542** — Playwright `test.use({ launchOptions })` override per-describe for headless vs headed isolation in a single run
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Default project config: headless: true
// This describe block forces headed mode for visual regression tests only
test.describe('Visual regression — header component', () => {
  test.use({
    launchOptions: {
      headless: false,
      slowMo: 50,
    },
    viewport: { width: 1280, height: 900 },
  });

  test('header renders correctly at 1280x900', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/');
    await expect(page.locator('header')).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('header-1280x900.png');
  });

  test('nav links are visible at 1280x900', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/');
    const links = page.locator('nav a');
    await expect(links).toHaveCount(5);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Forcing `headless: false` in a describe block makes those tests incompatible with headless-only CI environments (e.g., Docker without Xvfb). Wrap the override in a condition checked via an environment variable (`process.env.CI ? {} : { launchOptions: { headless: false } }`) to restore CI compatibility.

---

**Pattern 543** — Vitest `aroundAll` generator hook for file-scoped database schema migration with guaranteed teardown
```typescript
import { test as base, beforeAll, afterAll } from 'vitest';
import { runMigrations, rollbackMigrations, getDb } from '../db/test-helpers';

// Use aroundAll at the file level to bracket the entire file's test suite
// with schema setup and teardown as a single atomic operation.
const test = base.extend<{ db: ReturnType<typeof getDb> }>({
  db: async ({ }, use) => {
    const db = getDb();
    await use(db);
  },
});

test.aroundAll(async function* () {
  const schemaVersion = await runMigrations('test_schema_cycle57');
  try {
    yield; // All tests in the file run here
  } finally {
    await rollbackMigrations('test_schema_cycle57', schemaVersion);
  }
});

test('inserts a record correctly', async ({ db }) => {
  const id = await db.insert('users', { name: 'Alice' });
  expect(id).toBeGreaterThan(0);
});

test('reads back an inserted record', async ({ db }) => {
  await db.insert('users', { name: 'Bob' });
  const users = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?', ['Bob']);
  expect(users).toHaveLength(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: `aroundAll` runs once per file, so a schema migration failure blocks ALL tests in the file with a single error. For large test files this can mask individual test failures. Prefer splitting large files into focused modules with one `aroundAll` each rather than a single monolithic file.

---

**Pattern 544** — Playwright `worker`-scoped fixture for authenticated API client shared across tests in a worker
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { ApiClient } from '../lib/api-client';

type WorkerFixtures = { authedApiClient: ApiClient };

const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  authedApiClient: [
    async ({ }, use) => {
      // Login once per worker — expensive operation shared across all tests in worker
      const client = new ApiClient(process.env.API_BASE_URL!);
      await client.login({
        email: process.env.TEST_USER_EMAIL!,
        password: process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!,
      });
      await use(client);
      // Teardown: invalidate the session after last test in worker
      await client.logout();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('worker-shared client can list resources', async ({ authedApiClient }) => {
  const resources = await authedApiClient.get('/resources');
  expect(resources.status).toBe(200);
});

test('worker-shared client can create a resource', async ({ authedApiClient }) => {
  const result = await authedApiClient.post('/resources', { name: 'new-item' });
  expect(result.status).toBe(201);
});
```
Tradeoff: A worker-scoped authenticated client shares session state across all tests in that worker. If any test mutates the session (e.g., changes the user's email or invalidates the token), all subsequent tests in the worker will fail. Use worker-scoped auth only for read-heavy suites; write tests should use test-scoped clients.

**Pattern 545** — Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers({ now })` + `test.extend()` fixture for deterministic Date and timer isolation
```typescript
import { test as base, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';

type TimerFixtures = { frozenAt: (isoDate: string) => void };

const test = base.extend<TimerFixtures>({
  frozenAt: async ({ }, use) => {
    let installed = false;
    const freeze = (isoDate: string) => {
      vi.useFakeTimers({ now: new Date(isoDate).getTime() });
      installed = true;
    };
    await use(freeze);
    if (installed) vi.useRealTimers();
  },
});

test('calculates days until expiry correctly on 2026-05-14', ({ frozenAt }) => {
  frozenAt('2026-05-14T00:00:00.000Z');
  const expiry = new Date('2026-06-14T00:00:00.000Z');
  const daysLeft = Math.ceil((expiry.getTime() - Date.now()) / 86_400_000);
  expect(daysLeft).toBe(31);
});

test('generates an ISO timestamp with the frozen date', ({ frozenAt }) => {
  frozenAt('2026-05-14T12:00:00.000Z');
  expect(new Date().toISOString()).toBe('2026-05-14T12:00:00.000Z');
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces the global `Date` constructor and `setTimeout`/`setInterval`. Third-party libraries that capture a reference to the real `Date` before the fixture runs (common in polyfills and some ORM connection pools) will not see the faked time. Ensure `frozenAt()` is called before any module that caches `new Date()` at import time.

**Pattern 546** — Playwright `page.route()` + `fulfill()` for network-level API isolation without a mock server
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('User profile page — isolated from real API', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    // Intercept all calls to the users endpoint and return a controlled payload
    await page.route('**/api/users/42', async (route) => {
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({
          id: 42,
          name: 'Alice Isolation',
          email: 'alice@example.com',
          role: 'admin',
        }),
      });
    });
  });

  test('renders user name from mocked API response', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/users/42');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Alice Isolation' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('shows admin badge for admin role', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/users/42');
    await expect(page.getByText('Admin')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.route()` matches URLs using glob patterns; the `**` prefix is required to match regardless of scheme and host. Without it, the route only matches exact origins, breaking tests when the app is served from a different port in CI. Always use `**/` as a prefix or a full regex for port-agnostic matching.

**Pattern 547** — Vitest `test.extend()` with a `scope: 'file'` in-memory SQLite fixture for zero-migration unit tests
```typescript
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import Database from 'better-sqlite3';

type DbFixtures = { db: Database.Database };

const test = base.extend<DbFixtures>({
  db: [
    async ({ }, use) => {
      // File-scoped: create schema once per test file, wipe rows between tests
      const db = new Database(':memory:');
      db.exec(`
        CREATE TABLE users (
          id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
          name TEXT NOT NULL,
          role TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'user'
        );
      `);
      await use(db);
      db.close();
    },
    { scope: 'file' },
  ],
});

// Per-test cleanup — rows reset between tests without schema re-creation
test.beforeEach(({ db }) => {
  db.exec('DELETE FROM users;');
});

test('inserts and retrieves a user', ({ db }) => {
  db.prepare('INSERT INTO users (name, role) VALUES (?, ?)').run('Alice', 'admin');
  const user = db.prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?').get('Alice') as { name: string; role: string };
  expect(user.role).toBe('admin');
});
```
Tradeoff: `better-sqlite3` is synchronous; the `async` fixture wrapper is required for Vitest's `scope: 'file'` to work correctly even though no actual async I/O occurs. Using the sync `Database` constructor inside an async fixture is safe because SQLite in-memory databases are thread-local in the Node.js process, but be aware that parallel workers each get their own in-memory DB instance.
