**Pattern 548** — Playwright `test.step()` nested steps for structured fixture-level tracing in slow tests
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow with stepped fixture tracing', async ({ page }) => {
  await test.step('Navigate to product listing', async () => {
    await page.goto('/products');
    await expect(page.getByRole('list', { name: 'products' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  const productName = await test.step('Select first available product', async () => {
    const firstProduct = page.getByTestId('product-card').first();
    const name = await firstProduct.getByRole('heading').innerText();
    await firstProduct.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
    return name;
  });

  await test.step('Verify cart badge incremented', async () => {
    await expect(page.getByTestId('cart-badge')).toHaveText('1');
  });

  await test.step(`Checkout with product: ${productName}`, async () => {
    await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Cart' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText(productName)).toBeVisible();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/checkout');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.step()` names appear in Playwright's HTML report and trace viewer, making long E2E tests easier to debug. However, steps do not create fixture isolation boundaries — a failure in one step does not trigger automatic cleanup for resources acquired in a previous step. Always pair with fixture-level teardown rather than relying on steps for resource management.

**Pattern 549** — Vitest `vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')` with `mockResolvedValueOnce` for sequential multi-request isolation
```typescript
import { test, vi, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { fetchUserWithPosts } from '../services/userService';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.restoreAllMocks();
});

test('fetchUserWithPosts makes two sequential fetch calls and merges results', async () => {
  const fetchSpy = vi.spyOn(globalThis, 'fetch')
    .mockResolvedValueOnce(
      new Response(JSON.stringify({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }), {
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      }),
    )
    .mockResolvedValueOnce(
      new Response(JSON.stringify([{ id: 10, title: 'First Post' }]), {
        status: 200,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      }),
    );

  const result = await fetchUserWithPosts(1);

  expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
  expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenNthCalledWith(1, 'https://api.example.com/users/1');
  expect(fetchSpy).toHaveBeenNthCalledWith(2, 'https://api.example.com/users/1/posts');
  expect(result).toEqual({ id: 1, name: 'Alice', posts: [{ id: 10, title: 'First Post' }] });
});
```
Tradeoff: `mockResolvedValueOnce` queues responses in call order — the spy returns them in strict FIFO sequence. If the implementation changes the fetch call order (e.g., swaps user and posts requests for a parallel `Promise.all`), the test will silently pass with incorrect data because each mock returns the next queued value regardless of the URL. Always pair with `toHaveBeenNthCalledWith` assertions that verify the URL for each call position.

**Pattern 550** — Playwright `{box: true}` fixture option to suppress fixture steps from appearing in trace viewer
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Verbose low-level fixture — we want it hidden from the trace
const test = base.extend<{ seedDatabase: () => Promise<void> }>({
  seedDatabase: [
    async ({ request }, use) => {
      const seed = async () => {
        await request.post('/test-api/seed', {
          data: { scenario: 'checkout-happy-path' },
        });
      };
      await use(seed);
      // Cleanup — also hidden from trace
      await request.delete('/test-api/seed');
    },
    { box: true },  // Collapses fixture internals to a single "seedDatabase" step
  ],
});

test('checkout completes after seeding', async ({ page, seedDatabase }) => {
  await seedDatabase();
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Place order' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `{box: true}` hides the fixture's internal actions from the Playwright trace viewer, making the trace cleaner for high-level review. The downside is that when the fixture itself is the source of a failure, the trace provides no internal steps for diagnosis — you lose the request/response timeline for the seed API call. Reserve `box: true` only for stable, well-tested fixtures.

**Pattern 551** — Node.js `t.mock.module()` with a factory returning per-test state via closure for ESM isolation in `node:test`
```typescript
import { test, mock, before, after } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('module mock with per-test closure state', async (t) => {
  let capturedPayload: unknown = null;

  // Mock BEFORE dynamic import of the module under test
  t.mock.module('./emailService.js', {
    namedExports: {
      sendEmail: async (payload: unknown) => {
        capturedPayload = payload;
        return { messageId: 'mock-id-001' };
      },
    },
  });

  // Dynamic import AFTER the mock is installed — gets the mocked version
  const { notifyUser } = await import('./notificationService.js');

  await notifyUser({ userId: 42, event: 'welcome' });

  assert.deepStrictEqual(capturedPayload, {
    to: 'user42@example.com',
    subject: 'Welcome!',
    body: expect.stringContaining('42'),
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.mock.module()` in `node:test` is scoped to the test context `t` — the mock is automatically restored when the test ends. However, because ESM module instances are cached after the first import in a given module namespace, the `notificationService.js` module must not have been previously imported at the file's top level. If it was, its internal `import` of `emailService` was already bound to the real module before `t.mock.module()` ran.

**Pattern 552** — Vitest `test.extend()` with `onCleanup` for async resource cleanup ordering guarantees
```typescript
import { test as base, onTestFinished } from 'vitest';

interface HttpServerFixture {
  server: { url: string; close: () => Promise<void> };
}

const test = base.extend<HttpServerFixture>({
  server: async ({ }, use) => {
    // Inline module to avoid file-level imports polluting other tests
    const { createServer } = await import('../test-helpers/mock-http-server');
    const instance = await createServer({ port: 0 }); // port 0 = OS-assigned

    // Register cleanup with onTestFinished — runs after use() resolves
    // even if the test throws, ensuring the port is always released
    onTestFinished(async () => {
      await instance.close();
    });

    await use({ url: `http://localhost:${instance.port}`, close: instance.close });
    // Note: teardown is handled by onTestFinished above, not here,
    // so a test throw cannot skip the close() call.
  },
});

test('mock HTTP server responds with 200', async ({ server }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${server.url}/health`);
  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
});
```
Tradeoff: Using `onTestFinished` instead of post-`use()` cleanup code guarantees teardown runs even when the test body throws before `use()` resolves (e.g., if `await use(...)` is never awaited due to an early assertion failure). The tradeoff is that `onTestFinished` callbacks run in reverse registration order — if multiple fixtures register cleanup with it, the teardown order is last-in-first-out, which may not match the initialization order of dependent fixtures.

**Pattern 553** — Playwright `mergeTests()` for combining page-object fixtures and data fixtures without namespace collisions
```typescript
import { mergeTests } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as pageObjectTest } from './fixtures/page-objects';
import { test as dataFixtureTest } from './fixtures/data-fixtures';

// pageObjectTest provides: loginPage, dashboardPage, settingsPage
// dataFixtureTest provides: seedUser, seedOrg, cleanupData

// Merge without conflicts — each fixture namespace is kept orthogonal
export const test = mergeTests(pageObjectTest, dataFixtureTest);
export { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// In tests:
// import { test, expect } from './combined-fixtures';
// test('user can log in', async ({ loginPage, seedUser }) => {
//   await loginPage.goto();
//   await loginPage.fill(seedUser.email, seedUser.password);
//   await loginPage.submit();
//   await expect(loginPage.page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
// });
```
Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` raises a runtime error if both fixture sets define a fixture with the same name. When composing fixtures from different teams or libraries, name-prefix your fixture types (e.g., `authLoginPage` vs `dataLoginUser`) to prevent collisions before they become runtime failures. There is no static TypeScript warning for duplicate fixture names across merged test objects — the error only surfaces at test run time.

**Pattern 554** — Vitest `detectOpenHandles` config + `scope: 'worker'` fixture teardown for eliminating async handle leaks
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectOpenHandles: true,   // Report tests that leave open handles
    pool: 'forks',              // Separate process per worker — handles don't bleed across workers
  },
});

// In test fixture file:
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { createRedisClient } from '../lib/redis';

const test = base.extend<{}, { redis: ReturnType<typeof createRedisClient> }>({
  redis: [
    async ({ }, use) => {
      const client = createRedisClient({ lazyConnect: false });
      await client.connect();
      await use(client);
      // Explicit disconnect prevents the open TCP handle from triggering
      // Vitest's detectOpenHandles warning after the worker's last test
      await client.disconnect();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

test('redis fixture disconnects after worker finishes', async ({ redis }) => {
  await redis.set('key', 'value');
  expect(await redis.get('key')).toBe('value');
});
```
Tradeoff: `detectOpenHandles: true` adds measurable overhead to each test worker because Vitest tracks all async resources via `async_hooks`. In suites with thousands of tests this can increase total run time by 5–15%. Enable it only in CI or during active debugging of handle-leak issues; disable it in local development runs via a `vitest.config.local.ts` override.

**Pattern 555** — Playwright `page.clock.install()` + `clock.fastForward()` for isolating time-dependent polling components
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('auto-refresh banner disappears after 5s countdown', async ({ page }) => {
  // Install the fake clock BEFORE navigation so the page never sees real time
  await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('2026-05-14T10:00:00Z') });

  await page.goto('/dashboard');

  // Trigger an action that starts the 5-second auto-dismiss countdown
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Refresh data' }).click();
  const banner = page.getByRole('alert', { name: /Refreshing in/ });
  await expect(banner).toBeVisible();

  // Jump the fake clock forward — no real waiting required
  await page.clock.fastForward(5000);

  // After 5 virtual seconds the banner should have dismissed itself
  await expect(banner).toBeHidden();
  // Real wall-clock time elapsed: < 100ms
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.clock.install()` must be called before `page.goto()` or `page.reload()` — if the page navigates before the clock is installed, script-level timers created during initial load (e.g., `setTimeout` in module initialization code) use the real clock and will not respond to `fastForward`. If retrofitting existing tests, wrap the `clock.install()` + `goto()` sequence in a single `test.step()` to make the ordering constraint visible in traces.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha G346: Vitest `detectOpenHandles: true` reports false positives for `scope: 'worker'` fixtures whose teardown runs after the last test — the handle is not leaked but the detection fires before worker-scoped teardown completes**
A worker-scoped fixture (e.g., a database connection pool or Redis client) is torn down after the last test in the worker finishes. Vitest's open-handle detection fires at the point the last test result is recorded, before the worker-scope teardown phase. This causes the teardown handle to appear as an unclosed resource even though it will be properly closed milliseconds later.
Why this matters: Teams see spurious "open handle" warnings in CI that cause flaky test runs or false failures in strict mode, leading to wasted debugging time chasing a non-existent leak.
Fix: Upgrade to Vitest >=2.1 where worker-scoped fixture teardown is tracked separately from the test result timeline. For older versions, add an explicit `afterAll(() => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 50)))` in the worker fixture file to give teardown time to complete before the handle scanner fires — this is a workaround, not a fix.

---

**Gotcha G347: Playwright `mergeTests()` silently picks the LAST registered fixture when two merged test objects define the same fixture name — the first fixture's implementation is permanently shadowed**
When `mergeTests(testA, testB)` is called and both `testA` and `testB` expose a fixture named `page` (or any other name), Playwright uses `testB`'s implementation with no warning. If `testA` extends the built-in `page` fixture (e.g., to add automatic route interception) and `testB` passes through the unmodified built-in `page`, `testB`'s version wins and the interception logic is silently dropped.
Why this matters: Page-object fixtures that augment built-in fixtures are a common pattern. Merging them with another fixture set that happens to also extend the same built-in will silently break the augmentation, causing tests to pass locally (before the merge) but fail after integration.
Fix: Before calling `mergeTests()`, audit both fixture sets for overlapping names using TypeScript's intersection type: `type Conflicts = keyof FixtureA & keyof FixtureB`. Rename conflicting fixtures in one set, or use explicit re-export aliasing before merging.

---

**Gotcha G348: Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` does not isolate modules that are imported at the top level of the test file — only modules imported INSIDE the `isolateModulesAsync` callback are isolated**
Developers use `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` to get a fresh module instance per test. However, if the module under test is imported at the file's top level (`import { myModule } from './myModule'`), that import is evaluated once when the test file loads. The `isolateModulesAsync` call creates a fresh registry only for dynamic imports made INSIDE its callback — the top-level import is already cached and will not be re-evaluated.
Why this matters: Tests that call `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` while keeping top-level static imports silently share module state between tests, defeating the purpose of isolation. The test file compiles without errors and the mocks appear to register correctly, but the module under test never sees a fresh import.
Fix: Remove all top-level imports of the module under test and move them inside the `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` callback as dynamic `await import()` calls. Apply the same rule to any modules that transitively import the target module.

---

**Gotcha G349: Vitest `vi.useFakeTimers()` blocks `Promise` microtask queue flushing when `shouldAdvanceTime: false` (the default) — `await`-based code inside the test may never resolve**
`vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces `setTimeout` and `setInterval` but does NOT replace microtask scheduling (`queueMicrotask`, `Promise.resolve().then()`). However, some Vitest internals and community plugins schedule cleanup work via `setImmediate` or `process.nextTick`, which ARE replaced by fake timers. If a test `await`s a promise whose resolution depends on a `setImmediate` callback, and fake timers are active without manual advancement, the test hangs indefinitely.
Why this matters: Tests that mix `await`-based async code with `vi.useFakeTimers()` occasionally produce silent hangs in CI with no error output — the test times out rather than failing with an assertion error, making the root cause invisible.
Fix: When using fake timers with async code, always pair timer advancement with microtask flushing: call `await vi.runAllTimersAsync()` (Vitest ≥1.6) instead of `vi.runAllTimers()`. The async variant flushes the microtask queue between each timer callback, preventing the hang.

---

**Gotcha G350: Node.js `t.mock.module()` does not support mocking built-in Node.js modules (e.g., `node:fs`, `node:path`) — the mock silently has no effect and the real built-in is used**
`t.mock.module()` in `node:test` works for user-land ESM and CJS modules by intercepting the module loader. Built-in modules (those prefixed with `node:` or matching Node.js core module names) bypass the user-land module loader entirely — they are resolved through a separate native binding layer that `t.mock.module()` cannot intercept.
Why this matters: Developers attempting to mock `node:fs` to test file-reading logic will find their mock factory is never called and the real `node:fs` functions execute. This causes tests that write to disk, read real files, or depend on OS-specific paths to fail in unexpected ways or produce real side effects.
Fix: Use a manual dependency-injection approach — accept the `fs` module as a parameter to the function under test instead of importing it directly. Alternatively, wrap `node:fs` calls in a thin user-land adapter module (e.g., `./lib/fs-adapter.ts`) that CAN be mocked with `t.mock.module()` because it is a regular user-land module.

### Patterns

**Pattern 556** — Jest `globalSetup` + `globalTeardown` for One-Time External Resource Lifecycle
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';
export default defineConfig({
  globalSetup: '<rootDir>/test/global-setup.ts',
  globalTeardown: '<rootDir>/test/global-teardown.ts',
});

// test/global-setup.ts
import { MongoMemoryServer } from 'mongodb-memory-server';
export default async function globalSetup(): Promise<void> {
  const mongod = await MongoMemoryServer.create();
  process.env.MONGO_URI = mongod.getUri();
  // Attach to globalThis so teardown can find the handle
  (globalThis as Record<string, unknown>).__MONGOD__ = mongod;
}

// test/global-teardown.ts
import type { MongoMemoryServer } from 'mongodb-memory-server';
export default async function globalTeardown(): Promise<void> {
  const mongod = (globalThis as Record<string, unknown>).__MONGOD__ as MongoMemoryServer;
  await mongod?.stop();
}
```
Tradeoff: `globalSetup` runs in a separate worker context — `globalThis` mutations are visible to `globalTeardown` but NOT to test files. Share state into tests only through `process.env` (serializable strings). Using `globalThis` for non-string payloads across all test files requires a custom environment or `setupFilesAfterEnv`.

**Pattern 557** — Vitest `test.extend()` with `scope: 'worker'` for Shared Authenticated API Client
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from 'vitest';
import { ApiClient } from '../src/api-client';

interface WorkerFixtures {
  apiClient: ApiClient;
}

export const test = base.extend<Record<never, never>, WorkerFixtures>({
  apiClient: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Runs once per worker — auth handshake paid only once
      const client = new ApiClient({ baseURL: process.env.API_URL! });
      await client.authenticate({ token: process.env.API_TOKEN! });
      await use(client);
      await client.logout();
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// Each test that requests `apiClient` shares the same authenticated session
test('fetch user profile', async ({ apiClient }) => {
  const profile = await apiClient.get('/me');
  expect(profile.status).toBe(200);
  expect(profile.data).toHaveProperty('id');
});

test('list repositories', async ({ apiClient }) => {
  const repos = await apiClient.get('/repos');
  expect(repos.status).toBe(200);
  expect(Array.isArray(repos.data)).toBe(true);
});
```
Tradeoff: Worker-scoped fixtures are shared across all test files running in the same worker. If tests mutate shared state on the client (e.g., changing default headers), those mutations bleed into subsequent tests. Keep worker-scoped fixtures read-only or stateless; use `scope: 'test'` for any fixture that tests modify.

---

**Pattern 558** — Jest `setupFilesAfterEnv` Global `afterEach` for Timer and Mock Hygiene
```typescript
// jest.setup.ts  (referenced in jest.config.ts setupFilesAfterEnv)
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

afterEach(() => {
  // Restore real timers if any test activated fake timers without cleanup
  jest.useRealTimers();
  // Clear all call records so assertion counts never bleed between tests
  jest.clearAllMocks();
  // Restore any spied implementations (jest.spyOn) to originals
  jest.restoreAllMocks();
});

// Individual tests may still opt into fresh mocks via jest.resetAllMocks()
// when they need implementation resets, not just call-record resets.

// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';
export default defineConfig({
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/jest.setup.ts'],
  // Belt-and-suspenders: config-level reset as well
  clearMocks: false, // Handled by afterEach above for visibility
  restoreMocks: false,
});
```
Tradeoff: Placing cleanup in `setupFilesAfterEnv` makes teardown implicit — developers may not realise why a `jest.spyOn` is restored between tests. Add a brief comment in `jest.setup.ts` explaining the intent. Avoid duplicating these calls in individual `afterEach` blocks; double-invocation is harmless but adds noise to test output.

---

**Pattern 559** — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` + `afterEach(vi.unstubAllEnvs)` for Environment Variable Isolation
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { getFeatureFlag } from '../src/feature-flags';

describe('getFeatureFlag', () => {
  // Restore all env stubs after every test in this suite
  afterEach(() => vi.unstubAllEnvs());

  test('returns true when env flag is "1"', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('ENABLE_NEW_UI', '1');
    expect(getFeatureFlag('ENABLE_NEW_UI')).toBe(true);
  });

  test('returns false when env flag is "0"', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('ENABLE_NEW_UI', '0');
    expect(getFeatureFlag('ENABLE_NEW_UI')).toBe(false);
  });

  test('returns false when env flag is absent', () => {
    // No stub — tests the true absence; vi.unstubAllEnvs in afterEach
    // ensures previous test's stub is not visible here
    delete process.env.ENABLE_NEW_UI;
    expect(getFeatureFlag('ENABLE_NEW_UI')).toBe(false);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv()` stores the original value and restores it on `vi.unstubAllEnvs()`. If a test manually deletes a key (line 3 above) rather than stubbing it, `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` cannot restore it because no original was recorded. Prefer always using `vi.stubEnv(key, undefined)` instead of `delete process.env[key]` to keep the restore path consistent.

---

**Pattern 560** — Vitest `onCleanup` in `test.extend()` for Async Resource Disposal Ordering
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from 'vitest';

interface TestFixtures {
  tempDir: string;
  writeFile: (name: string, content: string) => Promise<void>;
}

const test = base.extend<TestFixtures>({
  tempDir: async ({}, use, { onCleanup }) => {
    const { mkdtemp, rm } = await import('node:fs/promises');
    const { join } = await import('node:path');
    const { tmpdir } = await import('node:os');

    const dir = await mkdtemp(join(tmpdir(), 'vitest-'));
    // Register cleanup BEFORE yielding — runs even if use() throws
    onCleanup(async () => {
      await rm(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
    });
    await use(dir);
  },
  writeFile: async ({ tempDir }, use) => {
    const { writeFile: fsWrite } = await import('node:fs/promises');
    const { join } = await import('node:path');
    await use((name, content) => fsWrite(join(tempDir, name), content, 'utf8'));
  },
});

test('writes and isolates temp files per test', async ({ tempDir, writeFile }) => {
  await writeFile('hello.txt', 'world');
  const { readFile } = await import('node:fs/promises');
  const { join } = await import('node:path');
  const content = await readFile(join(tempDir, 'hello.txt'), 'utf8');
  expect(content).toBe('world');
});
```
Tradeoff: `onCleanup` can only be called once per fixture invocation — a second call throws `FixtureAccessError` in Vitest ≥4.1. If you need multiple teardown steps, either compose them into a single `onCleanup` callback or use multiple fixture layers, each with its own `onCleanup`.

**Pattern 561** — Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` for Per-Test Singleton Re-initialisation
```typescript
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

describe('AppConfig singleton', () => {
  test('reads NODE_ENV at import time — development', async () => {
    process.env.NODE_ENV = 'development';
    const { AppConfig } = await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      // Dynamic import inside the callback gets a fresh module registry
      const mod = await import('../src/app-config');
      return mod;
    });
    expect(AppConfig.env).toBe('development');
  });

  test('reads NODE_ENV at import time — production', async () => {
    process.env.NODE_ENV = 'production';
    const { AppConfig } = await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
      const mod = await import('../src/app-config');
      return mod;
    });
    expect(AppConfig.env).toBe('production');
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    delete process.env.NODE_ENV;
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Every `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` call re-evaluates the entire module graph rooted at the target — transitive dependencies are re-required too. This can be slow for deep dependency trees. Scope the import inside the callback to the minimum necessary module; import shared utilities outside the callback to avoid redundant re-evaluation.

---

**Pattern 562** — Playwright `test.use()` for Per-Describe Locale and Timezone Isolation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Default suite runs in UTC
test('price formats in USD', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/pricing');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('price-display')).toHaveText('$9.99');
});

describe('German locale suite', () => {
  // Override locale + timezone for this describe block only
  test.use({
    locale: 'de-DE',
    timezoneId: 'Europe/Berlin',
  });

  test('price formats in EUR with German separators', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/pricing');
    // German locale formats 9.99 as "9,99 €"
    await expect(page.getByTestId('price-display')).toHaveText('9,99 €');
  });

  test('date renders in DD.MM.YYYY format', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/invoice');
    await expect(page.getByTestId('invoice-date')).toHaveText(/\d{2}\.\d{2}\.\d{4}/);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.use()` options apply to the entire describe block including nested describes. If a nested describe needs a different locale, add another `test.use()` inside it — later options shadow outer ones. Be aware that Playwright launches a fresh browser context per `test.use()` combination, so mixing many locale permutations multiplies context-creation overhead.

---

**Pattern 563** — Vitest `vi.mock(import(...))` Type-Safe Module Factory with Auto-Typed Return
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';

// Type-safe mock using the import() promise form — the factory's return type
// is inferred from the real module, catching typos at compile time.
vi.mock(import('../src/email-service'), () => ({
  sendEmail: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'mock-id-001' }),
  validateAddress: vi.fn().mockReturnValue(true),
}));

import { sendEmail, validateAddress } from '../src/email-service';
import { registerUser } from '../src/user-registration';

describe('registerUser', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.mocked(sendEmail).mockClear();
    vi.mocked(validateAddress).mockClear();
  });

  test('sends welcome email on successful registration', async () => {
    vi.mocked(validateAddress).mockReturnValue(true);
    await registerUser({ email: 'alice@example.com', name: 'Alice' });
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(sendEmail).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'alice@example.com', subject: 'Welcome!' }),
    );
  });

  test('rejects registration when email is invalid', async () => {
    vi.mocked(validateAddress).mockReturnValue(false);
    await expect(
      registerUser({ email: 'not-an-email', name: 'Bob' }),
    ).rejects.toThrow('Invalid email address');
    expect(sendEmail).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: The `vi.mock(import(...))` form requires Vitest ≥1.3 and the `@vitest/expect` package. The import path in `vi.mock(import('../src/email-service'))` must be a literal string — it cannot be a variable or computed expression. If the module path is dynamic, fall back to the string-literal `vi.mock('../src/email-service', factory)` form and cast the return type manually.

---

**Pattern 564** — Jest `jest.replaceProperty()` for Non-Configurable Property Isolation
```typescript
import { jest, test, expect, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { getProcessPlatform } from '../src/platform-utils';

// jest.replaceProperty allows replacing properties that Object.defineProperty
// marked as non-configurable — something jest.spyOn cannot do.
afterEach(() => {
  jest.restoreAllMocks(); // Also restores replaceProperty patches
});

test('returns "win32" on Windows platform', () => {
  jest.replaceProperty(process, 'platform', 'win32');
  expect(getProcessPlatform()).toBe('win32');
});

test('returns "linux" on Linux platform', () => {
  jest.replaceProperty(process, 'platform', 'linux');
  expect(getProcessPlatform()).toBe('linux');
});

test('returns "darwin" on macOS platform', () => {
  jest.replaceProperty(process, 'platform', 'darwin');
  expect(getProcessPlatform()).toBe('darwin');
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.replaceProperty()` works by temporarily redefining the property descriptor. It does NOT support replacing methods (use `jest.spyOn` for those). If the property's getter has side effects, replacing the value directly may bypass them — test the side effects separately. The replacement is automatically reverted by `jest.restoreAllMocks()` but not by `jest.clearAllMocks()` or `jest.resetAllMocks()`.

---

**Pattern 565** — Vitest `aroundAll` Generator for File-Scoped Database Seeding
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createPool, type Pool } from '../src/db';
import { seedTestData, clearTestData } from '../test/db-helpers';

interface FileFixtures {
  pool: Pool;
  seedId: string;
}

const test = base.extend<FileFixtures>({
  pool: [
    async function* () {
      // aroundAll: generator runs setup before ANY test in the file,
      // and teardown after ALL tests complete — single pool for the file.
      const pool = createPool({ connectionString: process.env.TEST_DB_URL! });
      const seedId = await seedTestData(pool, { users: 10, orders: 50 });
      yield { pool, seedId };
      await clearTestData(pool, seedId);
      await pool.end();
    },
    { scope: 'file' },
  ],
  seedId: async ({ pool }, use) => {
    // Exposed as a separate fixture so tests can reference the seed ID
    await use((pool as unknown as { _seedId: string })._seedId);
  },
});

test('lists seeded users', async ({ pool }) => {
  const result = await pool.query('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users');
  expect(Number(result.rows[0].count)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(10);
});

test('lists seeded orders', async ({ pool }) => {
  const result = await pool.query('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders');
  expect(Number(result.rows[0].count)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(50);
});
```
Tradeoff: `aroundAll` generator syntax (yield-based) is available in Vitest ≥4.1. Earlier versions must use `beforeAll`/`afterAll` within a custom test object. The generator approach ties setup and teardown together in a single function, preventing the common mistake of writing setup in `beforeAll` and forgetting the matching `afterAll`.

---

**Pattern 566** — Playwright `page.route()` with `fulfill()` for Deterministic API Response Isolation
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('renders error banner when API returns 500', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept the specific endpoint before navigation
  await page.route('**/api/v1/products', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 500,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/shop');

  // The banner must appear without any real server involvement
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toHaveText(/Something went wrong/);
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toBeVisible();
});

test('renders product grid on success', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.route('**/api/v1/products', async (route) => {
    await route.fulfill({
      status: 200,
      contentType: 'application/json',
      body: JSON.stringify([
        { id: 1, name: 'Widget', price: 9.99 },
        { id: 2, name: 'Gadget', price: 19.99 },
      ]),
    });
  });

  await page.goto('/shop');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card')).toHaveCount(2);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.route()` intercepts at the browser network layer — requests never leave the machine. This makes tests fast and hermetic but means server-side cookie handling, redirects, and authentication flows are bypassed. For testing auth-dependent behaviour, prefer a real test server with controlled state; use `page.route()` only for third-party APIs or heavy endpoints where a real server would add latency.

---

**Pattern 567** — Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` + `--runInBand` Fallback for Memory-Leak Isolation
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  // Kill and restart a worker if it exceeds 512 MB after becoming idle
  // This prevents one leaky test file from poisoning subsequent files
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '512MB',

  // Per-test teardown: always dispose large objects
  setupFilesAfterEnv: ['<rootDir>/test/memory-guard.setup.ts'],
});

// test/memory-guard.setup.ts
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

afterEach(() => {
  // Release any WeakMap or Set entries holding DOM nodes or large buffers
  jest.clearAllMocks();
  jest.restoreAllMocks();
  // Allow GC to reclaim module-level caches if resetModules is true
});

// Usage: if a single test file is suspected of leaking, run it with:
//   jest --testPathPattern="leaky-module" --logHeapUsage
// Compare heap usage across tests; if it grows monotonically, the leak
// is within that file's beforeEach/afterEach lifecycle, not globalSetup.
```
Tradeoff: `workerIdleMemoryLimit` causes Jest to restart the worker process, which re-runs `setupFiles` and `setupFilesAfterEnv` for the next test file. This adds startup overhead per restart. Set the limit conservatively (512 MB is a reasonable default for Node.js; lower it to 256 MB for memory-constrained CI runners). Do not set it below the baseline heap size of the test environment or every test file will restart the worker.

---

**Pattern 568** — Vitest `vi.setTimerTickMode('interval')` for Polling-Based Async Logic
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { HealthPoller } from '../src/health-poller';

describe('HealthPoller', () => {
  let poller: HealthPoller;
  const mockFetch = vi.fn();

  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    // 'interval' mode: vi.advanceTimersByTime() ticks timers
    // at their natural interval — accurate for setInterval-based pollers
    vi.setTimerTickMode('interval');
    globalThis.fetch = mockFetch;
    poller = new HealthPoller({ intervalMs: 1000, endpoint: '/health' });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    poller.stop();
    vi.useRealTimers();
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
  });

  test('polls endpoint every 1000ms', async () => {
    mockFetch.mockResolvedValue({ ok: true, json: async () => ({ status: 'ok' }) });
    poller.start();

    // Advance 3 full intervals
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(3000);
    expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
    expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/health');
  });

  test('stops polling after stop() is called', async () => {
    mockFetch.mockResolvedValue({ ok: true, json: async () => ({ status: 'ok' }) });
    poller.start();
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1500);
    poller.stop();
    await vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(3000);
    expect(mockFetch).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.setTimerTickMode('interval')` is available in Vitest ≥4.1. In older versions, use `vi.runAllTimers()` or `vi.advanceTimersByTime()` without the tick mode API. The `interval` mode runs timers at their natural cadence, which can cause `advanceTimersByTimeAsync` to take longer than `nextTimerAsync` mode — use `nextTimerAsync` when you only care that the next pending timer fires, not about the wall-clock delta.

---

**Pattern 569** — Vitest `vi.mockObject()` with `spy: true` for Deep Object Spy Without Factory
```typescript
import { describe, test, expect, vi, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import { OrderService } from '../src/order-service';
import type { PaymentGateway } from '../src/payment-gateway';

describe('OrderService', () => {
  let gateway: PaymentGateway;
  let service: OrderService;

  beforeEach(() => {
    // vi.mockObject wraps every method as a vi.fn() spy,
    // preserving the original implementation by default when spy: true
    gateway = vi.mockObject<PaymentGateway>(
      {
        charge: async (amount, token) => ({ transactionId: 'real-tx' }),
        refund: async (txId) => ({ success: true }),
        getStatus: (txId) => 'settled',
      },
      { spy: true },
    );

    service = new OrderService(gateway);
  });

  test('calls gateway.charge with correct amount', async () => {
    await service.placeOrder({ items: [{ price: 49.99 }], paymentToken: 'tok_test' });
    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith(49.99, 'tok_test');
  });

  test('refunds on order cancellation', async () => {
    vi.spyOn(gateway, 'charge').mockResolvedValue({ transactionId: 'tx-001' });
    await service.placeOrder({ items: [{ price: 20.00 }], paymentToken: 'tok_x' });
    await service.cancelOrder('tx-001');
    expect(gateway.refund).toHaveBeenCalledWith('tx-001');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.mockObject()` with `spy: true` (Vitest ≥3.2) wraps the real implementation rather than replacing it, so integration tests can verify call counts without losing real behaviour. However, if the gateway implementation throws in tests (e.g., network errors in CI), the spy still forwards the call to the real method. Always pair `spy: true` mocks with `mockResolvedValue`/`mockReturnValue` overrides for the specific error paths you want to simulate.

---

**Pattern 570** — Jest `resetModules: true` Config + `jest.requireActual` for Partial Module Mocking
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';
export default defineConfig({
  resetModules: true, // Fresh module registry per test file
});

// __tests__/config-loader.test.ts
import { jest, test, expect, beforeEach } from '@jest/globals';

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.resetModules(); // Extra per-test reset for singleton re-init
});

test('loads config from YAML when CONFIG_FORMAT=yaml', async () => {
  process.env.CONFIG_FORMAT = 'yaml';

  jest.mock('../src/yaml-parser', () => {
    // Spread real module, then override only parse()
    const real = jest.requireActual<typeof import('../src/yaml-parser')>('../src/yaml-parser');
    return {
      ...real,
      parse: jest.fn().mockReturnValue({ db: { host: 'localhost' } }),
    };
  });

  const { loadConfig } = await import('../src/config-loader');
  const config = await loadConfig('./config.yaml');
  expect(config.db.host).toBe('localhost');
});

test('loads config from JSON when CONFIG_FORMAT=json', async () => {
  process.env.CONFIG_FORMAT = 'json';
  // No yaml-parser mock needed — clean registry from resetModules
  const { loadConfig } = await import('../src/config-loader');
  const config = await loadConfig('./config.json');
  expect(config).toHaveProperty('db');
});
```
Tradeoff: Combining `resetModules: true` in config with `jest.resetModules()` in `beforeEach` provides belt-and-suspenders isolation but doubles the module teardown overhead per test. For test files that do NOT need isolation, the per-file `resetModules: true` config option already provides file-level isolation — the `beforeEach` call is only necessary when tests within the same file must see different module states.

---

### Community Gotchas

**G351** — Vitest `test.override()` Silently Falls Through to Parent Fixture When Called Inside a Nested `describe`
When `test.override()` (Vitest ≥4.1) is used inside a `describe` block that is itself nested inside another `describe`, the override applies to ALL tests in the file that share the same fixture name — not just the tests in the inner `describe`. This is because `test.override()` patches the fixture definition on the shared test instance, not on a lexically scoped copy.
Why this matters: Teams migrating from `test.scoped()` (deprecated in 4.1) to `test.override()` expect per-describe scoping. Instead, tests outside the inner `describe` see the overridden value, causing unexpected behaviour in otherwise-passing tests and making test order matter for correctness.
Fix: Create a new `const innerTest = test.extend({ myFixture: [...overriddenValue...] })` and use `innerTest` inside the nested `describe` instead of calling `test.override()`. This gives a genuinely scoped fixture without polluting the outer test instance.

---

**G352** — Jest `clearMocks: true` in Config Clears `mockReturnValue` But Does NOT Reset `mockImplementation` Factories
`clearMocks: true` in `jest.config.ts` runs `jest.clearAllMocks()` before each test, which resets call counts, instances, and results arrays. However, it does NOT reset mock implementations set with `mockImplementation()` or `mockReturnValue()` — those persist until `jest.resetAllMocks()` or `jest.restoreAllMocks()` is called.
Why this matters: A test that calls `myMock.mockImplementation(() => 'special value')` leaves that implementation active for all subsequent tests in the file when only `clearMocks: true` is configured. This causes later tests to receive the `'special value'` return unexpectedly, making them pass or fail depending on test order.
Fix: Use `resetMocks: true` in `jest.config.ts` (or call `jest.resetAllMocks()` in `afterEach`) when you need implementation resets. If you need call-count isolation only, `clearMocks: true` is sufficient — document which level of isolation is used in the setup file to prevent confusion.

---

**G353** — Vitest `vi.stubGlobal()` Does Not Restore Globals Across Worker Restarts in `vmThreads` Pool
When running tests with `pool: 'vmThreads'` and `isolate: true`, each test file gets a fresh VM context. However, `vi.stubGlobal()` patches `globalThis` in the current VM context. If a test file uses `vi.stubGlobal('fetch', mockFetch)` without a corresponding `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` or `afterEach`, the stub leaks into subsequent test files that happen to land in the same worker, because the VM context is reused across test files within one worker lifecycle.
Why this matters: Stubs on `globalThis.fetch`, `globalThis.localStorage`, or other web APIs bleed across test files in vmThreads mode, causing network-dependent tests to use a stale mock without realising it. The issue is intermittent — it only reproduces when multiple test files share a worker, which is non-deterministic.
Fix: Always call `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in a global `afterEach` registered via `setupFilesAfterEnv`. Alternatively, upgrade to Vitest ≥4.0's reworked pool model and set `pool: 'forks'` for true process-level isolation at the cost of higher overhead.

---

**G354** — Playwright Fixture Defined in `test.extend()` Cannot Access `page` if Its Scope Is `'file'` or `'worker'`
A fixture with `scope: 'file'` or `scope: 'worker'` cannot depend on `page` because `page` is a `scope: 'test'` fixture (a new page is created per test). Attempting to destructure `page` inside a file-scoped or worker-scoped fixture factory causes Playwright to throw `"Cannot use test-scoped fixture 'page' in file-scoped fixture"`.
Why this matters: Developers attempting to write a file-scoped fixture that pre-navigates to a URL and shares the authenticated session across tests naturally reach for `{ page }` in the fixture arguments. This pattern is impossible in Playwright's fixture scoping model and causes a cryptic runtime error rather than a compile-time one.
Fix: Use `scope: 'test'` for any fixture that needs access to `page`, `context`, or `request`. To share authenticated state across tests without re-logging in per test, use `storageState` in `test.use()` combined with a one-time `globalSetup` that runs the login and writes the storage state file.

---

**G355** — Node.js `t.mock.fn()` Replacement Does Not Apply Retroactively to Already-Bound References
When using `node:test`'s `t.mock.fn()` to replace a module export, the replacement only intercepts future calls made through the module's export object. If the module under test captured a reference to the original function at import time (e.g., `const doWork = require('./worker').doWork` in CommonJS, or `import { doWork } from './worker'` in ESM), that reference is bound before the mock is applied and will never call the mock.
Why this matters: The test appears to set up a mock, the assertion `mock.calls.length === 1` fails with `0`, and there is no error — the real function simply ran instead of the mock. This is one of the most common sources of "my mock isn't working" confusion in `node:test` suites.
Fix: Ensure the module under test accesses its dependencies through the module namespace object at call time (e.g., `workerModule.doWork()`) rather than a destructured local binding. In ESM, this means the module under test must import the full namespace (`import * as workerModule from './worker'`) or use a DI parameter. Alternatively, use `t.mock.module()` to replace the entire module before importing the module under test.

## Cycle 59 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 571** — Vitest `aroundEach` + `AsyncLocalStorage.run()` for Request-Scoped Context Isolation
```typescript
import { test } from 'vitest';
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';

interface RequestCtx { traceId: string; userId: string }
const ctx = new AsyncLocalStorage<RequestCtx>();

export const isolatedTest = test.extend<{ requestCtx: RequestCtx }>({
  requestCtx: async ({}, use) => {
    const value: RequestCtx = { traceId: crypto.randomUUID(), userId: 'test-user' };
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) =>
      ctx.run(value, async () => {
        await use(value);
        resolve();
      })
    );
  },
});

isolatedTest('handler reads correct trace id', ({ requestCtx }) => {
  const result = ctx.getStore();
  expect(result?.traceId).toBe(requestCtx.traceId);
});
```
Tradeoff: Wrapping `use()` inside `AsyncLocalStorage.run()` guarantees that every `await` inside the test body remains within the correct async context, but requires care not to call `ctx.run()` again inside the test as it creates a nested scope that shadows the fixture-provided store rather than extending it.

**Pattern 572** — Jest `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` + `jest.unstable_mockModule()` for Per-Test ESM Singleton Reset
```typescript
import { jest } from '@jest/globals';

beforeEach(async () => {
  await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
    jest.unstable_mockModule('../src/db-client', () => ({
      db: { query: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue([]) },
    }));
    const { db } = await import('../src/db-client');
    (db.query as jest.Mock).mockResolvedValueOnce([{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }]);
    const { getUser } = await import('../src/user-service');
    const user = await getUser(1);
    expect(user.name).toBe('Alice');
  });
});

test('second test starts with a fresh module registry', async () => {
  const { db } = await import('../src/db-client');
  // db.query is the real implementation, not the mock from the previous test
  expect(jest.isMockFunction(db.query)).toBe(false);
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` creates a fully independent module registry for the duration of its callback, preventing ESM singleton state from leaking between tests. The cost is that every dynamic `import()` inside the callback re-executes module-level side effects (logging, DB pool creation), which can slow suites that rely on expensive initialisation paths.

**Pattern 573** — Playwright `storageState({ indexedDB: true })` for Firebase Auth Token Capture
```typescript
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

const test = base.extend<{ authedPage: typeof base.prototype }>({
  authedPage: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.fill('[name=email]', process.env.TEST_EMAIL!);
    await page.fill('[name=password]', process.env.TEST_PASSWORD!);
    await page.click('[type=submit]');
    await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
    // Capture IndexedDB-based Firebase token alongside cookies/localStorage
    await context.storageState({
      path: 'playwright/.auth/user.json',
      indexedDB: true,
    });
    await use(page);
    await context.close();
  },
});

test('authenticated user sees dashboard', async ({ authedPage }) => {
  await expect(authedPage.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: Including `indexedDB: true` in `storageState()` captures Firebase/Supabase auth tokens stored in IndexedDB, enabling true auth session reuse across test workers. The storage state file grows significantly (often 50-200 KB) compared to cookie-only captures, and stale IndexedDB tokens may not be cleared by `page.evaluate(() => indexedDB.deleteDatabase(...))` if the test runner context is reused — always regenerate the auth file in global setup rather than committing it.

**Pattern 574** — Vitest `vi.setTimerTickMode('interval')` for Polling-Based Async Logic
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from 'vitest';

beforeEach(() => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  vi.setTimerTickMode('interval');
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
});

async function pollForResult(maxAttempts: number): Promise<string> {
  for (let i = 0; i < maxAttempts; i++) {
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 500));
    if (i >= 2) return 'ready';
  }
  throw new Error('Timed out');
}

test('polling resolves after three ticks', async () => {
  const promise = pollForResult(5);
  // 'interval' mode auto-advances fake clock on each microtask drain
  const result = await promise;
  expect(result).toBe('ready');
});
```
Tradeoff: `'interval'` tick mode automatically drains the fake timer queue whenever the real event loop yields, making `await`-based polling tests work without manual `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` calls. However, this mode can mask real timing bugs where two timers must fire in a specific order; use `'manual'` mode when timer-ordering correctness is part of what is being tested.

**Pattern 575** — Node.js `node:test` `t.mock.module()` for ESM Module Isolation Without Jest
```typescript
import { test, mock } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

test('getUsers returns mocked data', async (t) => {
  t.mock.module('../src/http-client.ts', {
    namedExports: {
      get: async (url: string) => {
        assert.match(url, /\/api\/users/);
        return { data: [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }] };
      },
    },
  });

  // Dynamic import AFTER mock registration picks up the mock
  const { getUsers } = await import('../src/user-service.ts');
  const users = await getUsers();
  assert.deepEqual(users, [{ id: 1, name: 'Alice' }]);
});
```
Tradeoff: `t.mock.module()` is automatically restored when the test ends (unlike `jest.unstable_mockModule()` which requires explicit `jest.unstable_unmockModule()`), making it ideal for lightweight ESM isolation in projects that have adopted `node:test`. The limitation is that `t.mock.module()` does not support `jest.requireActual()`-style partial mocking — the entire module must be either real or mocked; mixing real and mock exports requires manually re-exporting selected real values from the mock factory.

**Pattern 576** — MSW `server.use()` One-Time Handler for Single-Test Network Override
```typescript
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';
import { afterAll, afterEach, beforeAll, test, expect } from 'vitest';

const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/api/config', () => HttpResponse.json({ theme: 'light' }))
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'error' }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

test('uses default theme', async () => {
  const res = await fetch('/api/config');
  const data = await res.json();
  expect(data.theme).toBe('light');
});

test('overrides theme for this test only', async () => {
  server.use(
    http.get('/api/config', () => HttpResponse.json({ theme: 'dark' }), { once: true })
  );
  const res = await fetch('/api/config');
  const data = await res.json();
  expect(data.theme).toBe('dark');
  // server.resetHandlers() in afterEach removes the one-time override
});
```
Tradeoff: The `{ once: true }` option in `server.use()` removes the handler after one match, but the handler entry remains in the stack until `server.resetHandlers()` is called. Omitting `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())` allows handlers to accumulate across tests, causing later tests to match stale one-time handlers that should have been consumed — this is one of the most common causes of MSW-based test flakiness.

**Pattern 577** — Vitest `vi.mockObject()` with `spy: true` for Deep Object Spy Isolation
```typescript
import { vi, test, expect, beforeEach } from 'vitest';
import type { DatabaseClient } from '../src/db';

const realClient: DatabaseClient = {
  query: async (sql: string) => [{ id: 1 }],
  transaction: async (fn: (tx: DatabaseClient) => Promise<void>) => fn(realClient),
  close: async () => {},
};

let spyClient: DatabaseClient;

beforeEach(() => {
  // vi.mockObject wraps every method in a spy while preserving the real implementation
  spyClient = vi.mockObject(realClient, { spy: true });
});

test('service calls query with correct SQL', async () => {
  const { fetchUsers } = await import('../src/user-service');
  await fetchUsers(spyClient);
  expect(spyClient.query).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.stringContaining('SELECT * FROM users')
  );
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.mockObject()` with `spy: true` wraps every enumerable method in a `vi.spyOn()` while keeping the real implementation active, eliminating the need for manual `vi.spyOn(obj, 'method')` calls per method. The tradeoff is that deeply nested object properties (e.g., `client.pool.acquire`) are not automatically wrapped — only top-level enumerable methods are spied on; nested objects require separate `vi.mockObject()` calls.

**Pattern 578** — Jest `workerIdleMemoryLimit` for Memory-Leak Isolation Between Test Files
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  workerIdleMemoryLimit: '256MB',
  // Workers that exceed the limit are recycled before the next test file
  // This prevents memory-accumulating singletons from corrupting later tests
  maxWorkers: 4,
  testEnvironment: 'node',
  globals: {
    // Force re-evaluation of module-level state per worker lifecycle
  },
});

// src/__tests__/cache.test.ts
import { globalCache } from '../src/cache';

test('cache starts empty', () => {
  // Worker recycling via workerIdleMemoryLimit guarantees globalCache
  // is the post-require() initial state, not accumulated state from
  // a previous test file that ran in the same worker
  expect(globalCache.size).toBe(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `workerIdleMemoryLimit` recycles a worker process when its idle RSS exceeds the threshold, which clears module-level singleton state between test files. This is a coarser form of isolation than `resetModules: true` (which resets per-test) and is more appropriate for large integration test suites where module reset overhead is prohibitive. The worker recycle adds ~200 ms of startup cost per recycled worker, which can slow CI on memory-intensive test suites.

**Pattern 579** — Playwright `test.abort()` for Invariant-Violation Fail-Fast from Route Handlers
```typescript
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('checkout flow completes without payment errors', async ({ page }) => {
  // Abort the test immediately if the payment service returns a server error
  await page.route('**/api/payment', async (route) => {
    const response = await route.fetch();
    if (response.status() >= 500) {
      await test.abort(`Payment API returned ${response.status()} — stopping test`);
    }
    await route.fulfill({ response });
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.click('[data-testid=pay-button]');
  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.abort()` triggers an immediate, clean teardown of the test — fixtures run their cleanup logic and the test is marked as failed with the provided message. This prevents downstream assertions from running against a corrupted application state, making failure messages more actionable. However, aborting from inside a route handler means the abort message is generated before the full request/response cycle completes; log the response body before calling `test.abort()` to capture diagnostic information.

**Pattern 580** — Vitest `detectAsyncLeaks` for Surfacing Unresolved Promise Handles
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    detectAsyncLeaks: true,
    // Reports tests that leave open handles: unresolved promises, timers,
    // active EventEmitters, or unclosed streams
    pool: 'forks', // async leak detection requires process isolation
  },
});

// src/__tests__/event-stream.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createEventStream } from '../src/event-stream';

test('stream emits three events then closes', async () => {
  const stream = createEventStream();
  const events: string[] = [];

  await new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => {
    stream.on('data', (e: string) => events.push(e));
    stream.on('end', resolve);
    stream.on('error', reject);
    stream.start();
  });

  expect(events).toHaveLength(3);
  // If stream.destroy() is missing here, detectAsyncLeaks will report
  // an open handle and fail the test with a precise stack trace
  stream.destroy();
});
```
Tradeoff: `detectAsyncLeaks: true` in Vitest requires `pool: 'forks'` because it tracks Node.js async resource IDs at the process level. This means each test file runs in a separate subprocess, significantly increasing memory usage and startup time for large suites. Consider enabling `detectAsyncLeaks` only in a separate CI job targeting files with known handle-leak history rather than as the default for all runs.

**Pattern 581** — Jest `fakeTimers.enableGlobally` + `doNotFake` for Project-Wide Timer Isolation
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    enableGlobally: true,
    doNotFake: ['nextTick', 'setImmediate'],
    // Keeps Node.js microtask queue real so Promise chains resolve correctly
    // while Date, setTimeout, and setInterval are faked
    timerLimit: 2000,
  },
});

// src/__tests__/retry.test.ts
import { jest, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { retryWithBackoff } from '../src/retry';

test('retries three times with exponential backoff', async () => {
  const fn = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('fail 1'))
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('fail 2'))
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('ok');

  const promise = retryWithBackoff(fn, { attempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 100 });
  // Advance fake clock without touching real nextTick/setImmediate
  await jest.runAllTimersAsync();
  await expect(promise).resolves.toBe('ok');
  expect(fn).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Tradeoff: `enableGlobally: true` eliminates per-test `jest.useFakeTimers()` / `jest.useRealTimers()` boilerplate but means every test in every file runs with fake timers unless explicitly opted out. Tests that assert against `Date.now()` differences or use third-party libraries that rely on real timer semantics (e.g., `p-retry` with jitter) will silently stall because the clock never advances without an explicit `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()`. Audit all test files for real-timer assumptions before enabling globally.

**Pattern 582** — Testcontainers `PostgreSqlContainer` per-Suite Lifecycle with Jest `globalSetup`
```typescript
// jest.global-setup.ts
import { PostgreSqlContainer, StartedPostgreSqlContainer } from '@testcontainers/postgresql';
import { writeFileSync } from 'node:fs';

declare global {
  // eslint-disable-next-line no-var
  var __PG_CONTAINER__: StartedPostgreSqlContainer;
}

export default async function setup() {
  const container = await new PostgreSqlContainer('postgres:16-alpine')
    .withDatabase('test_db')
    .withUsername('test')
    .withPassword('test')
    .start();

  global.__PG_CONTAINER__ = container;
  // Share connection URL with test workers via environment variable
  process.env.DATABASE_URL = container.getConnectionUri();
  writeFileSync('/tmp/jest-pg-url', container.getConnectionUri());
}

export async function teardown() {
  await global.__PG_CONTAINER__?.stop();
}
```
Tradeoff: Starting a single container in `globalSetup` and sharing the connection URL through `process.env` is the most cost-efficient approach for integration suites: one Docker pull, one startup, all test files share the same instance. The isolation risk is that test files sharing the same database can corrupt each other's data if they do not use separate schemas or run within rolled-back transactions. Use `CREATE SCHEMA test_<uuid>` per test file and `DROP SCHEMA` in `afterAll` for file-level data isolation without per-file container overhead.

**Pattern 583** — Vitest `test.signal` (AbortSignal) for Cancelling In-Flight Async Resources
```typescript
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';

async function streamData(
  url: string,
  signal: AbortSignal
): Promise<string[]> {
  const res = await fetch(url, { signal });
  const chunks: string[] = [];
  const reader = res.body!.getReader();
  while (true) {
    const { done, value } = await reader.read();
    if (done || signal.aborted) break;
    chunks.push(new TextDecoder().decode(value));
  }
  return chunks;
}

test('stream aborts cleanly on test timeout', async ({ signal }) => {
  // test.signal is aborted when the test times out, is bailed, or Ctrl-C is pressed
  const dataPromise = streamData('https://example.com/stream', signal);

  signal.addEventListener('abort', () => {
    // Verify the stream was cleaned up — no afterEach needed
    expect(signal.aborted).toBe(true);
  });

  const chunks = await dataPromise;
  expect(chunks.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
}, { timeout: 5000 });
```
Tradeoff: `test.signal` provides a zero-boilerplate cancellation path for async resources that naturally accept an `AbortSignal` (fetch, EventSource, WebSocket). For resources that do not accept a signal (e.g., legacy database clients, custom EventEmitter streams), a `test.signal` listener that manually calls a `close()` or `destroy()` method achieves the same effect. The limitation is that `test.signal` fires only on abnormal test termination — it does not fire on a normally-completing test, so teardown that must run regardless (e.g., releasing a database connection) still belongs in `onCleanup` or `afterEach`.

**Pattern 584** — Node.js `node:test` `TestContext.mock` Auto-Restore for Dependency Injection
```typescript
import { test, describe } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

interface Logger { log: (msg: string) => void }
interface Mailer { send: (to: string, body: string) => Promise<void> }

function createNotificationService(logger: Logger, mailer: Mailer) {
  return {
    async notify(userId: string, message: string) {
      logger.log(`Notifying ${userId}`);
      await mailer.send(`${userId}@example.com`, message);
    },
  };
}

describe('NotificationService', () => {
  test('logs and sends email', async (t) => {
    const logSpy = t.mock.fn();
    const sendSpy = t.mock.fn(async () => {});

    const service = createNotificationService(
      { log: logSpy },
      { send: sendSpy }
    );

    await service.notify('u1', 'Hello');

    assert.strictEqual(logSpy.mock.calls.length, 1);
    assert.strictEqual(logSpy.mock.calls[0].arguments[0], 'Notifying u1');
    assert.strictEqual(sendSpy.mock.calls[0].arguments[0], 'u1@example.com');
    // t.mock.fn() mocks are automatically restored after the test — no afterEach needed
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `TestContext.mock.fn()` creates a spy that is automatically torn down when the test ends, making it safer than `jest.fn()` in a non-reset-mock environment. The constructor injection pattern means the module under test receives collaborators as parameters rather than importing them directly, which avoids the need for module-level mocking entirely. The downside is that this pattern requires refactoring existing code to accept dependencies as parameters — modules that hard-code their dependencies via `require()` / `import` cannot use this approach without structural changes.

**Pattern 585** — Playwright `mergeTests()` for Compositional Fixture Isolation Without Coupling
```typescript
import { test as base, mergeTests, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { test as dbTest } from './fixtures/db-fixture';
import { test as authTest } from './fixtures/auth-fixture';
import { test as a11yTest } from './fixtures/a11y-fixture';

// Merge independent fixture sets into a single test function
// Each fixture file owns its own setup/teardown without knowing about the others
const test = mergeTests(base, dbTest, authTest, a11yTest);

test('authenticated user can create a record', async ({
  page,
  dbConnection,    // from db-fixture
  authSession,     // from auth-fixture
  a11yChecker,     // from a11y-fixture
}) => {
  await page.goto('/records/new');
  await page.fill('[name=title]', 'Test Record');
  await page.click('[type=submit]');

  const record = await dbConnection.query(
    'SELECT * FROM records WHERE title = $1', ['Test Record']
  );
  expect(record.rows).toHaveLength(1);

  const violations = await a11yChecker.analyze(page);
  expect(violations).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `mergeTests()` composes fixture sets by merging their `test.extend()` definitions without either set needing to know about the other, preventing the "fixture pyramid" antipattern where one giant fixture file accumulates all concerns. The limitation is that if two fixture sets define a fixture with the same name, the last merged definition wins silently — use a naming convention (e.g., `dbConn`, `authConn`) to avoid collisions and add a lint rule that flags duplicate fixture names across merged sets.

### Community Gotchas

**G356** — Vitest `aroundAll` Receives Fixture Context in v4.1 — Breaking Change for Existing Suite Hooks
In Vitest 4.1, the `aroundAll` callback signature changed: it now receives `(suite, runSuite)` where `suite` is the fixture context for the current test file, rather than just `(runSuite)`. Existing `aroundAll` callbacks written as `(runSuite) => { await runSuite(); }` now silently treat `suite` as `runSuite` and never call the actual suite runner, causing the entire test file to be skipped without error.
Why this matters: The failure mode is silent — tests neither pass nor fail, they simply do not run. In CI, a silently-skipped file may pass the job because no assertions fail, masking a regression that removes all tests from coverage.
Fix: Update all `aroundAll` callbacks to the two-argument signature: `async (suite, runSuite) => { await runSuite(); }`. Add a lint rule or type check that flags `aroundAll` callbacks with fewer than two parameters.

---

**G357** — Jest `resetMocks: true` Clears `jest.spyOn()` Return Values But Leaves the Spy Wrapper in Place
`jest.resetMocks()` (or `resetMocks: true` in config) calls `mockReset()` on every mock, removing all `mockReturnValue()` / `mockResolvedValue()` implementations and setting them to return `undefined`. It does NOT restore the original implementation — the function is still a spy wrapper, not the original. Tests that assert on the return value of a spied-on method after reset will receive `undefined` instead of the real return value.
Why this matters: A test that spies on `fs.readFileSync` and uses `resetMocks: true` will find that the next test's call to the real `fs.readFileSync` returns `undefined` and throws a `TypeError`, even though the test never explicitly mocked it. The error message points to the test under investigation, not the spy setup in a previous test.
Fix: Use `restoreMocks: true` (not `resetMocks: true`) if you need the original implementation back between tests. Use `resetMocks: true` only when all mocks are `jest.fn()` (not `jest.spyOn()`) or when the return value is always set explicitly at the top of each test.

---

**G358** — MSW `{ once: true }` Handler Entry Persists in Stack Until `resetHandlers()` Is Called
When `server.use(handler, { once: true })` is called, the handler fires exactly once — but the exhausted entry remains in the handler stack. A subsequent `server.use()` call for the same route will be appended below the stale entry. If `resetHandlers()` is never called, the stale one-time entries accumulate and can match routes in an unexpected priority order during later tests.
Why this matters: In suites with many `server.use()` overrides and no `afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers())`, the handler stack grows unboundedly. The 20th test in a file may receive a response from a one-time handler registered in the 3rd test because the stack was never cleared.
Fix: Always call `server.resetHandlers()` in `afterEach` — not `afterAll`. This clears all runtime handlers (including exhausted `once` entries) while preserving the initial handlers passed to `setupServer()`. If some handlers should persist across multiple tests, pass them to `setupServer()` as baseline handlers instead of registering them at runtime.

---

**G359** — Playwright `page.route()` Intercept Without `route.fulfill()` or `route.abort()` Hangs the Test
If a `page.route()` handler is registered but the handler callback does not call `route.fulfill()`, `route.continue()`, or `route.abort()` on every code path (e.g., the handler returns early on a condition check), the intercepted request remains pending indefinitely. Playwright will wait until the test timeout before reporting a failure, making the timeout the only signal that the route handler has a bug.
Why this matters: A route handler that conditionally aborts for 5xx responses but falls through for 4xx responses leaves 4xx requests hanging silently. The test times out after 30 s with a generic "Test timeout exceeded" message, not a "route handler did not respond" message, making root cause analysis difficult.
Fix: Always include a `fallthrough` path that calls `await route.continue()`. Use `route.fallback()` (Playwright v1.49+) as a default catch-all at the end of complex handler logic. Enable `page.on('requestfailed', ...)` in `beforeEach` to surface hanging requests as explicit assertion failures.

---

**G360** — Node.js `--test-global-setup` Shares Module-Level Singleton State with All Test Workers
Unlike Jest's `globalSetup`, which runs in a separate subprocess and communicates with workers only through serialised `global` values or environment variables, Node.js 24's `--test-global-setup` runs in the **same process** as the test runner. Any module-level singleton initialised in the global setup file (e.g., a database connection pool, an in-memory cache, a logger) is the exact same object reference visible to all test workers.
Why this matters: Tests that mutate shared singletons (e.g., adding cache entries, modifying logger configuration) affect every subsequent test in the same run without any teardown occurring between test files. This is the opposite of the isolation contract that `globalSetup` implies.
Fix: Treat `--test-global-setup` as a one-time environment bootstrap (e.g., starting Docker containers, writing temp files) rather than as an initialisation point for shared objects. Initialise all singletons that must be isolated inside each test file's `before` hook or via `t.mock.module()` so that they are scoped to the test file's module registry.

## Cycle 60 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 586** — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` with `unstubEnvs: true` for Automatic Env Variable Restoration
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    unstubEnvs: true,    // restore all vi.stubEnv() stubs after each test automatically
    unstubGlobals: true, // same for vi.stubGlobal()
  },
});

// auth.test.ts
import { vi, describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';

describe('auth service', () => {
  it('uses production endpoint when NODE_ENV=production', async () => {
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'production');
    vi.stubEnv('API_BASE_URL', 'https://api.prod.example.com');
    // No manual cleanup needed — unstubEnvs: true restores both after this test
    const { getApiUrl } = await import('../auth');
    expect(getApiUrl()).toBe('https://api.prod.example.com');
  });

  it('uses staging endpoint by default', async () => {
    // NODE_ENV is back to its original value here
    const { getApiUrl } = await import('../auth');
    expect(getApiUrl()).toContain('staging');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `unstubEnvs: true` auto-calls `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` after every test, eliminating a whole category of env-leak bugs for free, but it only restores the `process.env` snapshot captured at first-stub time within that test — if a test calls `vi.unstubAllEnvs()` manually mid-test and then stubs again, the new stub's baseline is the post-restore state, not the original process env, which can leave residual values when `unstubEnvs` fires at test end.

**Pattern 587** — Vitest `pool: 'vmForks'` for True Per-File Module Registry Isolation
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    pool: 'vmForks',
    // Each test file runs in a separate child process with its own Node.js
    // VM context — module singletons are never shared across files
    poolOptions: {
      vmForks: {
        memoryLimit: '512MB',
      },
    },
  },
});

// singleton.test.ts — can safely mutate module-level state
import { getCounter, increment } from '../counter';

test('counter starts at 0', () => {
  expect(getCounter()).toBe(0);
  increment();
  expect(getCounter()).toBe(1);
  // No cleanup needed — the entire module registry is discarded
  // when this file's vmFork process exits
});
```
Tradeoff: `vmForks` is the strongest isolation guarantee Vitest offers — each file gets its own child process AND its own V8 VM context, so module-level singletons, `globalThis` mutations, and native module state are fully contained. The cost is spawn overhead: `vmForks` is the slowest pool option, roughly 2–4× slower than `threads` for large suites. Reserve it for suites that share singleton-heavy infrastructure (DB clients, loggers, feature-flag caches) and use `pool: 'threads'` with explicit `vi.resetModules()` for everything else.

**Pattern 588** — Jest `jest.doMock()` + `jest.resetModules()` for Per-Test Module Variant Isolation
```typescript
// feature-flag.test.ts
import { jest, describe, beforeEach, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';

beforeEach(() => {
  jest.resetModules(); // clear module registry before each test
});

test('feature is enabled when flag is on', async () => {
  jest.doMock('../config', () => ({ FEATURE_X_ENABLED: true }));
  const { processRequest } = await import('../handler');
  const result = await processRequest({ userId: '42' });
  expect(result.featureX).toBe(true);
});

test('feature is disabled when flag is off', async () => {
  jest.doMock('../config', () => ({ FEATURE_X_ENABLED: false }));
  const { processRequest } = await import('../handler');
  const result = await processRequest({ userId: '42' });
  expect(result.featureX).toBeUndefined();
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.doMock()` (unlike `jest.mock()`) is not hoisted by `babel-jest`, so it must be paired with `jest.resetModules()` + a dynamic `import()` inside the test body — the module under test must be loaded after the mock is registered, not at the top of the file. This pattern is the only correct way to swap module-level constants between tests in the same file without splitting them into separate files.

**Pattern 589** — Playwright Worker-Scoped Auth Fixture with Per-Worker `storageState` File
```typescript
// fixtures/auth.fixture.ts
import { test as base, BrowserContext } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'path';

type WorkerAuthFixtures = { workerStorageState: string; authedContext: BrowserContext };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerAuthFixtures>({
  workerStorageState: [async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
    const stateFile = path.resolve(
      __dirname, `../playwright/.auth/worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}.json`
    );
    const context = await browser.newContext();
    const page = await context.newPage();
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.fill('[name=email]', `worker${workerInfo.workerIndex}@test.com`);
    await page.fill('[name=password]', 'secret');
    await page.click('[type=submit]');
    await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
    await context.storageState({ path: stateFile });
    await context.close();
    await use(stateFile);
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  authedContext: async ({ browser, workerStorageState }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ storageState: workerStorageState });
    await use(ctx);
    await ctx.close();
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Scoping auth setup to `worker` means the login flow runs once per parallel worker (not once per test), cutting suite runtime by the number of tests per worker. The limitation is that any test that mutates server-side auth state (e.g., changes the password, revokes the token) will corrupt the shared worker state and silently break all subsequent tests on that worker. Guard against this with an `afterEach` assertion that the session is still valid, or use a test-scoped `authedContext` fixture for tests that touch auth state.
