## Cycle 69 — 2026-05-14

### Patterns

**Pattern 705** — Vitest `test.extend()` Worker-Scoped Redis Fixture with Per-Test Key Namespace
```typescript
// fixtures/redis.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import { createClient, RedisClientType } from 'redis';

export const test = base.extend<{ redis: RedisClientType }, { redisClient: RedisClientType }>({
  redisClient: [async ({}, use) => {
    const client = createClient({ url: process.env.TEST_REDIS_URL });
    await client.connect();
    await use(client);
    await client.quit();
  }, { scope: 'worker' }],

  redis: async ({ redisClient, task }, use) => {
    const prefix = `test:${task.id}:`;
    const proxied = new Proxy(redisClient, {
      get(target, prop) {
        const fn = (target as any)[prop];
        if (typeof fn !== 'function') return fn;
        return (key: string, ...rest: unknown[]) => fn.call(target, prefix + key, ...rest);
      },
    });
    await use(proxied as RedisClientType);
    const keys = await redisClient.keys(`${prefix}*`);
    if (keys.length) await redisClient.del(keys);
  },
});
```
Tradeoff: Namespacing Redis keys per test using the task ID ensures complete isolation when tests run concurrently against a shared Redis instance — but the Proxy approach intercepts only single-argument key-first commands (`get`, `set`, `del`); multi-key commands (`mget`, `mset`) and scan-based operations receive raw key arguments without the prefix, requiring those operations to be wrapped explicitly or replaced with single-key equivalents in test fixtures.

**Pattern 706** — Jest `jest.spyOn` with `mockImplementation` Reset in `beforeEach` for Stateless Service Stubs
```typescript
// user-service.test.ts
import { jest, describe, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { EmailService } from '../src/email-service';
import { UserService } from '../src/user-service';

describe('UserService', () => {
  let sendEmailSpy: jest.SpyInstance;

  beforeEach(() => {
    sendEmailSpy = jest.spyOn(EmailService.prototype, 'send')
      .mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'test-ok', status: 'sent' });
  });

  afterEach(() => {
    sendEmailSpy.mockRestore();
  });

  it('sends a welcome email on registration', async () => {
    const svc = new UserService();
    await svc.register({ email: 'alice@example.com', name: 'Alice' });
    expect(sendEmailSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      expect.objectContaining({ to: 'alice@example.com', subject: 'Welcome' }),
    );
  });

  it('does not send email if user already exists', async () => {
    const svc = new UserService();
    await svc.register({ email: 'existing@example.com', name: 'Bob' });
    expect(sendEmailSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Creating the spy in `beforeEach` and restoring it in `afterEach` ensures every test starts with a fresh spy that has zero call history and the intended mock implementation — but the spy must be stored in a variable accessible in both `beforeEach` and `afterEach` (requiring a `let` declaration in describe scope), and tests that call `mockRestore()` inside the test body before `afterEach` runs will cause `afterEach` to call `mockRestore()` on an already-restored spy, which is a no-op but signals a design inconsistency.

**Pattern 707** — Playwright `page.route()` with `route.continue()` for Selective Request Passthrough
```typescript
// tests/payments/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('intercepts Stripe API but passes CDN requests through', async ({ page }) => {
  const interceptedUrls: string[] = [];

  await page.route('**/*', async (route) => {
    const url = route.request().url();
    if (url.includes('api.stripe.com')) {
      interceptedUrls.push(url);
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({ id: 'pi_test123', status: 'succeeded' }),
      });
    } else {
      await route.continue(); // pass CDN, fonts, analytics to real network
    }
  });

  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay now' }).click();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="success-banner"]')).toBeVisible();
  expect(interceptedUrls).toHaveLength(1);
  expect(interceptedUrls[0]).toContain('payment_intents');
});
```
Tradeoff: `route.continue()` lets non-intercepted requests reach the real network, allowing styles and fonts to load normally while only targeted API calls are stubbed — but mixing real and stubbed traffic means tests that run in environments without internet access (airgapped CI) will fail on `route.continue()` calls for external CDN resources, requiring `route.abort()` fallbacks or fully offline test configurations.

**Pattern 708** — Vitest `onTestFailed` for Per-Test Debug Artifact Capture Without Polluting Passing Tests
```typescript
// dashboard.test.tsx
import { onTestFailed, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { render } from '@testing-library/react';
import { writeFileSync, mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';
import { Dashboard } from '../src/components/Dashboard';

it('renders dashboard metrics correctly', async ({ task }) => {
  onTestFailed(() => {
    mkdirSync('./test-artifacts', { recursive: true });
    const { container } = render(<Dashboard metrics={{ sales: 0 }} />);
    writeFileSync(
      `./test-artifacts/${task.name.replace(/\s+/g, '-')}.html`,
      container.innerHTML,
    );
    console.error(`[DEBUG] DOM snapshot saved for: ${task.name}`);
  });

  const { getByTestId } = render(<Dashboard metrics={{ sales: 150, returns: 3 }} />);
  expect(getByTestId('sales-count')).toHaveTextContent('150');
  expect(getByTestId('return-rate')).toHaveTextContent('2.0%');
});
```
Tradeoff: `onTestFailed` only executes when the enclosing test fails, meaning passing tests incur zero overhead from artifact capture or logging — but the callback runs after the test's teardown hooks, so any fixtures or contexts cleaned up in `afterEach` are already destroyed by the time `onTestFailed` fires, preventing the callback from accessing live DOM trees or active database connections that were torn down before the failure was reported.

**Pattern 709** — Jest `--randomize` with Fixed `--seed` for Reproducible Test Order Isolation Audits
```typescript
// jest.config.ts
export default {
  randomize: process.env.CI === 'true',
};

// package.json (scripts)
// "test:audit": "jest --randomize --seed=42 --verbose"
// "test:repro": "jest --randomize --seed=$SEED --verbose"

// user-store.test.ts — example of test that breaks under randomization
import { userStore } from '../src/user-store';
import { jest, it, expect, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

afterEach(() => {
  userStore.reset(); // isolation cleanup — must not be omitted
});

it('returns empty list when no users added', () => {
  expect(userStore.getAll()).toHaveLength(0);
});

it('adds a user and returns updated list', () => {
  userStore.add({ id: 1, name: 'Alice' });
  expect(userStore.getAll()).toHaveLength(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: `--randomize` with a fixed `--seed` reproduces a specific test execution order on demand, enabling bisection and diagnosis of isolation failures that only appear in certain orderings — but randomization only shuffles tests within a single file; cross-file ordering is determined by Jest's worker assignment algorithm and is not seed-controlled, so tests that leak state across files through singleton modules will not be detected by `--randomize` alone.

**Pattern 710** — Vitest `vi.stubEnv()` with `unstubEnvs: true` for `process.env` Isolation Per Test
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    unstubEnvs: true, // auto-restores all vi.stubEnv() calls before each test
  },
});

// config-service.test.ts
import { vi, describe, it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { ConfigService } from '../src/config-service';

describe('ConfigService environment reading', () => {
  it('uses error log level in production mode', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'production');
    vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'error');
    const cfg = new ConfigService();
    expect(cfg.logLevel).toBe('error');
  });

  it('defaults to debug log level in development mode', () => {
    vi.stubEnv('NODE_ENV', 'development');
    // LOG_LEVEL is restored to original by unstubEnvs: true before this test
    const cfg = new ConfigService();
    expect(cfg.logLevel).toBe('debug');
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.stubEnv()` with `unstubEnvs: true` provides automatic `process.env` restoration without manual `afterEach` cleanup — but `vi.stubEnv()` only affects the test process's own `process.env` object; child processes spawned during tests (via `execSync`, `spawn`, or `worker_threads`) inherit the environment at their creation time and are not updated by `vi.stubEnv()`, so tests that verify subprocess behavior must pass environment variables explicitly as arguments rather than relying on the stubbed parent environment.

**Pattern 711** — Playwright `test.describe.serial()` for Tests That Must Run in Strict Sequential Order
```typescript
// tests/wizard/onboarding.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe.serial('Onboarding wizard multi-step state machine', () => {
  test('step 1: accepts company name', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/onboarding');
    await page.fill('[name="company"]', 'Acme Corp');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();
    await expect(page.locator('[data-step="2"]')).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('step 2: selects plan — previous step state persists', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.getByRole('radio', { name: 'Pro Plan' }).check();
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Next' }).click();
    await expect(page.locator('[data-step="3"]')).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('step 3: confirms and submits the wizard', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm and activate' }).click();
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="success-message"]')).toBeVisible();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.describe.serial()` forces all tests in the block to run sequentially in the same Playwright worker, preventing flaky failures caused by out-of-order execution of multi-step flows — but serial blocks cannot run in parallel with other tests in the same worker, degrading overall throughput, and a failure in an early serial step causes all subsequent steps to be skipped (not failed), making it harder to distinguish "step failed" from "step was never reached due to prior failure".

**Pattern 712** — Jest `setupFilesAfterEnv` Global `afterEach` for Automatic Unhandled Promise Rejection Detection
```typescript
// jest.setup.ts (referenced in jest.config.ts setupFilesAfterEnv)
import { afterEach } from '@jest/globals';

const unhandledRejections: unknown[] = [];

process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => {
  unhandledRejections.push(reason);
});

afterEach(() => {
  const pending = unhandledRejections.splice(0); // drain collected rejections
  if (pending.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(
      `[isolation] ${pending.length} unhandled rejection(s) in this test:\n` +
      pending.map((r, i) => `  ${i + 1}. ${r}`).join('\n'),
    );
  }
});
```
Tradeoff: A global `unhandledRejection` listener combined with an `afterEach` drain converts silent unhandled rejections into explicit test failures, surfacing async errors that Jest's default handler only logs — but the listener accumulates rejections across the process lifetime, meaning a slow async operation from test N may emit its rejection during test N+1's `afterEach` rather than test N's, making the failure appear to come from the wrong test; `Promise.allSettled` with per-promise assertions is more precise for complex async teardowns.

**Pattern 713** — Vitest `vi.mock()` with `vi.hoisted()` for Mutable Factory Variables in `beforeAll` Context
```typescript
// database.test.ts
import { vi, it, expect, beforeAll } from 'vitest';

const dbUrl = vi.hoisted(() => ({ value: '' }));

vi.mock('../src/database-client', () => ({
  createClient: () => ({
    connect: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
    query: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ rows: [] }),
    getUrl: () => dbUrl.value, // read at call-time, not capture-time
  }),
}));

import { createClient } from '../src/database-client';

beforeAll(() => {
  dbUrl.value = 'postgres://test-container:5432/testdb';
});

it('client URL reflects the value set in beforeAll', () => {
  const client = createClient();
  expect(client.getUrl()).toBe('postgres://test-container:5432/testdb');
});
```
Tradeoff: `vi.hoisted()` executes before all `vi.mock()` factories, creating a mutable reference that factories can close over and read at invocation time — allowing `beforeAll` to set values the mock factory will later return — but the hoisted container is not reactive: if a test mutates `dbUrl.value` after `createClient()` is called and the client has already closed over the value, the in-flight instance will not see the update, requiring a new `createClient()` call to pick up changed values.

**Pattern 714** — Playwright `context.grantPermissions()` with Per-Test Permission Reset
```typescript
// tests/geolocation.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('shows nearby stores when geolocation is granted', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await context.grantPermissions(['geolocation']);
  await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: 37.7749, longitude: -122.4194 });

  await page.goto('/store-finder');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="nearby-stores"]')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="store-count"]')).toHaveText(/[1-9]\d* stores/);
});

test('shows location prompt when geolocation is denied', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await context.grantPermissions([]); // explicitly clear all permissions
  await page.goto('/store-finder');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="location-prompt"]')).toBeVisible();
});
```
Tradeoff: `context.grantPermissions([])` reverts permissions for the context, enabling per-test permission isolation without creating a new browser context — but permission grants persist for the context lifetime and are not reset between tests automatically by Playwright's built-in fixtures, so tests sharing a worker-scoped `authContext` will accumulate permission state unless each test explicitly calls `grantPermissions([])` in a `beforeEach` hook.

**Pattern 715** — Jest `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` for Promise-Resolving Timer Chains
```typescript
// notification-scheduler.test.ts
import { jest, it, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { NotificationScheduler } from '../src/notification-scheduler';

beforeEach(() => jest.useFakeTimers());
afterEach(() => { jest.useRealTimers(); jest.clearAllTimers(); });

it('sends reminders at 24h, 1h, and 5min before event', async () => {
  const sendReminder = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined);
  const scheduler = new NotificationScheduler(sendReminder);
  const eventTime = Date.now() + 25 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
  scheduler.scheduleFor(eventTime);

  // Advance 24 hours — first reminder should fire
  await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
  expect(sendReminder).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  expect(sendReminder).toHaveBeenLastCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({ type: '24h' }),
  );

  // Advance another 23 hours — second reminder should fire at 1h mark
  await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(23 * 60 * 60 * 1000);
  expect(sendReminder).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync()` advances the fake clock and flushes all microtasks and pending promise continuations resolving within the window, enabling testing of timer-based flows that mix `setTimeout` with `await` — but it can only advance time forward, so tests simulating time reversal (NTP corrections, DST transitions) cannot use fake timers and must directly manipulate the `Date` constructor or use a library like `@sinonjs/fake-timers`.

**Pattern 716** — Vitest `test.runIf()` for Platform-Specific Isolation of OS-Dependent Tests
```typescript
// file-watcher.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import * as os from 'node:os';

const isLinux = os.platform() === 'linux';
const isMacOS = os.platform() === 'darwin';

test.runIf(isLinux)('detects file changes via inotify events', async () => {
  const { FileWatcher } = await import('../src/watchers/inotify-watcher');
  const watcher = new FileWatcher('/tmp/test-dir');
  const changes: string[] = [];
  watcher.on('change', (path) => changes.push(path));
  await watcher.waitForChange({ timeout: 2000 });
  expect(changes.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
  await watcher.close();
});

test.runIf(isMacOS)('detects directory moves via FSEvents', async () => {
  const { FileWatcher } = await import('../src/watchers/fsevents-watcher');
  const watcher = new FileWatcher('/tmp/test-dir');
  expect(watcher.isSupported()).toBe(true);
  await watcher.close();
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.runIf(condition)` marks a test as explicitly skipped when the condition is false (visible in reporter as skipped), which is clearer than a runtime `if` guard that produces a vacuous passing test — but `test.runIf` evaluates its condition at module evaluation time using only synchronous values, so dynamic readiness checks requiring `execSync` (e.g., verifying a kernel feature flag) must be executed synchronously before the module is parsed, and async checks are impossible without pre-computing them in `globalSetup`.

**Pattern 717** — Jest `jest.createMockFromModule()` for Auto-Generated Type-Safe Module Mocks
```typescript
// order-service.test.ts
import { jest, it, expect, beforeEach, describe } from '@jest/globals';

jest.mock('../src/payment-gateway');

import { PaymentGateway } from '../src/payment-gateway';
import { OrderService } from '../src/order-service';

const MockPaymentGateway = jest.createMockFromModule<typeof import('../src/payment-gateway')>(
  '../src/payment-gateway',
);

describe('OrderService payment handling', () => {
  let gateway: jest.Mocked<PaymentGateway>;

  beforeEach(() => {
    gateway = new MockPaymentGateway.PaymentGateway() as jest.Mocked<PaymentGateway>;
    gateway.charge.mockResolvedValue({ transactionId: 'txn_test', status: 'success' });
    gateway.refund.mockResolvedValue({ refundId: 'ref_test', status: 'refunded' });
  });

  it('marks order as paid after successful charge', async () => {
    const svc = new OrderService(gateway);
    await svc.processPayment({ orderId: 'ord_1', amount: 49.99 });
    expect(gateway.charge).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ amount: 4999, currency: 'usd' });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.createMockFromModule()` generates a mock that mirrors the real module's exported shape at call time, ensuring TypeScript types are preserved and all exported functions exist as `jest.fn()` — but the generated mock initializes all functions with no implementation (returning `undefined`), requiring explicit `mockResolvedValue` calls in each test's `beforeEach`; real module methods added after mock generation are absent from existing mocks until the mock is regenerated.

**Pattern 718** — Vitest `expect.addSnapshotSerializer()` for Stable Serialization of Volatile Object Fields
```typescript
// test-setup.ts
import { expect } from 'vitest';

expect.addSnapshotSerializer({
  test(val) {
    return typeof val === 'object' && val !== null
      && ('id' in val || 'createdAt' in val);
  },
  print(val, serialize) {
    const stable = { ...(val as Record<string, unknown>) };
    if ('id' in stable) stable.id = '<uuid>';
    if ('createdAt' in stable) stable.createdAt = '<timestamp>';
    if ('updatedAt' in stable) stable.updatedAt = '<timestamp>';
    return serialize(stable);
  },
});

// entity.test.ts
import { it, expect } from 'vitest';
import { createUser } from '../src/user-factory';

it('created user has expected shape', () => {
  const user = createUser({ name: 'Alice', email: 'alice@example.com' });
  expect(user).toMatchSnapshot();
  // Snapshot contains '<uuid>' and '<timestamp>' — stable across runs
});
```
Tradeoff: Custom snapshot serializers normalize volatile fields (UUIDs, timestamps, random IDs) before comparison, making snapshots stable across runs without per-field `expect.objectContaining()` assertions — but serializers are registered globally and affect all snapshot comparisons matching the `test()` predicate; a serializer that matches too broadly (any object with an `id` field) will normalize fields in unrelated snapshot tests, hiding legitimate regressions in those tests.

**Pattern 719** — Playwright `request` Fixture for API-Only Test Isolation Without Browser Overhead
```typescript
// tests/api/users.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('POST /api/users creates a new user', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.post('/api/users', {
    data: { name: 'Test User', email: `user-${Date.now()}@example.com` },
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.TEST_API_TOKEN}` },
  });

  expect(response.ok()).toBeTruthy();
  const body = await response.json();
  expect(body).toMatchObject({ name: 'Test User', id: expect.any(String) });
});

test('GET /api/users/:id returns 404 for unknown user', async ({ request }) => {
  const response = await request.get('/api/users/nonexistent-id-12345', {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.TEST_API_TOKEN}` },
  });

  expect(response.status()).toBe(404);
  const body = await response.json();
  expect(body.error).toContain('not found');
});
```
Tradeoff: The `request` fixture makes HTTP requests without spinning up a browser or rendering any page, reducing test execution time by 60-80% for pure API tests — but `request` uses a separate cookie jar from the `page` fixture, so tests verifying cross-cutting concerns that require both browser session state and API auth (e.g., a session cookie readable by both) must use `page.request` instead of `request`, as `page.request` shares the page's cookie context while `request` is fully isolated.

### Community Gotchas

**G401** — Vitest `vi.mock()` Auto-Mock Generates `undefined` for Non-Function Exports — Constants Silently Lose Values
When `vi.mock('../src/config')` is called without a factory function, Vitest auto-generates a mock module where every exported function is replaced with `vi.fn()`. However, non-function exports (constants, enums, plain objects, and class definitions) are replaced with `undefined`, not their original values. Code under test that reads `config.MAX_RETRIES` (a number constant) receives `undefined` and behaves unexpectedly.
Why this matters: A service that guards logic with `if (retries < config.MAX_RETRIES)` sees `retries < undefined` which is always `false`, causing the service to behave as if all retries are exhausted. The test passes because the mock makes the service return immediately, but the wrong code path is exercised — the `MAX_RETRIES` boundary is never actually tested, and the test provides false coverage confidence.
Fix: Always provide a factory function when mocking modules that export non-function values: `vi.mock('../src/config', () => ({ MAX_RETRIES: 3, TIMEOUT_MS: 5000, createClient: vi.fn() }))`. Use `vi.importActual()` inside the factory to preserve real constant values while replacing only functions: `vi.mock('../src/config', async () => ({ ...(await vi.importActual('../src/config')), createClient: vi.fn() }))`.

**G402** — Jest `jest.mock()` Hoisting Prevents Factory From Accessing Module-Scope `const` Variables
Jest's Babel transform hoists `jest.mock()` calls to the top of the file before any `import` statements execute. A factory function that references a variable defined in module scope (even a `const` declared before the `jest.mock()` call in source order) will receive `undefined` for that variable at hoisting time, because the `const` hasn't been initialized when the factory runs.
Why this matters: `const TIMEOUT = 5000; jest.mock('./retrier', () => ({ retry: jest.fn().mockImplementation((fn) => fn({ timeout: TIMEOUT })) }))` — at runtime, `TIMEOUT` is `undefined` in the factory because the factory is hoisted before the `const` assignment. Tests that rely on the timeout value produce behavior as if `timeout: undefined` was passed, without any error or warning, silently testing the wrong code path.
Fix: Inline all constants needed by the factory directly into the factory body: `jest.mock('./retrier', () => ({ retry: jest.fn().mockImplementation((fn) => fn({ timeout: 5000 })) }))`. Alternatively, use `jest.mock()` with `jest.requireActual()` inside the factory to read the real module's constants at factory-execution time rather than at module-scope initialization time.

**G403** — Playwright `storageState` from `globalSetup` Is Stale After Session Expiry — Tests Silently Pass Unauthenticated
`globalSetup` logs in once and writes `storageState` to disk. All test files then reference this file via `storageState: '.auth/user.json'`. If the test session's auth token has a short expiry (e.g., 1-hour JWTs), tests that run more than 1 hour after `globalSetup` completed will load a `storageState` with an expired token. The browser loads successfully, but API requests return 401 errors.
Why this matters: Components that receive a 401 response often silently redirect to the login page rather than throwing. Tests checking for authenticated content may see a login form instead, causing `expect(locator).toHaveText('Dashboard')` to fail with a timeout rather than a meaningful authentication error, making the root cause hard to diagnose and leading developers to incorrectly blame test infrastructure rather than token expiry.
Fix: Increase the test JWT expiry in the test environment to outlast the full test run duration. Alternatively, check the token expiry in a `beforeAll` hook and refresh it if it will expire within the next 10 minutes. For CI environments with strict token lifetimes, use `test.beforeAll` to refresh `storageState` at the beginning of each worker rather than relying on a single `globalSetup` state file.

**G404** — Vitest `clearMocks: true` Does Not Reset `mockReturnValue` — Only Clears Call History
`clearMocks: true` in `vitest.config.ts` calls `vi.clearAllMocks()` before each test. This clears call history, instances, and contexts for every mock — but it does NOT reset `mockReturnValue`, `mockResolvedValue`, or `mockImplementation` values. A test that sets `mockFn.mockResolvedValue('data-A')` will leave `'data-A'` as the active return value for the next test, even after `clearMocks: true` runs.
Why this matters: Test B relies on a default (unconfigured, returns `undefined`) behavior of `mockFn`. Test A ran before it and set `mockFn.mockResolvedValue('data-A')`. After `clearMocks: true`, test B calls `await mockFn()` expecting `undefined` but receives `'data-A'`. The failure message `expected undefined but received 'data-A'` appears to be a data regression but is actually mock state leakage — a pattern extremely common in codebases that migrate from `resetMocks: true` to `clearMocks: true` for performance reasons.
Fix: Use `resetMocks: true` instead of (or in addition to) `clearMocks: true` to also reset mock implementations between tests. Alternatively, call `vi.mocked(mockFn).mockReset()` explicitly in `beforeEach` for mocks whose return values must not persist. Recommended config for maximum isolation: `clearMocks: true, resetMocks: true, restoreMocks: true`.

**G405** — Jest `--testPathPattern` Bypasses `globalSetup` in Some IDE Test Runner Integrations — Infrastructure Not Started
When Jest is invoked via `jest --testPathPattern` from the CLI, `globalSetup` runs normally. However, some IDE Jest integration plugins invoke the Jest worker directly, bypassing the Jest configuration's `globalSetup` module. Tests that depend on `process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL` set by `globalSetup` receive `undefined`, causing connection errors that appear to be environment configuration problems rather than missing infrastructure.
Why this matters: A developer runs a single failing test file from their IDE using a Jest integration plugin. The plugin invokes the Jest worker directly without running `globalSetup`, so `TEST_DATABASE_URL` is undefined. The test fails with `connection refused` rather than a test assertion failure. The developer adds a `DATABASE_URL` env var globally to fix it, masking the test's actual dependency on `globalSetup` infrastructure and creating a CI/local environment divergence that resurfaces unpredictably.
Fix: Validate required environment variables at the top of test files that depend on `globalSetup` infrastructure: `if (!process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL) throw new Error('TEST_DATABASE_URL not set — run tests via npm test, not directly')`. Document in the test file that it requires `globalSetup` to have run. For IDE integration, configure the Jest plugin to use the project's `jest.config.ts` rather than a bare runner invocation.

**Pattern 720** — Playwright v1.60 `BrowserContext` Page Lifecycle Event Mirroring for Context-Scoped Resource Auditing
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/context-lifecycle-fixture.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type ResourceSummary = { pagesOpened: number; pagesClosed: number; frameNavigations: number };

export const test = base.extend<{ contextSummary: ResourceSummary }>({
  contextSummary: async ({ context }, use) => {
    let pagesOpened = 0;
    let pagesClosed = 0;
    let frameNavigations = 0;

    // v1.60: BrowserContext now mirrors page-lifecycle events directly on the context object.
    // These fire for every page created inside this context — including popups.
    context.on('page', () => pagesOpened++);
    context.on('pageclose', () => pagesClosed++);
    context.on('framenavigated', (frame) => {
      if (frame === frame.page().mainFrame()) frameNavigations++;
    });

    await use({ pagesOpened, pagesClosed, frameNavigations });

    // Isolation assertion: every page opened during this test must be closed by test end.
    // Unclosed pages cause BrowserContext teardown to stall, leaking resources into the next test.
    expect(pagesOpened, 'test leaked unclosed pages').toBe(pagesClosed);
  },
});

// tests/oauth.spec.ts
import { test } from './fixtures/context-lifecycle-fixture';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('OAuth popup opens, authenticates, and closes cleanly', async ({ page, contextSummary }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  const [popup] = await Promise.all([
    page.waitForEvent('popup'),
    page.click('[data-testid="oauth-github-btn"]'),
  ]);
  await popup.waitForLoadState('load');
  // Simulate completing OAuth flow — popup should close itself
  await popup.close();

  await page.waitForSelector('[data-testid="user-menu"]');
  // contextSummary fixture auto-asserts pagesOpened === pagesClosed after test
  expect(contextSummary.frameNavigations).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(1);
});
```
Tradeoff: Playwright v1.60's `BrowserContext` page lifecycle event mirroring (`pageclose`, `framenavigated`, `frameattached`, `framedetached`, `download`, `pageload`) allows context-level resource auditing without per-page event wiring — but the `framenavigated` event fires for every frame in every page, not just main-frame navigations; tests that embed `<iframe>` elements or single-page applications with hash-routing will see higher `frameNavigations` counts than expected and must filter by `frame === frame.page().mainFrame()` to count only top-level navigations.

**Pattern 721** — Vitest 4.1 `--coverage.changed` for Differential Coverage in Pull-Request Isolation Workflows
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — CI configuration for differential coverage
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      // --coverage.changed: only emit coverage data for files modified in the current branch.
      // In CI, this is equivalent to running `git diff --name-only origin/main | xargs vitest --coverage`.
      // The option is set via CLI: `vitest run --coverage --coverage.changed`.
      // When combined with a per-PR coverage threshold, this creates a "you own what you touch" policy.
      thresholds: {
        // These thresholds apply only to CHANGED files when --coverage.changed is active.
        lines: 80,
        branches: 75,
        functions: 80,
        statements: 80,
        // perFile: true means each changed file must meet the threshold individually,
        // not just the aggregate across all changed files.
        perFile: true,
      },
    },
  },
});

// .github/workflows/pr.yml (relevant excerpt)
// jobs:
//   test:
//     steps:
//       - name: Run tests with differential coverage
//         run: npx vitest run --coverage --coverage.changed
//         # Fails the PR if any changed file drops below the per-file threshold.
//         # Only changed files are measured — reduces noise from untouched legacy code.
```
Tradeoff: `--coverage.changed` (Vitest 4.1+) measures coverage only for files touched in the current branch diff, making PR coverage gates actionable — developers must maintain coverage on code they write, without being blocked by legacy files that have never had tests. However, `--coverage.changed` uses `git diff` against the current branch's base, which means it is only accurate when run in a full git checkout (not a shallow clone); CI pipelines that use `fetch-depth: 1` shallow clones will see an empty diff and report 100% coverage vacuously. Set `fetch-depth: 0` in the GitHub Actions `checkout` step when using this feature.

**Pattern 722** — Vitest 4.1 GitHub Actions Reporter with Automatic Job Summary for Per-Test Isolation Traceability
```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — CI-aware reporter configuration
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    reporters: process.env.GITHUB_ACTIONS
      ? [
          // github-actions reporter auto-generates a Job Summary with test statistics,
          // flaky test permalinks, and failure details — no extra setup required in CI.
          // It is enabled by default in Vitest 4.1+ when GITHUB_ACTIONS=true.
          'github-actions',
          // default reporter still runs for terminal output during PR checks.
          'default',
        ]
      : ['default'],
    // The 'agent' reporter (Vitest 4.1+) emits minimal output — failures only.
    // Use when running Vitest as a sub-process from an AI agent or script pipeline
    // where token/output budget matters. Reduces CI log noise by 90%+ on green runs.
  },
});

// For manual activation of the agent reporter (CI pipelines with output budget constraints):
// vitest run --reporter=agent
//
// The agent reporter outputs:
//   - Nothing on passing tests (complete silence on green)
//   - Full failure details including file path, line number, and diff on failures
//   - A one-line summary: "N tests passed, M failed, X skipped"
//
// This is NOT a replacement for the full reporter in normal development — it is optimized
// for automated pipelines that process test output programmatically rather than for humans.
```
Tradeoff: The Vitest 4.1 `github-actions` reporter posts per-failure annotation directly to the GitHub Actions workflow, linking each failure to its source line in the PR diff view — significantly faster to diagnose than reading a wall of terminal output. However, the annotations are only visible in the GitHub Actions UI and not in terminal output during `vitest run --reporter=github-actions` without also including `default`; run both reporters in CI to preserve human-readable terminal output for debugging locally replicated failures.

**Pattern 723** — Jest Monorepo `fakeTimers.enableGlobally` with Per-Project `doNotFake` Override for Selective Timer Isolation
```typescript
// jest.config.base.ts — shared root config for all packages
import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from 'jest';

export const rootConfig = defineConfig({
  fakeTimers: {
    enableGlobally: true,       // All tests start with fake timers — no per-test `jest.useFakeTimers()`
    doNotFake: [
      'nextTick',               // Keep real nextTick — some async utilities rely on it for ordering
      'queueMicrotask',         // Keep real microtask queue — Promise.resolve() chaining must work
      'performance',            // Keep real perf.now() — timing assertions in benchmarks
    ],
    now: new Date('2026-01-01T00:00:00Z').getTime(), // Deterministic epoch for all tests
    timerLimit: 100,            // Prevent infinite timer recursion from misconfigured intervals
  },
});

// packages/payment-service/jest.config.ts — override for a specific package
import { defineConfig, mergeConfig } from 'jest';
import { rootConfig } from '../../jest.config.base';

export default mergeConfig(
  rootConfig,
  defineConfig({
    fakeTimers: {
      // OVERRIDE: payment service uses Temporal.Instant in real-time audit logs.
      // Faking Temporal.Now breaks audit log timestamps in integration tests.
      doNotFake: [
        ...rootConfig.fakeTimers!.doNotFake!,
        'Date',         // Keep real Date in this package — payment timestamps must be real
      ],
    },
    testTimeout: 15_000,        // Integration tests are slower; real timers + I/O
  }),
);

// usage in a unit test — no jest.useFakeTimers() needed:
import { jest, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';

test('retries with exponential backoff', async () => {
  const onRetry = jest.fn();
  const retrier = new ExponentialBackoff({ onRetry });

  retrier.start();

  await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(1_000);
  expect(onRetry).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);   // 1st retry at 1000ms

  await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(2_000);
  expect(onRetry).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(2);   // 2nd retry at 2000ms (1000 + 2000 = 3000ms total)
  // Fake timers restored automatically before next test — no afterEach needed.
});
```
Tradeoff: `fakeTimers.enableGlobally: true` eliminates per-test `jest.useFakeTimers()` / `jest.useRealTimers()` boilerplate, but introduces a subtle danger: any code that executes a `setTimeout` at *module evaluation time* (before any test body runs) will have that timer captured by the fake clock, meaning the timer never fires unless a test explicitly advances the clock. Libraries that schedule background cleanup or heartbeat timers at import time (e.g., some HTTP connection pool implementations) will appear to hang or produce stale connections in every test. Fix: add the library's timer-using APIs to `doNotFake` for the affected project, or refactor the library to defer timer creation until an explicit `init()` call.

**Pattern 724** — Vitest `test.extend()` Builder Chain with Typed Config + Server Fixture Dependency
```typescript
// tests/fixtures/server-fixture.ts
import { test as base } from 'vitest';
import http from 'node:http';

interface ServerConfig {
  port: number;
  host: string;
  prefix: string;
}

// Step 1: extend base test with a config fixture
const withConfig = base.extend<{ config: ServerConfig }>({
  config: {
    port: 3099,
    host: 'localhost',
    prefix: '/api/v1',
  },
});

// Step 2: extend further with a server fixture that DEPENDS on config.
// This is the Vitest 4.1 typed builder chain pattern:
// each .extend() call returns a new test function that preserves prior fixture types.
export const test = withConfig.extend<{ serverUrl: string }>({
  serverUrl: async ({ config }, use) => {
    // Arrange: spin up a real HTTP server on the config-provided port
    const server = http.createServer((req, res) => {
      res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
      res.end(JSON.stringify({ ok: true, path: req.url }));
    });
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) =>
      server.listen(config.port, config.host, resolve),
    );

    // Act: provide the base URL to the test
    await use(`http://${config.host}:${config.port}${config.prefix}`);

    // Teardown: guaranteed to run even if the test throws
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.close(() => resolve()));
  },
});

// tests/api.spec.ts — override config per-test with test.use()
import { test } from './fixtures/server-fixture';
import { expect } from 'vitest';

// Default config (port 3099)
test('GET /api/v1/health returns 200', async ({ serverUrl }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`${serverUrl}/health`);
  expect(res.ok).toBe(true);
});

// Override config for one describe block
test.describe('on port 3100', () => {
  test.use({ config: { port: 3100, host: 'localhost', prefix: '/api/v2' } });

  test('GET /api/v2/health on alternate port', async ({ serverUrl }) => {
    const res = await fetch(`${serverUrl}/health`);
    expect(res.ok).toBe(true);
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: The Vitest `test.extend()` builder chain provides full TypeScript type inference through each extension layer — `config` is typed in the `serverUrl` fixture without casting. However, each `.extend()` call creates a new `test` function object; if the chain is long (4+ layers) and the fixture modules are heavy, import time increases noticeably. Keep fixture chains to 2-3 layers maximum and use `mergeTests()` to compose parallel fixture sets rather than deeply nesting `.extend()` chains.

### Community Gotchas

**G406** — Vitest `clearMocks: true` Does Not Reset `mockReturnValue` — Only Clears Call History, Causing Silent Cross-Test Contamination
`clearMocks: true` in `vitest.config.ts` calls `vi.clearAllMocks()` before each test. This clears call history, instances, and contexts for every mock — but it does NOT reset `mockReturnValue`, `mockResolvedValue`, or `mockImplementation` values set by prior tests.
Why this matters: Test A sets `mockFn.mockResolvedValue('data-from-A')`. Test B runs next and expects `mockFn()` to return `undefined` (the default), but instead receives `'data-from-A'` because `clearMocks` only wiped the call history, not the configured return value. The failure message `expected undefined but received 'data-from-A'` appears to be a data regression but is actually mock state leakage — extremely common in codebases that migrated from `resetMocks: true` to `clearMocks: true` for performance. Fix: use `resetMocks: true` (resets implementations and history), or add `vi.resetAllMocks()` to `beforeEach` in affected suites.

**G407** — Jest 30 Requires Case-Exact `jest.mock()` Paths — Wrong-Case Paths Compile Fine but Fail at Runtime on Case-Sensitive File Systems
`jest.mock('./path/to/MyService')` where the actual file is `./path/to/myService.ts` worked silently in Jest 29 on macOS (HFS+ is case-insensitive by default). Jest 30 introduced strict case-sensitive path matching for mock registration, aligning with case-sensitive Linux CI file systems.
Why this matters: A TypeScript project developed on macOS with wrong-case mock paths passes all tests locally but fails in CI (Linux) with `Cannot find module './path/to/MyService'`. The developer sees a "works on my machine" failure that is masked in the development environment. Fix: audit all `jest.mock()` calls to ensure the path string exactly matches the casing of the file on disk. Run `grep -rn "jest.mock" tests/ | grep -v "node_modules"` and cross-reference each path against the actual file system casing.

**G408** — Playwright `storageState` File Written by `globalSetup` Is Stale When JWT Expiry Is Shorter Than Test Suite Duration
`globalSetup` logs in once and saves `storageState` to `.auth/user.json`. All tests load this file via `storageState: '.auth/user.json'` in their project config. If the JWT in the storage state expires mid-suite (common with 1-hour expiry in test environments), tests that start after the expiry window load an invalid token, but the browser loads the page successfully (redirecting to a login screen rather than throwing).
Why this matters: Tests checking for authenticated content see the login page instead, failing with `expect(locator).toHaveText() expected: 'Dashboard', received: 'Sign In'` — a misleading assertion failure that looks like a UI regression rather than an auth expiry. Teams waste hours investigating frontend changes when the root cause is a 3600-second token limit. Fix: increase JWT expiry in the test environment to exceed the longest CI suite run (e.g., 8 hours), or add a `beforeAll` hook that refreshes the token when remaining lifetime drops below 30 minutes.

**G409** — Vitest Auto-Mock Generates `undefined` for Non-Function Exports — Constants, Enums, and Config Objects Silently Lose Their Values
When `vi.mock('../src/config')` is called without a factory function, Vitest generates a mock module where exported functions become `vi.fn()` instances but non-function exports (plain constants, numeric enums, string constants, plain objects) are replaced with `undefined`.
Why this matters: A service that reads `config.MAX_RETRIES` (a numeric constant) receives `undefined` in tests using auto-mock. The service guard `if (retries < config.MAX_RETRIES)` evaluates `retries < undefined` which is always `false`, silently bypassing the retry logic. The test passes because the wrong code path is exercised, creating false coverage confidence — the retry boundary is never exercised at all. Fix: always provide a factory when mocking modules with non-function exports: `vi.mock('../src/config', () => ({ MAX_RETRIES: 3, TIMEOUT_MS: 5000, createClient: vi.fn() }))`. Use `vi.importActual()` inside the factory to preserve real constant values: `vi.mock('../src/config', async () => ({ ...(await vi.importActual('../src/config')), createClient: vi.fn() }))`.

**G410** — Jest 30 Renamed `--testPathPattern` to `--testPathPatterns` (Plural) — IDE Integrations Hard-Coding the Old Flag Run the Entire Suite Silently
Jest 30 renamed `--testPathPattern` to `--testPathPatterns` (plural) to support multiple patterns simultaneously. IDE Jest runner plugins that hard-code the old flag name (`--testPathPattern`) silently fall back to running the full test suite when Jest 30 ignores the unrecognized flag, causing developers to wait for all tests to finish when they intended to run a single file.
Why this matters: A developer clicks "Run This Test File" in their IDE extension. The plugin invokes `jest --testPathPattern="path/to/my.test.ts"`. Jest 30 does not recognize `--testPathPattern` (singular) and runs the entire suite. The test output shows 2000 tests instead of 12, making it appear the single test passed (mixed in with the broader run). The developer gains false confidence that their targeted test works when in fact a completely different test suite ran. Fix: update IDE plugins to use `--testPathPatterns` (plural); check the IDE's Jest plugin settings for a "Jest CLI flags" override and update the flag name manually if the plugin has not been updated yet.

### Patterns

**Pattern 725** — Jest `expect.assertions(n)` at AAA Arrange Phase to Enforce Async Teardown Completeness

In asynchronous tests with `try/finally` teardown, a thrown assertion inside the `try` block that is
not awaited before the `finally` runs can silently swallow the failure. Placing
`expect.assertions(n)` as the *first* line of the Arrange phase guarantees Jest will fail the test if
exactly `n` assertions were not executed — catching silent swallowing regardless of `finally` order.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect, beforeEach, afterEach } from '@jest/globals';
import { sendNotification } from './notifications';
import type { NotificationService } from './types';

let mockService: jest.Mocked<NotificationService>;

beforeEach(() => {
  mockService = {
    send: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 'msg-1', status: 'sent' }),
    shutdown: jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined),
  };
});

afterEach(async () => {
  // teardown is real async — must be awaited
  await mockService.shutdown();
});

test('sendNotification calls service.send with correct payload', async () => {
  // Arrange — declare assertion count FIRST; catches async swallowing
  expect.assertions(3);

  const payload = { to: 'user@example.com', subject: 'Hello', body: 'World' };

  // Act
  const result = await sendNotification(mockService, payload);

  // Assert
  expect(result.status).toBe('sent');
  expect(mockService.send).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
  expect(mockService.send).toHaveBeenCalledWith(payload);
});
```
Tradeoff: `expect.assertions(n)` requires updating the count whenever assertions are added or
removed, creating a maintenance burden in frequently-changed tests. Reserve it for async paths where
silent assertion skipping is a realistic risk — primarily `try/catch/finally` flows, Promise rejection
tests, and tests with `done` callbacks. Do not add it to synchronous AAA tests where Jest's normal
assertion failure propagation is sufficient.

**Pattern 726** — Vitest `test.concurrent` + Per-Test `vi.stubEnv()` for Environment Variable Isolation Under Parallelism

`vi.stubEnv()` uses `process.env` which is a shared mutable object in the Node.js process. When
`test.concurrent` runs multiple tests in the same worker thread simultaneously, two concurrent tests
calling `vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', ...)` race on the same key. Vitest's `vi.stubEnv` and
`vi.unstubAllEnvs()` are *not* concurrency-safe on their own. The fix: use `pool: 'forks'` to get
separate processes, or encode the env state in isolated worker data rather than `process.env`.

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts — safe concurrent env isolation via forks pool
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    pool: 'forks',          // Each worker is a separate process — process.env is not shared
    poolOptions: {
      forks: {
        singleFork: false,  // One process per worker, not one shared process
      },
    },
  },
});

// service.test.ts — concurrent tests now safely isolate process.env
import { vi, test, expect, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { createLogger } from './logger';

afterEach(() => {
  vi.unstubAllEnvs(); // Restore process.env after each test in this file
});

test.concurrent('logger uses DEBUG level when LOG_LEVEL=debug', () => {
  // Arrange
  vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'debug');
  // Act
  const logger = createLogger();
  // Assert
  expect(logger.level).toBe('debug');
});

test.concurrent('logger uses INFO level when LOG_LEVEL=info', () => {
  // Arrange
  vi.stubEnv('LOG_LEVEL', 'info');
  // Act
  const logger = createLogger();
  // Assert
  expect(logger.level).toBe('info');
});
```
Tradeoff: `pool: 'forks'` provides process-level env isolation at the cost of higher memory usage
and slower worker startup (fork overhead vs thread overhead). For CPU-bound test suites with hundreds
of concurrent tests, switching from `threads` to `forks` can increase total wall-clock time by
20-40%. Use `pool: 'threads'` only when env vars are not mutated across concurrent tests — prefer
marking env-mutation tests as `test` (non-concurrent) within a `threads`-pooled suite.

**Pattern 727** — Node.js `AsyncLocalStorage` Per-Test Request Context in Express Integration Tests

Express middleware commonly reads request-scoped context (tenant ID, trace ID, user) from a shared
singleton rather than attaching it to `req`. In integration tests, concurrent or sequential tests
that trigger multiple concurrent requests will read the wrong context unless each test's request is
isolated in an `AsyncLocalStorage` scope.

```typescript
// src/context.ts
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';

interface RequestContext {
  tenantId: string;
  traceId: string;
}

export const contextStore = new AsyncLocalStorage<RequestContext>();

export function getContext(): RequestContext {
  const ctx = contextStore.getStore();
  if (!ctx) throw new Error('No request context — call contextStore.run() first');
  return ctx;
}

// tests/middleware.test.ts
import { test, expect } from 'vitest';
import request from 'supertest';
import { app } from '../src/app';
import { contextStore } from '../src/context';

test('each request gets its own isolated context', async () => {
  // Arrange: inject context via AsyncLocalStorage before the request chain
  const capturedContexts: string[] = [];

  // Override the middleware to capture context inside the store scope
  const testContext1 = { tenantId: 'tenant-A', traceId: 'trace-001' };
  const testContext2 = { tenantId: 'tenant-B', traceId: 'trace-002' };

  // Act: fire two requests sequentially with different contexts
  const [res1, res2] = await Promise.all([
    contextStore.run(testContext1, () =>
      request(app).get('/api/context').expect(200),
    ),
    contextStore.run(testContext2, () =>
      request(app).get('/api/context').expect(200),
    ),
  ]);

  // Assert: each response reflects its own isolated context
  expect(res1.body.tenantId).toBe('tenant-A');
  expect(res2.body.tenantId).toBe('tenant-B');
});
```
Tradeoff: `AsyncLocalStorage` propagates context across `await` boundaries and `Promise.all`
automatically in Node.js 16+. However, context does NOT propagate across `worker_threads` — if a
request handler spawns a worker thread, the worker will have an empty store. In Node.js 24 the
`AsyncContextFrame` default makes propagation across `setImmediate`/`nextTick` reliable, but
`worker_threads` remain isolated by design. Pass context explicitly via `workerData` when worker
threads must participate in the same logical context.

**Pattern 728** — `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` + ESM Dynamic Import for Per-Test Singleton Refresh with `satisfies` Narrowing

Module-level singletons (database connection pools, caches, feature flag clients) initialised at
import time cannot be reset by `jest.resetModules()` alone in ESM because the module graph is cached
per-specifier. `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` creates a fresh module registry for a callback scope,
combined with a dynamic `import()` inside the callback to obtain a fresh singleton instance.

```typescript
import { jest, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';

test('FeatureFlagClient reads flags from env at import time', async () => {
  // Arrange: override env before module evaluation
  process.env.FEATURE_NEW_UI = 'true';

  let isEnabled!: () => boolean;

  await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
    // Fresh module registry — singleton is re-created with the new env value
    const { FeatureFlagClient } = await import('../src/feature-flags');
    // `satisfies` narrows the type without casting to `any`
    const client = new FeatureFlagClient() satisfies { isEnabled(flag: string): boolean };
    isEnabled = (flag: string) => client.isEnabled(flag);
  });

  // Act
  const result = isEnabled('new-ui');

  // Assert
  expect(result).toBe(true);

  // Teardown: restore env so next test gets a clean state
  delete process.env.FEATURE_NEW_UI;
});

test('FeatureFlagClient returns false when flag is absent', async () => {
  // Arrange: env is clean — previous test's env mutation is fully isolated
  let isEnabled!: (flag: string) => boolean;

  await jest.isolateModulesAsync(async () => {
    const { FeatureFlagClient } = await import('../src/feature-flags');
    const client = new FeatureFlagClient() satisfies { isEnabled(flag: string): boolean };
    isEnabled = (flag: string) => client.isEnabled(flag);
  });

  // Act
  const result = isEnabled('new-ui');

  // Assert — clean module instance, flag absent
  expect(result).toBe(false);
});
```
Tradeoff: `jest.isolateModulesAsync()` is substantially slower than a plain import because it
creates a new module registry, re-evaluates all transitive imports, and re-runs all module-level
side effects (e.g., console statements, file reads, timer creation). For modules with heavy
initialization (GraphQL schema compilation, Prisma client generation), per-test isolation can add
500ms+ per test. Prefer mock-based isolation (`jest.mock()` with factory) when the singleton's
behavior can be controlled without re-evaluating the module.

**Pattern 729** — Vitest `vi.spyOn` with `using` Declaration for Deterministic Spy Lifecycle

TypeScript 5.2+ `using` declarations invoke `[Symbol.dispose]()` at block exit, providing
deterministic spy cleanup without an `afterEach` hook. Vitest's `vi.spyOn()` returns a spy that
implements `Symbol.dispose` as of Vitest 4.0 — calling `mockRestore()` automatically when the
enclosing block exits.

```typescript
import { vi, test, expect } from 'vitest';
import { processOrder } from './orders';
import * as mailer from './mailer';

test('processOrder sends confirmation email on success', async () => {
  // Arrange: `using` ensures spy.mockRestore() is called when the test block exits
  using sendSpy = vi.spyOn(mailer, 'sendEmail').mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'msg-abc' });

  const order = { id: 'ord-1', customerId: 'cust-1', total: 99.99 };

  // Act
  await processOrder(order);

  // Assert
  expect(sendSpy).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  expect(sendSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
    expect.objectContaining({ to: 'cust-1@example.com', subject: expect.stringContaining('ord-1') }),
  );
  // spy.mockRestore() called automatically at block exit — no afterEach needed
});

test('processOrder does NOT send email when order total is zero', async () => {
  // Arrange: fresh spy — previous test's spy was already restored
  using sendSpy = vi.spyOn(mailer, 'sendEmail').mockResolvedValue({ messageId: 'msg-xyz' });

  const freeOrder = { id: 'ord-2', customerId: 'cust-2', total: 0 };

  // Act
  await processOrder(freeOrder);

  // Assert
  expect(sendSpy).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
});
```
Tradeoff: `using` declarations require TypeScript 5.2+ and the `"lib": ["ES2022", "ESNext"]` or
`"useDefineForClassFields": true` tsconfig settings to compile correctly. Projects on TypeScript
<5.2 must use `afterEach(() => spy.mockRestore())` instead. Additionally, `using` only covers the
*current test block* — if the spy is declared in a `describe` scope and needs to persist across
multiple tests, `afterAll(() => spy.mockRestore())` remains the correct pattern. Do not use `using`
in `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks; the dispose fires at hook block exit, not at test end.

**Pattern 730** — Playwright `test.use({ baseURL })` Per-`describe` Environment Override for Multi-Environment Test Isolation

Playwright `test.use()` inside a `describe` block overrides fixture values for that scope only,
providing hermetic per-describe environment isolation without separate config files.

```typescript
// tests/api/orders.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Default baseURL from playwright.config.ts applies to tests outside describe blocks

test.describe('staging environment', () => {
  // Override baseURL for this describe block only — no other tests are affected
  test.use({ baseURL: 'https://staging.example.com' });

  test('GET /api/orders returns 200 on staging', async ({ request }) => {
    // Arrange (implicit — baseURL set by test.use)
    // Act
    const response = await request.get('/api/orders');
    // Assert
    expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
  });

  test('POST /api/orders creates order on staging', async ({ request }) => {
    // Arrange
    const newOrder = { customerId: 'c1', items: [{ sku: 'WIDGET', qty: 2 }] };
    // Act
    const response = await request.post('/api/orders', { data: newOrder });
    // Assert
    expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
    expect(await response.json()).toMatchObject({ status: 'pending' });
  });
});

test.describe('production readonly checks', () => {
  test.use({ baseURL: 'https://api.example.com' });

  test('GET /api/health returns healthy on production', async ({ request }) => {
    const response = await request.get('/api/health');
    expect(response.status()).toBe(200);
    expect(await response.json()).toMatchObject({ status: 'healthy' });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `test.use()` inside `describe` only affects the fixture value for tests in that describe
scope. It does NOT affect tests outside the describe block or in sibling describes, making it safe
for multi-environment suites in a single file. However, Playwright resolves `test.use()` at
collection time — dynamic `test.use()` calls inside `beforeAll` or `beforeEach` are silently ignored.
Always call `test.use()` at the top level of a `describe` block, never inside a lifecycle hook.

**Pattern 731** — Jest `moduleNameMapper` Dual-Entry Isolation for Tree-Shaken Bundle Testing

When a library ships separate ESM (tree-shakeable) and CJS entry points via `package.json`
`"exports"` field, Jest's CommonJS transform may resolve the CJS entry point — missing
tree-shaking side effects and export differences present only in the ESM build. Use
`moduleNameMapper` to force Jest to load the specific entry point under test.

```typescript
// jest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'jest';

export default defineConfig({
  moduleNameMapper: {
    // Force the ESM (tree-shakeable) entry point for the analytics library
    '^@company/analytics$': '<rootDir>/node_modules/@company/analytics/dist/index.mjs',
    // Force the CJS entry point for a Node.js-only util library
    '^@company/node-utils$': '<rootDir>/node_modules/@company/node-utils/dist/cjs/index.js',
  },
  transform: {
    '^.+\\.mts?$': ['ts-jest', { useESM: true }],
    '^.+\\.cts?$': ['ts-jest', { useESM: false }],
  },
});

// analytics.test.ts — verifies that the ESM entry point correctly tree-shakes
import { jest, test, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { trackEvent } from '@company/analytics';

test('trackEvent is a named export in the ESM build', () => {
  // Arrange (implicit — module resolved to ESM entry via moduleNameMapper)
  // Act
  const type = typeof trackEvent;
  // Assert — verifies the named export exists in the mapped module
  expect(type).toBe('function');
});
```
Tradeoff: `moduleNameMapper` overrides are applied globally to all tests in the Jest project —
every test importing `@company/analytics` will resolve to the mapped path. This is intentional for
bundle-entry isolation but can cause confusion when the mapped `.mjs` path does not exist yet (e.g.,
after a dependency update that changes the dist layout). Add a CI check that validates all
`moduleNameMapper` target paths exist: `Object.values(config.moduleNameMapper).forEach(p => existsSync(p.replace('<rootDir>', process.cwd())))`.

**Pattern 732** — Vitest `workspace` Project-Level `setupFiles` for Framework-Specific Global Fixture Registration

In a Vitest workspace with multiple projects (React components, Node.js services, CLI utilities),
each project needs different global setup — JSDOM globals for React, fetch polyfills for Node.js
services, file system mocks for CLI utilities. Using a single root `setupFiles` pollutes all
projects. Per-project `setupFiles` in `vitest.workspace.ts` keeps global fixture registration hermetic.

```typescript
// vitest.workspace.ts
import { defineWorkspace } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineWorkspace([
  {
    // React component tests — needs JSDOM + @testing-library/jest-dom matchers
    extends: './vitest.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'components',
      include: ['src/components/**/*.test.tsx'],
      environment: 'jsdom',
      setupFiles: ['./tests/setup/react-setup.ts'],
    },
  },
  {
    // Node.js service tests — needs undici fetch polyfill + global fetch mock reset
    extends: './vitest.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'services',
      include: ['src/services/**/*.test.ts'],
      environment: 'node',
      setupFiles: ['./tests/setup/node-setup.ts'],
    },
  },
  {
    // CLI tests — needs memfs virtual file system, no DOM globals
    extends: './vitest.config.ts',
    test: {
      name: 'cli',
      include: ['src/cli/**/*.test.ts'],
      environment: 'node',
      setupFiles: ['./tests/setup/cli-setup.ts'],
    },
  },
]);

// tests/setup/react-setup.ts
import '@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest';
import { vi, afterEach } from 'vitest';
import { cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';

afterEach(() => {
  cleanup(); // Unmount React trees after every test
  vi.clearAllMocks();
});

// tests/setup/node-setup.ts
import { afterEach, vi } from 'vitest';

// Install undici fetch globally for Node.js projects
import { fetch, Headers, Request, Response } from 'undici';
Object.assign(globalThis, { fetch, Headers, Request, Response });

afterEach(() => {
  vi.resetAllMocks(); // Reset mock implementations between service tests
});
```
Tradeoff: Per-project `setupFiles` means setup logic is duplicated across files (e.g., both
`react-setup.ts` and `node-setup.ts` call `vi.clearAllMocks()`). Extract shared primitives into a
`tests/setup/shared.ts` module imported by each project setup file. Avoid importing from
`vitest/config` inside `setupFiles` — use `vitest` (runtime imports) instead. Mixing `vitest/config`
imports in runtime setup files causes Jest-style module resolution failures in some Vite
configurations.

**Pattern 733** — Jest `--testNamePattern` + `--randomize` + `--seed` FIRST Independent Property Audit Workflow

The FIRST **Independent** property requires that tests pass regardless of execution order. The
standard audit workflow: run the suite with `--randomize` + a fixed seed repeatedly, then run
a targeted single test with `--testNamePattern` and the `--runInBand` flag to verify it passes in
isolation. A test that passes in a full run but fails in isolation has a hidden setup dependency.

```typescript
// package.json scripts for the audit workflow
// {
//   "scripts": {
//     "test:audit:randomize": "jest --randomize --seed=12345",
//     "test:audit:isolate": "jest --testNamePattern='$TEST_NAME' --runInBand --verbose"
//   }
// }

// Example: a test with a hidden dependency on a previous test's module state
// BEFORE fix — will fail when run in isolation:
import { jest, describe, it, expect } from '@jest/globals';
import { initCache, getFromCache } from './cache';

let cacheReady = false;

describe('cache module', () => {
  it('initialises successfully', () => {
    initCache({ maxSize: 100 });
    cacheReady = true; // side effect: sets shared mutable state
    expect(cacheReady).toBe(true);
  });

  it('returns undefined for missing key', () => {
    // BUG: depends on `cacheReady` being set by the previous test
    // When run in isolation via --testNamePattern, this fails because
    // initCache() was never called
    expect(getFromCache('missing-key')).toBeUndefined();
  });
});

// AFTER fix — each test is self-contained:
describe('cache module — fixed', () => {
  it('returns undefined for missing key', () => {
    // Arrange: initialise in this test's own Arrange phase
    initCache({ maxSize: 100 });

    // Act
    const result = getFromCache('missing-key');

    // Assert
    expect(result).toBeUndefined();
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: Running the full suite with `--randomize` on every CI push adds overhead proportional to
the number of randomization permutations. For suites >1000 tests, a single randomized run
(e.g., `--seed=$GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER`) catches most order-dependency bugs without running N! orderings.
Reserve exhaustive randomization (`--randomize` with 10+ seeds) for pre-release audits or when
flakiness is actively investigated.

**Pattern 734** — Playwright `page.addInitScript()` + `Symbol` for Cross-Frame Shared-State Poisoning Detection

In single-page applications with iframes (OAuth popups, embedded widgets, payment iframes), state
leaks can occur when the main frame and an iframe both access the same `localStorage` key or
`window` property. `page.addInitScript()` injects a poisoning probe before any frame script runs,
allowing tests to detect cross-frame state contamination.

```typescript
// tests/payment/checkout.spec.ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('payment iframe does not read main frame localStorage keys', async ({ page }) => {
  // Arrange: inject a Symbol-keyed poison before any frame script evaluates
  await page.addInitScript(() => {
    const POISON_KEY = '__test_isolation_probe__';
    // Write a poison value to localStorage from the main frame
    localStorage.setItem(POISON_KEY, 'POISONED');

    // Monitor iframe access attempts via a storage event listener
    const contaminated: string[] = [];
    window.addEventListener('storage', (e) => {
      if (e.key === POISON_KEY && e.storageArea === localStorage) {
        contaminated.push(e.url ?? 'unknown-frame');
      }
    });

    // Expose contamination list for the test to inspect
    (window as unknown as Record<string, unknown>)['__contamination__'] = contaminated;
  });

  // Act: load the checkout page which embeds a payment iframe
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.waitForSelector('iframe[data-testid="payment-frame"]');

  // Allow time for the iframe to initialize and potentially read storage
  await page.waitForTimeout(500);

  // Assert: no cross-frame localStorage reads of main-frame keys
  const contamination = await page.evaluate(
    () => (window as unknown as Record<string, unknown[]>)['__contamination__'],
  );
  expect(contamination).toHaveLength(0);
});
```
Tradeoff: `page.addInitScript()` runs in the main frame context — it does NOT automatically inject
into child iframes unless `page.addInitScript()` is called with `{ path }` before navigation and the
iframe shares the same origin. Cross-origin iframes are sandboxed by the browser and cannot be
probed directly; use `page.frame()` + `frame.addInitScript()` for same-origin frames. The
`waitForTimeout(500)` is a smell — replace with a proper `waitForFunction()` or
`expect(page.locator('...')).toBeVisible()` once the iframe renders, then read `__contamination__`.

### Community Gotchas

**G411** — Vitest `aroundEach` Hook Does Not Await Promises Thrown in `use()` — Async Errors in Fixture Body Swallowed Silently
When a Vitest `aroundEach` fixture's inner async function (the body between `use()` and end of the
generator/async function) throws, Vitest 4.1 swallows the rejection if the fixture was declared as
`async function*` rather than as an `async` function with explicit `try/finally`. The test is
reported as passed even though teardown errored.
Why this matters: A database rollback fixture using `async function*` syntax that throws in the
cleanup step (e.g., the transaction was already committed by the SUT) silently leaves the DB in a
dirty state, causing the next test to fail with a confusing data integrity error rather than the
actual teardown failure. Fix: always use the `async ({ use }) => { try { await use(); } finally {
... } }` pattern for `aroundEach` fixtures (the object-style API) rather than `async function*`
generator syntax. The object-style pattern surfaces errors from the teardown phase as a dedicated
`afterEach` failure.

**G412** — Jest 30 `expect.arrayOf()` Does Not Accept `expect.objectContaining()` as Its Inner Matcher — Only Type Primitives Allowed
`expect.arrayOf(expect.objectContaining({ id: expect.any(String) }))` compiles with TypeScript's
type checker but throws `Matcher is not a valid type constructor` at runtime in Jest 30. The
`arrayOf` matcher was designed for type-uniform primitive arrays (e.g., `expect.arrayOf(Number)`,
`expect.arrayOf(String)`) — it accepts a *constructor function*, not an asymmetric matcher.
Why this matters: Teams migrating from `expect(arr).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining([...]))` to
`expect.arrayOf()` for "cleaner" assertions nest `objectContaining` inside `arrayOf` and see runtime
errors that TypeScript did not catch. Fix: use `expect.arrayContaining([expect.objectContaining({
id: expect.any(String) })])` for arrays of objects. Reserve `expect.arrayOf(Number)` for
primitive-typed arrays where the element constructor is known.

**G413** — Node.js `node:test` `mock.module()` Requires `--experimental-vm-modules` on Node.js <23 — Silent No-Op Without the Flag
`node:test`'s `mock.module()` API for ESM module mocking relies on the VM module API which requires
`--experimental-vm-modules` on Node.js 20 and 22. Without the flag, `mock.module()` call
succeeds (no error thrown) but the module is NOT mocked — the real module is loaded, and tests pass
against real implementations.
Why this matters: A CI pipeline running Node.js 22 without the `--experimental-vm-modules` flag
will import real external modules (e.g., an email sender or Stripe client) in tests that appear to
mock them. Tests pass because the real module returns real data in a test environment, but the test
is not exercising mock-controlled behavior. The bug is completely invisible in the test output. Fix:
add `--experimental-vm-modules` to the test runner invocation on Node.js <23, or set
`NODE_OPTIONS=--experimental-vm-modules` in the CI environment. Node.js 24+ enables the VM module
API by default and does not require the flag.

**G414** — Playwright `test.use()` Inside `beforeAll` Is Silently Ignored — Fixture Overrides Must Be at `describe` Top Level
`test.use({ storageState: '.auth/admin.json' })` called inside a `beforeAll` hook does not apply the
fixture override to any tests in the enclosing describe block. Playwright collects fixture overrides
at test collection time (before any hooks run), so `test.use()` calls inside lifecycle hooks are
silently discarded.
Why this matters: A test file that conditionally sets `storageState` based on an environment
variable check inside `beforeAll` appears to work (the call executes without error) but all tests
run with the default `storageState` (typically unauthenticated). Authentication-dependent tests pass
in the development environment (where the default state happens to be authenticated) but fail in CI
with `expected: 'Dashboard', received: 'Login'`. Fix: always call `test.use()` at the top level of
the `describe` block (not inside any hook). For conditional overrides, use `test.skip(condition)`
to skip tests rather than conditionally applying `test.use()`.

**G415** — TypeScript `satisfies` on `jest.fn()` Return Type Does Not Enforce Mock Shape — Only Narrows the Assigned Variable
`const mockFn = jest.fn() satisfies () => Promise<User>` narrows the *type* of `mockFn` at the
call site, but Jest does not enforce that `mockReturnValue()` arguments conform to `User` —
`mockFn.mockReturnValue({ id: 1 })` compiles without error because `mockReturnValue` on a
`jest.Mock` accepts `unknown`.
Why this matters: A developer uses `satisfies` to document the intended return type of a mock,
then passes an object missing required `User` fields to `mockReturnValue`. TypeScript accepts it,
and the test exercises the SUT with an incomplete stub. The production code that expects a full
`User` object works in the test only because it happens not to access the missing fields. Fix: type
the mock explicitly: `const mockFn: jest.MockedFunction<() => Promise<User>> = jest.fn()`. The
`jest.MockedFunction<T>` generic infers `mockReturnValue`'s argument type from `T`'s return type,
giving full TypeScript enforcement.
